exp.0:0:
This verse says that the list of families of God's people begins with three names: Adam, Seth, and Enosh. They are the first links in a chain of generations. The names are still written as they appear in that older translation; the one called Enosh is the son of Seth.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, although there is not complete agreement. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their identity. That is why it begins with a genealogy, running from Adam to Israel. In this way it showed them that their history came from God from the very beginning of humanity.

For today: God does not overlook people, even when they appear only as names in a list. Your life is also part of his story. Today you can thank those who passed on the faith to you, and think about how to live so that others after you can come to know God.
exp.0:1:
This verse continues a list of names. After Adam, Seth and Enosh, the names Kenan, Mahalaleel and Jared appear. They are descendants of Seth, and the list moves from father to son.

The book of Chronicles does not have a confirmed author; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for the Jews who were returning from exile. It begins with Adam to remind them that their history goes back to the very beginning and that they are part of God's plan for all humanity.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those who are hardly mentioned in the Bible. Your life and your family matter to Him. Today you can thank Him for those who passed on the faith to you, and pray for those who will come after you.
exp.0:2:
This verse continues a list of names: Enoch, Methuselah, and Lamech. They are part of the line of descendants running from Adam to Noah.

The book of Chronicles begins with genealogies, and Jewish and Christian tradition often attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots and their identity. Beginning with Adam shows that the history of Israel sits within the history of all humanity.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those the Bible mentions only in passing. You too are part of his story. Today you can give thanks for those who went before you in the faith, and live faithfully, even when no one sees what you do.
exp.0:3:
This verse continues the list of ancestors that goes back to Adam. Here appear Noah and his three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. They are the sons of Noah, the ones who survived the flood with him.

The book of Chronicles begins with genealogies, that is, lists of families. We do not know with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but that is an opinion. It was written for the people who were returning from exile, and it reminded them where they came from and that God had cared for their history from the beginning. After Noah, the list divides into the nations that came out of his sons.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even when a name appears only in a list. You also have a place in his story. Today, thank God for your family and trust that he cares for your life faithfully.
exp.0:4:
This verse lists the seven sons of Japheth, one of Noah's three sons. They are the founders of families that later became peoples.

The book does not have a narrator identified with certainty; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but there is no certainty. It was written for the Israelites who were returning from exile and needed to remember their roots. That is why it begins with Adam and moves through the nations before reaching Israel. Scholars debate where each people mentioned lived, so it is wise to be cautious about identifications.

For today: God knows each person and each people by name. Today we can treat with respect those who are different from us, remembering that all of humanity comes from one common origin and that God values each of them.
exp.0:5:
This verse lists the three sons of Gomer, who was a son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah: Ashchenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The names appear in the older spelling used in that Bible translation, which would be written differently today (Riphath, Togarmah). They are names of individuals who were later associated with peoples.

The book of Chronicles, written by an author whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), begins with long genealogies. They were addressed to the Israelites returning from exile in Babylon, to remind them that they had roots, identity, and a place in God's history. This list is similar to Genesis 10 and shows all of humanity descending from Noah. Which exact peoples these names relate to is debated by scholars.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. You matter to him too. Give thanks that your life has value to him, and treat others with that same respect.
exp.0:7:
This verse names the four sons of Ham, one of the sons of Noah: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. The names appear in the older spelling used in the Reina-Valera 1909 (Châm for Ham, Chûs for Cush, Phuth for Put). Mizraim is the Hebrew word commonly used for Egypt.

The book does not say who wrote it, although Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra. It was written for the people returning from exile, and it begins with long lists of families to remind them where they came from. These names repeat Genesis 10, and many are associated with peoples and regions, though it is not always known exactly which ones.

For today: God knows the names of every family of humanity, not just one people. Today we can treat every person as someone with a history and worth before Him, without looking down on anyone because of their origin.
exp.0:11:
This verse names two peoples descended from Mizraim, which is Egypt: Pathrusim and Casluhim. From them came (that is, descended) the Philistines and the Caphtorim. The text is brief and does not clearly explain the relationship. Scholars debate whether the Philistines come from Casluhim, from Caphtor, or from a mixture of peoples.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (although this is not certain), writes after the exile. He begins with long lists of families to remind Israel where it comes from and how it relates to the other nations. The Philistines were neighbors and rivals of Israel, yet they also appear in this story.

For today: God knows the origin and the name of every people, even of those we find difficult to like. Today we can treat everyone with respect, remembering that every person matters to God.
exp.0:13:
This verse continues the list of Canaan's descendants. It names peoples: the Hittite, the Jebusite, the Amorite, and the Girgashite. The word "al" repeats the idea that Canaan fathered these peoples, or that they descended from him.

Here no individual speaks; it is the chronicler, who reviews the genealogies from Adam onward. The first chapters of Chronicles were written for the people returning from exile, to remind them of their origins and their place among the nations. These peoples appear later in the land of Canaan, although scholars do not always agree on how they relate to other historical sources.

For today: God knows each people and each person by name, even when for us they are only a list. Today we can treat with respect those who seem foreign or unimportant, remembering that all of them have a place in the history that God sustains.
exp.0:14:
This verse continues a list of the descendants of Canaan, son of Ham. It names three more peoples: the Hivites, the Arkites, and the Sinites. In the Reina-Valera 1909 the names appear in an older spelling, which today would be written as Hivites, Arkites, and Sinites. These are names of groups that later lived in the region of Canaan or near it.

Here it is not a character who speaks, but the chronicler, who is writing a genealogy. He begins with Adam to show where the nations come from and where Israel comes from. It is thought that he wrote for the people who were returning from exile, and that he wanted to remind them of their identity. Scholars do not have certain information about where each of these peoples lived exactly.

For today: God knows the names of all people, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today you can treat each person with respect, knowing that each one has value before God.
exp.0:15:
This verse ends a list of peoples descended from Canaan, son of Ham. It names three groups: the Arvadites (from Arvad, a coastal city), the Zemarites (from Zemar, probably near the coast of Phoenicia), and the Hamathites (from Hamath, in northern Canaan).

Here no single character speaks; the chronicler, traditionally identified with Ezra though this is not certain, reviews history from Adam onward. He writes for the people of Israel who returned from exile, and he wants to show them their roots and their place among the nations. These peoples also appear in Genesis 10.

For today: God knows the names and the history of all peoples, even of those almost no one remembers. This invites us to value every person and culture, despising no one, because all of them have a place in God's plan.
exp.0:16:
These verses list the sons of Shem, one of Noah's three sons. The names are Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech. The spellings in the older translation (such as "Asshur" or "Arphaxad") are written today as Asur and Arfaxad. The last four names, according to Genesis 10:23, appear as sons of Aram.

This is part of a genealogy that opens the book of Chronicles. The author, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not known for certain), wrote for the people who returned from exile. He wanted to remind them where they came from and that God had guided their history from the beginning, through Shem to Abraham.

For today: the names in this list remind us that every person matters to God and has a place in his story. Value your family roots and give thanks to those who came before you in the faith.
exp.0:23:
This verse begins the list of Shem's descendants, one of the sons of Noah. It names three generations: Shem, his son Arphaxad, and Arphaxad's son Shelah. They are only names, but they mark the path of a family that continues.

The chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes after the exile in Babylon. He wants to remind the people of Israel where they come from. After speaking of other branches, this list follows the line that leads to Abraham and then to Israel.

For today: God pays attention to every generation, even those we hardly know. Your faith and your family are part of a larger story. Give thanks for those who came before you, and live in such a way that those who come after will find in you a good example.
exp.0:24:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Eber had Peleg, and Peleg had Reu. It is the line of descendants running from Shem, son of Noah, down to Abraham. The names are written in the older style of this translation.

The book of Chronicles does not clearly say who wrote it. Jewish tradition points to Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written after the return from exile in Babylon. Its purpose was to remind the people that they had deep roots and that God had guided their history from the beginning. This list connects Israel with all of humanity and with the promise made to Abraham.

For today: God knows names that sometimes seem unimportant to us. Every person is part of his plan. Remember that your life also has value to him. Give thanks today for those who came before you in the faith, and live in a way that others can follow your example.
exp.0:25:
This verse continues a list of names. Serug, Nahor, and Terah are three ancestors who come in a direct line from Shem to Abraham. The old spelling in the Reina-Valera 1909 is not relevant to the reader, so the names are simply given as they appear in the verse above: Serug, Nahor, and Terah, the father of Abraham.

The book of Chronicles begins with long genealogies. It is not known with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is debated. It was written for the people who were returning from exile. They needed to remember who they were, where they came from, and that God had guided their history from the beginning. This list connects Shem with Abraham, the man of the promise.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those who barely appear in the stories. Your life also counts in his plan. Give thanks for those who passed on the faith to you, and live in such a way that others can receive it from you.
exp.0:27:
This verse says that Abraham had two main sons in this list: Isaac and Ishmael. The word "and" appears here as the connecting word that joins the two names. It is only the beginning of a family list that continues on.

The book of Chronicles does not clearly say who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was addressed to the Israelites who were returning from exile. With these genealogies, it reminded them where they came from and that they were still part of God's story. Here Ishmael is named first, but the account will then continue with Isaac, the son of the promise.

For today: our story is not by chance. God works through families and generations, even when there are complicated stories. We can be thankful for those who came before us and trust that God also has a purpose for our life and our family.
exp.0:29:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Ishmael, the son Abraham had with Hagar. Here eight names appear: Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah. Together with the four names before them, that makes twelve sons.

The author of Chronicles is unknown, though a Jewish tradition mentions Ezra. He wrote for the people who were returning from exile, and he begins with lists of families to remind them of their roots. Ishmael is named before the account moves on to Isaac because the history of Israel is set among all the nations. The twelve sons recall the promise God made to Abraham about Ishmael in Genesis 17:20.

For today: God keeps his promises and forgets no one. If he remembers these almost unknown names, he also knows you. Today you can value each person as someone important to God.
exp.0:31:
This verse names two of Abraham's grandsons, Sheba and Dedan, sons of Jokshan. The text is spelled differently in the original, but it refers to the same Jokshan mentioned in the verse before, the son of Keturah. Keturah was a secondary wife of Abraham, a woman of lower rank than a principal wife.

The speaker is the chronicler, who according to tradition may have been Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes for the people who returned from exile. He begins with long lists of families to remind them where they come from. Here he mentions the peoples related to Israel before he turns to Isaac and his line.

For today: God knows the names of people whom almost no one remembers. If your life feels small or unnoticed, remember that to God every person counts. Treat with respect and courage today those who go unnoticed.
exp.0:32:
This verse lists the five sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. It says that all of them are descendants of Keturah, a concubine of Abraham, that is, a wife of secondary rank.

The one speaking is the chronicler, an author whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, although this is not certain. He writes for the people who returned from exile and wants to remind them of their roots. Before continuing with the line of Isaac, he mentions the other sons of Abraham. In this way he shows that God kept his promise to give Abraham many descendants.

For today: God knows and remembers even the names that no one mentions. You are not a number to Him. You can live with the confidence that your life matters, even when others overlook it.
exp.0:34:
This verse names the five sons of Esau, the brother of Jacob (Israel). The names are given in the spellings used in this version: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. They are the heads of the families that later formed the people of Edom.

The text is part of a long list of families at the beginning of 1 Chronicles. No one is speaking; it is a genealogical record. It was probably compiled for the people returning from exile, and it shows where the neighboring nations came from and how Israel fits among them. Here Esau is reviewed first, and then Israel will follow.

For today: God remembers names, even those of people who did not follow the path of the promise. This invites us to value each person and not to despise anyone. Today you can pray for someone who seems far from God, trusting that He knows them by name.
exp.0:36:
This verse lists the four sons of Reuel, who was a son of Esau: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the names of leaders or families who later became part of the Edomite peoples. The names are written in the older style of the text.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra, though this is not certain, begins his book with long lists of families. He wanted to remind the people who had returned from exile where they came from, and also to place the neighboring peoples, such as Edom, descended from Esau. No one in particular is speaking here; it is a historical record.

God forgets no one, not even people of whom only the name remains. Today we can remember that every person, even one who seems to go unnoticed, has worth before God. It encourages us to value and pray for those whom others overlook.
exp.0:37:
This verse lists the seven sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. Seir is the ancestor of the Horites, the people who lived in the mountainous region of Seir, south of the Dead Sea. These are the names of a family list, with no further explanation.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written after the exile in Babylon. It begins with long genealogies to remind the people who returned to their land of where they came from. Here the inhabitants of Seir are mentioned because the descendants of Esau, the Edomites, mixed with them and occupied that region.

For today: God does not forget people, not even those who lived thousands of years ago and whom we hardly know. Every name matters to Him. Today you can remember that you too are known by your name, and treat with respect those whom people often overlook.
exp.0:38:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Lotan, a descendant of Seir, had two sons, Hori and Homam, and that he had a sister named Timna.

The book of Chronicles was written by a Jewish author after the exile in Babylon. Many think it was Ezra, but this is not certain. He begins with lists of names to remind his people where they came from, and here he mentions neighboring peoples, such as those of Seir, who lived in the region of Edom. Some believe this Timna is the same one who appears in Genesis 36, but the Bible does not make it clear.

For today: God overlooks no one. Although these names barely appear anywhere else, they were written down. Today you can remember that your life also matters to God, and that you can value the people others ignore.
exp.0:40:
This line is part of a family list. It says that Dishon was the son of Anah, and that Dishon had four sons: Amram, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. In Genesis 36 one of the names appears slightly differently (Hemdan), and it is not known for certain why.

The author of Chronicles, whom many believe was Ezra, though this is not certain, reviews the families from Adam onward. Here he lists the descendants of Seir, ancient inhabitants of the region of Edom. He writes for a people who were returning from exile and needed to remember their origins and their place in God's history.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even people who are rarely mentioned. Your name and your story matter to him. Today you can value those who go unnoticed and thank them.
exp.0:41:
This verse continues listing the descendants of Seir the Horite, whose sons lived in the land of Edom. It mentions the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zavan, and Jakan, and the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran. These are simply family names, a list of lineages.

The author of Chronicles, traditionally identified with Ezra though this is not known for certain, wrote for the people who returned from exile in Babylon. His purpose was to remind them who they were, connecting their history all the way back to Adam. Lists like this one of neighboring peoples, such as Edom, show where Israel fit among all the nations. Some of these names also appear in Genesis 36, with small differences in spelling.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who seem like mere names in a list. If He recorded them, you matter to Him too. Thank Him for knowing you and caring for you personally.
exp.0:42:
This verse begins the list of the kings who ruled in Edom, the land of Esau's descendants. It says that they reigned before Israel had a king. The first was Bela, son of Beor, and his city was called Dinhabah.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who writes after the exile in Babylon. It is not known with certainty who he was, although Jewish tradition often names Ezra. He repeats the list from Genesis 36 to show where the neighboring peoples of Israel came from. Some believe Bela could be the same Bela mentioned in Genesis 36:32, but this is understood in several ways.

God knows the name of every person, even of those who seem unimportant in history. Today we can trust that our lives matter to him, even when no one else remembers them. Let us live faithfully in what is simple.
exp.0:44:
This verse says that, when Jobab died, another man named Husham became king of Edom. Husham came from the land of the Temanites, that is, from Teman, a region associated with Edom. Note that he was not a son of the previous king, so the throne did not pass from father to son.

These words are part of the long lists of names with which 1 Chronicles begins. The author is not known for certain; Jewish tradition often names Ezra, but this is not sure. He writes for the people of Israel who were returning from exile and wanted to remember their roots. He includes Edom, a descendant of Esau, the brother of Jacob, to show the place of each people in history. Genesis 36 contains a very similar list.

For today: kings come and go, and sometimes only their name remains written down. God cares for every generation, and their stories matter. Live today with humility and serve with faithfulness, trusting that God is the true King who endures.
exp.0:45:
It says that when King Husham died, Hadad, son of Bedad, ruled in his place. This Hadad defeated the Midianites in the field of Moab, and his city was called Avith.

This is part of the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, where the author, whom Jewish tradition identifies as Ezra though this is not known for certain, lists the kings of Edom, the land of the descendants of Esau. The first readers were Israelites returning from exile, and they needed to remember their roots and their place among the nations.

For today: rulers pass away one after another, but God remains. We can live with humility, knowing that our positions and achievements are temporary, and trust in the Lord, whose kingdom never ends.
exp.0:48:
This verse tells us that when King Saul of Rehoboth died, a man named Baal-hanan, son of Achbor, took the throne in his place. It is a list of kings, one after another. Note that this Saul is not the king of Israel, but a king of Edom.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), goes through the genealogies to remind God's people of their roots. Here he lists the kings of Edom, the descendants of Esau, brother of Jacob. These kings did not inherit the throne from father to son, and each one reigned for a time and then died. The readers, who were returning from exile, needed to remember this history.

For today: human power is passing. Even kings give their place to others. It is better to live with humility and to serve God and others, because only His kingdom remains forever.
exp.0:49:
This verse continues the list of the kings of Edom. It says that when Baal-hanan died, Hadad reigned in his place, and that his city was called Pai. It also mentions his wife, Mehetabel, daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab.

In other biblical texts, Hadad appears as Hadar, and scholars explain that difference in several ways.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, reviews the genealogies from Adam onward. He writes for the people who were returning from exile. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was a neighbor of Israel, which is why its history is recorded. It is unusual for him to name the wife and her ancestors.

For today: kingdoms and offices pass away, but God knows every name and every story. Live with humility and serve God faithfully, knowing that He remembers what the world forgets.
exp.1:1:
This verse completes the list of the twelve sons of Israel, that is, of Jacob. Here appear Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. The names are written in an older spelling, such as "Naphtali," which we would write today as Neftalí.

It opens the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. The author, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes after the exile in Babylon. He wanted to remind the people who returned who they were: a family with roots, identity, and promises from God. That is why he begins with the twelve sons, the basis of the twelve tribes.

God knows each person by name and does not forget any of them. These names, which today may seem to be only a list, are part of the story of his faithfulness. If you ever feel insignificant, remember that God knows you and includes you in his family and in his plan.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that Perez had two sons: Hezron and Hamul. It is part of a family list.

The book of Chronicles does not clearly name its author; Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. Perez was born of Judah and Tamar, a difficult story full of human failings. Even so, from this line would come King David and, according to the New Testament, Jesus (Matthew 1:3).

For today: God can work through imperfect families and broken stories. Your past, or that of your family, does not prevent him from fulfilling his purpose with you. Trust in his grace and keep moving forward.
exp.1:7:
It says that Azariah was a son of Ethan. This is a line from a genealogy, that is, a list of family members. Ethan was one of the five sons of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, so Azariah belongs to that branch of the family.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra though this is not certain, writes after the return from exile. He wants to remind the people who they are and where they come from. The verse before mentions Achar, who brought trouble by disobeying God, and then the list continues with Hezron and the line that leads to David. Simple names also matter in this story.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your worth does not depend on being famous. Live faithfully in your place, because God sees what you do and keeps you in mind.
exp.1:10:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Nahshon was the father of Salma, and Salma was the father of Boaz. The line moves forward from Judah toward Boaz.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes for the people who returned from exile. He wants to remind them of their roots and that God preserved the tribe of Judah. This line leads to Jesse and to David. Boaz also appears in the book of Ruth, and the New Testament includes him in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

For today: God works through the ordinary stories of families, even in names we rarely read. Your daily life and your faithfulness also matter in God's plans, even when you do not see the whole result.
exp.1:12:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Jesse, the father of David. It names the first three: Eliab, the eldest, then Abinadab, the second, and Shimma, the third.

This is part of the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, written for the people of Israel after the exile. It is not known for certain who wrote them; tradition often points to Ezra, but this is not sure. Their purpose was to remember the people's origins and to highlight the line of Judah, from which David would come. The verses that follow reach David, the seventh son.

For today: God does not look at birth order or outward appearances. David was the youngest, and yet he was chosen. If you feel small or overlooked, remember that God sees you and can use your life.
exp.1:15:
It says that Zeruiah and Abigail were sisters, and that Zeruiah had three sons: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel. Here the wording about who was born to whom simply points to family descent. The verse notes that these women are sisters of the sons of Jesse, although the verse does not say so directly; from the context, it is understood that they belong to that family.

It is a genealogical list within 1 Chronicles, written by an author whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra, though this is not certain. Its purpose was to remind the people who returned from exile of their roots in the tribe of Judah and the family of David. Joab, Abishai, and Asahel later appear as important men in David's army.

For today: God values families and real people, with names and surnames. Your family history, with its lights and shadows, is not foreign to him. Thank God for the people who have shaped your life, and serve where he has placed you.
exp.1:17:
Caleb, son of Hezron, had children by his wife Azubah. The children are named: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon. The Hebrew text here is difficult, and some Bible versions read Jerioth as another wife or as a daughter rather than as a son of Azubah.

The book of Chronicles, written for the people of Israel after the exile, goes through the families of the tribe of Judah. Its author, often identified with Ezra though this is not certain, wanted to remind them of their origin and their place in God's promises. This Caleb belongs to the line of Hezron, and it is not clear that he is the same spy from the book of Numbers.

God knows our names and values the ordinary life of every family, even when no one else remembers it. Today you can thank him for your family and pray for them by name.
exp.1:22:
This verse tells how Geshur and Aram took from the descendants of Jair their towns, along with Kenath and its villages, sixty places in all. "Villages" are small settlements that depended on a larger town. At the end it makes clear that all those places belonged to the sons of Machir, father of Gilead.

The passage is part of the genealogies of Judah in Chronicles, which were written to record the origin and inheritance of the people. No character speaks here; the chronicler records family and territorial details. It is not known with certainty how or when this conquest happened, or whether the "sixty" include the twenty-three towns of Jair. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

What we receive as an inheritance can be lost if it is not cared for. Today we can ask ourselves what blessings we have, such as faith, family, or the teaching we have received, and protect them with prayer, perseverance, and gratitude.
exp.1:24:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Jerahmeel, the firstborn son of Hezron, had five sons: Ram (the firstborn), Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah.

Here no single character is speaking. The book of Chronicles has an unknown author, and Jewish tradition often attributes it to Ezra, though there is no certainty. It was written for a people who were returning from exile. These genealogies reminded them that they had roots in the tribe of Judah, and that God had cared for their history. This branch, the line of Jerahmeel, appears before the line leading to David.

For today: God does not forget people, not even those who are hardly mentioned. Remember that your name and your life matter to Him. Give thanks today for your family and for those who went before you in the faith.
exp.1:25:
It says that Jerahmeel, a descendant of the tribe of Judah, had a second wife named Atarah, and that she was the mother of Onam.

These words are part of a long list of families at the beginning of 1 Chronicles. The author does not name himself in the text; Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. He wrote for a people who were returning from exile, and he wanted to remind them who they were and which families they came from. Here he details the line of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron, within the tribe of Judah. That he mentions a second wife shows that he records the family history as it happened, without embellishing it.

For today: God pays attention to people, even to names that almost no one remembers, such as Atarah. Today you can live with the confidence that your life also matters to Him, even if you go unnoticed.
exp.1:26:
This verse lists the three sons of Ram: Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. Ram was the firstborn son of Jerahmeel, and Jerahmeel in turn was the firstborn of Hezron, of the tribe of Judah. It is part of a family list.

No one speaks in this passage. The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the genealogies of Judah. He probably did so to help the people returning from exile remember their roots, their identity, and God's promise concerning the line of Judah, from which David would come.

For today: God knows names that history has almost forgotten. Maaz, Jamin, and Eker do not appear in other accounts, yet God holds them in mind. If sometimes you feel that your life goes unnoticed, remember that to God no person is insignificant. Live faithfully in your place, even when no one else notices.
exp.1:27:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Onam, son of Jerahmeel and of his wife Atara, had two sons: Shammai and Jada. Then it names the sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur. They are simply names, one after another, to show who descended from whom.

There is no character speaking here. The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), gathers long genealogies of the tribe of Judah. He probably does this so that the people, returned from exile, would remember their roots and their identity. This group comes from the line of Jerahmeel.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those whom almost no one remembers. Your name and your life matter to him, even when they seem small. Today you can thank those who came before you and live faithfully where you are.
exp.1:28:
This verse says that the wife of Abishur was named Abihail, and that she bore two sons: Ahban and Molid.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews here the families of Judah, in the line of Jerahmeel. He probably wrote for the people returning from exile, to remind them who they were and that God had cared for their families. After this verse, the list goes on with other descendants.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even people we barely know. This list names a mother and her sons. That invites us to value each person, to remember our ancestors with gratitude, and to believe that our everyday life matters to God.
exp.1:29:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Nadab had two sons, Seled and Appaim, and that Seled died without having children. The phrase "died without children" means that his family line did not continue through him.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records these genealogies. He wrote for the people of Israel who were returning from exile and needed to remember their roots and their identity. This list belongs to the clan of Jerahmeel, within the tribe of Judah. Even the branches that came to an end were recorded.

For today: God forgets no one, even when a life seems small or without visible fruit. Your worth does not depend on what you leave behind or on how well you are remembered. Live faithfully and trust that your name matters to God.
exp.1:30:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Appaim had a son named Ishi, that Ishi had Sheshan, and that Sheshan had Ahlai.

There is no person speaking in a speech. It is the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He records the genealogies of the families of Judah, here the line of Jerahmeel. He probably does this to remind the people, after the exile, who they were and where they came from. The names are little known, and we know nothing more about them.

For today: God cares for every person, even for those whom almost no one remembers. Your name and your story matter to Him. Be encouraged to value those who came before you and to live faithfully in your generation.
exp.1:31:
This verse mentions the sons of Jada, the brother of Shammai: Jether and Jonathan. It says that Jether died without children, so his family line did not continue. "Brother of Shammai" only shows Jada's place within the family.

It is part of a long genealogy of the tribe of Judah, in the branch of Jerahmeel. No one is speaking; the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the names. He probably does this so that the people, returning from exile, would remember their roots and identity. Even the lines that ended are recorded, and Jonathan's line did continue.

For today: God remembers each person, even when the world forgets their name or they leave no great visible legacy. Live faithfully, and trust that your life has value before God.
exp.1:32:
This verse names the sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. The text then closes this part by saying that all of them are descendants of Jerahmeel. It is part of a family list, where each name marks a branch of the family.

First Chronicles has no narrator who identifies himself; Jewish tradition usually attributes it to Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. Jerahmeel belonged to the tribe of Judah. This list includes Jether, who died without children, and Jonathan, whose line did continue. In this way the memory of each family is preserved.

For today: God forgets no one, not even those who barely appear in the story. Your life and your family matter to Him, even though others may not notice them. Serve faithfully in small things.
exp.1:33:
This verse says that Sheshan, a descendant of Judah through the line of Jerahmeel, had no sons. He had only daughters. In that time, sons were usually the ones who carried on the family name and inherited the land.

The narrator here is not a character speaking, but the chronicler, who records the genealogies of Israel. He probably wanted to preserve the memory of the families after the exile. The next verse shows that Sheshan's line continued through a daughter who was married to Jarha, an Egyptian servant. So the account does not end in an empty space, but goes on.

For today: God does not depend on our structures or our expectations to carry on his work. Where we see an ending, he can open a way. Value each person in your family, regardless of their place, because God also takes them into account.
exp.1:35:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Attai had a son named Nathan, and that Nathan had a son named Zabad.

The Chronicles book does not name its author, and Jewish tradition often attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. Here the line of Sheshan is followed, who had no male sons. His daughter married Jarha, an Egyptian servant, and so the family continued. This shows that God works even when things do not turn out as expected.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to names that almost no one remembers. Your life, though it may seem ordinary, matters and can leave a mark on your family. Live with faithfulness and trust in God.
exp.1:41:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Caleb, the brother of Jerahmeel, had sons: his firstborn was named Mesha, who is presented as the father of Ziph. In these lists, "father of" usually indicates the founder or leader of a town or clan. The verse also mentions the sons of Mareshah, the father of Hebron. The Hebrew text is difficult here, and scholars debate whether "Mesha" and "Mareshah" are people or places.

The author of Chronicles, writing after the exile, gathers the genealogies of Judah to remind the people who they were and where they came from. He wanted to reaffirm their identity and their place in God's history.

For today: God knows our names and our families, even when they seem minor. Give thanks today for those who went before you in the faith, and live in such a way that you leave a testimony worth remembering.
exp.1:44:
This verse says that Maon was the son of Shammai, and that Maon was the "father" of Beth-zur. In genealogies, "father" does not always mean a biological father. It can indicate the founder or leader of a town. Beth-zur was a city in Judah, so Maon was probably the one who founded it or governed it.

Here a single character is not speaking. The chronicler, who writes after the exile in Babylon, lists the families of Judah, in this case the descendants of Caleb. He wanted the people to recover their identity, their roots, and their right to the land. Scholars do not know for certain who wrote the book, although tradition points to Ezra.

For today: God remembers names that we would overlook. Your life and your service, though they may seem small, matter before Him. Give thanks today for those who built your faith.
exp.1:45:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Ephah, a concubine (a wife of secondary rank, with fewer rights than the main wife) of Caleb, bore him three sons: Haran, Moza, and Gazez. It then adds that Haran had a son named Gazez.

There is no person speaking in a scene; it is the chronicler who writes, and we do not know his name with certainty. After the exile, the people needed to remember who they were and what tribe they came from. That is why even little-known names within the tribe of Judah are recorded. That Gazez appears twice may be due to a grandson with the same name, or to another way of ordering the list; it is not certain.

For today: God does not forget anyone, even those who are hardly mentioned. Value and pray for the humble people around you.
exp.1:46:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Jahdai had six sons: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph. "Sons" here means descendants of his family. Nothing more is explained about them. The Bible does not make clear for certain who Jahdai was or how he relates to Caleb, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

The author of Chronicles does not speak in the first person; he is a chronicler who records the genealogies of the tribes of Israel, here that of Judah, in the line of Caleb. These lists were preserved for a people who were returning from exile and needed to remember their roots, their land, and their identity as God's family.

For today: although we know almost nothing about these people, God preserved them in His Word. This reminds us that no name goes unnoticed by Him. If you sometimes feel small or forgotten, remember that God knows you personally and values you.
exp.1:50:
This verse mentions two descendants of Caleb: Salma, called the "father of" Bethlehem, and Hareph, the "father of" Beth-gader. In the Bible, "father of" often does not mean he was the literal father of a single son, but rather the founder, head, or leader of a town. That is why Bethlehem and Beth-gader appear here as places tied to these families.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition usually identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), gathers long lists of the families of Judah. He writes for the people who returned from exile, so that they would know where they came from and to which tribe and land they belonged. Bethlehem appears here only briefly, without yet revealing that David and, later, Jesus would come from it.

For today: God cares for names and small places. No one is insignificant to Him. Trust that He can use your family and your place, however humble they may seem.
exp.1:51:
This verse says that Shobal, who was the founder of the city of Kiriath-jearim, had descendants named Haroeh and half of the Manahethites. Here the word "father" does not always mean a direct father; it often refers to the leader or founder of a family or village. The Manahethites were a group or clan, and it is not entirely clear how they relate to Haroeh.

The chronicler speaks here, and no one knows for certain who he was (Jewish tradition usually points to Ezra). He wrote after the exile, so that the people would remember where they came from, which tribe they belonged to, and which cities were theirs. This list follows the descendants of Caleb, of the tribe of Judah, and shows how several families and cities were formed.

For today: God pays attention to people and their stories, even when their names seem distant or difficult to us. Value your own family and your own history, and give thanks for those who went before you in the faith.
exp.1:52:
This verse says that several families descended from the city of Kirjath-jearim: the Ithrites, the Puhites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites. From them later came the Zareathites and the Eshtaulites, who were inhabitants of Zorah and Eshtaol.

The author of Chronicles, whom many believe was a scribe living after the exile, is not describing a scene but recording family lists within the tribe of Judah. He probably wanted the people returning from exile to know where they came from and to what place they belonged. Some details in these lists are hard to pin down, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God takes notice of people and families, even the little-known ones. Give thanks for those who went before you in faith, and remember that your life also matters to God.
exp.2:0:
This verse opens a list of the sons David had in Hebron. "Firstborn" means the first male son. Someone "of Jezreel" is a person from the town of Jezreel, and "of Carmel" refers to a town in Judah. Amnon was the oldest, son of Ahinoam, and Daniel the second, son of Abigail.

The author of Chronicles cannot be named with certainty; many think of Ezra, but this is not known. He wrote for the people who were returning from exile, and he wanted to remind them of David's family and of God's promise about his descendants. In 2 Samuel 3:3 the second son appears as Chileab; we do not know for certain why the name changes.

For today: God pays attention to royal families, with their strengths and failures, and He forgets no one. Value your family history and pray for your loved ones. God can work even in imperfect homes.
exp.2:1:
This verse continues the list of the sons David had in Hebron. It names the third, Absalom, son of Maachah, who was the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur. Then it names the fourth, Adonijah, son of Haggith. The spellings here are those of this version; today we would write Absalom, Maacah, and Haggith as they appear in the verse above.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra (though this is not certain), wrote for the people who returned from exile. He wanted to remind them that David's family still mattered, because the promised king would come from it. It is striking that the list includes Absalom and Adonijah without commenting on their later failures. Absalom was the son of a foreign princess.

For today: God works through imperfect families. Our family history does not have to be perfect for God to use it. Even so, let us care for those God has entrusted to us, because raising children with love and discipline matters a great deal.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that the first six sons of David were born in Hebron, the city where he reigned seven years and six months. Afterward he moved to Jerusalem, and there he reigned thirty-three years. "Jerusalem" is the same city as Jerusalén. In total, his reign added up to about forty years.

This is part of a long list of families at the beginning of 1 Chronicles. No character is speaking; the chronicler, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records these details. He wrote for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots and the line of David, from which the Messiah would come according to God's promise.

For today: God works through the stages of our lives, long or short, and also through the messiness of families. Value your place and your time, and serve faithfully where God has placed you now.
exp.2:4:
This verse names four sons that David had in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. Their mother was Bath-shua, daughter of Ammiel. She is the same Bathsheba who appears in other books, where her father is called Eliam, a similar name.

The text is a family list, probably written after the exile by the Chronicler, whom tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. It wanted to remind the people that David's family was still important and that God's promises had not been lost. That is why names and places appear with such care.

For today: God does not forget families, not even those with painful or complicated stories. He can work through them. Trust that your story also matters to him, and follow his faithfulness step by step.
exp.2:5:
This verse is part of the list of the sons born to King David in Jerusalem. Here the names Ibhar, Elishama, and Eliphelet appear, which are the first of nine other sons. The names are written in the older spelling of the Reina-Valera translation, so they sound different from the ones we use today. The list continues in the next verse.

The chronicler, probably writing after the return from exile in Babylon, carefully records David's family. His purpose was to remind the people that David's royal line was still alive and that God's promises to that family had not been lost. Some names are repeated in the list (such as Elishama and Eliphelet), and scholars are not sure why; there are several possible explanations.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those who are rarely mentioned. Your name and your life matter to him, even when no one else notices them.
exp.2:6:
This verse continues a list of sons born to King David in Jerusalem. Three names appear here: Nogah, Nepheg, and Japhia. Nothing more is told about them; only their names are recorded.

The book of Chronicles was written long after David, probably for the people who were returning from exile. The author begins with long genealogies to remind them where they came from and that God had preserved David's line. This list of sons is part of that careful record. Some names repeat in the neighboring verses, and scholars explain this in several ways, with no certain answer.

For today: God knows and remembers even those whom history barely mentions. Your name and your life matter to Him, even when no one else notices them. Serve Him faithfully, even in what is hidden.
exp.2:7:
This verse ends a list of names: three more sons of King David born in Jerusalem. The names are Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet. There is something curious here: Elishama and Eliphelet had already appeared in the previous verse. Many scholars think they were two different sons with the same name, or that one of them died as a child and the name was repeated. There is no certainty.

The author of Chronicles, possibly the priest Ezra according to tradition, writes for the people who returned from exile in Babylon. He wants to remind them that David's family still lives on and that God keeps His promises. For this reason he records with care even the little-known sons.

For today: God knows the name of every person, even of those whom almost no one remembers. Your quiet work and your simple life also count for Him. Serve Him faithfully, without needing applause.
exp.2:9:
This verse is part of a list of kings. It says that Rehoboam was the son of Solomon, Abijah was the son of Rehoboam, Asa was the son of Abijah, and Jehoshaphat was the son of Asa.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the chronicler, an author whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes after the exile in Babylon. He wants to remind the people that the royal line of David continued, to give them hope and to show that God had not forgotten his promise to David.

For today: God works across generations, and also in what seems like a simple list of names. Your faith and your example can influence your children and grandchildren, so it is worth being faithful today, even if you do not see the fruit right away.
exp.2:10:
This verse continues the list of the kings of Judah, descendants of David. It says that Joram had a son, Ahaziah, and that Ahaziah had a son, Joash.

The book of Chronicles was written for the people of Israel after the exile. Many scholars think its author was Ezra, though this is not certain. The list reminded the people that David's family was still standing and that God had not forgotten his promise. Other books of the Bible tell that Joash, as a child, was saved from a royal massacre, so David's line nearly came to an end.

For today: God watches over his plan even when everything seems threatened. You can trust that he does not forget you, and that your life, though it may seem small, matters in his story.
exp.2:11:
It says that Amaziah was the son of Joash, that Azariah was the son of Amaziah, and that Jotham was the son of Azariah. Azariah also appears under the name Uzziah in other passages, and many consider them to be the same person.

It is part of the list of kings descended from David. We do not know for certain who wrote Chronicles; tradition names Ezra, but that idea is debated. It seems to have been written for the people who were returning from exile. The list reminded them that David's line was still standing and that God had not forgotten his promises.

For today: God works across the generations, even through imperfect people. Your faithfulness day to day, though it may seem small, can leave a mark on your children and on those who come after you.
exp.2:13:
The passage follows the list of the kings of Judah, descendants of David. It says that Amon had a son named Josiah.

The Chronicles text does not say with certainty who wrote it; a Jewish tradition names Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for the people who were returning from exile, and it reminded them that the line of David was still standing and that God had not forgotten his promises. According to 2 Kings, Amon was a wicked king, and his son Josiah was a king who sought God.

For today: your family past does not decide your future with God. Josiah was born into a difficult family and still chose to follow the Lord. You too can choose, today, to walk with God and change the story of those who come after you.
exp.2:14:
This verse lists the four sons of King Josiah: Johanan, the firstborn; Jehoiakim, the second; Zedekiah, the third; and Shallum, the fourth. The firstborn is the son who was born first. About Shallum, many understand him to be another name for Jehoahaz, though some dispute this.

The chronicler writes a list of the family of King David, following the line of the kings of Judah. He probably addresses the Israelites who were returning from exile, to remind them that their royal lineage had not been lost. It is a record, not direct teaching.

For today: God forgets no name. Even in lists that seem cold, he follows the story of every family. That reminds us that we too, with our name and our story, matter to him.
exp.2:15:
The verse names the sons of King Jehoiakim: Jeconiah, who reigned after him, and Zedekiah.

The author of Chronicles, traditionally associated with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes for the people who were returning from exile. He reviews the line of King David to show that, even after the fall of Judah, God had not forgotten his promise.

For today: God keeps his promises even through imperfect families and dark times. If your story today seems broken, trust that God is still at work and remembers your name.
exp.2:17:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions six more sons of Jeconiah, the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon: Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah. These are Hebrew names, and we know almost nothing about them.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes to the Jews who returned from exile. He reviews the line of David to remind them that God had not forgotten his promise. Even after the fall of the kingdom, the royal family still existed. Pedaiah, mentioned here, is the father of Zerubbabel in the following verse.

For today: God remembers people whom we would see as unimportant. If you feel forgotten, trust that your name and your life matter to him, and that he can work quietly for generations.
exp.2:18:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Pedaiah had two sons, Zerubbabel and Shimei. Then it names the sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam, Hananiah, and a daughter, Shelomith. The names sound old, but they are simply real people from one family.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records here the descendants of King David. He writes for the people who returned from exile in Babylon. This list shows that David's line was still alive. Other texts say that Zerubbabel was the son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2), so some think of a kinship through a levirate marriage; this is not known for certain.

For today: God pays attention to every person and every family, even to those who seem to be only a name in a list. You can trust that your life matters to Him. Today, give thanks for your family and pray for them by name.
exp.2:20:
This verse continues a family list. It says that Hananiah had as sons Pelatiah and Jesaiah. Then other names appear: Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah. It is not known for certain how they are related: they may be descendants of Jesaiah or separate branches. The Hebrew text is not clear, and the ancient translations vary.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile in Babylon, and tradition says its author was Ezra, though this is not certain. This list follows the line of King David down to the time after the exile, passing through Zerubbabel. It was meant to remind the people that God had not forgotten his promise to David.

For today: God knows every name, even the ones almost no one remembers. Your life and your faithfulness, though they may seem small, can be part of what God does in your family for generations.
exp.2:21:
Here is what it says: Shemaiah was the son of Shechaniah, and he had six sons: Hattush, Igeal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat. This is part of a family list of David's descendants. Note: the names are written in an old style, and the text says "six" even though only five names appear here. Some scholars believe Shemaiah himself is counted, or that a name was lost when the text was copied. This is not known with certainty.

The author of Chronicles, probably writing after the exile in Babylon, gathers the genealogies to show that David's family was still alive. In this way the people returning from exile could remember their identity and God's promise about the royal line.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even people who appear only as names on a list. Your life and your family matter to him. Today you can thank him for those who came before you in the faith, and live in a way that future generations will remember you as faithful.
exp.2:23:
This verse gives the list of the seven sons of Elioenai: Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah, and Anani. It is part of a genealogy, that is, a record of family descent. The phrase "seven" only indicates how many sons he had.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), writes after the exile in Babylon. This list closes the line of King David, which continues through his descendants to a late period. For the people who were returning home, these names showed that David's family still existed and that God's promises had not been lost. Scholars debate exactly when these last descendants lived.

For today: God knows and remembers even the names that almost no one mentions. Your life counts for Him, even when it goes unnoticed. You can live with peace and faithfulness, trusting that God keeps His promises from generation to generation.
exp.3:1:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Reaiah, son of Shobal, had a son named Jahath, and that Jahath had two sons: Ahumai and Lahad. From them came the families known as the Zorathites.

The book of Chronicles was written after the people of Israel returned from exile in Babylon. Jewish tradition usually credits it to Ezra, though this is not certain. Its purpose was to remind the people who they were, which tribe they came from, and that God remained faithful to his promises. Here the tribe of Judah is detailed, the tribe from which King David would come.

For today: God knows the names of people we barely remember. No one goes unnoticed by him. Today you can rest in the knowledge that your life matters to him, even if you feel that your work or your service goes unseen.
exp.3:3:
This verse is part of a list of families from the tribe of Judah. It says that Penuel was the father of Gedor, and Ezer the father of Hushah. It also presents these men as descendants of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah and the founder of Bethlehem. The word "father" here can mean a literal father, but it can also mean founder or leader of a town.

The author of Chronicles, of Jewish tradition, compiled genealogies after the exile in Babylon. He wants to remind the people where they came from. Here he names Bethlehem, a place that would later become important because of David. It is not known for certain whether each name refers to a person or to a town, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God pays attention to families and names, even the little-known ones. You also matter to Him. Think of those who went before you in the faith and give thanks for them, and live today in such a way that you can be a blessing to those who come after.
exp.3:12:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Kenaz (in other versions, Kenez) had two sons, Othniel and Seraiah. It then mentions Hathath as a son of Othniel. The comma at the end shows that the list continues in the next verse.

The book of Chronicles has no narrator speaking to a single person; it is a historical record. Many believe Ezra wrote it, though this is not certain. It was written for the people of Israel after the exile, so that they would remember who they were and where they came from. An Othniel with this kinship appears in Joshua and Judges as a deliverer of Israel, but this text does not explain that.

For today: God does not forget the names of those who serve Him. Even when your work seems small or little seen, it has value before Him. Live faithfully, because your example can shape your family.
exp.3:15:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Jehaleleel had four sons: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asareel. The names are spelled in an old way; today they are usually written Ziph, Ziphah, Tirias, and Asareel. Nothing more is told about them.

No one speaks here directly. The chronicler, who according to Jewish tradition was Ezra (though this is not certain), writes a long genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He does so for the people who were returning from exile, so that they would remember their roots and their place before God. Jehaleleel appears only here, and we do not know with certainty how he relates to the other families in the list.

God knows and remembers people, even those whom history barely mentions. If today you feel overlooked or unimportant, remember that your name has value to God. And you can follow his example: value and thank those who serve quietly around you.
exp.3:19:
This verse is part of a list of families. It names the sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah (called a son of Hanan), and Tilon. It also names the sons of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth. Some scholars think "Ben-hanan" may have been a single name, but this is not certain.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; an ancient tradition attributes it to Ezra. It was written for a people who were returning from exile, and the genealogies reminded them of their roots, their history, and that God had not forgotten them. Here the tribe of Judah is recorded, the tribe from which King David would come. About these people we know very little.

For today: God keeps in His Word names that almost no one remembers. This teaches us that no one goes unnoticed by Him. If you feel unimportant, remember that your name is known by God, and that your everyday, faithful life also counts.
exp.3:23:
The verse lists the five sons of Simeon, one of the sons of Jacob: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul. It is the beginning of the list of Simeon's family. Other biblical lists give some variants of the names, such as Jemuel in place of Nemuel, something that can be explained in several ways.

The book of Chronicles has an uncertain author, although one tradition attributes it to Ezra. It seems to have been written for the people who were returning from exile, to remind them of their roots and that God had kept every tribe and every family. That is why there are so many genealogies.

For today: God does not see people as mere numbers. Every name matters to Him. Today you can thank Him for your family and for those who came before you in the faith, and remember that you too are known by your name and have a place in His story.
exp.3:24:
This verse continues the list of Simeon's descendants. After Saul, the text names his son Shallum, then Mibsam, and then Mishma, as a chain of fathers and sons. It tells no story about them; it simply leaves their names written down.

The book of Chronicles was written by an unknown author, whom many believe was Ezra, though this is not certain. He was writing for the people returning from exile. He wanted to remind them who they were, where they came from, and that God had not forgotten any family, not even the little-known ones.

For today: God knows your name even when no one else remembers it. Your faithfulness day by day, in the simple and hidden things, has value before Him. And what you teach your children or those who follow you can reach further than you imagine.
exp.3:25:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Mishma had a son named Hamuel, and that from him came Zacchur, his son, and then Shimei, his son. These are names passed from father to son, generation after generation, within the tribe of Simeon.

The author of Chronicles is unknown; Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. He wrote after the exile in Babylon, when the people needed to remember who they were and to whom their inheritance belonged. That is why he records genealogies, even of small tribes like Simeon. The following verse makes clear that this family did not grow as large as Judah.

For today: God knows people by name, even those who are little remembered. If you feel that your life goes unnoticed, remember that every person matters to God. Today you can encourage someone quiet in your church or family, telling them that their service does count.
exp.3:27:
This verse is part of a list of cities in the south of Judah where the tribe of Simeon lived. It says they dwelt at Beer-sheba, Moladah, and Hazar-shual. These places were in the dry region of the Negev, an arid land with few resources.

The author of Chronicles is not identified with certainty; many believe he wrote after the return from exile in Babylon. His purpose was to remind his people where they came from, with which families, and in which lands. Lists like this gave identity and hope to a community that was rebuilding itself.

For today: God takes notice of names and places that seem small. If your life feels hidden or set in a dry place, remember that He knows you and sustains you. Serve faithfully where you are.
exp.3:28:
This verse is part of a list of towns where the descendants of Simeon lived. It names three places: Bilhah, Ezem and Tolad. Other translations spell them differently. We do not know exactly where they were, but they are located in the south of Judah, near the Negev.

Here the chronicler speaks, an author who wrote after the exile in Babylon, and no one knows for certain who he was. He wanted to remind the people of God who they were and where their families had lived. Simeon received his territory within that of Judah, and this list goes back as far as the time of David.

For today: God does not forget any name or any place, even when they are small or little known. If at times you feel insignificant, remember that God knows you and has a place for you in his story.
exp.3:29:
This verse continues a list of cities where the tribe of Simeon lived. It names three places: Bethuel (also called Betul in other texts), Hormah, and Ziklag. These were villages in the south of Israel, near the Negev desert.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile in Babylon. Its author, whose name is not known for certain, recalled the lists of families and territories so that the people could recover their identity and know that they had roots and a place before God. The text says that these cities belonged to Simeon until the kingdom of David.

For today: God pays attention to the small things and to each person, even to little-known places. Your life, though it may seem ordinary, does not go unnoticed by Him. Today you can thank Him for the place and the people He has placed around you.
exp.3:31:
This verse mentions five small towns, called villages, that belonged to the tribe of Simeon: Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan. The villages were smaller settlements that surrounded the main cities. Some scholars think that Etam here is different from other places with that name, and not all of the locations are known with certainty.

The chronicler, who wrote after the exile in Babylon, goes over the genealogies of the tribes of Israel. Here he lists the territory of Simeon, in the south, next to Judah. He wants to remind the people who returned from exile that they had roots, family, and a land given by God.

For today: God pays attention to the small things. These almost forgotten villages were recorded in his Word. If your life or your work seems unimportant, remember that God sees you, knows you by name, and values your faithfulness in everyday things.
exp.3:33:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three men: Meshobab, Jamlech, and Joshah, the son of Amaziah. They are part of a series of leaders of the tribe of Simeon. The phrase "son of" shows their family line, and the names continue in the next verse.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), compiled genealogies for the people who were returning from exile. In this passage he speaks of the tribe of Simeon, which lived in the south, near Judah. These lists reminded the Israelites of their identity, their inheritance, and that God had preserved his people despite everything. We know nothing more about these men.

For today: God knows the names of people the world forgets. If you ever feel that your life goes unnoticed, remember that for God every person matters. Serve faithfully, even when no one applauds you.
exp.3:34:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Joel and Jehu, who was the son of Josibiah, grandson of Seraiah, and great-grandson of Asiel. The phrase "son of" here shows the family line, that is, whose descendant each one was.

The text has no speaker as such; it is the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, although this is not certain. He is recording the leaders of the tribe of Simeon. Lists like this helped the people, after the exile, remember their roots, their inheritance, and their place among the tribes of Israel.

God knows each person by name, even those whom history barely mentions. No one is invisible to Him. Today you can rest in the knowledge that your life, though it may seem small or hidden, has value before God. You can also honor those who came before you and were faithful in silence.
exp.3:35:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions seven men: Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, and Benaiah. It says nothing more about them, only that they are part of a larger group.

We are in the genealogies of the tribe of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:24-43). The author, traditionally identified as Ezra, though this is not certain, records these names. According to the passage that follows, they were heads of their families, and their people grew greatly. The first readers, who were returning from exile, needed to remember their roots and their place among God's people.

For today: God knows people by their names, even those whom history hardly mentions. If today you feel small or little noticed, remember that your life and your faithfulness count before God.
exp.3:36:
This verse names Ziza and recalls his family line: he was the son of Shiphi, the grandson of Allon, and his ancestors were Jedaiah, Shimri and Shemaiah. It is part of a list of leaders of the tribe of Simeon. The phrase "son of" can mean a direct son or a descendant.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes after the exile. He wants the people to remember their roots. The verses that follow say that these families grew greatly and searched for pasture for their flocks. So the list shows how God cared for the tribe of Simeon and made it grow.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today we can value those who serve without being seen, thank them, and remember that our faithful work also matters to God.
exp.3:37:
These men named above were the leaders of their families. Over time, their households grew very large.

Here the chronicler reviews the family lines of the tribe of Simeon. It is not a speech but a family record. Its purpose was to remind a people returning from exile who they were and where they came from. Afterward, the text tells how those growing families went out to look for pasture and found wide, peaceful land.

For today: God pays attention to names and families, not only to the great figures of history. Give thanks for those who went before you in the faith, and think about how you can leave a good inheritance for those who come after you.
exp.3:38:
A group of families from the tribe of Simeon came as far as the entrance to Gedor, on the east side of the valley. They were looking for pasture for their sheep and herds. Herds are the flocks of animals they took care of.

The passage comes from 1 Chronicles, a list of the families of Israel. Its author is not named in the text; tradition often mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. The verses that follow say this happened in the days of King Hezekiah. The location of Gedor is not entirely clear, and some ancient manuscripts read a different place name instead. The account explains how this tribe grew and settled.

For today: the need to feed their families moved them to act. We may seek our livelihood with effort, but also with justice and trust in God, taking care not to take advantage of others to achieve it.
exp.4:0:
It says that Reuben was the firstborn son of Jacob (also called Israel), but he lost the rights of the firstborn because he dishonored his father by lying with his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22). Those rights passed to the sons of Joseph. The phrase "defiled his father's bed" means he committed a serious sexual wrong against his father. The "birthright" is the privilege of the eldest son, which included a double portion of the inheritance.

The text is written by the Chronicler, perhaps Ezra according to tradition, though this is not certain. He writes for the people who were returning from exile and needed to remember their origins. That is why he presents the genealogies and explains why Reuben, being the oldest, does not head the list. Judah received the leadership and Joseph received the double portion.

For today: our decisions have consequences that can affect what God meant to give us. But God continues to work with mercy. We can ask him for forgiveness and live with integrity, caring for what has been entrusted to us.
exp.4:1:
This verse explains a detail about the tribes of Israel. Judah prevailed above his brothers, and the chief ruler would come from him. Instead, the birthright, that is, the double portion of the inheritance that the firstborn son would normally receive, passed to Joseph.

The author of Chronicles, whom many believe wrote after the exile in Babylon (this is debated), is presenting the genealogies of Israel. When speaking of Reuben, the firstborn, he makes clear why Reuben did not receive that place: because of his sin against his father. The text shows that the privileges were divided between Judah and Joseph, from whom came Ephraim and Manasseh.

For today: our mistakes have consequences, but God continues to work with purpose. Value what God has entrusted to you and care for it with integrity, because character matters more than position.
exp.4:2:
This verse gives the list of the four sons of Reuben, the firstborn son of Jacob, who is also called Israel. Their names appear in the English spelling of the verse: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. The firstborn son is the eldest, the one who would normally receive the largest share of the inheritance.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews the families of Israel for the people who were returning from exile. Here he makes clear that Reuben lost the rights of the firstborn because of his sin against his father. Those rights passed to Joseph, while Judah became the leader of the family. Even so, the descendants of Reuben are remembered by name.

For today: our mistakes have consequences, and it is worth taking care of how we act. But God does not erase anyone from his story. If you have failed, seek God's forgiveness and live with integrity from today onward.
exp.4:3:
This verse is part of a family list. It names some descendants of Joel, who belonged to the tribe of Reuben: Shemaiah, Gog and Shimei, each the son of the one before. We do not know for certain how Joel is related to Reuben, because the text does not explain it here.
