The book of Chronicles, written by an author whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the genealogies of Israel. It does so for a people who were returning from exile and needed to remember who they were and where they came from. This list of Reuben continues down to Beerah, who was carried away captive by Assyria. In this way it shows that even the tribe of the firstborn lost its place of honor.

God pays attention to every person, even to names that almost no one remembers. Your life and your family matter to Him, even if you are not famous. Today you can thank Him for those who came before you in the faith and live faithfully, knowing that God knows you by name.
exp.4:4:
This verse continues a list of names. It says that Joel had a son named Shemaiah, and the line goes on with Gog, Shimei, Micah, Reaiah and Baal. Each one is the son of the one before him. Here "Baal" is a personal name, not a reference to the false god. Everyone in the list belongs to the tribe of Reuben.

The text is a genealogy, and it does not say clearly who its author was. Tradition attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for the people who were returning from exile. They needed to remember their roots and their place in Israel. This line ends with Beerah, who was taken captive by Assyria. So the names also recall a story of loss.

For today: God knows the names of people whom almost no one remembers. Your simple, hidden life also matters to Him. Today, take a moment to thank God for someone in your family who taught you to live with faith, and pray for the next generation.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that Bela, a descendant of the tribe of Reuben, kept extending his territory eastward until he reached the edge of the desert beside the Euphrates River. The reason is simple: he had a great many animals, and his livestock needed more pasture and room.

The writer of Chronicles, who wrote for the people who returned from exile, recalls the genealogies of the tribes to show that Israel has a history and an inheritance. Here he lists the descendants of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob, and explains how they grew and settled in Gilead.

For today: the blessings God gives us, whether work, possessions, or talents, tend to grow and call for more room. It is good to manage them with gratitude and wisdom, remembering that everything comes from his hand.
exp.4:11:
This verse gives the names of the leaders of the tribe of Gad who settled in Bashan, east of the Jordan River. Joel was the chief, and after him came Shapham, Jaanai, and Shaphat. The verse's wording reads "Joel the chief, and Shapham the next, and Jaanai, and Shaphat in Bashan." "Chief" means that he was the leader or head of the group.

The author of Chronicles is not describing a scene; he is a chronicler who arranges family lists. His purpose was to remind a people returning from exile who they were, which families they came from, and what land fell to them. We do not know much more about these men; only their names are preserved, and that is already significant.

God remembers people whom the world would forget. Today you may serve in humble places, without applause, and still your work matters. Do it with faithfulness, trusting that God sees and remembers what you do.
exp.4:13:
These are the sons of Abihail, who is listed here with the seven brothers mentioned earlier. The verse then names his ancestors one by one, going back to Buz. It is a family list, much like a family tree.

Here "Gilead" seems to be the name of an ancestor from the tribe of Gad, though nothing more is known about him.

We are in a list of the tribe of Gad, which lived east of the Jordan River. According to tradition, the author of Chronicles may have been Ezra, but this is not certain. Lists like this helped the people, who were returning from exile, remember their origins, their families, and their lands.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even people about whom we know almost nothing. Your name and your story matter to him. Give thanks today for your family and for those who passed on the faith to you, and think about how you can pass it on yourself.
exp.4:15:
This verse says that the descendants of Abihail, of the tribe of Gad, lived in the region of Gilead and in Bashan, with their villages. They also occupied all the pasturelands of Sharon, that is, the grazing lands on the outskirts of the towns, as far as their borders reached. Sharon here does not seem to be the coastal plain by the sea, but an area east of the Jordan.

It is part of a list of families in 1 Chronicles. The chronicler is probably not a character who speaks, but a writer who reminds Israel of its history after the exile. He records where each family lived to reaffirm their identity and their inheritance in the land that God gave them.

For today: God pays attention to specific places and families, not only to great names. Give thanks for the place where you live, and faithfully care for what He has entrusted to you, whether your home, your work, or your community.
exp.4:17:
This verse tells us that the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, who settled east of the Jordan River, had an army of 44,760 men. They were brave and well prepared: they carried shield and sword, they were ready to shoot with the bow, and they were skilled in war, meaning they were able fighters.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, goes through the genealogies of Israel to remind his people who they are and where they come from. This census is set in the days of King Jotham of Judah and King Jeroboam of Israel. The verses that follow explain that they won a war against the Hagrites, but not by their strength alone: they cried out to God and trusted in him.

For today: prepare yourself and do your best with what you have, but do not put your trust only in your own abilities. Before facing a difficulty, pray and wait on God.
exp.4:18:
This verse says that the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh fought against the Hagarites and against other neighboring peoples: Jetur, Nephish, and Nodab. The Hagarites are the descendants of Hagar, Abraham's servant, also called Ishmaelites. Jetur, Nephish, and Nodab were groups related to Ishmael, according to Genesis 25:15.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, reviews the genealogies of Israel. He tells us that these tribes lived east of the Jordan and that, being trained warriors, they confronted their neighbors. The verses that follow explain that they won because they cried out to God and trusted in him. For a people who had returned from exile, it was a reminder that God sustains those who wait on him.

For today: when you face a struggle, do your part responsibly, but cry out to God and trust in him. Preparation and prayer go together.
exp.4:20:
It says that the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, after defeating the Hagrites, carried off many animals as spoil: camels, sheep, and donkeys. They also took a hundred thousand people, that is, prisoners. The animals were the livestock they kept for raising and herding.

The chronicler tells this story to remind the people, after the exile, how God gave victory to their ancestors who sought him. The verse before explains the reason: they cried out to God in the battle and trusted in him. The numbers are very large, and some scholars debate how they should be understood, but the emphasis is on God's help.

For today: when you face a struggle, pray and trust God before your own strength. And if he gives you a victory, remember that it was a blessing from him, and use it with gratitude and justice.
exp.4:22:
This verse says that the half tribe of Manasseh, the part that stayed east of the Jordan River, lived in a large region to the north. It stretched from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon, which are areas of mountains and pastureland. It says they multiplied greatly, meaning they grew very large in number.

The chronicler, who writes long after these events, reviews the history of the tribes of the east. Earlier he tells how God gave them victory in war, and here he shows the results: land and growth. But the next verse reveals that, even with so much blessing, they later rebelled against God and followed other gods.

For today: when God blesses us with abundance, let us not take it as something we have earned. Let us use those moments to give thanks to him and remain faithful, because prosperity can also be a test for the heart.
exp.5:0:
This verse begins the list of the descendants of Levi, one of the twelve sons of Jacob. It names his three sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. From them came the three great families of the Levites.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written after the exile in Babylon, to remind the people of their roots. The Levites served in worship, and so this genealogy was important: it showed who could minister and where the priesthood came from, since Aaron and Moses descend from Kohath.

For today: God knows names and families, not just great deeds. Those who serve quietly also matter to Him. Today we can honor those who came before us in the faith and serve faithfully where God has placed us, knowing that He remembers our work.
exp.5:1:
This verse names the four sons of Kohath, who was a son of Levi: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. It is part of a family list. The word "sons" can also mean descendants, not only direct children.

The book of Chronicles does not clearly say who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. This list follows the line of Levi, the tribe of the priests and temple servants. From Amram would come Aaron, Moses, and Miriam, as the next verse shows.

For today: God cares for families and remembers names, even those that seem small. You matter to Him too. Think of those who went before you in the faith, give thanks for them, and ask yourself what legacy of faith you want to leave to those who come after.
exp.5:6:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Meraioth was the father of Amariah, and Amariah was the father of Ahitub. The word that means "was the father of" can sometimes in the Bible also indicate a more distant descendant, not only a direct son.

These names belong to the genealogy of the priests of the tribe of Levi, within 1 Chronicles, a book usually associated with the period after the exile in Babylon. The author is not identified with certainty. It records these family lines to remind the people of their identity, their history, and who served in the worship of God. This stretch leads toward Zadok, an important priest.

For today: God values people who seem to be just names on a list. Your everyday faithfulness, even when it goes unnoticed, is part of a larger story. Serve with constancy and leave a trace of faith for those who come after you.
exp.5:15:
The verse says Levi had three sons: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. Their names are the heads of the three great Levite families, and from these families would come those who served in Israel's worship.

Context: No single character is speaking here; the chronicler is writing after the exile in Babylon. The verse before this one ended with the removal of Jehozadak. Now the author returns to the origin of the Levites, to show those who came back that their service to God had ancient roots and had not been lost. The verses that follow describe each family in detail.

For today: God pays attention to people and to their service, even when their names may seem like nothing more than a list. Your humble work in the church or in your family also counts for Him. Serve Him faithfully, even when no one notices.
exp.5:17:
This verse gives the names of the four sons of Kohath (also spelled Kehath), who was a son of Levi: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. It is part of a family list, and it does not tell any story.

The book of Chronicles was written by an author who is not named; Jewish tradition often thinks of Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for the people who were returning from exile. It was meant to remind them who they were and who served God in the temple. The tribe of Levi had that duty, and that is why their families are recorded with such care. From Amram came Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, according to 1 Chronicles 6:3.

For today: God knows the names of those who serve him, even of those whom almost no one remembers. Today you can serve him faithfully in small things, trusting that he sees them and values them.
exp.5:19:
This verse begins to list the descendants of Gershom, one of the sons of Levi. The list follows a line from father to son: Libni, Jahath, and Zimmah. The phrase "his son" means that each one was the son of the one before him. In the Bible, these lists sometimes summarize several generations, so they do not always include everyone.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies as Ezra (though this is not certain), writes after the return from exile in Babylon. He wants to remind the people who the Levites are, the ones who served in the worship of the temple. These genealogies showed that their service had ancient and legitimate roots.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those whose names we hardly know. Your daily faithfulness, though it may seem small or quiet, has value before Him and can influence those who come after you.
exp.5:20:
This verse continues the list of descendants of Gershon, son of Levi: Joah, Iddo, Zerah and Jeaterai. Each one appears as "his son," that is, the next in the family line. In biblical genealogies, "son" can also mean descendant, so it is not always clear whether there is only one generation between one name and the next.

The author of Chronicles is not known for certain. Many believe he wrote after the return from exile in Babylon. Lists like this helped the people remember who they were and which families served in the worship of God. The Levites had that service, and that is why their names were preserved.

Today, this verse reminds us that God values people whom almost no one remembers. Your humble service, though it goes unnoticed, is not forgotten by Him. Serve faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.5:21:
These verses list descendants of Kohath, one of the sons of Levi: Amminadab, his son Korah, and Korah's son Assir. In genealogies like this one, "son" often means descendant, not always a direct son. Some believe Amminadab is another name for Izhar, but this is not certain.

The author of Chronicles, traditionally linked with Ezra though this is not known for sure, wrote for the people who returned from exile. He wanted to remind them of their history and of who served in worship. The Korah mentioned here is the same man who rebelled against Moses, but his family continued, and later some of his descendants served in the temple.

Today: God does not define you by the failures of your family. You can be faithful to God even if your family history carries wounds.
exp.5:22:
This verse is part of a family list of the Levites, descendants of Kohath. It says that Elkanah had a son named Ebiasaph, and that Ebiasaph had a son named Assir. In the Bible, "his son" can sometimes mean descendant, so the list may skip generations. Some of these names also appear in Exodus 6:24, and scholars do not always agree on how the two lists are related.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile in Babylon, remembers where the people came from. He wants to show that the Levites, who were in charge of worship and music in the temple, had a real and well-known lineage. In this way he encourages a people who were starting over.

For today: God knows and remembers people, even those who seem to be only a name in a list. Your faithfulness each day, though no one notices it, can be part of what God does through the generations.
exp.5:23:
This verse is part of a list of descendants. It names Tahath, his son Uriel, his son Uzziah, and his son Shaul. The older spelling of Tahath appears in the verse as the form that corresponds to Tahath, and Uzziah is the name that corresponds to the older spelling here. This Shaul is not the king of Israel but a Levite.

This is the genealogy of the Levites, of the family of Kohath. Tradition attributes the book to Ezra, although this is not certain. It was written after the exile to remind the people of their history and their roots, and the Levites of their service in worship. Other lists of this family in the same chapter give somewhat different names, and scholars do not agree on the reason.

Today: God knows and remembers even those whom almost no one mentions. Your faithful service, though small and hidden, has value before Him. Serve with constancy, without seeking applause.
exp.5:24:
In this list the name Elkanah appears several times, and it is not always clear whether it refers to the same person or to different relatives.

It is part of the genealogy of the Levites, the tribe responsible for service in the temple. Tradition attributes the book to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for the people who were returning from exile, to remind them of their roots, their identity, and the importance of worshiping God.

Today: God does not forget names. Many of these people have no famous stories, but each one was part of his plan. If your service seems small or hidden, remain faithful. God sees it and remembers it.
exp.5:25:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Elkanah had a son named Zophai, and that Zophai had a son named Nahath. These names are written in an older style. In other passages of the Bible, these same names appear in slightly different forms (for example, Zuph and Toah), and the reason is not known for certain; some think they are variants of the name or of the list.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, recorded the genealogies of the Levites. He wrote for the people who returned from exile, to remind them who they were, which family they belonged to, and who served in the worship of God. This line reaches down to Samuel.

For today: God remembers people whom almost no one remembers. Your name and your everyday faithfulness have value before Him, even when no one else notices them.
exp.5:26:
This verse is part of a family list. It names three men of the tribe of Levi, one after another: Eliab, his son Jeroham, and the son of that man, Elkanah. "His son" means that each one is the direct descendant of the one before. The names are written as they appear in the version of 1909, such as Elkanah, which today is sometimes read the same way.

This is not a character speaking in a scene. The chronicler, who writes after the exile, copies the genealogies of the Levites, the men in charge of worship. He wanted to show the people who were returning that their history and their service to God had roots. This line leads toward Samuel, who appears shortly after. Some scholars note that the names in these lists vary between passages, and it is not easy to explain all the differences.

For today: God takes notice of families and of lives that are little known. Perhaps no one will remember your name, but your faithfulness can prepare the way for those who come after. Serve God with constancy.
exp.5:28:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Merari had descendants named Mahli, and then come Libni, Shimei and Uzza, each one the son of the one before. It tells no stories; it only names people, one generation after another.

The writer of 1 Chronicles, whom many believe wrote after the return from exile, wants to show his people where they come from. Merari was one of the sons of Levi, and his family served in the work of the house of God. This list prepares the next verse, where the Levites whom David placed in charge of the music in worship are mentioned. Who each person in the list is is not always clear.

For today: God does not forget ordinary people who serve him faithfully, even when no one remembers them. Today you can serve steadily in small things and pass your faith on to those who come after you.
exp.5:29:
This verse continues a list of names from the family of Levi, in the line of Merari: Shimea, his son Haggiah, and his son Asaiah. It is simply a chain of fathers and sons, one generation after another. The names vary a little from translation to translation, and some of these men are not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), wrote after the exile. He wanted to remind the people who were returning of their history, their roots, and who served in worship. These lists show that the Levites, including the musicians, had a place and an inheritance set in order by God.

For today: God sees people whom the world forgets. Even if your service is simple or little seen, he knows it and values it. Serve faithfully, and trust that your name is important to him.
exp.5:30:
This verse says that David put certain men in charge of the music in the house of the Lord. He did this after the ark had rest, that is, when it had been settled in one fixed place and no longer moved from one spot to another.

Here the chronicler speaks, an author who writes after the exile and whose name we do not know for certain. He is presenting the families of the Levites, and that is why he gives lists of names. He wants to remind the people that worship had an order and that each family had a service. The singers served beside the tent of the tabernacle, before the temple that Solomon built existed.

For today: music in the church is a real service, not an ornament. If you have a gift for singing, playing, or helping in worship, offer it with steady commitment and humility, even though no one may remember your name.
exp.5:31:
This verse says that the Levites in charge of the music sang in service before the tabernacle, which here is called the "tent of meeting," because there was what recalled God's covenant with his people. They did this until Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. Then they continued in their service, but according to the order they already had.

The author of Chronicles, whose name we do not know for certain, writes after the exile. He wants the people to remember their roots and the importance of worship. Here he lists the families of Levite singers whom David put in charge of the music when the ark found its resting place in Jerusalem.

For today: serve God faithfully, even though places and circumstances change. The singers worshiped first in a tent and then in a temple, but their hearts and their service remained steadfast. Worship with constancy, without depending on the setting.
exp.5:33:
This verse is part of a list of the ancestors of Heman, the singer. The names are read backward: Heman was the son of Joel, and from there the family line goes up: Elkanah, Jeroham, Eliel and Toah.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records these genealogies to show the Israelites who were returning from exile who served in worship. Heman was from the tribe of Levi, of the line of Kohath, and he directed the singing before the tabernacle, and later in the temple of Solomon.

For today: God notices people we sometimes forget. Each name here is a reminder that faithful service, even when it is simple and quiet, is part of God's story. Today you can thank those who taught you to worship, and serve faithfully wherever God has placed you.
exp.5:34:
This verse is part of a list of the ancestors of Heman, the singer. It says that Heman descended from a long line of men: Amasai, Mahath, Elkanah and Zuph. The word "son" here can mean descendant, not always a direct son. Some names are repeated, such as Elkanah, and the lists in Chronicles have variants with other genealogies of the tribe of Levi.

The writer of Chronicles wrote after the exile in Babylon. He wanted to remind the people that the Levites had an ordered lineage and an ordered service. David appointed Heman and others to lead the singing in the house of God. The list shows that his ministry was not improvised but was part of a family history.

For today: God values the people hidden in lists of names. Give thanks to those who passed on your faith to you, even though few remember them, and serve faithfully in your own place, knowing that God sees and remembers.
exp.5:36:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors. It follows the family line backward: Tahath, Assir, Ebiasaph, and Korah. The names come in reverse order, from the more recent to the more distant, until reaching Levi. Korah is the same man who rebelled against Moses in the wilderness.

Here the chronicler speaks, writing down the genealogies of Israel after the exile. He is presenting the family of Heman, a Levite singer who served in the music of the temple. Some names repeat or vary in other lists, and scholars do not always agree on how they fit together. Even so, the point is to show that service to God had roots and order.

For today: God notices ordinary people and remembers their names. Give thanks for those who passed on your faith, and think about what legacy of service and worship you want to leave to those who come after you.
exp.5:37:
This verse closes the list of ancestors of Heman, the singer. It says that his line comes from Izhar, from Kohath, from Levi and, at the end, from Israel, that is, Jacob. These are ancient names that show that Heman belonged to the tribe of Levi.

The author of Chronicles, whom many believe was Ezra, though this is not certain, recorded these genealogies for the people who were returning from exile. He wanted to show who served in worship and that their service came from a legitimate inheritance. Here the list connects Heman, a musician from the time of David, with the origins of his tribe.

For today: God values people, not only the famous. Even little-known names matter to Him. Serve with gratitude where God has placed you, knowing that your service is part of a larger story.
exp.5:39:
This verse is part of a list of the ancestors of Asaf, a Levite musician. It says that Asaf came from a line that passed through Malchiah, Baaseiah, and Michael. "Son of" here means descendant, not always a direct father. The names appear in the older spelling used in the Reina-Valera 1909.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile in Babylon, and scholars are not sure who its author was; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra. The chronicler records these genealogies to show that the returning people kept their history and that the temple service had ancient roots. Asaf appears here at the right hand of Heman, leading the music in worship during the time of David.

For today: God notices people that others would overlook. These almost unknown names were part of a story of faith that reached down to Asaf. Your faithful service, even when no one notices, can also be a link that God uses to bless others.
exp.5:41:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors: Ethan, Zimmah and Shimei. "Son of" here can mean descendant, not always a direct son. They are links in the family line of the musician Asaph, who came from Gershon, son of Levi.

The author is the chronicler, and tradition often points to Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. He wants to show that the temple singers, appointed by David, had a legitimate lineage. This Ethan is different from the Ethan of Merari who appears in the following verse.

Today it reminds us that God values people whom almost no one mentions. Perhaps no one will remember your name, but your faithfulness passes on to others. Today, serve steadily in small things, for God sees and remembers.
exp.5:42:
This verse is part of a list of family members. It says that a certain man was a son of Jahath, who in turn was a son of Gershom, and Gershom was a son of Levi. In this way the chain of names is completed, reaching back to the ancestor of the whole tribe of the Levites.

This genealogy is written by the author of Chronicles, written for the people who were returning from exile. In this passage he presents the family of the singer Asaph, who served with music in the sanctuary. By reaching Levi, it becomes clear that their service had ancient and legitimate roots. Who wrote Chronicles, and exactly when, is debated among scholars.

For today: God remembers names that the world forgets. Your service, even if it seems small or hidden, is part of a larger story. Serve with faithfulness, knowing that God knows your name and values your place.
exp.5:43:
This verse says that the descendants of Merari, relatives of the other Levites, stood on the left side. Among them was Ethan, son of Kishi, grandson of Abdi and great-grandson of Malluch.

The text is part of a list of the Levites whom David put in charge of the singing in the house of the Lord. The singers stood in three groups: Heman in the center, Asaph on the right, and the sons of Merari on the left. The writer of Chronicles, who wrote after the exile (tradition identifies him with Ezra, though this is not certain), wants the people to remember that their worship had an order and a history.

For today: God notices every place of service, not only the most visible ones. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even if you are placed on the left.
exp.5:44:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Ethan, the singer from the sons of Merari, descended from Hashabiah, who was the son of Amaziah, and he in turn the son of Hilkiah. It is a chain of fathers and sons going back in time, all the way to Levi.

Here no character speaks in a scene; the author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies as Ezra, though this is not certain, records the families of the Levites. They served in the music of worship in the time of David. The names reminded a people returning from exile that their service to God had ancient roots.

For today: God knows people by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Honor those who came before you in the faith, and serve faithfully wherever you are, without seeking to be famous. Your service also matters.
exp.5:45:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors. It says that a certain Levite was the son of Amasai, who was the son of Bani, and Bani was the son of Shamer. It is one link in a family chain that goes back through Merari and even to Levi.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the families of the Levites who served in the music of worship. Ethan, of the line of Merari, stood at the left hand. This list reminded the people, after the exile, that their service to God had ancient roots and order.

For today: God notices people whose names almost no one remembers. Your faithful service, even if it seems small or hidden, matters to Him. Serve with steadiness wherever you are placed.
exp.5:46:
This verse closes a list of names. It says that the ancestor mentioned was a descendant of Mahli, who came from Mushi, and Mushi from Merari, a son of Levi. In other words, the family line goes back to one of the sons of Levi, the father of the priestly and service tribe.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), recorded genealogies for the people who were returning from exile. Here the family of Heman, a Levite singer, is shown. The Levites of the line of Merari had duties in the service of the tabernacle. The names gave identity and legitimacy to their service.

God notices people, even when their names seem distant or little known to us. Each generation served in its place. Today we can serve faithfully in simple tasks, without seeking recognition, trusting that God values what we do and remembers his children by name.
exp.5:48:
This verse says that Aaron and his descendants were in charge of offering the incense and the burnt offerings on the altars. They also worked in the most holy place, the most sacred space of the sanctuary. Their task included making atonement, that is, offering sacrifices to cover the sin of the people. They did everything just as Moses had commanded.

The one speaking is the Chronicler, who writes after the exile in Babylon. Earlier he spoke of the Levites in general, who attended the tabernacle. Here he clarifies that the priesthood was reserved for the family of Aaron. Then he continues with his list of descendants. This probably aimed to remind the people of the order of worship that God had established.

For today: God values that we worship him with reverence and obedience, not in our own way. We can ask ourselves whether our life of prayer and service seeks to please him. In addition, Christians believe that Jesus is the perfect priest who gives us access to God.
exp.5:50:
This verse is part of a list of names. It continues the line of priests descending from Aaron: Bukki, son of Abishua, then Uzzi, and then Zerahiah. The names are written as in the older version (Uzzi is Uzzi, Zerahiah is Zerahiah). No story is told about them; the text only notes that each one was born of his father and remained in the family.

The writer is the chronicler, an author whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though there is no complete certainty. He writes for the people who returned from exile. He shows them that the priesthood came from Aaron and from the instructions of Moses. In this way they could recognize who served legitimately in worship and how God had preserved his people through the generations.

For today: God notices people who sometimes seem unimportant. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one notices; your life also forms part of what God does from generation to generation.
exp.5:51:
The verse continues the list of Aaron's descendants, the priesthood: Meraioth, his son Amariah, and his son Ahitub. "His son" can mean a direct son or a descendant, because biblical genealogies sometimes summarize generations.

The book does not say who wrote it. Many think it was written after the exile in Babylon, perhaps by Ezra, though this is not certain. Its purpose seems to be to remind the people who returned who the priests were and that service to God had an unbroken line. This list prepares the mention of Zadok, and then of the cities that were given to the sons of Aaron.

Today it reminds us that God values faithfulness that passes from one generation to the next. Perhaps no one remembers your name, but God does. Serve steadily where you are, and pass your faith on to those who come after you.
exp.5:52:
This verse continues a list of fathers and sons in the priestly family. It says that Zadok was the son of Ahitub, and that Ahimaaz was the son of Zadok. In this older version, the phrase "his son" means that each name is the heir who carries on the line. The names appear in the older spelling, such as Achimaaz, which is now written Ahimaaz.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records the genealogies of the Levites. He does this for the people who were returning from exile, to show who served legitimately in worship and that God had watched over that priestly line through the years.

For today: God pays attention to people whose names we almost never remember. If your service is quiet, do not think it has no value. Be faithful where you are, and leave your children or others an example of trust in God.
exp.5:55:
It says that the fields and the villages around the city of Hebron were not given to the priests, but to Caleb, son of Jephunneh. The fields are the lands for farming and grazing; the villages are the small towns nearby. The descendants of Aaron received the city itself, along with its common lands, that is, the pasture ground next to it.

This passage is a list of cities that Israel gave to the Levites. The writer of Chronicles presents it as a historical record. Hebron was given to the priests, but Caleb had already received those lands as an inheritance, according to Joshua 14 and 21. In this way, both promises were kept.

For today: God attends to the details and fulfills what he has promised to each person. We can learn to honor our agreements and to share justly, without taking from others what God has already given them.
exp.5:63:
This verse says that the people of Israel gave the Levites cities to live in, along with their suburbs. The suburbs were the pasturelands around the city, where the Levites could keep their livestock.

The writer of Chronicles, who was writing to a people returning from exile, goes over the lists of the Levites. The Levites did not receive a land of their own like the other tribes, because their inheritance was to serve God. So the other tribes gave them cities from their own territories, spread throughout Israel. In this way there were servants of God near all the people. The lists of cities vary a little between books, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: let us generously care for those who serve God among us, such as pastors, teachers, and missionaries. When we give joyfully from what we have, we help teaching and spiritual care reach everyone.
exp.5:66:
This verse says that the Levites, of the family of Kohath, were given cities in the territory of Ephraim. Among them were Shechem, located in the hill country of Ephraim, and Gezer. The cities of refuge were places where a person who had killed someone without intending it could flee for protection. The pasturelands around each city were set aside for grazing.

The chronicler lists the cities that the tribes of Israel gave to the Levites, who did not receive a territory of their own because their task was the service of God. These lists remind us that God cared for them and distributed them among the people to teach and guide them spiritually. Shechem was one of the six cities of refuge.

God provides a place of protection and of service for each person. Today we can be like those cities: places of refuge, justice, and mercy for those who are wounded or need help. We should also support with generosity those who dedicate their lives to serving.
exp.5:67:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It says that the descendants of Kohath, of the tribe of Levi, were also given Jokmeam and Beth-horon, along with their suburbs, which were the grazing lands around each town, used for livestock.

The writer of Chronicles, who wrote for the people returning from exile, reviews how the Levitical towns were distributed. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, so they lived in towns within other tribes. Here the towns mentioned are those in Ephraim. Some names vary a little from other biblical lists, and scholars do not always agree on why.

For today: God cares that those who serve others have a home and provision. We can support with generosity and gratitude those who teach and care for us spiritually, and remember that no service to God goes unnoticed by Him.
exp.5:69:
From the half tribe of Manasseh, two towns were given, Aner and Bileam, with their pasturelands. The pasturelands were the open grounds around each town, where the livestock were raised. These towns were for the descendants of Kohath who had not yet received their portion.

This is part of a long list of towns that Israel gave to the Levites, the tribe set apart for the service of God. The chronicler, who writes after the exile, recalls these details to show that the Levites had a place in the land. Some names here differ from other lists in the Bible, and the reason is not known with certainty.

For today: God cares for those who serve others. We can support with generosity and gratitude our pastors, teachers, and servants, so that they have what they need to live and to devote themselves to their work.
exp.5:75:
This verse is part of the list of cities that the tribe of Naphtali gave to the Levites, the descendants of Gershon. The names given here are Kedesh in Galilee, Hammon, and Kirjathaim. It is worth noting that some names here differ from the parallel list in Joshua 21, and scholars explain those differences in several ways, for example, copying variants or alternate names for the same place.

The chronicler writes after the exile, and he goes over how Israel distributed cities to the Levites, who did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. In this way he reminded the people that service to God always had a place and a livelihood within the community.

Today we can support with generosity those who serve in our church, making sure they have what they need to devote themselves to teaching and walking alongside others.
exp.5:77:
This verse continues the list of cities given to the Levites. It says that, on the other side of the Jordan River, opposite Jericho, the tribe of Reuben gave Bezer, in the wilderness, and Jahzah. The pasture lands around each city, where the Levites could keep their livestock, are the common lands that belonged to each city.

The text is part of the genealogies in Chronicles, written to remind the people of their history and their identity. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, but cities scattered among all the tribes (Numbers 35; Joshua 21). In this way they lived close to the people to teach them the law of God. Bezer, moreover, was a city of refuge, according to Deuteronomy 4:43.

For today: God cares for those who serve and places his people near others. We can generously support those who serve in the church, and live out our faith near our neighbors.
exp.5:79:
This verse says that the tribe of Gad gave the Levites two cities: Ramoth, in the region of Gilead, and Mahanaim. Each one included its surrounding lands and pastures, the fields around the city where livestock could be raised.

It is part of a long list of cities that Israel gave to the Levites, the tribe dedicated to the service of God. They received no territory of their own, so they lived scattered among the cities of the other tribes. The chronicler's text recalls this arrangement for a people who were returning from exile. Ramoth in Gilead is also mentioned as a city of refuge in other passages.

For today: God cared for those who served him through the generosity of the people. We can gratefully support those who serve in our church, and give them what they need to live with dignity.
exp.6:0:
This verse begins the list of the tribe of Issachar, one of the twelve sons of Jacob. It says that he had four sons: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron. The names appear in the older spelling used in the 1909 version. Here the word "sons" can also mean descendants.

Context: there is no one speaking; it is a genealogical record within Chronicles. Its author is unknown, although a tradition attributes it to Ezra. It was probably written for the people who were returning from exile, to remind them of their identity, their land, and their history. The verses that follow show how this family grew, especially through its brave men.

For today: God remembers every name, even those that almost no one remembers. You also matter to Him. Value your family history and give thanks for those who came before you, remembering that your life also leaves a mark on others.
exp.6:1:
This verse mentions the six sons of Tola, who was a son of Issachar. They were heads of their families, that is, leaders of their households. It also says that in the time of King David, the descendants of Tola numbered 22,600 men of great valor, that is, strong and capable warriors ready for battle.

These lists of families come from the book of Chronicles, written after the exile in Babylon. The author is unknown; tradition names Ezra, but this is not certain. Its purpose was to remind the people of Israel of their roots and their identity, and that God had preserved every tribe. The censuses from the time of David show how the tribe of Issachar grew.

God pays attention to families and to every name, even to those almost no one remembers. Today we can be encouraged to build a faith in our homes that passes from generation to generation, and to serve with courage wherever God has placed us, without feeling insignificant.
exp.6:2:
This verse continues the line of Uzzi, a descendant of Issachar. It says that Uzzi had a son named Izrahiah, and that the sons of Izrahiah were Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Ishiah. In all there were five of them, all of them chief men, meaning leaders and important heads within their families.

No one speaks here. This is part of the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, which were written to remind the people of Israel who they were and where they came from. The passages around this verse speak of brave men ready for war in the days of David. Scholars do not agree on the exact date when this was written, though many place it after the exile in Babylon.

God does not forget names or families. Today we can give thanks for those who shaped us in the faith and ask ourselves what legacy of character and service we will leave to those who come after us.
exp.6:4:
This verse says that the relatives from the tribe of Issachar, counting all their families according to the records of their genealogies, numbered eighty-seven thousand men who were very brave and strong.

The author of Chronicles, traditionally identified with Ezra though this is not certain, compiled lists of families for the people who were returning from exile. He wanted to remind them of their identity and their roots, and that God had sustained every tribe. The numbers can be understood literally or as approximate figures; scholars debate this.

For today: God does not forget anyone, and every family and every person has a place in his story. Today we can give thanks for our family and for the faith we have received, and think about how to use our strengths to serve others and strengthen our community.
exp.6:5:
The verse says that Benjamin had three sons: Bela, Becher, and Jediael. Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob, and from his sons came families that formed one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Here only these three are named, as the beginning of the list.

The author is the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, although this is not certain. He wrote after the exile in Babylon. He wanted the people to remember who they were, what families they came from, and that God still considered them his own. Other lists of Benjamin in the Bible name more sons. Scholars explain this in several ways, for example, that they include grandsons or that they are other branches of the family.

Today it reminds us that God knows our names and our family history. Give thanks for those who went before you in the faith, and think about how you can pass it on to those who come after you.
exp.6:6:
Bela, son of Benjamin, had five sons: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri. Each of them was a head of a large family, the leader of a household line. They were mighty men of valour, strong and capable for war. Among their descendants were counted 22,034 men.

In this chapter the chronicler is not describing a scene; he is recording the genealogies of the tribes of Israel. He probably wrote after the return from exile, to remind the people who they were and to which family they belonged. Scholars do not agree on every detail of these lists, and some names reappear in other parts of the Bible.

For today: God knows names and families, not just crowds. Today you can give thanks for those who went before you in the faith and care for your own household, knowing that what you do faithfully leaves a mark on the generations that follow.
exp.6:9:
This verse is part of a list of family members. It says that Jediael had a son named Bilhan, and that Bilhan had seven sons: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar. The word for the son-line is simply the sons listed in the verse. Here "son" can also mean descendant.

No one is speaking in a scene; this is the account of the chronicler, an unknown author whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He wrote for the people who returned from exile, so that they would remember their roots. This list belongs to the tribe of Benjamin, and the verses that follow summarize it by counting the brave men of these families.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even the names that seem unimportant to us. Today we can remember our ancestors with gratitude, and those who taught us the faith, and live knowing that our lives matter before God.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that the descendants of Jediael, heads of their families, were very brave and well prepared men. They numbered seventeen thousand two hundred, ready to go out to fight. The phrase about going out to battle means they were of age and fit for war. Here the word "sons" can also refer to descendants.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, presents lists of Israel's families. This passage deals with the tribe of Benjamin. The numbers do not fully match the previous verse (twenty thousand two hundred), and scholars explain this in several ways: a different count, a different date, or different groups. These lists reminded the people of their identity after the exile.

God does not forget families or individuals. Every name and every contribution counts. Today we can serve with what God has given us, whether courage, perseverance, or care for others, knowing that He values our place among His people.
exp.6:11:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Shuppim and Huppim were sons of Ir, and that Hushim was a son of Aher. It tells no stories; it only gives names and family relationships. Some scholars think "Aher" might be another name for a relative already mentioned, but this is not known for certain.

This list is found in 1 Chronicles, a book that tradition attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for the people who returned from exile. They wanted to remember who they were, which tribe they belonged to, and that God had not forgotten them. This passage speaks of the tribe of Benjamin.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. You can rest in the knowledge that your life, though it may seem small, has value to Him. Today, also value someone who goes unnoticed, and thank them.
exp.6:14:
This verse is part of a family list from the tribe of Manasseh. It says that Machir married a woman named Maacah, who was the sister of Huppim and Shuppim. It also mentions Zelophehad, the one named second, and makes clear that he had only daughters. The text is difficult, and it is not clear how all the names are related; scholars interpret it in several different ways.

The chronicler is not describing a moment of action but recording genealogies. Lists like this helped the people of Israel, returning from exile, remember their roots, their tribes, and their lands. The mention of Zelophehad's daughters recalls that they appear in another passage of the Bible (Numbers 27), asking for an inheritance.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even those the world overlooks. Value today those who seem unimportant around you, and remember that your name matters to God too.
exp.6:15:
It says that Maachah, the wife of Machir, had a son whose name was Peresh. His brother was called Sheresh, and Sheresh's sons were Ulam and Rakem.

This is part of a genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh. The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), wrote for a people returning from exile. They wanted to remember who they were and which families they belonged to. That is why even little-known names are recorded, and also the names of women, which is notable in a list like this.

God pays attention to every person, even those almost no one remembers. These names appear in his Word, and that teaches us that your life and your family also matter to him. Today, thank God for those who came before you, and remember that your simple, hidden service has value before him.
exp.6:16:
It says that Bedan was a son of Ulam, and that this group of names belongs to the descendants of Gilead. Gilead was the son of Machir, and Machir was the son of Manasseh. It is part of a family list, like a summarized family tree.

Here no individual speaks; the chronicler, who writes after the exile in Babylon, is gathering the families of the tribes of Israel. He wanted to remind the people who were returning who they were, which tribe they belonged to, and that their roots were still alive. Some details of these lists are hard to reconstruct, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who barely appear mentioned by name. Your life and your family matter to Him. Give thanks today for those who came before you, and think about how you can pass on faith and a good example to those who come after.
exp.6:18:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Shemida had four sons: Ahian, Shechem, Likhi and Aniam. The names are written in an older form, but they are Hebrew names with no further explanation given here.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes after the exile in Babylon. This genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh showed the returning people that their families and their inheritance had not been lost. Shemida appears as a descendant of Manasseh, and the text gives no further details about these sons.

For today: God knows the name of every person, even of those whom history hardly mentions. If you sometimes feel overlooked, remember that your life has value before Him. And we can also learn to value those who serve in silence.
exp.6:19:
This verse is part of a list of the descendants of Ephraim. It names Shuthelah, and then Bered, Tahath, Eladah, and another Tahath, each one listed as the son of the one before him. The names appear in the old spelling used in that edition.

The speaker here is not a character in a story; it is the chronicler, who wrote these family records for the people of Israel after the exile. His purpose was to preserve the memory of the tribes, their lands, and their inheritance. Scholars do not agree on how some of these names fit with other lists, so it is wise to be cautious.

For today: God remembers each person by name, even those we barely know. This encourages us to value our family, those who came before us, and those who will serve after us, for no one is insignificant to God.
exp.6:21:
This verse says that Ephraim, the father of the sons who died, mourned their loss for many days. To mourn means to express deep sadness for someone who has died. His brothers, that is, close relatives from his tribe, came to comfort him, in other words, to be with him and encourage him in his grief.

It is part of the genealogies of Ephraim in Chronicles. The previous verse tells that men of Gath killed Ezer and Elad when they tried to steal their livestock. The text does not say how many years passed or describe the whole event in detail, and some scholars debate whether this Ephraim is the son of Joseph or a descendant with the same name. What is clear is a father's grief and the company of his family.

When someone suffers a loss, great speeches are not needed. We can visit them, listen to them, and accompany them with patience. God uses that simple presence to bring comfort.
exp.6:23:
This verse says that Sherah, a woman from the family of Ephraim, built or founded three towns: Lower Beth-horon, Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sherah. The word "built" can mean build, fortify, or have built. It does not say how she did it.

This passage belongs to the family lists in 1 Chronicles, and no speaker is talking. The writer records the descendants of Ephraim and mentions Sherah, which is unusual, because nearly all the names are of men. Many believe she was a woman of great influence, though the text gives no further details. Naming her shows that her work was remembered.

For today: God can use anyone, regardless of their gender or family history, to leave a lasting work. Faithfully do what is within your reach, because it may benefit many people after you.
exp.6:24:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Rephah was a son of Beriah, and then names Resheph, Telah, and Tahan as direct descendants in the line.

It is a genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim, within the records of the tribes of Israel in Chronicles. No character is speaking; the chronicler, traditionally thought to be Ezra though this is not certain, gathers names. He probably did so for the Israelites who were returning from exile, so that they would remember their origin, their tribes, and their inheritance. The list continues until it reaches Joshua.

For today: God remembers names that we overlook. If you feel forgotten or unimportant today, remember that for God every person counts. You can also value those who came before you in the faith, such as your family or your church, and thank them.
exp.6:25:
This verse is part of a list of descendants of the tribe of Ephraim. It names three generations in a row: Laadan, his son Ammihud, and the son of that one, Elishama. The phrase "his son" only shows who descended from whom. Through this chain of names the line reaches Joshua, the one who led Israel after Moses.

No one speaks in a scene here; the author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, gathers family records. He writes for the people who were returning from exile, and they needed to remember their identity, their tribe, and their land. After the list the places where they lived are given.

For today: God knows the names of people no one remembers. Your life counts, even when it seems hidden. Be faithful where you are, and leave a legacy of faith to those who come after you.
exp.6:26:
This verse is part of a list of descendants of the tribe of Ephraim. It says that Nun was the son of Elishama, and that Joshua was the son of Nun. The phrase "his son" only indicates that each one was the heir or direct descendant of the one before.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra although this is not certain, writes after the exile in Babylon. He wants to remind the people where they come from and which tribe each family belongs to. Here Joshua, the successor of Moses, is named. This is the only time his genealogy appears in Chronicles, and it is very brief.

For today: God remembers people, not only the great moments. Behind every leader there was a family that raised them and shaped their path. Honor those who came before you, and serve faithfully those who will come after you.
exp.6:27:
This verse lists the lands where the descendants of Ephraim lived. It mentions Bethel, with the towns nearby, called "villages" here. Eastward was Naaran, and westward was Gezer. It also names Shechem and Gaza with their towns.

The author of Chronicles, traditionally identified as Ezra, though this is not certain, gathers genealogies for the people who returned from exile. He wanted them to remember their roots and their lands. The list of names, which ends with Joshua, shows the line of Ephraim. Today it is hard to locate some of these places with exactness.

God is faithful and cares for the details: he gives each family a place and a name. Today we can trust that he also knows our story and our place. Thank God for your family and for the place where he has put you, and seek to serve him there faithfully.
exp.6:28:
This verse lists cities that belonged to the tribe of Manasseh: Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo and Dor, each with its villages, that is, the small towns that depended on them. It ends by saying that the descendants of Joseph, son of Israel (Jacob), lived there. The older names of Beth-shean, Taanach and Megiddo are written today as Beth-shean, Taanach and Megiddo.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records lists of families and territories. He wrote for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots and their land. These cities were in the north of Canaan, and the list shows that Ephraim and Manasseh, sons of Joseph, had their place within the people of God.

God remembers every family and every place. If sometimes you feel that your life goes unnoticed, remember that to God you have a name, a history and a place. Give thanks for this and live with confidence.
exp.6:29:
This verse begins the list of the descendants of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob. It names four sons: Imnah, Isuah, Ishuai, and Beriah, and also mentions a sister, Serah. It is uncommon for a genealogy to name a woman, so her inclusion stands out.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though there is no complete certainty, records the families of the tribes of Israel. He writes for the people who returned from exile in Babylon, to remind them who they were and to whom they belonged. This verse follows the list of cities of the sons of Joseph and opens the section about Asher.

For today: God does not forget any name, not even those that seem minor. If you sometimes feel overlooked, remember that for God your life and your family matter. Give thanks today for the people who are part of your story.
exp.6:30:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Beriah, son of Asher, had two sons: Heber and Malchiel. Malchiel was the father of Birzavith, which was probably a personal name, although some think it could also be a place.

The book of Chronicles has no author identified with certainty; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for the people who were returning from exile. These lists of tribes reminded them who they were, which family they belonged to, and that God had cared for their lineage. Here the tribe of Asher is recorded.

For today: God knows the names of people whom almost no one remembers. You are not a number to Him. You can live with peace knowing that your life, though it may seem simple, has value before God and that He cares for your family generation after generation.
exp.6:32:
This verse lists the three sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath.

The author of Chronicles, traditionally identified with Ezra although this is not certain, wrote these genealogies for the Israelites who were returning from exile. They wanted to remember who they were, what tribe they belonged to, and that God had preserved his people. Although these names hardly appear in other texts, they are recorded here with care.

For today: God does not forget anyone, even when a person's name seems unimportant to others. This invites us to value the ordinary people around us and to remember with gratitude those who came before us in faith and in family.
exp.6:33:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Shamer had four sons: Ahi, Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram. Shamer was a son of Heber and belonged to the tribe of Asher. Some names are spelled differently in other translations; for example, the name Jehubbah sometimes appears in other versions as Jehubah, and Shamer is called Shomer in verse 32 in some versions.

These lists are found in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. The author, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), wrote them for the people who were returning from exile. They wanted to remember who they were, which tribe they belonged to, and that God had cared for each family. There are no stories here, only names.

For today: God knows the name of every person, even of those whom almost no one remembers. Today you can value those who go unnoticed, and remember that you too are known and loved by God.
exp.6:34:
These verses give the names of four sons of Helem: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal. The verse says "his brother" because it refers back to Shomer (Shemer), mentioned earlier. These are names from the tribe of Asher, and nothing more is explained about them.

The book of Chronicles is anonymous, although tradition attributes it to Ezra. It was probably written for the people returning from exile. The lists of families reminded them where they came from, which tribe they belonged to, and that God had cared for their history. Some believe Helem is the same as Hotham in verse 32, but this is not certain.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those almost no one remembers. Today you can value your family and the believers around you who are unknown. Give them time, pray for them, and remind them that God sees them.
exp.6:35:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Zophah had five sons: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri and Imrah. Here the word "sons" can also mean descendants. The names sound unfamiliar because they are Hebrew, written in the old style of this translation.

The book of Chronicles does not clearly say who its author is, although Jewish tradition points to Ezra. It was written for a people who had returned from exile and needed to remember who they were. This list belongs to the tribe of Asher, and Zophah appears within the family of Helem. The records showed that each family had a place and an inheritance in Israel.

For today: God knows each person by name, even when the world forgets them. You can remember this when you feel small or unimportant. You can also honor those who work without being seen by thanking them for their service.
exp.6:36:
This verse continues a list of names. They are further sons of Zophah, of the tribe of Asher: Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera. The names are written as they appear in the Reina-Valera 1909; today some appear with other spelling, such as Shamma for Sama.

The book of Chronicles is a history of Israel that was written after the exile in Babylon. Jewish tradition often attributes it to Ezra, although this is not certain. Its purpose was to remind those who were returning to their land who they were, what tribe they belonged to, and that God had not forgotten his people. That is why it includes long lists of families, even of little-known tribes.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those no one remembers. You can rest in the fact that your life matters to Him. In addition, learn to value those who go unnoticed around you, and treat them with respect and kindness.
exp.6:38:
This verse gives the names of three sons of Ulla: Arah, Haniel, and Rezia. Ulla appears in the list of the descendants of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob. There are no hard words here; they are only proper names, and the Bible tells us nothing more about these people.

The book of Chronicles was written after the return from exile in Babylon, and no one knows for certain who its author was; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra. Here the writer does not speak in the first person but records genealogies. Lists like these helped the people remember where they came from and to whom their land belonged. The verse that follows shows that these descendants of Asher were brave men, fit for war.

For today: God knows the names of people whom history has almost forgotten. If you ever feel that your work or your life goes unnoticed, remember that to God every person counts. Today you can treat someone who seems of no account with honor and gratitude.
exp.7:3:
This verse is part of a list of names. It continues the sons of Bela, of the tribe of Benjamin: Abishua, Naaman, and Ahoah. These are names of people; there are no difficult words. In other lists some names appear in slightly different forms, and scholars do not always know why.

The author of Chronicles (tradition says it was Ezra, though this is not certain) writes after the return from exile in Babylon. He wanted the people to remember where they came from, what tribe and family they belonged to, and that their history had not been lost. Benjamin receives a great deal of attention in these chapters, perhaps because of its importance in Jerusalem.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who appear only as a name in a list. Today you can remember that your life and your family matter to Him. You can also give thanks for the little-known people who have sustained your faith.
exp.7:4:
This verse continues a list of names. It says that Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram were also sons of Bela, of the tribe of Benjamin. "Shephuphan" is the name as it is written in this reading; some connect it with "Shephuphan" in other lists, but that is not certain. The names are repeated in different lists, and it is not always clear whether they refer to the same people.

The author is the Chronicler, who according to tradition was Ezra, though this is not known with certainty. He wrote after the exile in Babylon. He wanted the people who were returning to remember their roots, their tribes, and their land. This genealogy showed them that, despite the exile, the history of Israel had not been lost.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. This encourages us to value others and to serve faithfully, even when no one notices. For God, no one is insignificant.
exp.7:11:
This verse gives part of the list of Benjamin's descendants. It says that Elpaal had three sons: Eber, Misham and Shamed. Shamed built the towns of Ono and Lod, along with their villages, that is, the small nearby settlements that depended on them.

There is no character speaking here; the chronicler, traditionally credited to Ezra though this is not known for certain, is the writer. He wrote after the exile in Babylon to remind the people where they came from. These genealogies showed that each family had a history, land and a place in Israel. The names of towns helped locate each clan.

For today: God notices what we do for others, even when it goes unnoticed. Shamed appears for building places where others would live. We can ask ourselves what we can build today, such as a healthy home, a friendship or a service in the church, that will benefit others after we are gone.
exp.7:12:
Beriah and Shema were heads of families who lived in Aijalon, a town of the tribe of Benjamin. The text says that they drove away the inhabitants of Gath, a Philistine city. It does not explain when or how this happened.

The author is unknown; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. This chapter is a list of families from Benjamin. It was probably written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their origin, their land, and their identity. That is why even brief events are recorded.

God remembers people who faithfully do their part, even when almost no one knows their names. Today you can serve steadily in your family or your church, without seeking applause, trusting that God sees and values what you do.
exp.7:13:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth are sons or descendants of the family of Benjamin, though here only their names are mentioned. The Bible does not explain who they were or what they did. Some texts connect these names with Beriah, but the verse itself does not make this clear.

The author, traditionally called the Chronicler, writes after the return from exile in Babylon. His purpose is to remind the Israelites who they were, which tribe they belonged to, and what their inheritance was. The genealogies showed that the people had roots and that God had preserved their families. This section speaks of the tribe of Benjamin and of the families of Aijalon.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom history almost does not remember. You can be encouraged to value quiet and faithful work without seeking applause. You can also remember with gratitude those who, though not famous, helped you in your faith.
exp.7:14:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Zebadiah, Arad, and Ader, who are counted among the descendants of Benjamin, according to the nearby context. The text does not explain who they were or what they did. Some translations write the third name differently, since Hebrew names vary a little in how they are spelled.

Here no single character is speaking. The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra, though this is not certain, gathers genealogies. His purpose was to remind the people who returned from exile what their roots, families, and tribes were. The names helped preserve Israel's identity and inheritance.

For today: God knows people by name, even those whom history barely remembers. This encourages us to value those who serve quietly and to trust that our lives, however small they may seem, matter to God.
exp.7:15:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Michael, Ispah, and Joha were sons of Beriah. The names sound different from how we write them today, so in this verse Michael is the same name as Michael, and Ispah is Ispah. Nothing more is told about them here.

The author, traditionally identified as Ezra though the text does not say so, records the families of the tribe of Benjamin. He writes for the people who returned from exile in Babylon, and he wanted to remember their roots, their lands, and their identity. Beriah appears in this genealogy as the head of a family household, and some scholars think his descendants were linked to the city of Aijalon, though the text does not make this clear.

God forgets no one, not even those who barely appear in the stories. Today you can remember that your life and your family matter to Him, even when you go unnoticed. Do your part faithfully, for God sees what others do not notice.
exp.7:16:
This verse is a simple list of four names: Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hezeki, and Heber. It tells no story; it only mentions several men from the same family. Hebrew names usually carry meaning, but here the text does not explain any of them.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile in Babylon. Its author, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), gathers genealogies to remind the people who they were and where they came from. This chapter deals with the tribe of Benjamin. Scholars debate exactly how these families are grouped, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who barely appear in the story. If you sometimes feel little noticed, remember that your name matters to God. Serve faithfully, even when no one sees it.
exp.7:18:
This verse is just a list of names: Jakim, Zichri, and Zabdi. According to verse 21, they are sons of Shimei, of the tribe of Benjamin. It tells no story about them; it simply records that they existed and belonged to this family.

The book of Chronicles is anonymous, although Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra. It seems to have been written for the people who returned from exile, and the genealogies reminded them where they came from, what tribe they belonged to, and that God had not forgotten their family. Scholars debate the exact purpose of some of the lists, but this idea is the most common.

For today: even when you sometimes feel like just one more name among many, God knows you personally. Live faithfully in the ordinary, because He values those whom no one else remembers.
exp.7:19:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three men: Elioenai, Silithai and Eliel. They are descendants of the tribe of Benjamin, and they are probably among the families descended from Shimei. Nothing more is said about them, neither what they did nor when they lived.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies as Ezra, though this is not certain, writes after the return from exile in Babylon. His purpose was to remind the people who they were, which families they came from, and that God had not forgotten them. For this reason he records genealogies carefully, even those of little-known people.

For today: God knows each person by name, even when no one else remembers them. If you sometimes feel that your work or your life goes unnoticed, remember that you are precious before God. Serve faithfully, without needing applause.
exp.7:20:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath were sons of Shimhi (another spelling of Shimei). The names are spelled in an older way, and today they are sometimes seen as Beraiah and Shimrath. The verse tells us nothing more about them.

It belongs to the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, within 1 Chronicles. The author, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes after the exile. He wanted the people to remember their families, their history and their place in God's promise.

For today: God knows people by their name, even those whom almost no one remembers. You can rest in the knowledge that your life and your everyday faithfulness do not go unnoticed by Him. Today, try to value and remember with gratitude someone who serves quietly.
exp.7:21:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three men: Ishpan, Heber, and Eliel. They are among the descendants of Benjamin, and in this passage they are counted among the sons of Shashak.

Context: First Chronicles has no narrator speaking in the first person. It is a historical book that tradition often attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for the people who were returning from exile. Lists of families reminded them who they were, which tribe they belonged to, and that God was still caring for their history.

For today: God knows our names, even when others overlook us. Today you can thank him for the people who worked quietly in your family or your church, and serve faithfully without needing applause.
exp.7:23:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Hananiah, Elam, and Antothijah, three men from the tribe of Benjamin. The text says nothing more about them; only their names appear. In this older version, the names are spelled differently from how they are written today; for example, Antothijah would be written differently now, and some scholars believe it may be related to the town of Anathoth, though this is not certain.

The book of Chronicles was written for the people of Israel after they returned from exile in Babylon. We do not know for certain who wrote it; Jewish tradition names Ezra, but that is an opinion, not a certain fact. These genealogies reminded the people who they were, which family they belonged to, and that God had not forgotten His people.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom history barely remembers. Today you can rest in the knowledge that your simple life and daily faithfulness matter to Him.
exp.7:24:
The verse mentions two sons of Shashak: Iphedeiah and Penuel. It is part of a list of names from the tribe of Benjamin. The older forms of the names (such as Iphedeiah) correspond to Hebrew names that today are sometimes written differently, such as Yifdeyah and Peniel.

The book of Chronicles, written after the return from exile in Babylon, reviews the genealogies of Israel. Its author is not known with certainty; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, though there is no full agreement. These lists helped the people who were returning to their land remember their roots, their families and their right to inheritance among the tribes.
