God does not see his people as a faceless crowd. Each person, even if they appear only once in the Bible, has a name and a place before him. Today we can remember that our worth does not depend on being famous or on being recognized. We can also honor the ordinary people around us, treating them with dignity and calling them by their name.
exp.7:26:
This verse gives only three names: Jaresiah, Eliah, and Zichri, who were sons of Jeroham. They are part of a list of family members from the tribe of Benjamin. "Sons of" may mean direct sons or also descendants; the text does not make this clear.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records genealogies after the return from exile. He wanted the people to remember their origin and their identity. The following verse says these were heads of families and lived in Jerusalem. We know nothing more about these three men from this passage.

For today: God does not forget people who seem unimportant. There are names that no story highlights, and yet they were written down in the Bible. You can rest in the knowledge that your simple and faithful life also has value before God. Today, value and remember with gratitude those who came before you in the faith.
exp.7:29:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Abiguibeón, who lived in Gibeon, had as his oldest son Abdon. The word "firstborn" refers to the first child born. It then names other sons: Zur, Kish, Baal, and Nadab.

The text comes from 1 Chronicles, whose author is unknown, although an ancient tradition attributes it to Ezra. It was probably written for the people who were returning from exile. They wanted to remember who they were, which families they came from, and how they had lived in Jerusalem. That is why even names that barely appear in other passages are recorded.

For today: God does not see anyone as a number. Even if the Bible mentions someone only once, their name is recorded. This encourages us to value the ordinary people around us, and to trust that God also knows your name and your story.
exp.7:30:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Gedor, Ahio and Zacher were sons or descendants of the family of Abi-gibeon, who lived in Gibeon, in the tribe of Benjamin. They are names without further detail.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes after the return from exile in Babylon. He wants the people to remember their roots and their identity. The list of Benjamin prepares the way to speak of King Saul, who appears in the verses that follow. Some names are repeated in other passages with variations, and scholars do not always agree on how they relate to one another.

For today: God forgets no one, even when history preserves only their name. Today you can value those who went before you in the faith, and remember that your life, even the most ordinary, matters to God.
exp.7:34:
This verse names the four sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. Micah was the grandson of Jonathan, the son of King Saul. These are names from a family list, written in the older spelling of this version.

The book of Chronicles has no confirmed author; Jewish tradition often names Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for the people returning from exile, and the genealogies reminded them where they came from and that they were still God's people. Here the line of Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin, is followed, although his reign ended badly. His family was not forgotten.

For today: God remembers people by name, even those whom almost no one mentions. You can trust that your life matters to Him, and also value those who serve quietly around you.
exp.7:36:
This verse continues the line of a family from the tribe of Benjamin. Moza had a son named Binea. Then come Rapha, Eleasah, and Azel, each a son of the one before.

Here the speaker is not a character but the author of Chronicles, who is not known with certainty; Jewish tradition often names Ezra, but this is not sure. He writes after the exile in Babylon. He wanted the people who were returning to know where they came from, and this genealogy reaches down to Azel, whose sons are named right after. This line belongs to the descendants of King Saul.

For today: God does not forget names that we would pass over. You can live at peace even if your work seems small or hidden. Serve faithfully in your family and in your church, because God sees and remembers.
exp.7:39:
This verse says that the sons of Ulam, of the tribe of Benjamin, were brave and strong men. They were skilled archers. Also, they had a very large family: 150 among sons and grandsons. The word "mighty" means full of strength.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the chronicler, whose identity is not known for certain (Jewish tradition often points to Ezra). He wrote after the return from exile in Babylon. His list of families helped the people remember their roots and their place in God's story. The tribe of Benjamin was known for its skilled archers.

For today: God looks at the faithfulness of families, and also at the abilities a person develops. We can ask him to help us use our strengths and talents with courage, and to leave our children and grandchildren a good example.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that the first people to return to live in their properties and cities, after the exile, were ordinary Israelites, priests, Levites, and the Nethinims. The Nethinims were helpers of the temple, devoted to service tasks; the Bible does not give much detail about their origin, and some think they descended from people who joined the service of the sanctuary.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes for the people who returned from Babylon. He reminds them of their roots and of their identity as God's people. After the punishment of the exile, the list shows that God had not abandoned them and allowed them to start again, with worship at the center.

For today: God knows how to restore what was lost, and in that restoration He values everyone, both those who hold visible positions and those who serve in silence. Serve with joy wherever you are; God sees you.
exp.8:4:
It says that among those who lived in Jerusalem was Asaiah, the firstborn of a man named Shiloni, together with the sons of Asaiah. The word "Shiloni" is usually understood to refer to the descendants of Shelah, son of Judah, although some scholars connect it with a different interpretation of the name. In the parallel text of Nehemiah 11:5, the name appears as Maaseiah, son of Shiloah, and it is not known with certainty whether this is the same person or whether there are differences from copying or in the name.

The author of Chronicles, who writes after the return from exile in Babylon, lists the families who settled again in Jerusalem. He wants to show that the people recovered their city, their lineage and their identity before God.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your faithful work and your family matter to Him, even when they go unnoticed.
exp.8:6:
This verse begins the list of the sons of the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem. Sallu is named, along with his father, his grandfather and his great-grandfather. In this way the list shows which family he came from and whose line he belonged to.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes for the people who returned from exile in Babylon. He wants to remind them who they are, which families they come from, and that God preserved them. For this reason he records carefully the names of those who settled again in Jerusalem.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those who seem to go unnoticed in history. Your life and your service, though they may be simple, matter to him. Today you can give thanks for those who served before you and live faithfully in the place where God has put you.
exp.8:7:
This verse continues a list of families from the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem. It names three men: Ibneiah, son of Jeroham; Elah, son of Uzzi and grandson of Michri; and Meshullam, son of Shephatiah, who in turn was the son of Reuel and grandson of Ibneiah. These are names of heads of families, along with their ancestors.

The writer is the chronicler, an author whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes for the people who returned from exile in Babylon. He reminds them who they were, which families they came from, and how they had returned to their land. The genealogies gave them identity and a link to their past.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom history barely remembers. Today you can give value to what is simple: your family, your church, your faithful work. And you can give thanks for those who, without being famous, passed on the faith to you.
exp.8:9:
This verse begins the list of the priests who returned to live in Jerusalem. It names three: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jehoiachin. Priests were men from the tribe of Levi, from the family of Aaron, responsible for worship in the temple.

No one speaks in this scene. The author of Chronicles, whom tradition calls Ezra, though this is not certain, is keeping a record. He wrote for the people who came back from exile in Babylon. He wanted to remind them who had sustained life in Jerusalem and that their service to God had ancient roots. That is why he notes names and families.

God knows and remembers the people who serve him, even those whom almost no one mentions. Today you can serve faithfully in your church or your family without seeking applause. Your quiet work does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.8:11:
This verse continues a list of priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. It names Adaiah, son of Jeroham, and Maasiai, son of Adiel. Each one appears with his family line, going back to Immer, one of the ancient priestly families.

Here it is not a single character who speaks; the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the names. He wanted to show the returning people that their lineage and their service in the temple were still alive. The verses that follow say there were one thousand seven hundred and sixty capable men for the work.

For today: God pays attention to particular people, even when no one else remembers their names. Your faithful service, though quiet, matters to God. Today you can serve steadily in your church or family, without seeking applause.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that the priests who returned to live in Jerusalem numbered 1,760 men. They were heads of their fathers' families. They are described as very able men, that is, highly capable and courageous, and they worked with dedication in the service of the temple, which here is called the house of God.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes after the return from exile in Babylon. He lists who settled again in Jerusalem: priests, Levites, and gatekeepers. His purpose is to remind the people that their identity and their worship had ancient roots and that God had restored them.

God notices faithful service, even when it goes unseen. These men were recorded for their dedication. Today you can serve in your church with steadiness and excellence, without seeking applause, knowing that God values what you do for Him.
exp.8:13:
This verse begins the list of the Levites who returned to live in Jerusalem. Shemaiah, son of Hasshub, is named, and his ancestors are traced back to Merari, one of the three sons of Levi. The word "Levites" refers to the tribe appointed to serve in the worship of God.

The author of Chronicles (tradition links him to Ezra, though this is not certain) writes for the people who returned from exile in Babylon. Through these lists of names he reminds them who they are, where they come from, and that God gave them a place to serve him. The descendants of Merari had important duties in caring for the sanctuary.

God pays attention to people and remembers their names, even those that almost no one notices. Today we can serve faithfully in humble places, without seeking applause, trusting that God values every task done with love for him.
exp.8:15:
This verse continues a list of Levites who returned to live in Jerusalem. It names Obadiah, a descendant of Idithun (another spelling of Jeduthun, a musician of the temple), and Berechiah, son of Asa and grandson of Elkanah. Of the latter it is said that he lived in the villages of the Netophathites, that is, in the towns near Netophah, close to Bethlehem.

Here no single character is speaking; it is the chronicler, who probably wrote after the return from exile in Babylon. He wanted to remind his people who served in the temple and that their family line had not been lost. That is why he records names and families with such care. It is thought that the list reflects those who settled again in the land, although scholars debate the exact period it describes.

For today: God notices simple and steady service. Berechiah lived in a village, far from the center, and still he was recorded. Serve where you are, without feeling small; God does not forget your work.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that the gatekeepers and their children took turns watching over the gates of the house of the Lord, that is, the place of worship that at that time was a tent, or tabernacle.

The text comes from the lists of families written by the Chronicler, traditionally credited to Ezra, though this is not certain. It shows that service in the temple had an ancient order, going back to David and Samuel. Scholars debate whether the list refers to the time of David or to the return from exile.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is simple and little seen. Look for a place where you can serve steadily, such as caring for others, welcoming people, or helping out, and do it with responsibility.
exp.8:23:
This verse says that the temple gatekeepers were stationed on the four sides of God's house: the east, the west, the north, and the south. The gatekeepers were the guards of the gates. The north and the south are the directions named here, and the phrase for the four directions refers to the four quarters.

The book of Chronicles was written after the return from exile, and it is not known with certainty who wrote it; many think of Ezra, but that is an opinion. In this passage the author reviews the lists of the Levite families who served in the temple. He wants to remind the people that the service of God had been well ordered since the days of David and Samuel, and that even simple tasks mattered.

For today: God values faithful service, even when no one applauds it. Ask yourself which "gate" you have been entrusted with: your family, your church, or your work. Keep watch over it with steadiness and care.
exp.8:24:
This verse says that the relatives of the gatekeepers, who lived in their villages outside Jerusalem, would come every seven days, that is, every week, to take their turns with them in the service.

It is part of a list of Levites who guarded the gates of the temple. The author of Chronicles, whose name the Bible does not state with certainty (tradition names Ezra), explains how the service was organized. The four chief gatekeepers lived near the house of God, and the others helped in turns. In this way the work was shared, and there was always someone on watch.

For today: serving God works best when it is shared. In your church or family, do not carry everything alone, and do not leave everything to others. Offer your turn faithfully and gladly, even when the task is simple.
exp.8:26:
This verse says that the Levite gatekeepers lived near the temple, the house of God, because the care of it was their responsibility. "Guard" means watchfulness and protection. They also had the task of opening the doors every morning.

The passage appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, written for the people who were returning from exile. Its author, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, recalls how service in the temple was organized. The gatekeepers were not the most visible, but their work was necessary. They guarded sacred places and objects, and they took turns with their brothers from the villages every seven days.

Today we can learn that God values faithful and constant service, even when it is little seen. Opening a door each morning seems small, but it sustained the worship of all. We can serve responsibly in simple things, such as arriving on time, caring for a space, or helping others, knowing that God sees and values that care.
exp.8:30:
It says that a Levite named Mattithiah, the firstborn son of Shallum, of the family of Korah, was in charge of preparing what was cooked in the pans. The word refers to a flat plate or griddle for baking. These were probably the grain offerings baked for use in worship at the temple.

The chronicler reviews how the Levites were organized after the return from exile. Each group had a specific task: some looked after the equipment, others the ingredients, others the bread. The passage is written to remind the people that serving God had order and that every person mattered. The exact details of that offering are not explained here, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

God values simple and unseen service. Baking did not seem like an important task, yet the name of the person who did it was recorded. Today you can serve joyfully in small things, knowing that God sees it.
exp.8:31:
This verse tells that some descendants of Kohath, from the tribe of Levi, were in charge of preparing the bread of the presence. These were loaves placed in the house of God, on a special table, and they were changed in order every day of rest, that is, every Sabbath.

The book of Chronicles was written after the return from exile in Babylon. Its author is unknown; Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. Here the families who served in the temple in Jerusalem are listed, to remind the people that worship had an order and that each person had a specific task.

For today: God values faithful service, even the kind that almost no one sees. Preparing bread every week seemed like something small, but it was part of worship. Today we can serve in the church or at home with consistency, without seeking applause, trusting that God sees what is done with love.
exp.8:32:
These verses speak of the Levites who were singers. They were heads of their families and lived in the rooms of the temple, free from other duties. "Exempt" means they did not have to do other work, because day and night they devoted themselves to that task, which was the music and praise in worship to God.

It is part of a list of families who returned to live in Jerusalem after the exile. The author, traditionally identified as Ezra (though this is not certain), goes through who had each responsibility in the temple. He wants to show that worship of God had order and that each service had people assigned to it.

For today: God values service that seems small or hidden, like singing or preparing something behind the scenes. Ask yourself what gift you have and offer it with steadiness and devotion, without seeking applause.
exp.8:35:
This verse is a list of names. It says that Abdon was the firstborn son and that his brothers came after him: Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, and Nadab. They are sons of Jehiel, who lived in Gibeon.

The writer is the Chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes for the people who returned from exile, to remind them who they were and where they came from. This list appears in a family of the tribe of Benjamin, the family of Saul, although the text mentions it alongside the Levites. Scholars explain that connection in different ways.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who are hardly mentioned. Your simple and faithful life also matters to Him. Today, give thanks for the ordinary people who have sustained your faith.
exp.8:37:
This verse says that Mikloth had a son named Shimeam. It also tells us that these descendants lived in Jerusalem, near their relatives.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, lists the families who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. This list of the tribe of Benjamin connects with the family of King Saul, who appears next. The names reminded the people of their roots and their identity.

For today: God pays attention to families and to individuals, not only to great leaders. Even if your name is not well known, God knows you and gives you a place. Today, value your family and your community, and live near them with love and support.
exp.8:42:
It says that from the family of Moza there came four generations: Moza was the father of Bina; Bina's son was Rephaia; Rephaia's son was Elasa; and Elasa's son was Asel. The word for "was the father of" is the one used in the verse itself, so no separate note is needed here.

This is part of a list of families from the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem. The writer of the history, traditionally called the Chronicler, gathers these names for the people who returned from exile. He wanted them to know where they came from, and that they had a place in the history of Israel. This line follows the descent of King Saul, and then focuses on Azel and his six sons.

For today: God does not forget people who seem little known. These names are almost never mentioned, but they were written down. Remember that your life, your family, and your daily faithfulness have value before God, even when no one else notices.
exp.8:43:
This verse ends the list of Azel's descendants, from the tribe of Benjamin. It says that he had six sons and gives their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. The phrase "these were the sons of Azel" marks where the list of his children closes.

These names come from the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. It is thought that the writer, traditionally identified as Ezra (though this is not certain), gathered them for the people returning from exile. They wanted to remember who they were, and which family and tribe they belonged to. This list repeats the Benjamin list of chapter 8, and these are the descendants of King Saul.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who barely appear in the Bible. Your name and your life matter to him. Today you can value the ordinary people around you, and give thanks for those who came before you in the faith.
exp.9:0:
This verse tells how the Philistines attacked Israel. The men of Israel fled before them, and many fell slain on Mount Gilboa. The phrase "fought against Israel" means they fought against Israel, and "slain" here refers to men struck down or killed in battle.

No one speaks in this verse; it is the account of the chronicler, an unknown author who wrote after the exile in Babylon. Many think it was Ezra, though this is not certain. He begins his history with the fall of King Saul, and then shows how God raised up David. The verses that follow narrate the death of Saul and his sons.

There are painful defeats that seem like the end, but God continues to work. If you are going through a loss today, trust that He can raise up something new, as He did with David after Gilboa.
exp.9:3:
Here the story of the end of Saul, the first king of Israel, is told. He is wounded by the arrows of the Philistines, and he asks his armourbearer, the soldier who carried his weapons, to kill him with the sword. He wants to prevent the uncircumcised (as the Israelites called the pagan peoples) from mocking him. The armourbearer refused, out of fear. Then Saul fell upon his own sword.

The narrator of Chronicles recounts the defeat of Israel on Mount Gilboa. Saul's sons have already died and the battle is lost. Saul acts out of fear of humiliation and abuse. The book presents this death as the close of a reign marked by disobedience to God (1 Chronicles 10:13).

For today: the fear of shame can lead us to desperate decisions. When everything seems lost, we should not keep our pain silent, but seek God and trusted people who can help us.
exp.9:4:
This verse tells that Saul's armourbearer, the soldier who carried his weapons, saw that the king was already dead. Then he too fell upon his own sword and died.

The narrator of Chronicles recounts the end of the battle of Gilboa against the Philistines. Saul, wounded, feared that the uncircumcised (the Philistines, who were not part of God's covenant) would humiliate him. The armourbearer obeyed out of fear and loyalty, but the Bible only describes what happened; it does not approve of it. Later, Chronicles explains that Saul died because of his unfaithfulness to God (1 Chronicles 10:13-14).

For today: when defeat or fear overwhelm us, we should not decide alone or give in to despair. Let us seek God and ask for help from trusted people. If anyone is thinking of harming themselves, they should speak with a family member, a pastor, or a professional.
exp.9:5:
Verse 6 says that Saul died together with his three sons, and that all his house died with him that same day. This is the tragic end of Israel's first king, which took place in the battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa. The phrase "all his house" most likely refers to his close family and to those who accompanied him in the battle, not necessarily to all his relatives.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, reports this defeat to show the end of Saul's dynasty. Right after, he gives the reason: Saul was not faithful to God and did not seek him (verses 13 and 14). In this way he prepares the way for the reign of David, whom Chronicles presents as the king after God's own heart.

For today: our decisions affect the people around us, and seeking God sincerely every day protects not only our own life but also the lives of our family.
exp.9:6:
It says that the Israelites who lived in the valley learned that their army had fled and that Saul and his sons had died. Then they abandoned their cities and ran away, and the Philistines came and settled in them.

Here the chronicler speaks, retelling the history of Israel after the exile. He recounts the defeat on Mount Gilboa to show the consequences of Saul's fall. The valley probably refers to the Jezreel area, though the text gives no further detail. The king's death left the people without protection or direction, and fear led them to lose their homes.

For today: the decisions of those who lead affect many people. We can pray for our leaders and, if we are called to guide others in the family, work, or church, do so faithfully before God, because others depend on us.
exp.9:7:
The day after the battle, the Philistines went out to the field to strip the fallen soldiers of their weapons and belongings. There they found the bodies of Saul and his sons lying on Mount Gilboa.

The one who tells the story is the chronicler of Israel (his name is not stated with certainty). He recounts the sad end of King Saul to prepare the way for David's arrival as king. Later in the same chapter, the text explains that Saul died because of his unfaithfulness to God and because he did not seek Him.

Today we can remember that our choices have consequences. Let us seek God sincerely every day, instead of trusting only in our own strength or our own plans.
exp.9:8:
When the Philistines had finished stripping Saul of his clothes and armor, they cut off his head and carried off his weapons. They sent messengers throughout their land to spread the news. They wanted it to be known in the temples of their idols and among the people.

The one who tells this account is the chronicler, who wrote long after these events. Many believe it was Ezra, though this is not certain. He recounts Israel's defeat at Gilboa to show the end of Saul's reign and to prepare the way for David's arrival. Later on, he explains that Saul fell because he was not faithful to God.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and trusting in ourselves leaves us without support. Today you can ask God to keep you faithful in small things, so that you do not turn away from Him.
exp.9:9:
The Philistines put Saul's weapons in the house of their god, and hung his head in the temple of Dagon. By doing this they meant that their gods had given them the victory over Israel. To strip the dead means to take away their weapons and clothing.

The one who tells the story is the writer of Chronicles, who wrote long afterward, for a people returning from exile. He wants to show how Saul's reign ended, a king who was not faithful to the Lord (v. 13). The account in 1 Samuel 31 gives some different details, and we do not know for certain how the two fit together; they may be details that complement each other.

For today: faithfulness to God matters more than power or success. Ask him to help you obey him in small things, so that your life does not depend on what others say about you.
exp.9:11:
It says that the brave men of Jabesh-gilead got up, gathered the bodies of Saul and his sons, carried them to their town, and buried their bones under a large tree (the tree that some translate as an oak or a tamarisk). Then they fasted seven days as a sign of mourning.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the end of Saul's reign, when he died in battle against the Philistines, who displayed his body and his armor. The people of Jabesh remembered that Saul had rescued them years earlier (1 Samuel 11). That is why they risked their lives to give him a worthy burial. The following verse explains the spiritual cause: Saul did not obey God.

For today: gratitude and loyalty are shown through actions. Think of someone who helped you in the past, and look for a concrete way to honor them, even if it costs you, and without expecting anything in return.
exp.10:1:
It says that the tribes of Israel recognize David as their leader. They remember that David was already leading the people in war while Saul was king, and that Saul's own sending out and bringing in of the army was carried on through him, meaning he guided them on their military campaigns and their returns. They also affirm that God promised him he would shepherd His people and be their ruler, that is, the one who governs them.

The speakers are representatives of all Israel, gathered in Hebron after the death of Saul. They want David to be king over all the tribes. They tell him they are his bone and his flesh, that is, his family. They appeal to his track record and to the word of God, which according to the text came through Samuel.

Today we can learn that good leadership joins service with proven character. If you lead in your home, your work, or your church, care for people like a shepherd, not only give orders.
exp.10:2:
It says that all the leaders of the tribes of Israel (the elders) went to Hebron to see David. There David made a covenant with them, a formal promise, with God as witness. Then they anointed him, that is, they poured oil on him as a sign that he was king. All of this fulfilled what God had said through Samuel.

The writer of Chronicles tells how all Israel came together under David after the death of Saul. The elders recognize that David had already led the people and that God had called him to shepherd Israel. Afterward, this united kingdom will advance toward Jerusalem.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when a long time passes. And whoever leads must do so with commitment, as one who is accountable to God, caring for others like a shepherd.
exp.10:3:
David, already recognized as king by all Israel, set out with the people toward Jerusalem. At that time the city was called Jebus, and the Jebusites lived there, a people who had inhabited that land from earlier times. The verse's wording that is set in quotation marks, along with the verse of the older word, is not included here since it does not appear in the verse on your screen.

Here the Chronicler speaks as the narrator of Israel's history. After the elders anointed David at Hebron, the next step is to conquer Jerusalem and make it his capital. Scholars believe the Chronicler wants to show that David reigned according to God's word, and that this city became a center of unity and worship for the whole people.

For today: when God confirms a calling, there may still be obstacles ahead. Move forward with courage and together with others, trusting that the One who gave you the promise will also sustain you along the way.
exp.10:5:
David offered a reward to whoever would lead the attack against the Jebusites, the people living in Jerusalem: that man would become commander of the army. Joab, son of Zeruiah, went up first and received that position.

David was already king over all Israel when this happened. The Jebusites felt safe in their stronghold and told him he would not get in. David needed to take that city to make it his capital. His offer encouraged the men to take risks. The passage in 2 Samuel 5 is similar, but it does not give this detail about Joab; the Chronicles text points it out.

For today: God often uses those who take the first step with courage. If He shows you something to do, do not wait for others to be bold first; take that step with faith and humility.
exp.10:8:
It says David kept advancing and growing stronger and greater, and that the reason was that the Lord of hosts was with him. That title means that God is Lord over all powers, both in heaven and on earth.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles, who writes to a people returning from exile who needed to remember their history. Here he summarizes how David was already king in Jerusalem, the city he took and strengthened. The author makes clear that his success came not only from his walls or his brave men, but from God's presence.

For today: we can work hard, but without forgetting that true growth comes from God. Before your plans, ask him to go with you, and thank him for every step forward, great or small.
exp.10:9:
This verse presents the chiefs of David's mighty men. It says that they supported him in his reign, along with all Israel, to make him king, just as God had said. "Chief" means the most outstanding among them, and "according to the word of the Lord" means in keeping with what God had announced.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra, though this is not certain, tells the story of David. He writes for a people who had returned from exile and needed to remember their roots. After recounting how David took Jerusalem and grew stronger because God was with him, he now presents the men who helped him. The emphasis is that David reigned by God's will, and also with the help of faithful people.

For today: God often carries out his plans through people who join together and serve. Think about who supports you in what you do, and thank them. And ask yourself how you might faithfully help others, even when no one sees you.
exp.10:14:
This verse tells how three of the thirty most valiant captains of David's army went down to the rock where he was, into the cave of Adullam. Meanwhile, the host of the Philistines had encamped in the valley of Rephaim.

The writer, the chronicler, recalls the brave men who supported David when he was not yet an established king. He lived on the run and sheltered in hard places, while the Philistines controlled the region. The verses that follow show that their loyalty risked everything. It is not known with certainty which three they were.

For today: true loyalty is shown in difficult times. We can ask ourselves whom we stand with when there is risk and sacrifice, and remember that God values those who serve faithfully, even when few notice them.
exp.10:21:
Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, is presented in this verse as a man of great courage, from Kabzeel, a town of Judah. Three of his deeds are recorded: he struck down the two lionlike men of Moab (some think these were two very strong warriors, others that they were animals; it is not certain). He also went down into a pit and killed a lion on a snowy day. The pit is a hole or cistern.

The writer of Chronicles is listing David's mighty men, the men who supported him in establishing his kingdom. Benaiah appears alongside other famous warriors. He stands out not only for his strength but for his courage in difficult and unexpected situations.

For today: courage is tested in uncomfortable and inconvenient moments. God can use us when we face with faith what others avoid, whether a problem, an injustice, or a difficult duty.
exp.10:22:
This verse tells how Benaiah faced a giant Egyptian, about two meters, twelve centimeters tall (five cubits). The Egyptian carried a thick spear, as big as the beam of a loom. Benaiah went down to fight him armed only with a staff, took the spear out of his hand, and killed him with his own weapon.

Here the chronicler is listing David's mighty men. Benaiah was a famous warrior, honored among the thirty, though he did not reach the top three. David placed him on his council. The account shows that the kingdom was upheld by brave and loyal men.

For today: many times our problems seem bigger and better armed than we are. This text encourages us to face them with courage, wisdom, and trust in God, without being discouraged by what we lack.
exp.10:23:
This verse sums up the deeds of Benaiah, son of Jehoiada: he struck down two lion-like champions of Moab, killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and defeated a giant Egyptian, taking his own spear away from him to kill him. For all of this he had the name among the three mighty men, that is, he was highly honored, although, as the text that follows says, he did not come to be one of the first three.

The writer of Chronicles is listing the brave men who supported David and helped him establish his kingdom. He does this to remind the people, who were returning from exile, that God had raised up faithful men around his chosen king.

For today: Benaiah did not wait for the perfect moment; he acted with courage in the face of what was set before him, even in difficult conditions like the cold and the pit. God often forms our character in small, hidden trials before entrusting us with something greater. Face with faith what lies before you today.
exp.10:24:
The verse speaks of Benaiah, a soldier of King David. It says that he was the most honored among the thirty mighty men, that is, the most respected within that group, but that he did not reach the level of the first three warriors. Even so, David set him over his guard, which here means that he gave him a place of trust, close to the king.

The author of Chronicles is unknown; Jewish tradition often attributes it to Ezra, although there is no certainty. The book was written for a people who had returned from exile and needed to remember the greatness of David's reign and those who supported it. That is why it lists its brave men in detail.

We can serve with dedication even if we are not the first or the most famous. Benaiah was not number one, but his faithfulness and courage were recognized and he was given responsibility. God and those around us value steadiness more than first place.
exp.10:26:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions two of David's warriors: Shammoth, who came from a place called Harorite, and Helez, who is called "Pelonite," that is, from a clan or town called Pelet. Some scholars believe that Harorite is a different way of spelling Harod, but there is no complete certainty.

Here the chronicler is not speaking in a speech but recording an official list. He tells who the brave men were who supported David when he was made king over all Israel. The names come from different tribes and peoples, which shows that the kingdom was strengthened by the union of many.

God does not forget those who serve in silence. Of these men only the names remain, but they were written down. Serve faithfully even when no one applauds you, for your work matters in God's plan.
exp.10:28:
The verse names two men from David's list of mighty warriors: Sibbecai, from Hushah, and Ilai, from the family or clan of Ahoh. The words in the verse that identify where each man came from, whether a place or a family, are the ones that tell us their origin. In other parallel passages, some of the names are spelled a little differently, so there is not complete certainty about every detail.

This is a list of the most outstanding warriors who supported David and strengthened his kingdom. The writer of Chronicles, writing after the exile, wants to remind the people that God raised up specific people, with personal names, to sustain the kingdom. These men came from many different places.

For today: God notices people who serve faithfully, even when almost no one remembers them. Your steady service, though it may be quiet, has value before Him and can sustain others.
exp.10:30:
This verse continues a list of names. Ithai, son of Ribai, came from Gibeah, a town in the tribe of Benjamin. Then Benaiah is named as "the Pirathonite," that is, a native of a place called Pirathon. This Benaiah seems to be a different man from the famous Benaiah son of Jehoiada.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; an ancient tradition attributes it to Ezra. Here the account lists the brave warriors who supported David when he was made king of Israel. It is notable that it includes people from different tribes, such as Benjamin, the tribe of the former king, Saul. All of them joined together to serve the king whom God had chosen.

For today: God values people who serve faithfully, even though almost no one remembers them. Today you can serve steadily in your church or family, without seeking applause, trusting that God sees and remembers every name.
exp.10:33:
The verse mentions two or more of David's mighty men: the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, and Jonathan, son of Shage the Hararite. Names ending in the form that marks a place of origin show where a man came from. The text is brief and difficult, and it differs from the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 23:32-33, so it is not entirely clear how many men are named.

This is part of the list of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:10-47). The Chronicler, who writes after the exile, wants to show that David's kingdom was sustained by many loyal men who supported him, and that God gave the victory through them.

For today: the list reminds us that God values those who serve without being famous. There are names that almost no one remembers, yet they were written down. Serve faithfully in small things; God sees and remembers your work.
exp.10:34:
This verse names two more men from the list of David's mighty warriors: Ahiam, son of Sacar, from a place called Harar, and Eliphal, son of Ur. The Hararite in the verse means that Ahiam came from that place or that family, though it is not known for certain where it was.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, speaks to a people who had returned from exile. He reminds them that David's reign was held up by many loyal men. This list resembles the one in 2 Samuel 23, but some names differ. We do not know the reason for certain: it may have been another way of writing the names, or different sources.

For today: God values those who serve without being famous. Even if few remember your name, your faithfulness in small things matters, and God keeps it in view.
exp.10:37:
This verse names two more of David's mighty men: Joel, brother of a man named Nathan, and Mibhar, son of Haggeri. It says nothing more about them, only who they were and where they came from.

The author of Chronicles, whose name we do not know for certain (tradition mentions Ezra), writes after the exile. He lists the men who supported David to remind the people how his kingdom was established. In the parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:36 some names appear differently, and this is explained in several ways, for example, by variations that arose when the texts were copied.

For today: God values faithful service, even when no one applauds it. Some people barely appear in the story, but their loyalty counts. Serve wherever you are, without seeking recognition.
exp.10:38:
This verse continues the list of David's mighty men. It names Zelek, who was an Ammonite, that is, from a foreign people neighboring Israel, and Naharai, from Beeroth. It says that Naharai was the armourbearer of Joab, that is, the one who carried his weapons and protected him in battle. Joab was the son of Zeruiah, David's sister.

The chronicler, writing after the exile, lists the men who supported David in making him king. There is no speech here, but a historical record. That an Ammonite is named shows that David had allies from outside Israel. We do not know more details about his story.

For today: God notices those who serve faithfully, even though almost no one remembers them. Your quiet work, like that of an armourbearer, has value, and God sees it.
exp.10:40:
This verse mentions two more men from the list of David's mighty warriors: Uriah the Hittite and Zabad, son of Ahlai. "Hittite" means that Uriah came from the people of the Hittites, a foreign nation. The text gives no further details about them.

The chronicler presents the list of the mighty men who supported David and helped him strengthen his kingdom. It is a list of names, not a speech. Many believe this Uriah is the same husband of Bathsheba, although the text here does not say so, and in 2 Samuel 23:39 a Uriah the Hittite also appears. Some see the same person in both places, but this is not certain.

For today: God notices people who often go unnoticed. There are names that almost no one remembers, yet they were written down. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even when no one applauds you; God sees and remembers what you do with love and loyalty.
exp.10:41:
Verse 42 mentions Adina, son of Shiza, of the tribe of Reuben. He was a captain of the Reubenites, that is, a leader or chief of his tribe. With him were thirty men, probably a group under his command. Some scholars think these thirty were part of his soldiers; others believe it refers to the elite group known as the thirty. The text does not make this entirely clear.

The chronicler (tradition says it was Ezra, though this is not certain) lists David's mighty men. He writes for the people who returned from exile, and he wants to remind them that David's kingdom was sustained by men from different tribes and backgrounds. Even foreigners appear, such as Uriah the Hittite. Each name shows that God used many people.

For today: God values those who serve faithfully, even when few remember them. Ask yourself where in your church or family you can offer quiet support, without seeking applause. God sees that service and remembers it.
exp.10:42:
This verse names two more men from the list of David's mighty warriors: Hanan, son of Maachah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite. The word that identifies Joshaphat's origin or family is not clear to us, so we do not know for certain where he came from. No deed of either man is told here; only their names are recorded.

This passage is part of a list the chronicler gives to show who stood with David when he was made king over all Israel. It is not the account of one particular person speaking. It is the writer's own record, written after the exile, most likely to remind the people that David's kingdom was built with the help of many faithful men.

For today: God notices people whom others overlook. Even if you have no visible role, your faithful service counts. Do your part with steadiness and humility, trusting that God remembers every name.
exp.10:43:
This verse names more men from the list of David's mighty warriors. Uzzia was from Ashtaroth, a town east of the Jordan. Shama and Jehiel were brothers, sons of Hothan, from a place or clan called Aroer. The phrases "the sons of" and "the Ashterathite" only indicate family and place of origin.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the chronicler, who writes after the exile. With this list he remembers the men who supported David when he was made king over Israel. They came from different tribes and regions, and many of the names appear only once. Why so few details are included is not known for certain, but the intention was to preserve their memory.

For today: God does not forget those who serve quietly. Even when no one knows your name or your work, He sees it. Serve faithfully wherever you are, without seeking applause.
exp.10:44:
This verse names two brothers, Jediael, son of Shimri, and Joha. The phrase "the Tizite" indicates that Joha belonged to a place or family called Tiz; scholars do not know for certain where it was. Both appear in the list of David's mighty men.

The one speaking is the chronicler, an author whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes to a people who had returned from exile. In listing these men, he reminds them that David's kingdom was sustained by many people who supported him with loyalty, not only by the king.

For today: God notices those who serve without becoming famous. We know almost nothing about Jediael and Joha, but their names were written down. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one notices. God does see it and remembers it.
exp.10:45:
This verse continues a list of David's mighty men. It mentions Eliel, who came from Mahavi (a place or clan whose meaning is uncertain), and Jeribai and Joshaviah, sons of Elnaam. It also names Ithmah, who was a Moabite, that is, from Moab, a people neighboring Israel.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra, though this is not certain, records these men who supported David in establishing his kingdom. The list includes men from different places, including a foreigner like Ithmah. The first readers, who were returning from exile, needed to remember their identity and their history.

God remembers ordinary people who serve him faithfully, even when almost no one mentions them. You can serve steadily in your church or family, trusting that God sees and values your devotion.
exp.11:1:
They say these warriors came armed with bows and could use both hands: with the right or the left they hurled stones with a sling or shot arrows. The "arrows" are the shafts shot from a bow, and the "sling" is a strap for hurling stones with force. Moreover, it clarifies that they were relatives of Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin.

The chronicler lists the men who joined David at Ziklag, when he was fleeing from Saul. It is remarkable that some from the king's own tribe crossed over to David's side. The Bible does not explain all their reasons here, but the account highlights that God was gathering support for David.

For today: God can use the abilities you already have, even the uncommon ones. Put them at the service of his work and, when the time comes, choose loyalty to what God is doing, even when it costs you.
exp.11:2:
This verse continues a list of warriors from the tribe of Benjamin. It names Ahiezer, who was the chief, and Joash, the sons of Shemaah, from Gibeah. It also names Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth, and Berachah and Jehu, from Anathoth. The words "Gibeathite" and "Anathothite" only indicate which town each man came from.

Here no single character speaks; it is the chronicler who records names. These men came to Ziklag, where David was living away from Saul because he feared him. They were Benjamites, the same tribe as Saul, and yet they sided with David. They were archers and slingers, skilled with both hands. The Bible gives no further details about most of them.

For today: God notices people whom sometimes no one remembers. Your faithfulness and your service, even when they go unnoticed, have value before Him. And sometimes following God requires making a courageous decision, even when it means breaking away from what others expect of you.
exp.11:4:
This verse continues a list of names: Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite. The word for his origin probably points to where he came from, perhaps a place called Harif or Haruf, though this is not known for certain.

Here it is not a character speaking, but the chronicler, who records the warriors who joined David at Ziklag while he was fleeing from King Saul. They were skilled with the bow and the sling, and many came from the tribe of Benjamin, the same tribe as Saul. The text highlights that they supported David even when that was risky. From this verse we know only their names; no further details about them are given.

God knows and remembers those who serve faithfully, even when no one else mentions them. Today we too can serve steadily in ordinary things, without seeking applause, trusting that our effort does not go unnoticed before God.
exp.11:6:
This verse names two more men: Joelah and Zebadiah, sons of Jeroham, from the town of Gedor. It is part of a list of warriors who joined David. Gedor was a town in Judah or in Benjamin; it is not known with certainty which, and scholars debate it.

The book of Chronicles is a historical narrative, and the author does not speak in the first person but records names. These men were from the tribe of Benjamin and supported David at Ziklag, when he was fleeing from King Saul. Almost nothing is known about them beyond this detail. Even so, they were written into the Bible.

For today: God notices those who serve without being famous. Your faithful support, though quiet, such as helping, praying, or walking alongside someone in a difficult season, has value before Him and is not forgotten.
exp.11:7:
Some men from the tribe of Gad left their own people and joined David when he was hiding in a stronghold in the wilderness. They were very brave warriors, trained for battle. Shield and buckler were defensive weapons: one small and one large, used to cover the body. They had faces like lions, that is, they were fearsome in appearance, and they were as swift as gazelles, which run through difficult terrain.

The author of Chronicles, whose name is not known with certainty, lists those who supported David before he became king. At that time he was fleeing from Saul, and joining him was risky. The account shows that God was preparing the support of all Israel for David's reign.

Today we can learn from their courage and loyalty. Supporting what is good and just sometimes costs something, but God sees those who remain firm. Ask Him for the courage to do what is right, even when it is not the most comfortable choice.
exp.11:8:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Ezer was the first, Obadiah the second, and Eliab the third. They are the first of eleven leaders from the tribe of Gad who joined David.

The book of Chronicles has no narrator who speaks in the first person; the author, who is unknown, reviews the history of Israel. Here it tells how brave warriors from the tribe of Gad came over to David when he was hiding from Saul in the wilderness. The text says they were strong men, with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles on the mountains. A large shield was carried by them.

God takes notice of people who serve with loyalty, even though almost no one remembers their names. Today you can faithfully support God's work in your family, your church, or your job, without needing to be recognized. What you do quietly has value before God.
exp.11:9:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Mishmannah was the fourth and Jeremiah the fifth among the warriors of the tribe of Gad who joined David. The phrase about them leaving their place means that they left where they were to go with him, and the other word in the source means ninth.

The writer of Chronicles is not speaking to a character but is recording the roster of those who supported David while he was in the stronghold in the desert, fleeing from King Saul. He describes them as brave, skilled with the shield, and with faces like lions. In naming each one, he makes clear that their loyalty was remembered and that each man showed courage.

For today: God notices the people who seem secondary in the story. If you serve quietly, without many noticing, remember that your faithfulness also counts. Seek to be steady and loyal where God has placed you.
exp.11:11:
This verse mentions two more men from a list: Johanan, the eighth, and Elzabad, the ninth. "Ninth" is an old way of saying the ninth in order. They are part of a group of warriors who joined David.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the chronicler, who is writing the history of Israel. This list is in the account of the Gadite warriors who went with David to Ziklag, when he was fleeing from Saul. The text says they were captains and that their troops were numerous. The author keeps their names so that they are not forgotten, though he gives no further details about each one.

For today: God notices the people who serve faithfully, even if almost no one else does. Today we can support God's work in our family, church or workplace with devotion, without needing applause. God remembers every name.
exp.11:12:
This verse follows a list of names. It mentions Jeremiah as the tenth and Machbanai as the eleventh among the warriors from the tribe of Gad who joined David.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records the names of these men with care. David was hiding from Saul in the wilderness, and these brave men from Gad came to support him. The verses that follow say they were army commanders, skilled and strong. Writing after the exile, the author wanted to remind the people that God had raised up faithful men for his chosen king.

For today: God pays attention to people who sometimes seem unimportant. Two nearly unknown names were kept in his Word. Your humble and steady service also counts, even when no one else notices it.
exp.11:13:
These men mentioned before were military leaders of the tribe of Gad. There was a great difference among them: the least of them was in charge of a hundred soldiers, and the greatest of them, of a thousand. That is, they were men with real capacity to command.

Here the speaker is the chronicler, who lists the warriors of Gad who joined David when he was hiding from Saul, in a remote place in the desert. Many understand that the author wants to show that David had broad support and that God was raising him up as king. The exact details of the historical context are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God values both the one who leads a hundred and the one who leads a thousand. Serve faithfully wherever you are, without comparing yourself; what matters is supporting God's cause with loyalty and courage.
exp.11:14:
They say these brave men from the tribe of Gad crossed the Jordan River in the first month of the year, right when the river had overflowed all its banks. Even so, they managed to drive out the people of the valleys, both to the east and to the west.

Here the chronicler speaks, listing the warriors who joined David while he was hiding from Saul. The Gadites were men very skilled in war. The text does not say which enemies they drove out, so it is best not to invent details. Its purpose is to show the courage and loyalty of those who supported David.

For today: when a right decision seems difficult, like a swollen river, do not wait for perfect conditions. Take the step with courage and loyalty, trusting that God walks with those who seek to serve him.
exp.11:16:
Here David goes out to meet a group of men from Benjamin and Judah who arrive at his stronghold. He tells them that if they come in peace and to help him, his heart will be joined with them. But if they have come to betray him and hand him over to his enemies, even though he has done nothing wrong, may God look into it and judge them.

David was fleeing from King Saul and living in hidden places, surrounded by people who kept coming to support him. Since he did not know the intentions of these men, he speaks frankly and leaves the matter in God's hands. Shortly afterward, Amasai answers with words of loyalty.

For today: when someone comes to you, be sincere and ask for sincerity in return. If people treat you unjustly, do not take revenge; commit your cause to God, who sees the heart.
exp.11:19:
As David came to Ziklag, men of Manasseh joined him. Seven are named: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zilthai. They were captains of thousands, that is, leaders who commanded groups of a thousand men. Joining him meant they left their former side and took his.

The narrator is the chronicler, who lists those who supported David before he became king. David was at Ziklag, fleeing from Saul, and the Philistines allied with him had sent him away from the battle out of distrust. Even so, these leaders of Israel followed him. The text shows that God was raising up help for David, until it formed a army of God.

For today: sometimes it becomes clearer whom God supports when everything is difficult. Choose to support what is right, even when it is not the most comfortable, and serve with courage wherever God places you.
exp.11:29:
This verse tells us that from the tribe of Ephraim came twenty-eight thousand... actually, it says twenty thousand eight hundred men. They were very brave, that is, soldiers of great courage. "Famous throughout the house of their fathers" means that they were respected and well known among their families and clans.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (although this is not known for certain), lists the tribes that went to Hebron to support David as king. This list shows that all Israel came together behind him. Ephraim is mentioned, a large tribe with great influence, and its support carried a great deal of weight.

God often unites his people when there is a common purpose. Today we can ask ourselves whether we set aside our own interests and differences to serve together what God wants. Unity requires decision and courage, and each person adds something, even if they are not famous.
exp.11:32:
This verse says that fifty thousand men from the tribe of Zebulun came to join David. They were soldiers ready for war, with all their weapons.

The author of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, lists the tribes that went to Hebron to make David king after Saul's death. He reminds the people that Israel united around the king chosen by God. The numbers can be understood in different ways, but the clear emphasis is the unity and loyalty of Zebulun.

Today, following Christ calls for a heart that is not divided. We can ask ourselves whether our commitment to Him is sincere and steady, not half-hearted. That devotion shows in simple things: keeping what we promise, serving with joy, and staying loyal even when it costs us.
exp.11:33:
It says that the tribe of Naphtali provided a thousand captains, or military leaders, and with them thirty-seven thousand soldiers armed with shield and spear. The shield served to protect and the spear to attack. It was a complete army, with good leaders and many willing people.

It is part of a list the chronicler presents of the tribes that went to Hebron to make David king over all Israel, after the death of Saul. It is not a speech by a character; the author is telling the story. Many believe he wrote after the exile, to remind the people of their unity. The numbers are large, and some scholars debate how to understand them, but the central message is clear: almost all of Israel came together.

For today: each person has a place. Naphtali provided leaders and also ordinary people. Ask yourself how you can contribute to your church or family, whether by leading or supporting, with a united and sincere heart.
exp.11:36:
These are the tribes that lived on the other side of the Jordan River, namely Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and 120,000 men came to Hebron. They came with all manner of weapons of war, that is, with every kind of equipment ready for battle.

The book of Chronicles does not name its author, and Jewish tradition often attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. Here a list is given of the warriors from all the tribes who went to Hebron to make David king after the death of Saul. The numbers are very high, and some scholars debate how they should be understood, but the central point is the great unity of the people.

Today we can learn that serving God and his purpose calls for unity and total commitment. All those tribes, even the most distant ones, left what was theirs and came with a sincere heart, without divided loyalty. Ask yourself how you can contribute to your church or your family with that same heart.
exp.11:37:
This verse says that all the warriors from the tribes of Israel, well prepared for battle, came to Hebron with a whole heart, that is, sincere and undivided, without duplicity. Their purpose was to make David king over all Israel. Moreover, the rest of the people thought the same way: they all had one mind, that is, one willingness and one desire.

The one speaking is the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, who tells how, after the death of Saul, the tribes gathered in Hebron to acknowledge David. He highlights this because the kingdom had been divided, and now there was unity and joy, as the feast that follows shows.

For today: unity springs from a sincere heart and a shared purpose. We can ask ourselves whether, in our family or church, we seek to serve with total devotion and in harmony, without hidden agendas.
exp.11:39:
It says that the neighbors of Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali, even from far away, brought a great deal of food to Hebron: bread, flour, cakes of figs, raisins, wine, oil, oxen, and sheep. They carried it on donkeys, camels, mules, and oxen. The cakes of figs were loaves of pressed figs. And the text gives the reason: there was joy in Israel.

The writer of Chronicles, not a character who speaks, tells how all Israel came together to make David king in Hebron. The warriors arrived with a whole and sincere heart, that is, with complete and honest loyalty. For three days there was celebration, and the northern tribes provided the food. Scholars understand this account as a picture of national unity under David.

Today we can learn that true joy is expressed by sharing. When something good unites us, such as the church, the family, or service to God, we can give generously of what we have. Ask yourself what you can bring this week to bless others.
exp.12:0:
This verse says that David gathered the leaders of the people to talk things over before making a decision. The captains of thousands and hundreds were military leaders who were in charge of groups of a thousand and of a hundred men. The other leaders refers to the rest of the people's leaders.

The book of Chronicles tells here how David, now king over all Israel, wants to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem. The ark was the symbol of God's presence, and it had been neglected since the days of Saul. Before acting, David consults the leaders and proposes that they also seek God's approval. The text does not detail how he sought it at that moment.

For today: even when we have authority, it is wise to listen to others and to ask ourselves whether what we are planning pleases God. Important decisions in the family, the church, or at work turn out better with counsel and prayer.
exp.12:1:
Here David speaks to the whole assembly of Israel. He proposes, if it seems good to them and is of the Lord our God, to send word everywhere to gather their brethren who were left in all the land of Israel. He also invites the priests and Levites who lived in their cities and in the grazing lands around them, so that they may join the people.

David had just been recognized as king over all Israel. Before bringing the ark of God to Jerusalem, he wants the whole people to take part, and not only the leaders. That is why he first consults the chiefs and then the assembly. The ark, as the following verse says, had been neglected since the days of Saul.

For today: before undertaking something important, seek counsel, include others, and ask whether it pleases God. What is done in unity and in prayer usually moves forward with more peace.
exp.12:2:
Here David proposes to the people that they bring the ark of God back, the sacred chest where the tablets of the law were kept and which symbolized God's presence among Israel. He says that "since the days of Saul we have not sought it," meaning that they had neglected it and no longer looked for it or took it into account.

David speaks before the leaders and the whole assembly of Israel, after consulting with the captains. He wants the decision to belong to everyone and also to please God. The ark had been for years in Kiriath-jearim, far from the center of the nation's life. David desires that worship return to the central place of the nation.

For today: it is easy to neglect God without realizing it, as happened with the ark. We can ask ourselves what we have set aside in our relationship with Him, such as prayer or reading the Bible, and give Him again a principal place at home and in daily life.
exp.12:6:
It says that the ark of God was taken out of the house of Abinadab and placed on a new cart. Uzza and his brother were driving that cart. The phrase "they carried" simply means that they took the ark away. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among his people.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who tells how David wanted to bring the ark to Jerusalem after years of it being in Kiriath-jearim. David gathered all Israel with good intentions and great joy. But the Law indicated that the ark was to be carried by the Levites on poles, not on a cart. This becomes clear in what happens afterward, although the text of this verse does not explain it directly.

For today: good intentions and enthusiasm in serving God are not enough. It is also wise to seek in his Word how he wants us to do things, and to obey him with humility and reverence.
exp.12:8:
This verse tells that, on arriving at a place called the threshing floor of Chidon (a threshing floor is a flat piece of ground where grain was beaten out), the oxen pulling the cart stumbled or bolted. Uzza, one of those guiding the cart, reached out his hand to steady the ark and keep it from falling.

It is a historical account. David and all Israel were bringing God's ark with great joy and music. But the law required that the ark be carried on the shoulders by the Levites, and not touched directly (Numbers 4:15). Here they were carrying it on a new cart, as the Philistines had done. Afterward, David acknowledged this mistake (1 Chronicles 15:13).

For today: sincerity and joy are valuable, but they do not replace obedience. We should seek God according to his Word, not only according to our own ideas.
exp.12:9:
The anger of God burned against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he reached out his hand and touched the ark. Uzzah died right there, in the presence of God. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among his people.

The account is told by the chronicler. David and all of Israel were bringing the ark up with celebration and music. But they were carrying it on a cart, and the Law commanded that it be carried by the Levites. Later on, David acknowledges that they did not seek God in the proper way (1 Chronicles 15:13). Uzzah tried to keep the ark from falling, but he touched something that God had declared holy. Some details of this punishment are hard to understand, and they have been interpreted in several ways.

For today: good intentions and great enthusiasm are not enough. We must approach God with reverence and obey his Word, not simply do things our own way.
exp.12:13:
The ark of God stayed in the house of Obed-edom for three months. During that time, the Lord blessed Obed-edom, his family, and everything he had. The name "Lord" is the name of God; "blessed" means that God gave him favor and well-being.

This is a account from the Chronicler. David wanted to bring the ark to Jerusalem, but Uzzah died when he touched it (1 Chronicles 13:9-10). David was afraid and left the ark at the house of Obed-edom, who was from Gath. The Bible does not detail what the blessing consisted of, so it is not wise to invent it. Later, David moved the ark with greater reverence (ch. 15).

For today: God's presence is not something to be feared or treated lightly. If we receive it with respect and obedience, He can bless our home. We can open our house to Him with prayer and daily reverence.
exp.13:0:
This verse tells that Hiram, king of Tyre, sent messengers to David. He also sent him cedar timber, stonemasons and carpenters to build him a house, that is, a palace.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, presenting a historical event. David had just been recognized as king over all Israel, and Tyre was a neighboring city with which a good relationship was being established. The following text says that David understood that God had confirmed him as king. Thus Hiram's help appears as a sign that God was affirming his kingdom. Hiram's political motives are not explained here.

God can use unexpected people to bless and support us. Let us recognize his hand in such help, give thanks with humility, and use what we have received to serve, not only to exalt ourselves.
exp.13:4:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three sons of David: Ibhar, Elishua, and Elpalet. They are the ones born in Jerusalem after David was recognized as king over all Israel. It is striking that Elpalet appears again in the next verse; some think these were two sons with the same name, though this cannot be stated with certainty.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, tells how God established David's kingdom. Just before this, he speaks of the house that Hiram, king of Tyre, built for him. The list of sons shows that the dynasty was growing, and among them was Solomon, the future king.

For today: God notices each person and remembers their name, even when they seem small in history. Value the people around you, and trust that your life also matters to Him.
exp.13:6:
This verse ends a list of the children born to David in Jerusalem: Elishama, Beeliada, and Eliphalet. They are simply names. In other passages the name "Eliada" appears in place of "Beeliada," and it is not known for certain why the form of the name changes. Some think it is an older variant.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra though this is not certain, tells this. After David was established as king, he notes that his household grew in Jerusalem. It is a sign that God was sustaining his reign. Right after this the Philistines come to attack him.

For today: God also cares for the simple details of life, such as family and names that no one remembers. Trust that He works in the everyday, and pray for your children or loved ones, knowing that each one matters to Him.
exp.13:7:
It says that the Philistines learned that David was now king over all Israel, and so they all went out together to look for him. When David heard about it, he went out to confront them. The phrase about being anointed means that he had been marked out and set apart to be king, and the words about going after him mean that they were pursuing him.

This is the account of the writer of Chronicles. It tells what happened right after David was recognized as king by all the people and settled in Jerusalem. While Israel was divided, the Philistines did not see David as a great threat. Now that he was united, they attacked him. The verses that follow show that David did not act alone: he sought God's counsel.

For today: when you begin something good or take a step of growth, pressures or attacks may come. Do not be caught off guard or react on impulse. Do as David did: pray first and seek God's guidance before you act.
exp.13:8:
This verse says that the Philistines, Israel's enemies, came with their army and spread out across the valley of Rephaim. That valley was near Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles is speaking. David had just been anointed king over all Israel, and the Philistines felt threatened, so they went to look for him. The important part comes next: David did not act on his own, but first consulted God. Some scholars think this shows his dependence on God rather than his military strength.

For today: when a threat or problem comes spreading like that army, do not react first with fear or with your own strength. Do as David did: pray, ask God for direction, and trust that he will guide you.
exp.13:15:
It says David did exactly what God had commanded him. So his army struck down the Philistine forces and chased them all the way from Gibeon to Gezer.

The narrator is the chronicler, who tells how David, already king of Israel, faced the Philistines a second time. Before fighting, David again asked God what to do. God gave him a strategy different from the previous one: go around the enemy and attack when he heard a sound in the tops of the trees. David did not rely on his earlier experience, but on God's guidance.

For today: before important decisions, seek God's direction in prayer and in his Word, even if you have already lived through something similar. What worked yesterday may not be the path for today. Obeying with trust opens the way to his help.
exp.14:0:
It says that David, now king, built houses for himself and his family in the city of David, which is Jerusalem. He also prepared a special place for the ark of God and set up a tent for it, that is, a tent where it would be kept.

Here the writer of Chronicles, who tells the story of Israel, speaks. This happens after David had settled in Jerusalem. The ark was the sign of God's presence with his people. Before bringing it, David made the preparations, and the next verse shows that he wanted to do it according to what God had commanded.

For today: before doing something important for God, it is worth preparing with order and care. We can ask ourselves whether we are making a real place in our lives for his presence, through our time, attention and obedience.
exp.14:6:
It says that among the descendants of Gershom (one of the sons of Levi), a man named Joel was the head or leader of the family. Together with his relatives they numbered one hundred and thirty people. "The chief" means the one who led or directed the group.

The passage is part of the account in Chronicles, which tradition attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain. David wants to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem, and this time he calls together the Levites, who were the ones responsible for carrying it. Earlier, an attempt had been made to move it in another way, and it ended badly. Now he gathers the families in order, with their leaders, so that it is done as God commanded.

For today: God values orderly and shared service. No one is just a number; every family and every leader had their place. Ask yourself in what simple task in your church you can serve faithfully.
exp.14:8:
