This verse is part of a list of families of the Levites. It says that from the descendants of Hebron, the chief was Eliel, and that with him there were eighty brothers, that is, relatives or members of his clan. The chief of that family was its leader or head.

The writer of Chronicles tells how David prepared the moving of the ark of God to Jerusalem. Earlier, the ark had been moved in the wrong way (1 Chronicles 13), and now David gathers the Levites, who were the ones appointed to carry it according to the law of Moses. That is why the names and numbers are recorded: each family had its place in serving God.

For today: God values every person who serves, even if their name is rarely mentioned. Doing things the way God intends, with order and commitment, matters. Ask yourself where you can serve faithfully in your church or community.
exp.14:11:
Here David speaks to the heads of the Levite families and asks them for two things: that they sanctify themselves, together with their brothers, and that they bring the ark of the Lord to the place he had prepared for it in Jerusalem. To sanctify oneself means to set oneself apart and purify oneself in order to serve God. To bring up means to move or carry the ark to its place.

David speaks after the first attempt to move the ark ended badly, when Uzza died. Now David wants to do it as God commanded, and that is why the following verses say that they had not sought God according to the ordinance before. The Levites were the ones who were to carry the ark.

For today: serving God matters not only for what we do, but for how we do it. Before a spiritual task, it is good to stop, examine the heart, and seek God with reverence and obedience.
exp.14:14:
This verse tells that the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders, using the poles or staves that were passed through the rings on the ark. This was as Moses had commanded, following what the Lord had ordered him.

Here David is speaking. The first time he tried to bring the ark to Jerusalem, he placed it on a new cart, and Uzza died when he touched it (1 Chronicles 13). Now David acknowledges that they had not sought God as He had directed. Therefore they consecrated the Levites and did it the right way.

For today: good intentions and enthusiasm are not enough. God invites us to seek Him according to His Word, not according to our own ideas. If we have gone wrong before, we can still correct our course with humility and obedience.
exp.14:16:
1 Chronicles 15:17 tells us that the Levites, following David's command, chose three leaders of music: Heman, son of Joel; Asaph, son of Berechiah; and Ethan, son of Kushaiah, who came from the family of Merari. The verse shows that they appointed these men to their role.

David had told the leaders of the Levites to choose singers from among their brothers. This happens when David brings the ark of God to Jerusalem, this time carried as Moses had commanded. The account presents praise as an orderly part of worship, not something improvised.

For today: worship of God deserves care, preparation and teamwork. If you serve in your church, whether by singing, playing an instrument or helping with practical tasks, do it with order and joy, knowing that every service, great or small, matters before God.
exp.14:23:
This verse lists seven priests who blew the trumpets before the ark of God as they carried it to Jerusalem. It also mentions Obed-edom and Jehiah as doorkeepers for the ark, that is, guards who watched over the entrance and protected the ark. To blow the trumpets means to sound them.

The passage is a historical account, not a speech. David organized the Levites and priests to bring the ark, this time as God had commanded, after the earlier failed attempt. Each person had a specific task: to sing, to play, to carry, or to keep watch. The names show that the worship was orderly and shared.

For today: God cares about the details and values the service of each person, even the kind that almost no one sees. Serve faithfully in the part that is yours, whether great or small, and do it with reverence and joy.
exp.14:24:
This verse tells how David, the leaders of the people, and the commanders of the army went to bring the ark of the covenant up from the house of Obed-edom. They did it with joy. "Elders" were the respected leaders of each tribe, and "commanders of thousands" were military officers who led large groups of men.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who recalls how David brought the ark up to Jerusalem. Earlier, an attempt to move it had ended badly because it had not been done the way God directed (1 Chronicles 13 and 15:13). This time the Levites carried it as was proper, and so there is celebration, music, and sacrifices.

For today: when we seek God, it is good to do so with reverence and obedience, but also with gladness. Joy is not carelessness; it is the natural response of a heart that draws near to God as He asks. Today you might ask yourself: is my worship sincere and joyful?
exp.14:25:
This verse tells us that the Levites were able to carry the ark of the covenant, and that God helped them in that task. As a sign of thankfulness, they offered as a sacrifice seven bullocks (young bulls) and seven rams (male sheep). The phrase "helped" means that God gave them strength and support.

The passage is narrated by the chronicler, who recalls when David brought the ark up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom. Earlier, a first attempt had failed (1 Chronicles 13). Now they were doing it as God had commanded, with the Levites carrying it. The number seven usually points to completeness, though the text does not explain more.

For today: let us not do God's work by our own effort alone. We can obey him, ask for his help, and when everything goes well, thank him with humility and joy.
exp.14:26:
This verse describes how David and those taking part in the bringing up of the ark were dressed. David, the Levites who carried the ark, and the singers wore robes of fine linen, a white and delicate cloth. Chenaniah led the singing. David also wore an ephod of linen, a simple garment similar to an apron or vest, used in the service of God.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the history of Israel. David brings the ark to Jerusalem with joy, after having earlier moved it in the wrong way. Now everything is done with order and reverence. That the king dressed the same as the Levites shows humility: he presented himself as just one more worshiper. This prepares the contrast with Michal, who despised him.

For today: when we worship God, we can do so with joy, but also with humility and order, without seeking to stand out above others.
exp.14:27:
This verse describes how all Israel brought the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem, in the middle of a great celebration. There were shouts of joy and music from many instruments. Some of the instruments were played with the breath, such as the horns and trumpets, the cymbals were struck to make a festive noise, and the stringed instruments were played to fill the air with music.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who recounts how David moved the ark, the symbol of God's presence. Earlier, the move had failed because it was not done as God commanded. Now the Levites carry it with care, amid sacrifices and praise. Shortly afterward, Michal, David's wife, looks down on him as she watches him celebrate.

For today: when we worship God, we can do so with sincere joy and with reverence. Let us not allow the criticism of others to take away our delight in praising him.
exp.14:28:
When the ark of the covenant came into the city of David, Michal, the daughter of Saul, looked out from a window and saw King David leaping and dancing. In her heart she despised him. The word "despised" here means looking down on someone with scorn, as if they were worth little.

The narrator is the chronicler, who tells how David brought the ark to Jerusalem during a great celebration, with songs, trumpets, and harps. Michal, the daughter of the king before him, watches from a distance and does not take part. The text does not explain her reasons. In 2 Samuel 6 more detail is given, and some think she felt it was unworthy of a king.

For today: worshiping God with sincere joy can be misunderstood by others. Make sure your worship is honest, and guard your own heart so that you do not look down on the joy of others in their faith.
exp.15:0:
They brought the ark of God successfully and placed it in the center of a tent that David had prepared for it. There they presented "burnt offerings" (offerings that were burned completely, as a total surrender to God) and "peace offerings" (offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving, of which a part was shared as a meal).

This is part of the account in the book of Chronicles. Earlier, David had brought the ark to Jerusalem after a first attempt had failed (1 Chronicles 13 and 15). The ark symbolized God's presence with Israel. The author, traditionally identified with Ezra although this is not certain, emphasizes the importance of worshiping God in the right place and in the right way.

For today: put God at the center of our lives, just as the ark was in the middle of the tent. We can begin the day by giving thanks to Him and handing over our plans, so that He is first and not last.
exp.15:1:
This verse says that David, after finishing presenting the offerings to God, blessed all the people in the name of the Lord. The burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole as a complete surrender to God. The peace offerings were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving, and a meal was also shared from them. To bless in the name of the Lord means to ask for God's good on the people, not to give one's own good.

The narrator is the chronicler of Israel. He tells of the moment when the ark of the covenant finally arrived in Jerusalem and was placed in a tent prepared by David. It was a day of great joy and renewed worship for the whole nation. David acts here as a king who leads the people toward God.

For today: before blessing others, it is worth coming near to God with devotion and gratitude. Someone who worships from the heart can encourage their family and friends with words that point to God.
exp.15:4:
This verse lists the Levites whom David appointed to serve with music before the ark. Asaph was the leader; the others played harps and lyres, which were stringed instruments. Asaph, by contrast, played the cymbals, metal plates that made a loud, ringing sound.

The chronicler tells how David brought the ark to Jerusalem and organized the worship. After the celebration and the offerings, he assigned these Levites to remember, give thanks, and praise the LORD. Some names are repeated, such as Jehiel, and it is not certain whether they are different people or a variant in the text.

For today: praising God is best done as a team, and each person has a place. Some lead, others accompany, and all are important. Serve where God has placed you, without seeking the spotlight, with gratitude and steadiness.
exp.15:7:
This verse invites three things: to give thanks to the Lord, which here means thanking him and acknowledging him publicly; to call upon his name, that is, to cry out to God and trust in him; and to make known his deeds, or in other words, to tell them to all the peoples.

David has just brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. On that festive day, he assigns Asaph and his brothers, the Levite musicians, to lead the praise. These words open a psalm of thanksgiving, which resembles parts of Psalm 105. The speaker is David, with the people gathered before the ark.

For today: think of something specific that God has done for you or your family, and tell someone about it this week. Giving thanks out loud strengthens your faith and can encourage others to seek God.
exp.15:9:
This verse invites us to glory, but not in ourselves; it calls us to glory in the holy name of God. "Glory" here means to rejoice and boast with gratitude. The phrase about those who seek the Lord refers to those who desire him and follow him. The joy of the heart is tied to seeking God.

These words are part of the psalm that David gave to Asaph and his brothers when the ark of the covenant came to Jerusalem. It was a time of celebration and thanksgiving. The text encourages the people to sing, to remember the works of God, and to seek him, not only on special days but continually, as the following verses say.

Today, when you feel tired or restless, take a few minutes to remember something specific that God has done for you. Give thanks aloud or with a song. Seeking God with gratitude can restore joy to the heart.
exp.15:10:
It says we should seek God and depend on his power, and that we do so always, without growing weary. To seek means to come to him with a sincere desire. His power is his strength. Being in his presence and enjoying his nearness is what it describes when it speaks of seeking him. Always, without stopping, means all the time.

This text is part of the psalm that David gave to Asaph and his brothers when the ark of the covenant arrived in Jerusalem. It was a moment of celebration and gratitude. The people were called to sing, to remember God's wonders, and to keep their relationship with him alive.

For today: don't seek God only when you have problems. Set aside a moment each day to pray, read the Bible, and ask him for strength for whatever you face. In this way your trust in him becomes a daily habit, not just a reaction to crises.
exp.15:11:
This verse invites us to remember. We are asked to keep in view the wonders God has done, his wonders (extraordinary deeds), and the judgments of his mouth, that is, the decisions and verdicts God has declared.

This song appears when David brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, and the book presents it as a hymn of thanksgiving that was given to Asaph and his brothers to sing. It is addressed to the people of Israel, descended from Jacob. It reminds them that their God has spoken and acted in their history, and that they should trust him.

For today: a simple habit is to write down, or count aloud, the times God has helped, cared for, or guided you. When doubt or weariness comes, that grateful memory will help you seek God with more confidence.
exp.15:13:
This verse says that the Lord is our God and that his judgments reach all the earth. "Judgments" means his decisions and his just way of ruling. In other words, the God of Israel is not a local god: his authority and his justice reach the whole world.

It is part of the song of thanksgiving that David handed over to celebrate that the ark of the covenant arrived in Jerusalem. According to the text, Asaph and his brothers sang it. It calls the people to remember what God has done and the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: when the world seems confusing or unjust, remember that God is still God over all the earth. Remember what he has done in your life and give him thanks, trusting that his justice has not stopped.
exp.15:16:
He made his promise to Jacob a firm decree, and to Israel an everlasting covenant that will never be broken. God made this promise sure and secure.

These words are part of the song of thanksgiving that David gave to Asaph and his brothers, the Levites, when the ark of the covenant was brought to Jerusalem. The people were to remember that God is faithful to his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He promised them the land of Canaan when they were few in number and lived as strangers there. God keeps what he promises even when his people are small and weak.

For today: when you feel small or insecure, call to mind God's promises and how he has sustained you. Write them down and give thanks, trusting that he remains faithful.
exp.15:22:
This verse calls all the earth to sing to the Lord.

David gave this song of thanksgiving when the ark of God arrived in Jerusalem. The preceding text recalls that God looked after the patriarchs when they were few and lived as strangers. That care shows why his people have reason to sing. A similar psalm appears in Psalm 96.

For today: make it a habit to tell someone, each day, one specific way God helped you. It can be in a prayer, in a song, or in a message to a friend.
exp.15:23:
This verse calls us to speak and sing of God's glory among the nations. "Peoples" here means the nations around us, and "wonders" are the amazing works that God has done. The invitation is not only for Israel, but for everyone to know who God is.

These words are part of the song of thanksgiving that 1 Chronicles attributes to David, when the ark of God was brought to Jerusalem. Asaph and his brothers were appointed to praise God. The song reminds us that the LORD is great and that the gods of the peoples are nothing, because only He made the heavens.

For today: think of something concrete that God has done in your life, and tell it this week to someone who does not know Him, simply and with gratitude.
exp.15:28:
This verse invites us to give God the honor that is due Him for who He is. The verse of the first word: to give or hand over. An offering is a gift brought to God. To bow down means to lower oneself in humility. The phrase about the beauty of holiness can be understood as worshiping Him in holy clothing or attitude, or as admiring how pure and perfect He is; scholars interpret it in both ways.

It is part of the psalm that David gave to Asaph and his brothers when the ark of the covenant came to Jerusalem. It was a time of great celebration and thankfulness. The psalm calls all peoples, not only Israel, to recognize that the Lord reigns.

For today: before asking God for something, take a moment to acknowledge who He is. Give Him thanks, bow before Him with simplicity, and offer Him your day, your time, or your service as a gift.
exp.15:30:
This verse invites the heavens to be filled with joy, and the earth too. It also asks that among the nations it be announced clearly that the Lord reigns, meaning that God is King and holds authority over everything.

This is part of the psalm that David handed over to Asaph and his brothers when the ark of God was brought to Jerusalem. It was a song of thanksgiving and celebration. The text calls all peoples to honor God and warns that he comes to judge the earth. Scholars understand that judgment as a just and upright rule.

For today: even when the world seems disordered, you can begin your day by remembering that God reigns. Thank him for something specific and speak of his goodness with someone close to you. In this way your joy rests on who God is, not on your circumstances.
exp.15:32:
It says that even the trees of the forests will sing for joy before God, because he comes to judge the earth. "Judge" here means to govern with justice, to set things in order.

The passage is a song of praise which, according to the account, David handed to the musicians when they brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. It invites all creation to celebrate that God reigns. The singing trees are poetic language; this is not something literal, but an image of all of nature joining in the praise.

For today: God's judgment is a reason for hope, not only for fear, because he will come to correct what is unjust. Today you can trust that God will set everything in order, and in the meantime, praise him with gratitude, even when you see injustice around you.
exp.15:38:
This verse tells us that David left the priest Zadok and his fellow priests at Gibeon, before the tabernacle of the Lord. "The high place" was an elevated place where worship took place. Here it refers to the site where the tabernacle stood, not to idol worship.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who describes how David organized worship after bringing the ark to Jerusalem. The ark was in Jerusalem with Asaph and his brothers, while at Gibeon the tabernacle and its altar remained. There Zadok and the priests offered the daily sacrifices, as the law commanded. In this way worship was never interrupted.

For today: God values faithfulness. Faith is sustained by small acts of devotion, such as praying and giving thanks each day, even when no one sees them.
exp.15:39:
This verse says that Zadok and the priests were to offer burnt offerings to God every day, morning and evening, on the altar. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned completely as a gift to God. The phrase "according to all that is written in the law of the Lord" means they did it just as God had commanded Israel through Moses.

The one telling this is the writer of Chronicles, writing long after these events. David had brought the ark to Jerusalem, and he left Zadok at Gibeon, where the tabernacle was, so that the daily worship would not be interrupted. The writer wants to highlight that the worship followed an order faithful to the law.

For today: God values steadiness. We can set aside a fixed moment each morning and each evening to pray and give thanks to him, not as empty routine, but as a sincere giving of our lives.
exp.15:41:
This verse tells us that David left Heman and Jeduthun in charge of the music in worship. They played trumpets, cymbals (metal plates that make a sound when struck together), and other instruments made for praising God. In addition, the sons of Jeduthun were appointed as gatekeepers, that is, guards of the entrances to the place of worship.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who reviews the history of Israel. He recounts that David had brought the ark to Jerusalem and organized the daily service before it. The morning and evening sacrifices followed the law, and the musicians were chosen by name to give thanks, because God's mercy endures forever.

For today: God values visible service, such as music, and quiet service, such as keeping a gate. Ask yourself what simple task you can do in your church, with gratitude and steadiness, to honor God.
exp.16:4:
God says that he has never lived in a fixed house since he brought Israel up out of Egypt. Rather, he moved from tent to tent, and from one tabernacle (the sacred tent where he was worshiped) to another. "Until this day" means until that moment in the time of David.

God speaks to the prophet Nathan during the night, and he tells him to carry a message to David. David wanted to build a temple for him, but God answers that it will not be David who builds it. God reminds him that he never asked for a house of cedar; he walked with his people in simplicity. Scholars agree that God does not reject David, but makes clear to him his plans and his timing.

God does not depend on buildings to be with us. What matters most to him is our closeness to him and our obedience. Today you can seek him anywhere: at home, at work, or on the road. And if a good desire does not come true the way you expected, trust that God has a better plan.
exp.16:5:
God asks David whether, in all the time he walked with Israel, he ever once complained to the judges, the leaders he appointed to look after his people, that they should build him a house of cedar. "Shepherd" means to look after and guide, the way a shepherd guides his sheep. Cedar was a fine and costly wood.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan on the same night that David wanted to build a temple for him. God reminds him that he had always been with his people in a tent, the tabernacle, which moved with them. His answer is not a rejection of David's desire, but a way of showing that God does not depend on buildings. Scholars explain in several ways why David would not be the one to build it.

For today: God values your closeness and your obedience more than your great projects for him. Serve him with humility, remembering that he walks with you in everyday life.
exp.16:6:
This verse is part of the message that God sends to David through the prophet Nathan. God reminds him where He took him from: He took him from the pastures where he tended sheep, from behind the flock, to make him a ruler, that is, a leader or governor, over Israel. The sheepcote is the place where the livestock is kept. "The Lord of hosts" is a title that highlights God's power and authority.

David wanted to build a temple for God. But God answers him that He had never asked for a house of cedar, since He had walked with His people in a tent. Before speaking of what David would do, God reminds him of what He had already done for David.

For today: if God has given you a place, a job, or a responsibility, remember that it comes from His grace, not from your merits. This helps us live with humility and gratitude.
exp.16:7:
God says that he was with David wherever he went. "Cut off" means removed or eliminated: God took his enemies out of the way. He also gave him a famous name, comparable to the name of the most important men in the world.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan, who brings this message to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God reminds him that he has always been with him, since he was a shepherd of sheep. Then he promises something greater: God himself will build David a house, that is, a lasting family and descendants.

For today: before trying to do something great for God, let us remember what he has already done for us. Looking back and giving thanks for his companionship gives us humility and confidence for the future.
exp.16:10:
God tells David that, when he dies, he will raise up one of David's own descendants who will be one of his sons. God will make his kingdom firm and stable.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a house for God, but God answers that He will build David a house, that is, a lasting royal family. The immediate fulfillment was Solomon. Christians also see in this a promise that points to Jesus, a descendant of David.

God keeps his promises even when we cannot see them fulfilled. We can serve faithfully today, pray for our children and the generations to come, and trust that God continues to work after we are gone.
exp.16:12:
He says that God will be like a father to David's son, and that this son will be treated as a true son. God promises not to take away his mercy, that is, his kindness and faithfulness, as he took it away from the one who came before you. The phrase about the one who came before you is commonly understood to refer to Saul, although the text does not give his name here. Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of Jesus, a descendant of David.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God promises that it will be he who establishes David's house, or dynasty. Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of Jesus, a descendant of David.

God treats us with a father's love, and his kindness toward those who are in Christ does not depend on our successes. Today you can approach him with confidence, knowing that he sustains you faithfully, and respond with grateful obedience.
exp.16:20:
In this verse, David asks a question to praise God: what other nation is there like Israel? God himself went to rescue a people to make them his own. In this way he made himself famous through great and awe-inspiring deeds, such as bringing his people out of Egypt and driving out the nations that were before them. "Redeem" means to set free by paying a price or by great effort.

David speaks in prayer, after God promised him through the prophet Nathan that his family would reign and that his descendant would build the temple. David feels deeply thankful and remembers what God has already done for Israel. That gives him confidence that God will also fulfill what he has just promised.

For today: when you doubt the future, remember what God has already done in your life and among his people. Thanking him for the past strengthens confidence in his promises.
exp.16:22:
This verse is a prayer. David asks God to keep the promise he made about David's family firm forever. The word "servant" refers to David himself, and "house" means his family and descendants. He ends by asking God to do as he has said, that is, to fulfill what he promised.

David speaks after the prophet Nathan brought him God's word: although David would not build the temple, God would establish a line of kings from him. David, thankful and humble, remembers how God rescued Israel from Egypt. With that history as his foundation, he trusts that God will also keep this new promise. Many Christians see in it a hope that points to Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when you pray, lean on what God has already promised in his Word. You can ask him with confidence, remembering how faithful he has been before, and rest in the knowledge that he keeps what he says.
exp.16:23:
David asks here that the name of God be honored forever, so that everyone will say: "The Lord of hosts is the God of Israel, and truly a God to Israel." He also asks that his family, the house of David, remain steadfast before God.

David speaks in prayer after God promised him, through the prophet Nathan, that his descendants would endure. David does not want blessing only for himself, but that what God said be fulfilled and that God be glorified. His prayer rests on God's word, and that is why he dares to ask with confidence.

For today: when you pray for your family or your plans, rest on God's promises and ask that, above all, his name be honored through your life.
exp.16:25:
It says that the Lord is the true God and that he himself promised something good to David, his servant. The idea that God has spoken this good thing about his servant means that God announced a blessing for David. The word "servant" here refers to someone who serves God with humility.

David speaks in prayer. He had wanted to build a temple for God, but God answered him through the prophet Nathan that instead he would establish a family and a dynasty for David. David, grateful, recognizes that everything comes from God's promise and not from his own merits. For that reason he dares to pray with confidence.

For today: when you pray, rely on what God has already promised in his Word. You can bring his promises before him with humility and gratitude, trusting that he is faithful and fulfills what he says.
exp.17:4:
These verses tell how the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer, king of Zobah, who was already at war with David. But David defeated them too and struck down twenty-two thousand of them. The word "struck" here means that he beat them in battle, causing many casualties.

The book of Chronicles is a historical account that recalls the reigns of Israel, probably to encourage the people after the exile. It is not told by a character but by the narrator. It shows how God established David's kingdom against its enemies. The following text explains it: "The LORD preserved David wherever he went." It should be read as ancient history of war, not as a model for justifying violence today.

For today: when you face problems that seem to grow or to receive reinforcements, remember that God is still your help. Trust in Him and act with courage, humility, and justice.
exp.17:5:
It says David placed garrisons, that is, groups of soldiers who watched over and controlled the place, in Syria of Damascus. The Syrians came under his rule as servants, meaning they were under his authority, and they paid him tribute with gifts or presents. The text gives the reason: the Lord gave David victory wherever he went.

This is part of the Chronicler's account of David's military victories. It came after David defeated Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and the Syrians who had come to his aid. The Chronicler writes for a people returning from exile, and he wants them to remember that David's kingdom was sustained by the hand of God, not by human strength alone.

For today: in what you face, recognize that success and protection come from God. Do your part with effort and honesty, but trust Him and give Him thanks, without relying only on your own abilities.
exp.17:6:
It says that David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants or officers of Hadarezer, king of Zobah, and brought them to Jerusalem. Some scholars believe they were ceremonial shields; the text only says that they were made of gold.

It is part of the Chronicler's account of David's victories. After defeating Hadarezer and the Syrians of Damascus, it notes that "the Lord gave victory to David wherever he went." The spoils came to Jerusalem, and the following passage tells how Solomon used another metal taken in those wars for the temple. In this way it shows that what was gained would serve God's purposes.

For today: what we receive, whether money, talents or achievements, is not only for ourselves. Let us ask God for wisdom to use it in a way that serves his work and blesses others.
exp.17:8:
This verse tells that Tou, king of Hamath, heard that David had completely defeated the army of Hadarezer, king of Zobah.

The text is historical narrative, and the writer of Chronicles recounts David's victories. Tou and Hadarezer were enemies, since there was war between them. So when he learned of the victory, Tou sent his son with gifts to greet and congratulate David. That event shows how the influence of Israel's king was growing among the neighboring nations. The verses that follow say that David dedicated those gifts to the LORD.

For today: when God gives you an achievement or a blessing, remember to whom it truly belongs. Follow David's example, who dedicated what he received to God, and use it with gratitude and generosity.
exp.17:9:
Tou, king of Hamath, sent his son Hadoram to David to greet him and congratulate him, because he had defeated Hadarezer, the enemy of Tou. Wishing him well and acknowledging his success is what the greeting meant here. He also sent him as a gift all kinds of vessels of gold, silver and brass.

The chronicler, who writes for the people of Israel, tells how David's kingdom grew. Tou was already at war with Hadarezer, so David's victory worked in his favor, and he wanted to gain David's friendship. In 2 Samuel 8:10 this son appears under the name Joram, and it is not known for certain why the name changes.

For today: when God gives you a victory, also acknowledge those who helped you, and receive their gifts with gratitude. Just as David did, dedicate the best to God (v. 11) and do not keep it only for yourself.
exp.17:15:
This verse names three officials of David's kingdom. Zadok and Abimelech were priests, that is, the ones who led worship and the sacrifices. Shavsha was the secretary, that is, the scribe who recorded and kept the king's documents.

The author of Chronicles, who is not named, gives a list of David's officials after his victories. It shows a well-ordered kingdom, where worship and administration had people responsible for them. In 2 Samuel 8:17 a similar list appears, but with some names that differ, such as Ahimelech and Seraiah. It is not known with certainty whether these are variants from copying or from how the names were written.

God uses both those who serve in visible roles and those who do simple tasks, like keeping records. Ask yourself: what small task can you do faithfully today, as for the Lord?
exp.18:1:
David said that he would show kindness to Hanun, the new king of the Ammonites, because Hanun's father Nahash had also been kind to him. So David sent messengers to comfort him over the death of his father. The phrase "show kindness" here means showing goodwill and loyalty. The verse says the messengers were sent to comfort Hanun, meaning to console him.

The speaker is David, king of Israel. The text does not explain what Nahash's kindness consisted of; it only says David remembered it and wanted to repay it in the same way. What follows shows that the Ammonite advisers suspected his intentions and treated the messengers badly, so a gesture of goodwill ended in offense.

For today: Be grateful in concrete ways. If someone has done you good, look for a sincere way to return it. And if someone misreads your good intentions, do not stop doing good because of it.
exp.18:3:
This verse tells that Hanun, king of the Ammonites, seized David's messengers, shaved off half of their beards, cut their garments in the middle, up to their buttocks, and sent them back. In that culture, this was a very serious public humiliation.

The chronicler recounts the event. David had sent envoys to offer condolences over the death of Hanun's father, who had earlier shown kindness to him. But the Ammonite officials, suspicious, told Hanun that the envoys were spies. He believed them without checking, gravely insulted David, and the matter ended in war.

For today: before judging someone's intentions, it is wise to find out the truth calmly. Suspicion without proof and bad advice can destroy relationships and turn a gesture of kindness into a major conflict.
exp.18:5:
This verse says that the Ammonites realized they had made themselves hateful to David by humiliating his messengers. So Hanun, their king, sent a thousand talents of silver (an enormous amount) to hire chariots and horsemen from several Aramean regions: Syria of the rivers (Mesopotamia), Maachah, and Zobah. "Hire" here means to pay for their service.

The narrator recounts what happened after David sent messengers to comfort Hanun over the death of his father. Hanun grew suspicious, humiliated them, and shaved them, and so provoked a conflict. Instead of asking forgiveness, he chose to prepare for war.

For today: when we have hurt someone out of pride or suspicion, the wisest course is to acknowledge the wrong and seek reconciliation. Spending energy defending ourselves from the consequences only makes the problem bigger.
exp.18:6:
This verse says that the Ammonites hired, paying for it, a huge army of allies: thirty-two thousand chariots and the king of Maachah with his people. They came and camped in front of Medeba, a city. The Ammonites also gathered together from their cities and came to fight. The figure of thirty-two thousand refers to chariots and fighting men; some scholars think it includes the soldiers.

The account comes from the Chronicler, who tells how the war began. David had sent messengers to comfort Hanun over the death of his father, but the Ammonites humiliated them. When they learned they had offended David, they prepared for war by buying allies with a thousand talents of silver.

For today: when we have done wrong or provoked a conflict, it is tempting to seek strength and support instead of acknowledging the mistake. Better that we seek peace and ask forgiveness in time, before the problem grows.
exp.18:7:
David learned that the Ammonites were gathering a large army with help from foreign soldiers. So he sent Joab, his commander, together with the whole army of his mighty men, that is, his best soldiers. The sentence explaining the wording about hearing of it has been removed, since it refers to words not found in the verse.

This is a historical account. The Ammonites realized they had offended David, and they paid a great deal of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Syria. David did not wait to be attacked; instead he responded by sending Joab with his army.

For today: when a serious problem arises, it is wise to act responsibly and not remain paralyzed. Listening well, preparing, and taking concrete steps is part of acting with wisdom, without ceasing to trust in God.
exp.18:9:
Joab, the commander of David's army, saw that the enemy was attacking him from the front and from behind. This verse says he chose the best soldiers of Israel, the most capable ones, and set them in formation against the Syrians.

Here the narrator of the book explains the background. David had sent Joab out with the army because the Ammonites, who had shamed David's messengers, hired Syrian soldiers to fight alongside them. Joab found himself caught between two fronts: the Ammonites in the city and the Syrians in the open field. So he divided his forces and placed himself against the stronger enemy.

For today: when you feel pressed in from every side, do not freeze. Think calmly, organize what you have, ask others for help, and trust that God is the one who gives the final outcome.
exp.18:10:
This verse tells us that Joab, commander of Israel's army, handed over the rest of his soldiers to his brother Abishai. Abishai was to set them in battle formation facing the Ammonites.

Israel was surrounded: the Ammonites in front, at the entrance of the city, and the Arameans behind them. Joab, as commander, divided his forces. He took the best of the men against the Arameans, and Abishai was left in charge of the rest against the Ammonites. Then they promised each other mutual help and entrusted the outcome to God.

When we face a big problem, we do not have to carry it alone. We can do our part well, ask for and offer help to others, and then trust that God will do what is best.
exp.18:15:
When the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they did not give up. They sent messengers to call up reinforcements from the Syrians who lived on the other side of the river (the Euphrates). They were led by Shophach, the commander of the army of Hadarezer, king of Zobah.

This is part of the account of David's war against the Ammonites and their Syrian allies. The chronicler does not speak in the first person here; he simply narrates. It shows that the defeat did not end the conflict: the Syrians regrouped with greater strength, which is why David had to go out and fight himself, as the text goes on to say.

For today: problems often return bigger after a first victory. Let us not lower our guard or trust only in what we achieved yesterday. We still need prayer, prudence, and dependence on God every day.
exp.18:17:
The Syrians (Arameans) fled before Israel's army. David defeated seven thousand men who fought in chariots and forty thousand foot soldiers. He also killed Shophach, the commander of their army.

The chronicler tells this after the Ammonites insulted David's messengers and hired Syrian allies to fight. David answered by defending Israel. The numbers in this account differ a little from 2 Samuel 10:18, and scholars explain the difference in several ways, such as differences in copies of the text or in the way numbers were counted.

For today: trusting in human power or alliances does not guarantee victory. When you face a great problem, act with courage and responsibility, but place your trust in God, who gives true security.
exp.18:18:
This verse tells how the war ended. The Syrians who served Hadadezer saw that Israel had defeated them, so they made peace with David and became his servants, meaning they came under his rule and paid him tribute. From then on, Syria no longer wanted to help the Ammonites.

It is part of the account in the book of Chronicles, written by a narrator who reviews the history of Israel. The Ammonites had insulted David's messengers and hired Syrian help to fight. When the Syrians failed, the Ammonites were left alone. The text shows how David strengthened his kingdom, and the writer presents these victories as part of the fulfillment of God's promises to Israel.

For today: human alliances can fail when they are based on pride or on an unjust conflict. Before supporting a fight, it is wise to ask ourselves whether it is just. And our greatest security is not in powerful people, but in God.
exp.19:0:
At the start of the new year, when kings used to go out to war, Joab led Israel's army. He laid waste the land of the Ammonites and laid siege to (surrounded to attack) the city of Rabbah. David stayed in Jerusalem, and Joab defeated Rabbah and destroyed it.

The writer of Chronicles recounts David's wars to remind the people of their history. Here he mentions that David stayed at home, but he does not tell what happened there. In 2 Samuel 11, that same moment appears alongside David's sin with Bathsheba. Why Chronicles leaves this out is not known for certain; some believe it wanted to emphasize other themes.

For today: ask yourself whether you are faithfully carrying out your responsibility in the place where God has put you. Times of carelessness or comfort can become dangerous. Stay alert, busy with what is good, and dependent on God.
exp.19:1:
The verse tells that David took the crown of the king of the Ammonites, which weighed a talent of gold (about 30 or 35 kilos, by estimate) and had precious stones in it. Then it was set on David's head. He also brought out of the city of Rabbah an exceeding great spoil.

The phrase "their king" can also be understood as referring to the image of their god Milcom; the Hebrew text allows both readings.

The book of Chronicles was written to encourage God's people after the exile, reminding them of David's reign. Here the account summarizes the victory over Ammon, won by Joab, the commander of the army, while David was in Jerusalem. Chronicles leaves out David's sin with Bathsheba, which happened during that same time, but the Bible reader knows it from 2 Samuel 11.

Victories and honors can be a gift from God, but they do not replace being in the place where God calls us. Let us guard our hearts when things go well for us.
exp.19:2:
The verse says that David brought out the people of Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, and put them to work with saws, iron threshing sledges, and axes. He did the same to all the other cities of Ammon, and then he returned to Jerusalem with his whole army.

The chronicler tells of the end of the war against the Ammonites, who had humiliated David's messengers. Scholars debate the exact meaning: some believe it was forced labor with those tools; others, a cruel execution. The Hebrew allows both readings. In any case, this is how wars were fought in that time.

For today: the Bible honestly recounts the harshness of history without disguising it. This reminds us that no human leader is perfect, not even David, and that only Jesus is the just and merciful King. We can trust in Him and be people who treat with compassion even those who have wronged us.
exp.19:3:
After this, the text says, war broke out again with the Philistines at a place called Gezer. There Sibbechai, from the family of the Hushathites, struck down Sippai, a descendant of the giants (the Rephaim), and the Philistines were brought under control. The word "subdued" means that they were defeated and lost their strength.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the victories from the reign of David, right after the capture of Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. Here it is not David who speaks, but the chronicler, who emphasizes that God gave victory to his people through different warriors, not only through the king. Each soldier had a part in that story.

For today: God uses ordinary and little-known people to overcome great difficulties. Do faithfully what is given to you, even when no one notices, and trust that God sees and values your service.
exp.19:5:
It says there was another war against the Philistines at Gath. There was a man there of great height, with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. He was also a descendant of Rapha.

Here the chronicler speaks, summarizing Israel's victories in the time of David. It is not a speech but a brief account. The text shows that these giants fell by the hand of David and his servants. The Israelites who read this, after the exile, remembered that God had given victory to his people against enemies who seemed invincible.

Today we can remember that no problem, however enormous it seems, is beyond God's care. He often acts through ordinary people who trust in him and support one another. Do not face alone only what frightens you: pray and seek help.
exp.19:6:
It says that a Philistine giant from Gath mocked and defied the people of Israel, and that Jonathan, David's nephew, struck him down and killed him. Jonathan was the son of Shimea, David's brother.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the last wars of David against the Philistines. Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator, who summarizes how the descendants of Rapha, men of great stature, fell. Some scholars think these accounts encouraged the people after the exile, reminding them that God gave victory over enemies who seemed invincible.

Today we can remember that God often works through ordinary people and united families, not only through great leaders. When something intimidates us or mocks our faith, we are not alone: God can raise up someone at our side to help us face it with courage.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that Satan stood against Israel and pushed David to take a census, that is, to count the people. The verse presents this as an attack on Israel, and the account moves forward from that point.

The narrator is the writer of Chronicles, who tells the story of Israel. Joab, the commander of the army, warns that the census will bring harm. Some readers note that 2 Samuel 24:1 says the anger of the Lord moved David to act; Bible scholars explain the two accounts in different ways. What is clear is that David acted out of pride or from trusting in his own strength, and that this was sin.

For today: when we feel the urge to trust in numbers, achievements, or resources more than in God, it is wise to stop and reflect. Listening to a wise counselor, like Joab, can save us from painful mistakes.
exp.20:1:
Here David orders Joab, the commander of his army, and the leaders of the people to travel through all of Israel, from Beersheba (in the south) to Dan (in the north), to count the people. He wants to know how many there are.

King David is the one speaking. The verse before this one says that Satan moved David to take this census. Joab objects, because he sees that it will bring harm to Israel, but the king insists. Many believe the problem lay in pride, or in trusting the number of soldiers more than God, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: let us be careful not to measure our security only by numbers, resources, or achievements. And if someone wise warns us, let us listen with humility before we go ahead.
exp.20:4:
This verse gives the result of the census: in Israel there were one million one hundred thousand men who drew the sword, that is, men who could fight. In Judah there were four hundred seventy thousand.

Joab, the commander of the army, hands the count to David. He had warned that the census would do harm, but the king insisted. The text says this displeased God. The figures in 2 Samuel 24 are different, and they are explained in several ways, such as counted groups or rounding. There is no single certain answer.

Today, let us not place our security in numbers, money, or our own strength, but in God. And when someone wise warns us, let us listen with humility before insisting on our own way.
exp.20:9:
God tells the prophet Gad to go to David and say that He offers him three possible punishments. David must choose one, and God will carry it out.

Here the Lord speaks. David had taken a census of the people, and the Bible presents this as a serious sin. David had already acknowledged his guilt and asked for forgiveness. God does not overlook sin: even after repentance, there are consequences. The punishments that follow are famine, defeat, or plague, and the text does not fully explain why God acts this way.

Today we can learn that asking for forgiveness is necessary, but it does not always remove the consequences of our actions. It is good to accept responsibility with humility and to trust in God's mercy, as David will do afterward.
exp.20:11:
God, through the prophet Gad, gives David three options for punishment: three years of famine, three months of being defeated before his enemies, or three days of plague sent by the angel of the LORD. The first sentence's explanation of old words must be removed since those words do not appear in the verse; the rest is translated.

Gad is a prophet who carries the LORD's message. Earlier, David had ordered the people to be counted, and this displeased God. The Bible presents this scene as the result of that sin, and the text does not fully explain why the census was so serious; it has been understood as pride or reliance on one's own strength.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and even so we can come to God with humility. David chose to fall into God's hands, because he trusted in His mercy. When we fail, it is good to return to Him without excuses.
exp.20:16:
It says that David looked up and saw the angel of the Lord standing between heaven and earth. He had a drawn sword in his hand, stretched out toward Jerusalem. When they saw him, David and the leaders of the people, the elders, fell face down to the ground. They were clothed in sackcloth, a rough cloth used as a sign of grief and repentance.

David had ordered a census of the people, and that displeased God. As a result, a plague came upon Israel. The text tells how God had compassion and stopped the angel. Here David recognizes the seriousness of the moment and humbles himself alongside the leaders. The exact reasons for the sin of the census are explained in several ways; the text only says that it was evil.

Today, when we fail, we can imitate David: not hide the mistake or blame others, but come before God with humility, acknowledge the wrong, and trust in his compassion.
exp.20:18:
This verse tells us that God, through his angel, gave an order to Gad, a prophet, to pass on to King David. David was to go up and build an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. A threshing floor was a flat, firm piece of ground where grain was beaten to separate the kernels from the straw. Mentioning that Ornan was a Jebusite shows that he belonged to the people who had lived in Jerusalem before.

David had sinned by ordering a count of the people, and a plague fell on Israel. He humbled himself and asked that the punishment fall on him and not on the people. Gad was the prophet who brought God's messages to him. The command to build an altar shows that God was opening a way of forgiveness and worship.

For today: when we fail, God does not ask us to hide, but to return to him with humility and obedience, and he shows us the way to be restored.
exp.20:20:
Ornan turned around and saw the angel. His four sons, who were with him, hid themselves out of fear. Meanwhile, Ornan kept threshing the wheat, that is, separating the grain from the straw on the threshingfloor, which was a flat, hard piece of ground for that work.

The angel of the LORD had commanded David, through the prophet Gad, to build an altar on that threshingfloor. David was seeking to stop the plague that was afflicting the people. Ornan was a Jebusite, an inhabitant of the region of Jerusalem. This moment shows that God made himself present in the middle of an ordinary man's work.

Today, God can make himself present in everyday life. Live attentive to his voice, and respond with reverence, not with indifference.
exp.20:21:
When David came to Ornan's threshing floor, Ornan saw him and came out from the place where he was threshing wheat. Then he bowed down to the ground before the king. The threshing floor was a flat, firm piece of ground where the grain was separated from the straw. Bowing down means lowering oneself until one touches the earth, as a sign of respect.

David was on his way to that place because the prophet Gad had told him, on God's behalf, to build an altar there. There was a plague upon Israel, and Ornan and his sons had just seen an angel. Ornan owned the land, and his reaction shows respect for the king and fear at what was happening.

For today: when God asks something of you, respond with humility and willingness. Ornan offered everything with generosity, and David wanted his worship to cost him something real. Worshiping God is not giving what is left over.
exp.20:22:
Here David asks Ornan for the place where he was threshing wheat. The threshing floor was a flat, firm piece of ground where the grain was separated from the chaff. David wants to build an altar to the LORD there, and he asks to buy it for its full price, that is, for its complete and fair value, so that the plague affecting the people will end.

David, the king of Israel, is speaking. A plague had fallen on the people after he ordered a census, and now he seeks a place to offer sacrifices and ask for mercy. Ornan, who is also called Araunah in other passages, wants to give him everything, but David insists on paying.

For today: our sincere worship of God should not be cheap. We can ask ourselves what we are willing to give, in time, effort, or resources, to serve him truly and not only when it is easy for us.
exp.20:25:
David paid Ornan six hundred shekels of gold for the place where the threshing floor was.

After the plague that fell on Israel because of David's sin in counting the people, the angel of the Lord stopped beside Ornan's threshing floor. David wanted to build an altar there to seek forgiveness. Ornan offered him the place for free, but David refused: he did not want to offer God something that cost him nothing.

Today, worshiping God truly involves commitment and sacrifice. Ask yourself what you give the Lord that costs you time, effort, or money, and not just what you have left over.
exp.20:27:
This verse says that God gave an order to the angel who was bringing punishment on Israel, and the angel stopped acting. The phrase about the sword going back into its sheath means that the angel put the sword back in its scabbard, that is, he halted the judgment.

David had sinned by taking a census of the people, and a plague came that killed many. When David bought the threshing floor of Ornan, he built an altar and offered sacrifices, and God answered with fire from heaven. After that, the angel stopped punishing. The text does not explain every detail, but it shows that God accepted the offering and stopped the punishment.

For today: when we fail, we can return to God with humility and sincerity. He is just, but he is also willing to forgive and to put a limit on the harm. His mercy has the last word.
exp.20:28:
David, seeing that the Lord had answered him on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, offered sacrifices right there. The threshing floor was a flat piece of ground where wheat was beaten out of the stalks. Having heard him meant that God had answered his prayer.

The narrator of Chronicles tells how David had sinned by taking a census, and a plague fell on Israel. When the angel stayed his sword, David recognized that God had heard him and worshiped in that place. The verses that follow explain that the tabernacle was far away, in Gibeon, and David was afraid to go there because of the sword of the angel.

For today: when God answers you in a difficult moment, do not carry on as if nothing happened. Stop, give thanks, and worship him right there. You do not need a special place to draw near to him with gratitude.
exp.21:0:
Here David declares that this place will be the site of God's temple and of the altar where the burnt offering will be presented, that is, the offering that was burned whole for God. "LORD" is the name of the Lord.

David speaks here after the sin of the census and the plague that followed. He had offered a sacrifice on the threshing floor of Ornan, and God answered there (1 Chronicles 21). Then David understands that this place is the chosen one. Although he will not be able to build the temple himself, he begins to prepare stone, iron, bronze and cedar so that his son Solomon can build it.

For today: God can turn a place of wrongdoing and pain into a place of worship. If you are carrying a failure today, bring it honestly before God. And, like David, prepare with faith what others will continue after you.
exp.21:4:
Here David says that his son Solomon is young and tender. The house for the Lord had to be exceeding magnifical, that is, very grand, so that his name would be honored in all countries. That is why David decides to make ready, that is, to prepare everything that was needed. And he gathered materials in great abundance before he died.

David speaks as an old man. God did not permit him to build the temple, so he devoted himself to getting everything ready for Solomon. Shortly afterward he gives Solomon the work directly. He had gathered iron, bronze, cedar and more, some of it brought by the Sidonians and Tyrians.

Today we can learn to serve God even when we do not see the final result. Perhaps you will not be the one to finish the work, but you can prepare the way: pray for your children, teach them the faith, or support those who come after you.
exp.21:5:
David called his son Solomon and charged him to build a house for the Lord God of Israel. Here the wording "house" means a temple, the place where God would be worshiped.

David was already old and knew that he would not be the one to build the temple. So before he died, he prepared materials in abundance and handed the task to his son, who was still young and inexperienced. Later, the text explains that God did not allow David to build it because of the wars he had fought.

We can learn from David to serve God even when we do not see the full result. He prepared the way for another. Today we can pray, teach, save, or serve in the church, with the aim of blessing those who will come after us.
exp.21:8:
God promises David that he will have a son who will be a "man of rest", that is, a man of peace and tranquility. God himself will give him rest from the enemies around him. That is why his name will be Solomon, which is connected with the Hebrew word for "peace". Furthermore, God promises that in the days of this son there will be peace and quietness over Israel.

David speaks to his son Solomon. He tells him that he wanted to build the temple, but God told him he would not do it, because he had taken part in many wars and shed much blood. That task would belong to Solomon, whose reign would be peaceful.

For today: sometimes God closes a door we desire, but opens another through someone else. We can accept his direction with humility, support those who carry on the work, and trust that God gives peace in his time.
exp.21:14:
Here David tells his son Solomon that he already has many skilled people ready to build the temple. He mentions officials, stonecutters (those who cut and shape the stone), masons and carpenters, along with every man who is skilled in any kind of work.

David speaks near the end of his life. God did not allow him to build the temple, so he spent his last years preparing materials and people. He wants to encourage Solomon, who is young, so that he will not fear such a great task. Just before this verse he reminded Solomon that obeying God is the foundation for prospering.

God often gives us resources and people before asking us to take on a great task. When you feel that a project is bigger than you, look with gratitude at what you already have: talents, friends, support. Take the first step trusting that God is with you and works through others, without trying to do everything alone.
exp.21:16:
This verse says that David also ordered all the leaders of Israel to help his son Solomon. The word "leaders" refers to the heads of the people, and the phrase "ordered" means that he gave a command. The colon at the end introduces what David is about to tell them next.

David speaks near the end of his life. God did not allow him to build the temple, so he prepared everything so that Solomon would be the one to build it. First he encouraged his son, and now he asks the leaders to support him. Solomon was young and the task was enormous, so he needed help.

For today: no one does a great work for God alone. We can encourage and support those who carry a responsibility, whether in the church, the family, or the workplace. Let us ask ourselves today whom we can help with a word, our time, or our labor.
exp.21:17:
He says that God is with the people and has given them rest on every side. David affirms that God put the inhabitants of the land under his hand, and that the territory was subdued before the Lord and before Israel. "Rest" means quiet and peace; "inhabitants" are the people who dwell in the land.

David speaks to the leaders of Israel at the end of his life. He had prepared materials for the temple, but God gave that work to Solomon. Now David asks the chief men to help his son. He reminds them that God has already given them peace, so this is a good time to build. Some understand that the conquest was not yet complete in every detail, but David speaks of the peace they were enjoying in his time.

Today, times of calm are an opportunity to serve God. We should not spend them only on comfort; let us use them to help others, support the work of the church, and seek the Lord.
exp.21:18:
Here David encourages Israel's leaders to give their whole heart and their entire being to seeking God. Then he calls them to rise up and build the sanctuary, to bring the ark of the covenant and the holy vessels into the temple that would be built in honor of the name of the Lord. The word "soul" in the verse refers to the inner self or being, and "sanctuary" refers to the place of worship.

David speaks to the leaders of Israel near the end of his life, after he had given his son Solomon the task of building the temple. God had given them peace with their neighbors, and David wants them to use that rest to obey and support Solomon.

For today: when God gives us a time of calm, it is not only for resting. We can use it to seek him sincerely and to serve in whatever he places before us, beginning with prayer before we act.
exp.22:3:
This verse says that of the 38,000 Levites counted, 24,000 would be in charge of overseeing and moving forward the work of the house of the Lord, that is, the temple. Another 6,000 would be officers and judges.

King David, now old, prepares everything so that his son Solomon can build the temple. He gathers the leaders, priests, and Levites, and organizes them by their tasks. The Levites were the tribe set apart for serving God. According to the text, he counted those from thirty years old and upward, although later in the chapter another age is also mentioned, and for that reason some scholars explain it in different ways.

For today: in God's work there is room for many different gifts. Some organize, others serve, others teach. Ask God in which task you can help with steadiness and joy in your church.
exp.22:4:
It says that of the counted Levites, four thousand would be gatekeepers, that is, responsible for guarding the doors and the entrance of the temple. Another four thousand would be devoted to praising the Lord with musical instruments that David had made for that purpose. To praise means to acknowledge and celebrate the greatness of God.

The passage describes what David did in his old age, when he left his son Solomon as king. David would not build the temple himself, but he prepared everything so that it could be raised up and function well. He organized the Levites by their tasks: work, judgment, watching, and music. The numbers are large, and some scholars take them literally, while others see them as figures that show a broad organization.

For today: God values the one who guards the door as much as the one who sings. In your church or family, serve wherever there is a need, without comparing tasks, doing everything as worship to God.
exp.22:6:
This verse says that Gershon, one of the sons of Levi, had two sons: Laadan and Shimei. It is the beginning of a list that arranges the Levites by their families. "Shimei" is another way of spelling the name, and in some versions it appears in that form.

Here the writer of Chronicles tells how King David, already old, organized the Levites for the service of the temple that Solomon would build. David divided them into groups according to the three sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Each group received tasks, such as keeping the gates or leading the praise. Some scholars note that this Shimei may not be the same as the one who appears in other passages, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God pays attention to each person and each family, not only to the famous ones. Serving God in simple things and with order has value before Him. Ask yourself what place you can faithfully fill in your church or community.
exp.22:7:
This verse names the three sons of Laadan: Jehiel, Zetham, and Joel. Saying that Jehiel was the "first" probably means he was the eldest or the head of the family.

The book of Chronicles, written by an author who is not named in the text, tells that David, now old, organized the Levites by their families for the service of the temple that Solomon would build. Laadan was a descendant of Gershon, one of the three sons of Levi. Some of the lists in this area are difficult to reconcile, and scholars explain them in different ways.

God knows and remembers by name people whom almost no one mentions. Today, your simple and steady service in the church or in the family also matters to God, even though no one applauds it. Serve it faithfully.
exp.22:9:
The verse lists four sons of Shimei from the tribe of Levi: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. It is part of a list of Levite families. This Shimei appears to be different from the one in the preceding verse, and scholars do not agree on how the two are related.

The passage tells how King David, now old, organized the Levites by families for the service of the temple that his son Solomon would build. The next verse explains that Jeush and Beriah had few sons, so they were counted as a single family. In this way the record was kept in order.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to names that almost no one remembers. Your service, however small or quiet it may seem, has value to Him. Serve faithfully where you are, without seeking recognition.
exp.22:12:
This verse says that Amram had two famous sons: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart to be dedicated to the most holy things, together with his sons, forever. His work was to burn incense before God, to serve him, and to bless the people in his name. "Set apart" means he was chosen and put aside for a sacred use.

The writer of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews the families of Levi. This takes place when David, now old, organizes the Levites for the service of the temple that Solomon would build. Aaron is highlighted because the priests came from his family. The sons of Moses, by contrast, are mentioned afterward as ordinary Levites.

For today: serving God is a calling, not just a task. Ask God how he wants to use you, and do what he entrusts to you with care and gratitude, whether in the church, in your home, or at your work.
exp.22:14:
This verse says that Moses had two sons: Gershom and Eliezer. It is a very brief family list. In the text, "sons" refers to the descendants who would carry on his line.

The author, whom tradition calls the Chronicler, reviews the families of Levi while David prepares the service of the temple. Aaron and his sons receive the priestly office. Moses' sons, though he was a man of God, are counted only as ordinary Levites. Their place is simple, and the text does not say why. This shows that service in the temple depended on God's calling, not on family fame.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is quiet. You do not need an important position or a great name to be useful in his work. Do with love what he has placed in your hands.
exp.22:15:
This verse says that the firstborn son of Gershom was named Shebuel. The word "was" is spelled differently in older texts, and "the first" means the eldest or the leader of that family. Shebuel also appears under other spellings, such as Shubael, in other passages, and the name is written in different ways depending on the text.

The book of Chronicles was written by an author who is not named in the text, and many believe it was written after the exile in Babylon. Here David is already old, and he organizes the Levites for service in the temple. The descendants of Moses are listed to show that they too had a place, even though they were not priests.

God takes account of every person, even those who seem quiet and unnoticed in the story. Today we can serve faithfully in ordinary things, without seeking recognition, trusting that God sees and values what we do for Him.
exp.22:16:
This verse says that Eliezer, son of Moses, had one son, named Rehabiah, who was both the first and the only one. But the family of Rehabiah grew greatly, with many descendants.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records here how David organized the Levites for the service of the temple. The family lists showed that each group had its place and its task. The descendants of Moses appear as ordinary Levites, without any special privileges.

For today: do not lose heart if your beginning seems small. Eliezer had only one son, and yet God multiplied that family. What matters is being faithful where God has placed you, because he can make grow what seems little.
exp.22:17:
This verse says that, among the descendants of Izhar, Shelomith was the chief or the leader.

Here the chronicler reviews the families of the Levites, the tribe responsible for serving in worship. David, already old, had made Solomon king and was organizing the Levites for service in the future temple. These lists show that each family had a defined place and task. We do not know much more about Shelomith from this verse.

For today: God pays attention to people and to their service, even when their name appears only in a list. You can serve faithfully in your place, without seeking applause, trusting that God sees and values what you do.
exp.22:18:
This verse lists the four sons of Hebron, who was a descendant of Levi through the family of Kohath: Jeriah, Amariah, Jahaziel, and Jekameam. The order of birth is given by the words "the first," "the second," and so on.

The book of Chronicles is a narrative that recalls the history of Israel, and its author is traditionally identified with Ezra, though this is not certain. Here David, now old, organizes the Levites for the service of the temple that his son Solomon would later build. That is why families and names are recorded: each one had a place and a task.

For today: though these names may seem distant to us, they remind us that God knows each person and gives them a place in his work. Ask yourself what simple task you can carry out faithfully in your church or community, without thinking it is small.
exp.22:19:
This verse says that Uzziel had two principal sons: Michah was the first, and Jesiah was the second. It is part of a list of Levite families. "The first" and "the second" indicate the order in which they are mentioned, probably by their rank or by birth order.

The book of Chronicles tells the history of Israel, and Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, though this is not known with certainty. Here the author describes how David, now old, organized the Levites to serve in the temple that his son Solomon would build. The lists of names showed that each family had a place and a task in worship.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your service, though it may seem small or little seen, matters. Serve faithfully where God has placed you.
exp.22:20:
It says that Merari, one of the sons of Levi, had two sons: Mahli and Mushi. Then it mentions that Mahli had two sons, Eleazar and Kish. It is part of a family list, and the names are written as they appear in this older version.

The author, who according to Jewish and Christian tradition is the Chronicler (many think it was Ezra, though this is not certain), records here the families of the Levites. David, already old, had made his son Solomon king and organized the Levites for the service of the temple that was going to be built. Merari was one of the three great Levite branches, along with Gershon and Kohath. This list shows who would serve and how the work would be arranged.

God looks at people and their families, not only at the great leaders. Even little-known names had a place in his house. Today you can remember that your service, though it may seem small or hidden, is valuable to God. Serve faithfully where you are.
exp.22:22:
This verse lists the three sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth. Mushi was a son of Merari, and Merari was a son of Levi. It is part of a list of families, and the words "three" simply tell us how many there were. Note that one of Mushi's sons has the same name as his uncle Mahli, which was common in ancient genealogies.

The author of the book, traditionally called the Chronicler, records here how the Levites were organized when David, now old, made Solomon king. David counted them and prepared them to serve in the temple that would be built in Jerusalem. Each name shows that no Levite was left out of serving God.

For today: God overlooks no one, even when a name appears only once. If your service is small or hardly seen, remember that God sees it and values it. Serve faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.22:24:
He says that David recognized God had given rest and peace to Israel, and that He dwells in Jerusalem forever. "Rest" means peace from enemies, a time free of conflict. "Dwell" means to live in or make one's home.

David speaks near the end of his life, when he prepares Solomon as king and organizes the Levites. Since there was now peace and the temple would be built, the Levites would no longer need to carry the tabernacle from place to place. That is why David expands their service, counting from the age of twenty. Some understand "forever" as a lasting promise, and others see it fulfilled in Christ.

For today: when God gives you a time of rest, don't use it only to relax. Ask Him how you can serve Him more fully, in your church or with the people around you.
exp.22:27:
This verse says that the Levites were under the direction of the priests, the descendants of Aaron, to help in the service of the temple. They took care of the courts (the yards) and the chambers (the rooms used for storing things). They also helped in the purifying, that is, in the cleaning of everything set apart for God, and in the rest of the work of the house of God.

The one narrating is the chronicler, and he tells what King David did at the end of his life. Since the temple would be permanent, the Levites no longer had to carry the tabernacle, the tent of worship that moved from place to place. David then gave them new tasks, more stable and varied.

For today: serving God is not always something visible. Cleaning, tidying, or helping with humility is also worship. Ask God what simple task you can do this week in your church or community.
exp.22:28:
This verse lists some of the duties of the Levites in the temple. They took care of the showbread, which was the bread set out each week before God in the holy place. They also looked after the fine flour for the grain offering, the unleavened wafers (thin cakes made without yeast), what was baked in a pan, and what was fried. In addition, they took care of every measure and size, that is, that everything was done with order and accuracy.

The account comes from the last stage of David's reign. He was already old and was organizing the service of the Levites for when his son Solomon would build the temple.
