The Levites assisted the priests, who were descendants of Aaron. Here the text shows that serving God included very practical and simple tasks.

For today: God values faithful service, even the kind that goes unnoticed. We can serve in the church or at home with order, care, and a good heart, as if serving God himself.
exp.22:29:
This verse says that the Levites were to be present every morning and likewise every evening, to give thanks and praise to the Lord. Here "give thanks" means publicly acknowledging and thanking God for who He is and for what He does.

The passage speaks of David, already old, who organizes the service of the temple before his son Solomon builds it. Here he describes the duties of the Levites, assistants to the priests. Besides caring for the place and preparing the bread and offerings, they had a constant task: praising God at the beginning and at the end of the day. In this way the worship had a daily, orderly rhythm.

For today: we can give God the beginning and the end of our day. A brief moment of gratitude in the morning and another at night is enough to remember that everything we have comes from Him.
exp.23:0:
The verse tells us that the descendants of Aaron, the first high priest, were also organized into groups or shifts of service. It names his four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The word "divisions" refers to these divisions or work groups.

Here the chronicler speaks, probably writing after the exile in Babylon, to remind the people how the temple service was arranged in the time of David. The verses that follow explain that Nadab and Abihu died without children, so the priesthood continued through Eleazar and Ithamar. David divided them into shifts so that worship would have order.

God values order and the participation of everyone in his work. Today we can ask ourselves what specific task falls to us in the church or the community, and carry it out faithfully, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.23:2:
This verse says that David organized the descendants of Aaron into groups. Zadok, from the family of Eleazar, and Ahimelech, from the family of Ithamar, helped him divide the priests into their divisions.

The passage is told by the chronicler, and it shows David preparing the service of the temple that his son Solomon would build. Nadab and Abihu had died without children, so only two lines remained in the priesthood. With so many priests, order was needed so that everything would be done with reverence.

For today: God cares about order and about the participation of everyone. In the church, the family, or the workplace, serving in turns and with responsibility prevents disorder and allows many to serve without anyone carrying the whole load.
exp.23:3:
This verse tells that when the priests were organized, it was found that the descendants of Eleazar had more heads of families than those of Ithamar. For that reason, Eleazar received sixteen family groups and Ithamar eight. The "heads of families" are the leaders of each household or clan. "Found" means it was checked or counted.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile, and tradition attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. Here the text tells what King David did: he arranged the shifts of service in the temple. Nadab and Abihu had died without sons, so only two priestly branches remained. The shifts were divided by lot, so that it would be fair and orderly.

For today: God cares for order and for the participation of everyone in his service. In your church or family, serve faithfully in the place that falls to you, without competing or looking down on others.
exp.23:10:
In the verse, it says that when the priests were divided into service shifts, the ninth lot fell to the family of Jeshua, and the tenth to the family of Shecaniah.

It is a list within a story that tells how David, with the help of the priests Zadok and Ahimelech, organized the descendants of Aaron into 24 groups. Each group would serve in the temple in turns. Lots were cast so that the order would be fair. The chronicler writes after the exile and wants to remind the people that worship of God has order and roots. We do not know much more about these two men, apart from their mention here.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it goes unnoticed. There are names that almost no one remembers, yet they were written down. Do your part in your church or family with joy, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.23:12:
This verse continues a list of shifts. The thirteenth shift fell to Huppah (in other versions, Hupah), and the fourteenth to Jeshebeab (Jesebab). The words for thirteenth and fourteenth in the list are simply the ordinal numbers for those positions.

The book of Chronicles tells how King David organized the priests descended from Aaron into twenty-four groups. Each group would serve in rotation in the worship of the temple. The turns were assigned by lot, so that the order would be fair and orderly. The one who tells the account is the chronicler, who wanted to record these names for the people. These men hardly appear in other passages.

For today: God values faithful service, even when no one remembers your name. Do your part in your family, your church, or your work with steadiness and order, as a service to God.
exp.23:13:
This verse says that the fifteenth turn of service in the temple fell to the family of Bilgah, and the sixteenth to that of Immer. The words "fifteenth" and "sixteenth" are the same as the verse's wording, so they need no further comment. They are two of the twenty-four groups of priests.

The chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, tells how David organized the priests. They cast lots before the king and the religious leaders, so that each group would know when it was its turn to serve. In this way worship was kept in order and no one was overlooked.

For today: God values those who serve in unglamorous places. Bilgah and Immer are not famous, yet they were recorded. Serve faithfully in what falls to you, even when no one applauds; God sees it.
exp.23:14:
This verse continues a list of shifts. It says that the family of Hezir received the seventeenth shift, and the family of Aphses (today it is often written Afses or Pisés) the eighteenth. The word that introduces each name means that each shift was assigned to a priestly household, that is, to a family descended from Aaron.

The author is the Chronicler, who tells how David organized the priests into twenty-four groups for service in the temple. The shifts were decided by lot, so that the order would be fair and no one would feel favored. Here there is no speech, only an orderly record. The names were preserved because each family had a real task.

For today: God values steady service, even when it is little seen. If today you are given a simple task in your church or family, do it faithfully. God knows your name and your place.
exp.23:15:
This verse continues a list of turns assigned to the priests. It says that the nineteenth lot fell to Pethahiah, and the twentieth to Jehezekel. Each name stands for a priestly family with its own turn of service.

The account is told by the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. It tells that King David, together with the leaders of the priests, organized the descendants of Aaron into 24 groups. They divided them by casting lots, so that the service in the temple would be orderly and without favoritism.

For today: God cares about order and values each person, even those whom almost no one remembers. Serve faithfully in the place that is yours, without comparing yourself to others, for your service matters.
exp.23:19:
This verse begins a list of Levites who were not priests. "The rest" are the other descendants of Levi, apart from Aaron's family. It names Shubael, from the line of Amram, and his son Jehdeiah. In other lists the name appears as Shebuel or Shebuel son of Gershom, so some details of the names are explained in different ways.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile, and its author is unknown (Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, but this is not certain). Here it describes how David organized the service of the temple in shifts. After arranging the priests, it also records the other Levites, so that the people would remember that worship had order and that each family had its place.

For today: God does not forget those who serve in silence. Many names here barely appear anywhere else, but they were written down. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one applauds you.
exp.23:20:
This verse says that, among the descendants of Rehabiah, Isshiah was the head or leader of the family. The phrase "the first" means he was the one who led that group. Rehabiah was the son of Eliezer, grandson of Moses, according to 1 Chronicles 23:17.

Here no one speaks within a scene. It is the chronicler, who carefully records the lists of the Levites. These lists show how service in the temple was organized, with families arranged for their ministry. It is part of a historical record, not a speech. Names are mentioned so that each family would know its place.

For today: God pays attention to each person and each service, even when it seems small or little known. Today you can serve faithfully in your church or family, without needing applause. God remembers those who serve with steadiness and order.
exp.23:24:
This verse continues a list of Levite families. It says that Isshiah was the brother of Micah, and that Zechariah was the son of Isshiah. These names belong to the family of Uzziel, a descendant of Kohath.

The book of Chronicles does not have a narrator who can be identified with certainty; tradition attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. Here it is told how David organized the priests and Levites for the service of the temple, and lots were cast to divide the duties. Even the less well-known names are recorded, because each person had a place in that service.

For today: God overlooks no one, not even those who are hardly ever mentioned. Your humble service in the church or in your family also has value. Do your task faithfully today, even if no one applauds it.
exp.23:27:
It says that from the family of Mahli, a descendant of Merari and a Levite, came Eleazar, who died without leaving sons. The phrase "who had no sons" means that he had no descendants to carry on his family line. Later it is clarified that he had daughters (1 Chronicles 23:22).

It is part of a list of Levite families that the chronicler presents while describing how David organized the priests and Levites to serve in the temple. The text is a historical chronicle, written after the exile, to remind the Israelites of their roots and their service to God. Here the one speaking is not a character but the narrator.

For today: our worth does not depend on leaving a great, visible legacy. God remembers even those who seem to have no continuity. Serve faithfully where you are; God sees what you do.
exp.23:30:
These likewise cast lots, as their brothers the sons of Aaron did, to decide their turns of duty. The Levites, that is, those who helped in the service of the temple, also drew lots to know their turn of work, just as the sons of Aaron, who were the priests, had done. Casting lots was a way of deciding without favoritism, like drawing something by chance. They did this in the presence of King David, the priest Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the families. The final phrase points out that the head of the family and the younger brother were entered into the same drawing.

The text is part of an account by the Chronicler, who lists how David organized the service of the temple. Earlier, the turns of the priests had been divided, and here the same method is applied to the other Levites. The purpose was that everything be done with order and with justice.

Today we can learn that in the church and in the family, service to God does not depend on importance or age. Everyone has a place and a valuable task. Let us serve with humility and without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.24:5:
This verse says that all the sons of Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman sang and played in the house of the Lord under the direction of their father. They used cymbals (metal plates), psalteries (stringed instruments, something like a lyre), and harps. All of this was for the service of the temple, by the order of King David.

The text is a historical account by the chronicler, who records how the music of worship was organized. The king is mentioned here without being named, and most readers understand him to be David. The author wants to show that worship had order, dedicated families, and a clear calling, not improvisation.

For today: worship grows stronger when it is learned and served in family and in community. If you have a gift, put it at the service of your church with humility and order, and help others, young people or children, to grow in it.
exp.24:6:
This verse says that the total number of musicians from the families of Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman, together with their relatives, was 288. All of them were trained (that is, taught and instructed) in singing and music for God, and all were skilled, meaning capable and qualified to serve.

Here the chronicler speaks, recalling how worship at the temple was organized in the days of David. The music was not improvised: teams were prepared to praise God. Then lots were cast to assign the shifts, and the young and the old, the teacher and the student, all took part alike.

For today: if you serve God with some talent, do not neglect it. Prepare yourself, practice, and keep learning with humility. And remember that in the church everyone counts, from the newest member to the most experienced.
exp.24:8:
This verse tells how the shifts of service for the temple musicians were divided. The first "lot," that is, the drawing of lots, fell to Joseph, of the family of Asaph. The second fell to Gedaliah. Each group had twelve people, counting their brothers and sons.

The book of Chronicles describes here the arrangement that King David made for worship in the temple. The author does not name himself; many think it was Ezra, but this is not certain. Lots were used so that the order would be fair: the young and the old, the teacher and the student, all took part on equal terms.

For today: God values the service of everyone, not only of the most gifted or visible. Serve where and when your turn comes, with faithfulness, without comparing yourself to others or seeking first place.
exp.24:14:
The eighth turn, or group of service, fell to Jeshaiah. His group had twelve people in all: he, his sons, and his brothers. The "eighth" points to the order that came up by lot.

This is part of a list in which the chronicler describes how King David organized the musicians of the temple. There were 24 groups of twelve, and the order of service was decided by casting lots (1 Chronicles 25:8). The passage was written to remind its readers that the praise offered in the temple had order, and that each family had an assigned place in it.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is seldom seen. No one named in this list is famous, yet each name is recorded. Let us gladly take the place given to us, serving alongside others and without comparing ourselves to them.
exp.24:15:
This verse says that the ninth lot, or turn of service, fell to Mattaniah. He took part with his sons and his brothers, and in total there were twelve people.

The passage is part of a list that describes how King David organized the musicians of the temple, together with the heads of the Levites. Lots were cast to divide the turns of service in praise. The passage gives us no further details about Mattaniah. It simply lists each leader with his group of twelve, which shows order and care.

For today: God values the service of every person, even the kind that seems small or hardly seen. If you have a simple place in your church or your family, do it faithfully and work as a team, knowing that God sees and remembers your labor.
exp.24:16:
This verse says that the tenth turn or lot fell to Shimei. He served with his sons and his brethren, and in total there were twelve people. The word "tenth" refers to the tenth group in the list.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks, describing how King David organized the musicians of the temple into 24 groups of twelve. They cast lots to divide the turns of service. Shimei here corresponds to the name that appears in verse 3 as Shimei, son of Jeduthun, though some scholars think there was a copying error in the list.

For today: God values orderly and shared service. No one did everything alone, and each group had its place. Look for ways to serve alongside others in your church, without seeking the spotlight.
exp.24:17:
The eleventh lot, or turn of service, fell to Azareel. He, together with his group of twelve made up of his sons and brothers, would serve together.

This is not a character speaking; it is the chronicler recording how King David organized the temple musicians into 24 groups of twelve, so that they would praise God in turns. The turns were assigned by casting lots, so that no one chose by preference.

The name Azareel also appears as Uziel in verse 4, and scholars often see it as another form of the same name, though this is not entirely certain.

For today: God values orderly and shared service, even service that seems small or unnoticed. You can serve faithfully in your church or family, without needing recognition, trusting that God sees your part.
exp.24:18:
This verse says that the twelfth group, or turn, fell to Hashabiah. His group was twelve people, counting his sons and his brothers, that is, his relatives.

The Chronicler tells how King David organized the Levites who served with music in worship. They were divided into twenty-four groups of twelve, and the turns were assigned by casting lots. In this way the service was kept in order and no one was preferred over another. Many understand that this helped make the praise in the temple continuous.

For today: God values orderly and shared service, even when no one sees our name. Do the task that falls to you in your church or family with joy, without comparing yourself to others, because every part counts.
exp.24:20:
This verse says that the fourteenth lot, in the list of temple musicians, fell to Mattithiah. He served together with his sons and his brothers, and in total there were twelve people.

Here no character speaks in a dialogue. This is the account in 1 Chronicles, which tells how King David organized the families of Asaph, Jeduthun and Heman to serve in music for worship. They were divided into 24 groups of twelve, and the text says that lots were cast (v. 8). In this way each family knew when its turn to serve would come.

For today: God values steady, orderly service, even when it is not very visible. Your place in the church or the family matters, and serving as a team helps everyone take part.
exp.24:21:
This verse says that the fifteenth lot, in the service of music in the temple, fell to Jeremoth. He, his sons, and his brothers formed a group of twelve people. The number fifteen is simply the fifteenth in order, and "brothers" here probably refers to relatives or fellow members of the same family line.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), tells how David organized the musicians for service in the house of God. They cast lots to divide the shifts among 24 groups, each of twelve. In this way favoritism was avoided and everything was kept in order. Jeremoth was a descendant of Heman, one of the musical leaders.

For today: God values the service of every person, even of those whom almost no one remembers. Serve wherever you are needed, with steadiness and without seeking recognition, because in the body of Christ every task has value.
exp.24:22:
It says that the sixteenth lot, among the groups of temple musicians, fell to Hananiah. His group was made up of him, his sons, and his brothers, twelve people in all. The phrase "the sixteenth" simply means the number sixteen.

The writer of Chronicles describes how King David organized the music service in the house of God. Lots were cast to divide 24 shifts among the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, who praised with harps, lyres, and cymbals. Each group had twelve people. The repetition of the pattern shows that the order was even, and that each family had an assigned place.

For today: God values steady, orderly service, even when no one applauds it. Your part in the church, the family, or the workplace, however small it may seem, counts before Him. Serve faithfully and joyfully in the turn that falls to you.
exp.24:23:
The seventeenth lot fell to Joshbekashah. He, together with his sons and his brothers, formed a group of twelve people.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the chronicler's account. King David organized the Levites to serve with music in worship. He divided them into 24 groups, and lots were cast to set the order of each one. This list repeats the same pattern for each group, so it shows order and the participation of everyone.

God values steady service, even when it is not conspicuous. Joshbekashah appears only once, but his place mattered. Today you can serve in your church or family faithfully, doing your part without comparing yourself to others, for God counts on each person.
exp.24:24:
This verse says that the eighteenth group of temple musicians was assigned to Hanani, together with his sons and his brothers, twelve people in all. The eighteenth is the number 18 in the order of the groups.

The passage is part of an account written by the chronicler, whose identity we do not know for certain, though many think it was Ezra. It tells how David organized the musicians to serve in the house of God. Lots were cast to divide the work into 24 shifts, each with twelve people. This list shows that worship was well ordered and that each person had his or her place.

For today: God values steady service, even the kind that almost no one sees. Hanani appears only once, but his work mattered. Think of a simple way you can serve in your church or family, and do it faithfully, without looking for applause.
exp.24:25:
The nineteenth group of temple musicians fell to Mallothi, along with his sons and his brothers, twelve in all.

King David organized the Levites to serve in the music of the temple. There were 24 groups of twelve, and the order of their service was decided by casting lots (1 Chronicles 25:8). Mallothi belonged to the family line of Heman. This list of names shows that each group had its place and its turn.

God values the service of everyone, including those whom almost no one remembers. Mallothi appears only in a list, but his work was part of the worship of the people. Today, serve faithfully in your place, even when it is simple or little seen.
exp.24:27:
This verse says that the twenty-first lot for service in the temple fell to Hothir (in this version, "Othir"), together with his sons and his brothers, twelve people in all. This was a group of musicians assigned to one shift of service.

Context: The chronicler, who according to Jewish tradition was Ezra (this is not certain), tells how King David organized the Levites. The sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun were set apart to minister with harps, lyres, and cymbals. The 24 families of musicians received their turn by lot, so no one was placed above another. Each group had twelve members.

For today: God values steady service, even when it is little seen. This man appears only in a list, but his place mattered. Serve where God has put you, faithfully and as part of a team.
exp.24:28:
This verse says that the twenty-second group of musicians fell to Giddalti. His group was made up of twelve people: him, his sons, and his brothers.

Here no particular person is speaking. The chronicler tells how King David, together with the leaders of the temple service, arranged the Levites into twenty-four shifts to sing and play instruments in the worship of God. Lots were cast to set the order of the shifts. The author includes each name to show that everyone had a place and a task.

For today: God values the service of each person, even when no one applauds it. Ask yourself what simple task you can do faithfully in your church or family, and do it as for the Lord.
exp.25:1:
This verse lists the sons of Meshelemiah, a Levite who served as a gatekeeper of the temple. The order of birth is given: Zechariah was the first, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, and Jathniel the fourth. "Firstborn" means the eldest son.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records how David organized the shifts of the gatekeepers, who guarded the doors and the entrance of the temple. He writes for a people who were returning from exile and needed to remember that worship of God had order, and that each family had its place. That is why so many names appear.

For today: God notices simple and steady service, even when no one applauds it. Guarding a door does not seem like much, yet it was written down. Serve faithfully wherever you are, because God sees you and remembers you.
exp.25:2:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Meshelemiah, one of the gatekeepers of the temple. Three are named here: Elam, the fifth; Jehohanan, the sixth; and Elioenai, the seventh. It is part of a family record, where each son appears in his order of birth.

The writer of Chronicles, whom tradition often associates with Ezra, though this is not certain, records how David organized the service shifts of the Levites. The gatekeepers guarded the doors and the entrance of the temple. Meshelemiah had many sons, and several of them served in this task. The list shows that each family had an assigned place.

For today: God notices services that seem small, like guarding a door, and knows by name those who perform them. If your work goes unnoticed, remember that God sees it and values it. Serve him faithfully wherever you are.
exp.25:3:
This verse lists five sons of Obed-edom: Shemaiah, the firstborn, followed by Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, and Nethaneel. They are part of a longer list, since the next verse adds three more sons and says that God blessed Obed-edom.

The passage is part of the Chronicler's account of how worship in the temple was organized in the time of King David. Here the families of the Levites who served as gatekeepers are named, the men who guarded the gates and the storerooms. Many believe this Obed-edom is the same man who hosted the ark of the covenant in his house, though not everyone affirms this with certainty.

Today we can learn that God notices faithful service, even in simple tasks like watching a gate. If you serve in your church or your family without many people noticing, remember that God knows your name and values your steadfastness.
exp.25:4:
This verse ends the list of the eight sons of Obed-edom: Ammiel was the sixth, Issachar the seventh, and Peulthai the eighth. It makes clear that having so many children was a sign that God had blessed him. Here, "blessed" means that God gave him favor and a large family.

It is part of the lists of Levites who served as gatekeepers of the temple in the time of King David. There is no direct speaker; the chronicler is the one recording the names. Obed-edom is probably the same man in whose house the ark of the covenant stayed (2 Samuel 6:11), although some scholars debate this. His family was honored with a service in the temple.

God cares for those who honor his presence. We do not have to measure his blessing only by the number of children or possessions; we also see it in a life of faithful service to God.
exp.25:9:
This verse introduces Hosah, a Levite from the family of Merari, and his son Simri, who was made the head over the sons of Hosah. Simri was not the firstborn, that is, the oldest son, but his father appointed him to lead the family.

This is a list of the gatekeepers of the temple, from the time when the service was organized, a period traditionally linked to the reign of David. The author, whom tradition identifies as the Chronicler, records names and duties to show that the worship of God had order. The text does not explain why the father chose Simri; it only says that he did.

For today: serving God does not depend on the place we hold by birth or by appearance. God can use the one we least expect. Serve faithfully wherever you are entrusted, and if you are asked to guide others, do so with humility and responsibility.
exp.25:11:
This verse says that the gatekeepers, that is, those in charge of guarding the doors of the temple, were organized into groups. The heads of each family took turns standing guard together with their brothers. All of them had the same purpose: to serve in the house of the Lord, that is, in the temple.

This is part of a list of the Levites whom David organized for the service of the temple. The writer of Chronicles, who writes long after these events, wants to remind readers that worship of God had order and that each family had its place. The verses that follow explain that they divided the gates by casting lots, both the small and the great.

For today: there are no small tasks in God's house. Even if guarding a door may seem like little, God values faithful service. This week, look for a simple way to serve in your church and do it with joy, together with others.
exp.25:16:
This verse describes how many Levites guarded each side of the temple: six to the east, four to the north, and four to the south, each day.

The author of Chronicles, writing after the exile, reviews how David organized the Levite gatekeepers for the service of God. No one speaks here; it is a record of shifts. He wanted to show that worship was to be carried out with order and care, protecting what belonged to God.

For today: God values small, steady tasks, even when few people notice them. If in your church or family you are assigned to watch over, open, clean, or accompany others, do it faithfully. And share the load with others, as they did, two and two.
exp.25:21:
This verse says that the sons of Jehieli, namely Zetham and his brother Joel, were placed in charge of the treasures of the temple. "House of the Lord" is the temple, and "were in charge" means they were given the responsibility of watching over and managing those treasures.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), describes how King David organized the service of the temple before Solomon built it. The Levites, the tribe dedicated to serving God, received different duties: gatekeepers, musicians, and keepers of the treasures. Those treasures were offerings and objects dedicated to God. The passage shows order and shared responsibility among several families.

For today: what God entrusts to us, whether possessions, gifts, or time, calls for care and honesty. Today you might ask yourself: am I faithfully managing what God has placed in my hands?
exp.25:22:
This verse names four families from the tribe of Levi, descendants of Kohath: the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites. They are clans, that is, family groups that came from a common ancestor. The verse serves as an introduction to a list, and the information continues in the following verses.

The book of Chronicles, written after the exile, recalls how David organized the Levites for service in the temple. In this chapter, tasks are divided, such as guarding the gates and the treasures. Who wrote Chronicles is not known with certainty; tradition often mentions Ezra, but that is an opinion, not a certain fact. Here the text shows that each family had a place and a responsibility.

For today: God notices faithful service, even when it is quiet. Ask yourself what simple task you have been entrusted with in your church or family, and carry it out with honesty and care.
exp.25:24:
This verse continues the family line of Eliezer, the other son of Moses. It names his descendants: Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram, Zichri and, at the end, Shelomith. The phrases quoted from the original wording and the comments on them are not carried over here, since they do not appear in the verse you are reading.

Here no single person is being spoken about. The chronicler presents a list of Levites assigned to take care of the treasures of the temple in the days of David. Shelomith, a descendant of Eliezer, was in charge of the gifts dedicated to God, together with his brothers. Little is known about these people outside this passage.

For today: God values those who faithfully look after what has been dedicated to him, even when no one sees them or remembers them. Today we too can serve honestly in small things, such as money, time, or the tasks of the church, knowing that God knows every name and every service.
exp.25:27:
She says that Shelomith and his brothers took care of everything that had been set apart for God since the days of Samuel. This included what was dedicated by Samuel the seer (that is, the prophet), by King Saul, by Abner, and by Joab, the military leaders. "Dedicate" means to set something apart for God. They also looked after what others dedicated afterward.

Here the chronicler lists the duties of the Levites in David's kingdom. The treasures of the temple, which came largely from spoils of war, had to be kept in good order and honesty. In this way resources were gathered to repair the house of the LORD. The text says nothing more about how this was organized.

For today: what we give to God deserves care. If you are entrusted with money, time, or tasks in your church, manage them with order, honesty, and gratitude, as one who gives an account to God.
exp.25:30:
This verse says that among the Hebronites, a family of Levites descended from Hebron, Jerijah was the chief. They were organized by lineages and families. In the fortieth year of David's reign, a count was made, and it was found that among them there were strong and capable men in Jazer of Gilead, a city east of the Jordan.

Here the chronicler speaks, who is not David but the author of the book. He writes a list of Levites assigned to duties in the temple and also to matters of the kingdom. David wanted the service to God and the government to be well ordered, and so he reviewed the abilities of the families. The identity of the author is not known for certain, although Jewish tradition mentions Ezra.

For today: God values orderly service and the abilities of each person. Think about what skills you have and offer them faithfully in your church or community, even if your work is not seen by everyone.
exp.25:31:
This verse says that the brothers of Jeriah, 2,700 valiant men and heads of families, were placed by King David as overseers of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh. Those tribes lived east of the Jordan. King David appointed them, and their responsibility covered both matters pertaining to God and the affairs of the king.

The one speaking is the writer of Chronicles, who is not David. Tradition attributes the book to Ezra, although this is not certain. This account shows how David organized the service of the Levites at the end of his reign. Its purpose was that the people, even in distant territories, would be guided with order in both spiritual and civil life.

Today, this passage encourages us to serve faithfully and not to separate our faith from our daily responsibilities. Whether at work, in the family, or in the church, we can act with integrity, as those who serve God.
exp.26:0:
This verse describes how service to the king was organized in Israel. The people were divided into twelve groups, and each group served one month of the year in rotation. Each group had twenty-four thousand men, with heads of families, leaders of thousands, leaders of hundreds, and officers.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, presents the order that David left at the end of his reign. The leaders of each month are listed in what follows. The purpose seems to be to show a well-ordered kingdom, where everyone took part and no one carried the whole year's load.

For today: service works best when it is shared in an orderly way. In the church, the family, or the workplace, dividing up tasks and respecting turns prevents exhaustion and allows more people to contribute their gifts.
exp.26:2:
This verse says that Jashobeam, the leader of the division for the first month, was a descendant of Perez. It also says he was in charge of all the commanders of the groups assigned to that month. The verse's notes on the old spelling and on the meaning of a word from the verse are not needed here, since the verse above is already in modern English.

This is not a character speaking in a speech. The chronicler, who according to Jewish tradition was Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews how David organized the service to the king. There were twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand men, and each one served for one month in turn. This kept things orderly and spread the burden among everyone.

For today: God values order and shared service. When each person serves in their turn and in their place, no one is worn out and everyone contributes. In church, in the family, or at work, we can offer our part with steadiness and humility, without wanting to carry everything ourselves or leaving everything to others.
exp.26:6:
This verse says that the fourth commander of David's army, for the fourth month of the year, was Asahel, the brother of Joab. After him, his son Zebadiah took that role. That unit had twenty-four thousand men.

Here the chronicler presents the military organization of King David: twelve groups of twenty-four thousand men, each serving one month a year. Asahel died young, in David's time (2 Samuel 2:23). For that reason it is understood that his son continued the role, although the text does not explain exactly how that was arranged. Some scholars think the name remained as the title of the unit.

For today: God values orderly and steady service, even when it is not seen. There is work that is done in shifts and without applause. Serve faithfully wherever you are, and think also of the people who will continue what you begin.
exp.26:7:
It says that the fifth commander, in charge of the fifth month of the year, was Shamhuth, of the family of Izrah (this is how the name is understood). Under his command were twenty-four thousand men. In other versions, his name appears as Shamhuth.

This passage is part of the list the chronicler gives of how King David organized his army. There were twelve divisions, and each one served one month of the year in rotation. In this way, the service was shared and did not always fall on the same people. The writer of Chronicles then records the order that existed in David's time, to remind the people of it.

For today: shared and well-organized work cares for people and sustains the mission. In the family, the church, or the workplace, dividing tasks fairly prevents exhaustion and lets each person serve with joy and steadiness.
exp.26:8:
This verse says that the sixth commander, for the sixth month of the year, was Ira, son of Ikkesh, from the town of Tekoa. Under his command was a group of twenty-four thousand men.

Here the chronicler describes how King David organized Israel. Each month, a group of twenty-four thousand men was on duty, with its own leader. In this way the service was shared, and no one carried the whole weight alone. The text is part of a list and says nothing more about Ira. Tekoa was a town in Judah, and the prophet Amos would later come from there.

For today: good order and shared service help take care of everyone. In your family, your church, or your work, do your part faithfully and let others do theirs. God values even the services that almost no one sees.
exp.26:10:
The eighth captain for the eighth month was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zarhites, and his company had twenty-four thousand men. This verse tells us that Sibbecai, from the town of Hushah and from the family of Zerah, was in charge of the soldiers for the eighth month. His group had twenty-four thousand men.

Here the chronicler lays out how King David's kingdom was organized. The army was divided into twelve groups, and each group served one month of the year, so that no one bore the whole burden. It is written as a list of names to help people remember the order that existed in Israel. Some scholars think this Sibbecai is the same man who appears among David's mighty men, though the text does not state this with complete clarity.

For today: orderly, shared service makes a community strong. In your church or family, do your part gladly, without expecting recognition.
exp.26:11:
Abiezer, a man from Anathoth who belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, was in charge of the ninth group of service. He was to serve during the ninth month of the year, at the head of twenty-four thousand men.

The chronicler describes how King David organized military or national service. There were twelve groups, each with a leader and twenty-four thousand men, who served one month in turn. It is not David who speaks here; it is the chronicler's account, which lists these names in order. Some details of their exact task are not explained in the text.

For today: God values orderly and shared service. No one does everything all the time. Serve faithfully when your turn comes, even when no one applauds you, and trust that God sees your faithfulness.
exp.26:12:
It says that Maharai, from Netophah, was the commander of the military group for the tenth month. He was a descendant of Zerah (the verse's wording points to his family line through Zerah) and was in charge of a unit of twenty-four thousand men.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not entirely certain), shows how King David organized the army. Each month, a group of twenty-four thousand men served under a commander, so that the service was spread across the whole year. The list shows order and the participation of several families and tribes.

For today: God values steady, shared service. If each person faithfully carries out their turn, no one is worn out and the whole community is strengthened. Ask yourself where you can serve regularly in your church or your family.
exp.26:13:
This verse says that the commander for the eleventh month was Benaiah, from the town of Pirathon and of the tribe of Ephraim. Under his command were twenty-four thousand men.

The author of Chronicles is describing how King David organized Israel's army. Each month, a group of twenty-four thousand men served under a leader, and then they were relieved by the next. In this way there was order, rest, and steady service. The text most likely aims to show David's good leadership and the value of each person in the people, although we do not know all the details of how it worked.

For today: God cares about order and values teamwork in service. We can serve faithfully in our church or family, knowing that our part, though it may seem small, matters and is done better when we share the load.
exp.26:14:
This verse closes the list of the twelve military commanders of King David. Heldai, from the town of Netophah and a descendant of Othniel, was in charge of the last month of the year. His group had twenty-four thousand men. The word "division" means the group or shift of service that he was assigned to lead.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records how David organized the kingdom in his final years. Each commander served one month in turn, so there was always an army ready without always burdening the same men. With Heldai the twelve-month cycle comes to an end.

For today: God values order and shared service. If each person does their part at the right time, no one is worn out and everyone serves better. Think about how you can serve in your church or family with steady faithfulness, without feeling you have to carry everything alone.
exp.26:17:
The verse names two tribal leaders. For Judah, it gives Elihu, described as one of David's brothers, and for Issachar, Omri, son of Michael. The names are given in the spelling used in this version.

The book is a chronicle of Israel's history. The author, who does not speak in the first person, lists how David organized the kingdom: armies, officials, and tribal leaders. About Elihu there is some uncertainty. Some think he is another name for Eliab, David's eldest brother, but this is not certain. What we do see is that each tribe had a recognized leader.

Today: God values each person in their place, even when their name appears only in a list. Ask yourself what responsibility God has given you in your family, your church, or your work, and carry it out faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.26:20:
This verse continues a list of leaders placed over each tribe of Israel. Here Iddo, son of Zechariah, is named over the other half of the tribe of Manasseh, the part that lived in Gilead (east of the Jordan). Jaasiel, son of Abner, is also named as leader of Benjamin.

It is part of a record of how the kingdom was organized in the time of King David, toward the end of his reign. The writer of Chronicles does not speak in the first person; he simply presents the list. He probably wants to show that Israel was well ordered, with each tribe represented and with responsible men known by name.

For today: God takes notice of people who serve in tasks that seem small or little known. Today you can serve faithfully where you are, without needing applause, trusting that God remembers your name and your work.
exp.26:22:
This verse says that David did not count the men under twenty years old when the census was taken. The reason is that God had promised to make Israel as numerous as the stars of the sky.

The one speaking here is the chronicler, who reviews the organization of David's kingdom. This census is the one Joab began on the king's orders, and which brought God's judgment on Israel (2 Samuel 24). Some understand that they did not count the young men out of respect for God's promise; others, that the census was left incomplete. The text gives no further details.

For today: God keeps his promises in his own time and in his own way, and we do not need to measure and control everything to feel secure. We can rest in his word, trust that he knows what he is doing, and avoid depending only on numbers, resources, or our own plans.
exp.26:27:
It says that King David placed Baal-hanan, from the city of Gader, in charge of the olive trees and the sycamore trees that were in the low plains. He gave Joash charge of the cellars where the oil was stored.

This list appears in the final part of David's reign. The chronicler, who writes after the exile, lists the men responsible for the king's possessions: lands, vineyards, livestock and storehouses. It shows a well-ordered kingdom, where each person had a specific responsibility. We do not know more details about these two men; the Bible only records their names and their task.

For today: God values faithful work, even when it is simple and little seen. Caring well for what has been entrusted to you, whether a home, a job or a service in the church, is a way of honoring God.
exp.26:28:
This verse names two men in charge of King David's large herds. Shitrai, the Sharonite, looked after the herds that grazed in that plain, and Shaphat, son of Adlai, looked after those that were in the valleys. The word "Sharonite" means that Shitrai was from the region of Sharon, an area of pasture land near the coast.

Here the chronicler, who does not identify himself in the text, gives a list of those who managed David's possessions. The list ends by saying that all of them were overseers of his property. He was probably trying to show that the kingdom was well organized, with responsible people for every task, even the simplest ones.

For today: God values faithful and orderly work, even the kind that almost no one sees. Caring well for what has been entrusted to you, whether at home, at work, or in the church, is a way of serving God and others.
exp.26:29:
This verse is part of a list of the officials who looked after King David's property. Obil, a descendant of Ishmael, was in charge of the camels. Jehdeiah, from Meronoth, was in charge of the donkeys, that is, the female donkeys. "Ishmaelite" indicates his family line, and "Meronothite" shows that he came from a place called Meronoth.

The author of the book, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra though this is not certain, does not speak in the first person. He presents how David's kingdom was organized: each official carried out a specific task. This shows an orderly government. It is striking that an Ishmaelite was put in charge of the camels, animals typical of desert regions.

God values faithful service, even in simple and little-seen tasks. Caring for camels or donkeys brought no fame, yet the work was recorded in the Bible. Do well what is yours to do today, without seeking applause.
exp.26:30:
It says that Jaziz, of Hagerite descent, was in charge of King David's flocks of sheep. The text then sums up that all those named were overseers of the king's property, that is, the people who managed the goods and possessions of the king. The Hagerites were a people who were related to Hagar, the mother of Ishmael.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, gives a list of the officials who organized David's kingdom. Earlier he mentions those who looked after the herds of cattle, camels, and donkeys. With this he shows that the kingdom was well ordered. It is interesting that Jaziz was a foreigner, although the Bible says nothing more about him.

For today: God values responsible work, even the kind that seems simple or goes unnoticed. Caring well for what we are entrusted with, in the home, at work, or in the church, is a way of serving God faithfully.
exp.26:31:
This verse mentions two men who were close to David. Jonathan, the king's uncle, was a counsellor, a wise man, and also a scribe, meaning someone who knew how to write, keep records, and handle documents. Jehiel, son of Hachmoni, was with the king's sons, probably looking after them or accompanying them in their upbringing, although the text gives no further details.

The author of Chronicles, traditionally identified with Ezra though this is not certain, lists the officials who served in David's kingdom. This list shows that the government was well organized: there were military leaders, managers of property, and counsellors. It is meant to remind us how the kingdom functioned in David's time.

For today: God uses both those who advise and those who guide the young. We can value wise counsel and, if God gives us the opportunity, devote time to accompanying and teaching children and young people with patience and good example.
exp.26:33:
After Ahithophel, the verse says, two other men served the king as counselors: Jehoiada, son of Benaiah, and Abiathar. Joab was the general, that is, the commander of the king's army.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who lists the main officials in charge of David's government. He wants to show that the kingdom was well organized, with counselors, priests, and military leaders. Ahithophel appears here as a counselor, although later, according to 2 Samuel, he supported Absalom's rebellion.

For today: no one should carry the weight of important decisions alone. Seek advice from wise and faithful people, and pray that God will give you wisdom. Still, remember that your final trust must be in God, not only in people.
exp.27:0:
David gathered in Jerusalem all the leaders of the kingdom: the heads of the tribes, the commanders of the army (the leaders of thousands and of hundreds), those in charge of the king's property, his sons, the court officials (here probably meaning officers of the royal household) and his most courageous warriors.

The passage belongs to the book of Chronicles, which describes a solemn assembly near the end of David's life. He is now an old man and wants to set everything in order. In the verses that follow, he explains that God did not allow him to build the temple, but that his son Solomon would. He brings everyone together so that they can witness and support that transition.

For today: when the time comes to pass a responsibility on to others, do it with clarity, humility, and in full view of everyone. Serving God is not only about what I accomplish, but also about preparing those who will carry the work forward.
exp.27:2:
This verse says that God refused David permission to build the temple. The reason God gave was that he was a "man of war" and had shed a great deal of blood. The phrase "build a house for my name" means building a temple where God would be worshiped.

David speaks before all the leaders of Israel, gathered in Jerusalem near the end of his life. He wants to explain why he will not be the one to build the temple, but his son Solomon will. He makes clear that his desire was good and that he had already prepared the materials. Scholars understand the scope of the matter of the blood in different ways, but the text ties it to his wars.

For today: sometimes God says "no" to a good desire, and that is not always a rejection. It may be that your part is to prepare the way for others. Trust that God knows what he is doing, and serve with joy in the place that is yours.
exp.27:3:
Here David recalls that God chose him to be king, and not by chance. God first chose the tribe of Judah to lead Israel, then the family of his father, and at last him, the youngest of his brothers.

David speaks before the leaders and the gathered people, now an old man. He explains that God did not allow him to build the temple because he had been a man of war. Before speaking of his son Solomon, David acknowledges that his own reign was a gift from God, not an achievement of his own.

For today: everything we are and have comes from the grace of God. Recognizing this helps us live with humility, and to accept with peace that sometimes God entrusts to others what we dreamed of doing ourselves.
exp.27:4:
In this verse, David says that God gave him many sons, but that of all of them he chose Solomon to reign. He says Solomon would sit upon "the throne of the kingdom of the Lord", meaning that the kingdom belongs to God and the king only represents him.

David speaks before the leaders of Israel, now an old man, to present Solomon as his successor. He explains that God did not allow him to build the temple because he had been a man of war. He also recalls that God had first chosen him. Thus, Solomon's choosing comes from God, not only from a human decision. God also gives him a condition: to obey his commandments.

For today: recognize that what you have is a charge from God, not only yours. If He gives you a task, whether in the family, at work, or in the church, care for it with humility and obedience, and trust that He guides those whom He calls.
exp.27:10:
This verse tells us that David handed his son Solomon the plans for the temple. The plans included the porch (the entrance), the buildings, the storehouses (probably the treasuries or rooms for keeping valuables), the upper chambers, the inner rooms, and the place of the mercy seat, which was the holiest place, where the ark was kept.

David speaks as a father and as an aging king. God did not allow him to build the temple, so he prepares everything so that Solomon can do it. The text says David had these plans, and other passages in this chapter indicate that he received them through the inspiration of God. Before giving them over, he asks Solomon to seek God with a sincere heart.

For today: God values our preparing the way for others. We can leave our children and those who follow us a solid faith, a good example, and guidance, knowing that God can use others to finish what we began.
exp.27:14:
It says that David handed over to Solomon gold and silver already weighed out, with the exact amount for each lampstand. There were lampstands of gold and of silver, and each one had its lamps, which were the small lamps where the oil and the wick were placed. The metal was divided according to the use of each piece in the temple.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting David's preparations before he died. David gave his son Solomon the plans for the temple, which according to the text he had received through the Spirit. The exact weight shows that nothing was left to chance, since everything was done with order and for the service of God.

For today: God values care in the details of service. Serve God with order and faithfulness, even in small tasks that no one sees.
exp.27:15:
It says David gave gold and silver, measured by weight, to make the tables for the bread of the Presence, which were the loaves set out before God in the sanctuary. There were tables of gold and also tables of silver.

Here the text tells how David prepared everything for the temple that his son Solomon would build. He gave exact plans and materials, which according to the account he received by the Spirit of God (v. 12). He did this so that the service to God would be carried out with order and care.

For today: God cares about the small details we do out of love for Him. No hidden service is insignificant. We can give our time, money and talents with order and generosity, knowing that God values what we give Him from the heart.
exp.27:16:
This verse lists the materials for the temple's utensils. David names pure gold for the fleshhooks (forks or hooks used to handle the flesh of the sacrifice), the basins (vessels for catching liquids), the censers, and the bowls of gold. He also mentions silver for other bowls. Everything was to be given by weight, that is, with an exact measure for each piece.

David speaks before Israel, near the end of his life. He hands his son Solomon the plans for the temple, which he himself would not be able to build. He says that God himself gave him to understand the design, so nothing was left to chance or to human taste.

For today: God cares about details and about order. We can serve him with care and excellence even in small things, without neglecting tasks that seem unimportant, because we do them for him.
exp.27:17:
This verse continues the list of materials that David hands over for the temple. It speaks of pure gold, weighed out, for the altar of incense and for the figure of the golden cherubim. This figure is described as being like a chariot: wings spread out, covering the ark of the covenant. Cherubim are angelic beings who appear in the presence of God.

David speaks to Israel and to his son Solomon, and gives him the plans for the temple. He says God himself made him understand the design. David will not build it, but he prepares everything with care so that Solomon can carry it out.

For today: God values preparation and generous giving, even when we do not see the final result. We can serve with what we have, do our own part well, and trust that God will accompany those who continue the work.
exp.27:20:
It says that Solomon will not be alone in building the temple. The priests and the Levites, organized into their groups, will take charge of the service of the house of God. Helpers will also join in: willing people with skill, ready for any kind of work. The princes, or leaders, and all the people will stand ready to carry out his commands.

David, now an old man, speaks to his son Solomon. He hands over the plans for the temple, which he says came from God, and encourages him not to be afraid. David will not be able to build it himself, but he leaves the human team in place to support his son in the work.

For today: God rarely calls us to an important task so that we carry it out alone. We can humbly accept the help of others and joyfully offer our abilities in the church or the community, knowing that every contribution counts.
exp.28:0:
In this verse, King David speaks to the whole assembled people. He tells them that God chose Solomon, his son, to build the temple. He points out that Solomon is young and tender, meaning inexperienced and fragile, and that the work is enormous, because the temple is not for a man but for the Lord God.

David is now old and hands over the kingdom and the plan for the temple to Solomon. He wants the people to support his son. Afterward he himself describes how much he has prepared and given for the work.

For today: when God entrusts us with something great, we do not depend only on our own strength or experience. We can prepare ourselves, give generously, and support others, remembering that the work belongs to God.
exp.28:1:
David says he gave everything he had to prepare the temple of God. He gathered gold, silver, bronze, iron and wood, each material for the work it was meant to do. He also gathered precious stones: onyx stones (probably onyx, though the word is translated in several ways), colored stones, and marble stones in abundance.

David speaks before the whole assembly of Israel. He had already said that God chose Solomon, young and inexperienced, for an enormous task, because the temple was for God and not for a man. David would not build the temple himself, but he gets everything ready for his son and encourages the people to give generously.

For today: you do not have to be the one who finishes the work in order to serve God. We can prepare the way for others with our time, gifts or resources, and do it with our whole heart, even if we never see the final result.
exp.28:3:
David says he gives three thousand talents of gold from Ophir and seven thousand talents of refined silver, that is, silver that has been purified. They would be used to cover the walls of the temple buildings. A talent was a very large unit of weight, and its exact modern equivalent is debated. Ophir was a region famous for its fine gold, but no one knows for certain where it was.

David speaks before the people and their leaders. His son Solomon would build the temple. David had already prepared a great deal of material, but he also gives from his own personal treasure, because he loved the house of God. Then he invites the others to give offerings.

Giving to God should come from affection and not from obligation. Ask yourself what you can offer him with joy, whether time, talents, or money, and take the first step, as David did, to encourage others by your example.
exp.28:4:
It says that David had already set aside gold for everything that would be made of gold, silver for what would be made of silver, and materials for the work of the craftsmen. "Craftsmen" here means the skilled workers or artisans. Then he asks: "Who is willing today to give to the Lord?", that is, who wants to give freely and gladly, and not out of obligation.

King David, already old, speaks before all the people. He himself had given a large amount of his personal wealth for the temple that his son Solomon would build. Now he invites the leaders to join in. The following verse shows that they responded with generosity.

God does not seek only our money, but a willing heart. David gave first and then invited others. We might ask ourselves what time, talent, or resource we can offer to God today with joy, without pressure.
exp.28:10:
This verse declares that all greatness belongs to God: the majesty (his splendid greatness), the power, the glory, the victory, and the honor. It says that everything that exists in heaven and on earth is his. It also affirms that the kingdom is God's and that he is exalted as head above every ruler.

David speaks in front of the whole people. Israel had just given offerings gladly for the building of the temple, which his son Solomon would later build. David does not boast about what was gathered, but praises God and acknowledges that everything comes from him.

For today: when you give your time, your money, or your talents, do it with gratitude and without pride. Remember that everything you have already belonged to God, and that you are only a joyful steward of what he has entrusted to you.
exp.28:14:
He says that we are strangers and sojourners before God, that is, travelers passing through who do not own the land. Just as our fathers were, we live only a short time: our days are like a shadow that passes, and there is none abiding, that is, there is no way to hold them back or to make sure they will last.

David speaks at the end of his life, before the whole people. They have just given generous offerings for building the temple, which his son Solomon would build. David acknowledges that nothing they give is truly theirs, since everything comes from God. His humility comes from knowing that they are passing through.

For today: since our life is brief and what we have is on loan, we can live with open hands. Think of one specific thing, time, money, or a talent, and use it today to bless others and honor God.
exp.28:16:
This verse says that David speaks to God with sincerity. He acknowledges that God tests the heart, that is, He examines the innermost part of each person thoroughly. It also says that God takes pleasure in uprightness, which means honesty and sincerity. David affirms that he gave everything with an upright heart and willingly, and he rejoices because the people also gave willingly, that is, of their own accord.

David speaks in prayer before all of Israel. Materials and offerings are being gathered to build the temple, which his son Solomon would later build. Before this verse, David acknowledges that everything comes from God and that they are strangers and sojourners on the earth.

For today: when you give your time, your money, or your service, do it with a sincere heart. God does not look only at how much we give, but at why we give it. Remember also that everything you have already comes from Him.
exp.28:20:
The people of Israel offered many sacrifices to God. The day after David's prayer, they presented a thousand bulls (young cattle), a thousand rams, and a thousand lambs. The burnt offerings were offerings that were burned whole on the altar. The drink offerings were liquids, such as wine, that were poured out as part of the offering.

This is the end of David's reign. He had already gathered materials to build the temple and had led the people in worship. Now that Solomon was going to be king, all the people celebrated with offerings, food, and joy before God. The text is not David speaking; it is the account of the writer of Chronicles.

For today: when God has been good to us, we can respond to him with generous gratitude. It is not about quantity, but about a thankful heart that gives and worships with joy, together with others.
exp.28:22:
This verse says that Solomon sat as king on the throne of the Lord, taking the place of his father David. It went well for him, and all Israel obeyed him.

The author is the chronicler, who tells the history of Israel after the exile. He has just described the great festival with sacrifices, feasting, and joy, where Solomon was anointed a second time. He calls the throne "of the Lord" because he presents the king as someone who rules under God's authority, not only by his own power. What follows shows that the princes also supported him.

For today: whatever responsibility we have, whether in the home, at work, or in the church, it is best to live it as something entrusted to us by God. That attitude leads us to serve with humility and to seek his guidance.
exp.28:25:
This verse sums up David's reign. It says he ruled over all Israel, that is, over the twelve tribes united together. "Son of Jesse" identifies him by his humble family, since his father was from Bethlehem. At first he reigned only over Judah, but afterward all the tribes accepted him.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not known for certain), closes the story of David here. Earlier it tells how Solomon was recognized as the new king. The verses that follow say that David reigned forty years and died in old age, honored. The book was written to remind the people, after the exile, of the importance of the kingdom and the temple.

God can take an ordinary person and use him for a great task. Today, instead of seeking prestige, we can serve faithfully where God has placed us, trusting that he gives the growth.
exp.28:26:
This verse sums up how long David ruled: forty years in total. For the first seven years he reigned in Hebron, and the other thirty-three years he reigned in Jerusalem.

The writer of Chronicles is the one speaking, and he does not identify himself with certainty. Jewish tradition often names Ezra, but this is not known for sure. Here he closes the story of David with a summary, just before telling of David's death and the beginning of Solomon's reign. The passage wants to show that God was faithful to his promise and sustained David's kingdom to the end.

For today: our lives also have seasons, some smaller and some greater, and God works in all of them. David did not begin in Jerusalem but in Hebron. We can trust that God cares for every season and be faithful where we are now, without despising simple beginnings.
exp.28:28:
This verse says that everything King David did, from the beginning to the end of his life, was written down in three records: the chronicles of Samuel, those of Nathan, and those of Gad. "Seer" is another word for prophet, someone to whom God revealed things. "Chronicles" means records or accounts of events.

Here the author of 1 Chronicles speaks, though he does not name himself and his identity is not certain. He is closing the account of David's reign. He mentions sources that we no longer have as separate books, so we do not know for certain what they were. His purpose seems to be to show that what he tells rests on the testimony of men of God.

For today: our lives also leave a record. Let us live with integrity, so that what others remember of us points to God and not only to our achievements.
exp.28:29:
This verse closes the account of King David. It says that his deeds, his reign, his power, and the times that came upon him, upon Israel, and upon the surrounding kingdoms were recorded in the writings of the prophets Samuel, Nathan, and Gad.

The phrase about the times that came over him refers to the events and eras that he lived through.

The one speaking is the author of Chronicles, who is not named; many believe it was Ezra, though this is not certain. He concludes the story of David and notes that his life was recorded by trustworthy witnesses. The books cited are not preserved as separate works, so we know of them only through this mention.

For today: our lives also have good and difficult times, and God sees them all. Live faithfully through each season, for what you do with sincerity leaves a mark on others.
exp.7:2:
This verse lists the sons of Bela, the firstborn son of Benjamin: Addar, Gera, and Abihud. It is part of a family record. The names are written just as they appear in your Bible.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, wrote after the exile in Babylon. His aim was to remind the people who were returning who they were, which families they came from, and that God had not forgotten them. The lists of Benjamin differ in some details from other biblical passages, and scholars explain these differences in various ways, perhaps because of different family records. Here there is no direct teaching, but a remembering of lineage.

For today: God knows names that we read without giving them attention. This encourages us to value ordinary people who receive no fame, including in our own family or church. Today, take a moment to thank God for someone who has influenced you quietly, and tell that person personally that you appreciate them.
exp.6:13:
This verse begins the list of the descendants of Manasseh. It says that Asriel was born through a concubine, a woman from Aram (Syria) who is named only by her homeland. The verse also says she gave birth to Machir, who became the father of Gilead.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles come from an unknown author. Jewish tradition connects them with Ezra, though this is not certain. They were written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots, their tribes, and their lands. The names here are hard to follow, and scholars understand them in various ways.

For today: God remembers each person by name, even a woman whom the list identifies only as a concubine from Aram. He values those who go unnoticed and treats everyone with dignity.
exp.0:51:
This verse continues a list of the chiefs of Edom. Three are named: Oholibamah, Elah, and Pinon. Their names appear in the list, but the list gives no further details about them.

Nobody is speaking in a sermon or story here. The chronicler (tradition often says it was Ezra, though this is not certain) presents family records. Edom comes from Esau, the brother of Jacob. By including this list, the author shows that God knows the history of all peoples, and that the promises made to Abraham continued on their course. A similar list appears in Genesis 36.

For today: God takes account of people, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your name and your life matter to Him, even when the world does not highlight them. Serve faithfully in the ordinary things.
exp.1:11:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Boaz was the father of Obed, and Obed was the father of Jesse. In the Bible, "father of" sometimes refers to a direct son and sometimes to a more distant descendant.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the line of the tribe of Judah. He writes for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. This line leads to King David, son of Jesse. Other passages, such as Ruth 4 and Matthew 1, show that this line also reaches to Jesus.

For today: God works through generations, even through people who are rarely mentioned. Your daily faithfulness, though it may seem small, can be part of what God is doing in your family and beyond your lifetime.
exp.0:35:
The verse lists the sons of Eliphaz, son of Esau: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz, and then, through Timna, Amalek. The names are given in a form close to the original spelling. In Genesis 36, Timna appears as a concubine of Eliphaz and the mother of Amalek, so here she could be a woman's name or the name of a clan. It is not entirely clear.

The author of Chronicles is unknown, although Jewish tradition often names Ezra. He writes for the people who returned from exile, and that is why he begins with long genealogies. Before moving on to Israel, he records the branches of other peoples, such as Esau's line, to show where each family stands in history.

For today: God knows the names and stories of people, even of those almost no one remembers. You can trust that your life also matters to him. And this invites you to value and respect every person.
exp.18:0:
Some time later, Nahash king of the Ammonites died, and his son succeeded him. This verse tells us that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, died, and that his son took the throne in his place. "Some time later" points back to the events the writer had already recorded, such as David's victories. The son's name is Hanun, and he is mentioned in the next verse.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of Israel and here presents a change of rule in a neighboring nation. This moment leads to a very delicate episode. David wants to show kindness to Hanun, but the Ammonite leaders suspect his intentions. The Bible does not explain in detail what the "kindness" Nahash had shown to David consisted of.

For today: when someone reaches out to us with good intentions, let us think well before assuming the worst. Suspicion without evidence can destroy relationships and cause great harm.
exp.7:35:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Ahaz was the father of Jehoaddah, and that Jehoaddah had three sons: Alemeth, Azmaveth and Zimri. Then Zimri was the father of Moza.

The book does not have one known author, though Jewish tradition often credits Ezra, and this is not certain. It was written for the people who returned from exile, to remind them who they were. This list traces the line of Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin, through Jonathan, his son. Their names were kept to preserve the identity of the people.

For today: God does not forget anyone, even when a name seems unimportant. Today you can value your family, give thanks to those who came before you, and remember that your life also has a place in God's story.
exp.0:26:
This verse tells us that Abram and Abraham are the same person. The list of names arrives at Abram at the end of the line from Shem, and here it is made clear that his name was changed. In Genesis 17:5, God gave him the name Abraham, which is understood to mean "father of multitudes."

The book of Chronicles is a history that focuses on family records. It is traditionally attributed to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. This list connects Israel with the beginnings of humanity, and Abraham marks the point where the history of God's promise begins.

For today: God knows who you are and can give you a new identity. Abraham received a new name together with a promise. If you trust God, your past does not define your future. Live today according to what He says about you.
exp.8:21:
This verse says that the men chosen as gatekeepers numbered two hundred and twelve. They were registered by their family line, in the villages where they lived. The phrase "positions of trust" means that they were appointed to their posts. The text says that David and Samuel the seer appointed them to that service.

It is part of the genealogical lists in 1 Chronicles, written for the people who were returning from exile. Their purpose was to remind them who served in the temple and how worship was organized. The author is not named in the text. Some think the men were organized from David's time, and others believe Samuel began the order earlier. The text gives no further detail, so it is best not to claim more than what is said.

God cares even for quiet work, such as opening and keeping watch over a gate. If you serve in something small or little seen in your church or family, do it faithfully, for God sees it.
exp.17:7:
This verse tells how David, after defeating Hadadezer, king of Zobah, took a large amount of bronze from two cities that belonged to him: Tibhath and Cun. Years later, Solomon used that bronze to make the bronze Sea (a huge basin of water for the temple), the pillars, and various other bronze articles.

The writer of Chronicles, who wrote for the people who returned from exile, summarizes David's victories. Just before this, he says that the LORD gave David victory wherever he went. It shows that God gave the victory, and that what was taken ended up serving the temple, even though David did not build it.
