For today: what God places in our hands, whether achievements, resources, or efforts, can serve a purpose greater than ourselves, even for future generations. We can ask ourselves how to use what we have for his work and not only for our own benefit.
exp.7:33:
It says that Jonathan, son of King Saul, had a son named Merib-baal, and that Merib-baal in turn had a son named Micah. In the reader's wording, Merib-baal "was the father of" Micah, which is the same idea as "had a son." In other passages of the Bible, Merib-baal appears under the name Mephibosheth, though not all scholars explain this change of name in the same way.

The author of Chronicles is unknown; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. He writes after the return from exile and reviews the family lines of the tribes, here that of Benjamin. He wanted the people to remember their roots and their identity. Including Saul's line shows that his family was not forgotten, even after his fall.

God cares for people and for their history, even for those who seem forgotten. Today we can remember with gratitude those who came before us in faith and family, and trust that our lives also have value before God.
exp.4:12:
This verse gives a list of seven men from the tribe of Gad, called "their kinsmen," meaning relatives of Joel and the other leaders mentioned just before them. They are listed by their families, which means by their households or clans. The verse says there were seven in all.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile in Babylon, and we do not know for certain who wrote it; Jewish tradition often names Ezra. Its purpose was to remind the people who they were, which tribes they came from, and that God had not forgotten them. Gad lived east of the Jordan, in the region of Bashan, and these lists preserved their memory and their inheritance.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today you can value and encourage those who serve quietly in your church or family, and remember that your life also counts before God.
exp.18:2:
The princes of the Ammonites warn their new king, Hanun, not to trust David. They ask him whether he really believes David is showing respect for his father by sending comforters to him. In their view, those servants actually came to explore the land, spy it out, and overthrow it.

Hanun had just inherited the throne, and the princes speak like worried advisers. David wanted to return a kindness that Nahash had shown him earlier. The Bible does not say that the princes had any proof; their accusation seems to arise from suspicion.

For today: before judging someone's intentions, let us think about whether we have evidence or only fear. Groundless suspicion can damage friendships and cause great conflicts. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern calmly and with love.
exp.28:21:
They ate and drank before the Lord that day, full of joy. Then, for the second time, they publicly recognized Solomon, David's son, as king. They made him king in a formal ceremony that confirmed his position before everyone. They anointed him before the Lord, pouring oil on him as a sign that God was setting him apart, and they installed him as ruler. They also anointed Zadok as priest.

David was already old, and he had gathered all Israel to prepare for the building of the temple. He had prayed and given his offerings, and the people offered sacrifices. The text says "the second time" because Solomon had already been proclaimed king before (1 Kings 1), and some understand that this ceremony confirmed him before everyone in peace and unity.

Today we can learn that celebrating with thankfulness before God and supporting those whom he places as leaders brings unity. Pray for your leaders and cooperate joyfully in what God is doing.
exp.23:4:
This verse says that the priests were divided into groups by drawing lots, so that no one was given special treatment. Both the descendants of Eleazar and the descendants of Ithamar had important leaders. The phrase "officers of the sanctuary" and "officers of God" refers to the chiefs in charge of the service in the temple. The word "divided" means that they were separated out and arranged into their groups.

Here the chronicler tells how David organized the priestly service. The shifts had to be arranged so that the work in the sanctuary was orderly and fair. Because the family of Eleazar had more leaders, lots were used to distribute the shifts impartially. Scholars agree that the aim was to avoid disputes and to acknowledge God's direction.

For today: serving God in the church calls for order and justice. Sharing tasks with humility, without competing or seeking the first places, helps everyone serve in peace.
exp.11:23:
This verse says that from the tribe of Judah came six thousand eight hundred troops, armed with shields and spears. Their weapons show that they were equipped and ready to fight. Shields and spears were common weapons of the time.

The author of Chronicles gives a list of the tribes that went to Hebron. They went to support David and to make him king over the kingdom that had belonged to Saul, according to the word of the LORD. Judah was David's own tribe, and here the count is given of how many of its men joined him. The numbers in these lists are hard to pin down precisely, and some scholars read them differently.

For today: God does great things through the combined effort of many committed people. Ask yourself how you can offer your support, prepared and faithful, to what God is doing in your church or community.
exp.20:6:
This verse says that the census David ordered was evil in God's sight, and for that reason He struck Israel with punishment. The word "command" here refers to the order David gave to count the people. "Struck" means that God sent a punishment on the nation.

The narrator of Chronicles tells that David ordered the fighting men to be counted, although Joab, his military commander, did not agree. The texts do not explain every detail of the motive, but the context suggests pride or confidence in military strength rather than in God. Afterward David acknowledges his sin and asks for forgiveness.

For today: let us be careful not to trust in our numbers, resources, or abilities more than in God. And if we make a mistake, let us do as David did: acknowledge the error quickly, with humility, and ask God for forgiveness.
exp.3:41:
This verse tells that five hundred men from the tribe of Simeon went out toward the mountainous region of Seir. Four leaders guided them: Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, sons of Ishi. "Led by" means these four were the leaders or chiefs of the group. The verse uses the word "these" to point back to the Simeonites already named.

The author of Chronicles is unknown; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. He is recording the genealogies of Israel and remembering events from the tribes. This expedition took place in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. The Simeonites were looking for pasture for their flocks, and they fought against peoples who lived there. The text presents that conquest as part of the history of the tribe, without giving more details. Some wonder how to judge these events, and the text does not explain it.

God uses people by name and surname, not only great figures. Even what we do in ordinary life, such as seeking provision for our families, matters. We can ask him for direction before taking an important step.
exp.5:68:
This verse names two more cities that were given to the descendants of Kohath, one of the Levite families: Aijalon and Gath-rimmon. The phrase "together with their pasturelands" refers to the open land around each city, where the people could graze their animals.

Here the chronicler reviews how the Levitical cities were divided among the tribes of Israel. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, because their inheritance was to serve God. So the people gave them cities in which to live. This passage follows the same list found in Joshua 21.

God cared for those who devoted themselves to his service, and his people responded with generosity. Today we can gratefully and practically support the pastors, teachers, and missionaries who dedicate their lives to serving the church.
exp.13:1:
David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel. "Realized" means he recognized and understood this clearly. "Established" means that the LORD had set him in place firmly. "Highly exalted" means that the LORD had raised his kingdom up. His kingdom was growing, but the text says this was the LORD's doing.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who summarizes the history of Israel. Shortly before, Hiram, king of Tyre, sent David cedar wood and workers to build him a house. That gesture from a foreign king was for David a sign that God was sustaining his reign. Moreover, the text says that his kingdom was exalted "for the sake of His people Israel," that is, for the good of Israel.

When we receive success, support, or responsibility, we can recognize that they come from God and not only from our own effort. That keeps us humble and reminds us that we should use what we have received to serve others.
exp.5:35:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors. It says that a certain man was a son of Elkanah, who was a son of Joel, who was a son of Azariah, who was a son of Zephaniah. These are names from the tribe of Levi.

Here no character speaks in a scene. The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies as Ezra though this is not certain, gathers the genealogies of the Levites. This line leads to Heman, the singer of the temple. The Israelites returning from exile needed to remember who they were and what their service to God was. The names repeat and vary between lists, and scholars explain them in different ways.

For today: God remembers people by name, including those who seem unimportant. Give thanks for those who passed on your faith, and serve faithfully, even when no one applauds you.
exp.1:6:
The verse says that Achar was a son of Carmi, and that he was the one who brought trouble upon Israel. This happened because he violated the ban on devoted things, which means he disobeyed God's command and took something that had been set apart for destruction or dedicated to Him.

The verse is part of a genealogy of the tribe of Judah. The chronicler does not tell the whole story here; he takes it for granted, since the account is given in Joshua 7. Some think the name "Achar" is a play on words with "Achan," and that it recalls the word for "troubler." This is a common interpretation, but not something entirely certain. Even in a list of names, we are reminded that his actions had consequences.

For today: our private decisions can affect others. Before giving in to something we know God does not approve of, let us think about who would bear the consequences, and seek to obey honestly.
exp.7:32:
This verse lists a family line: Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul, and Saul was the father of four sons: Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Esh-baal. "Was the father of" means a direct father-son relationship here. In the Bible, "father" can also mean an ancestor further back in the family line, so the word does not always point to an immediate son.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies as Ezra though this is not certain, writes after the exile in Babylon. His purpose was to remind the Israelites who they were. Here he presents the family of Benjamin, from which Saul came, the first king of Israel. Esh-baal appears to be the same person who is called Ish-bosheth in other texts. The names in this list connect the people with their past.

For today: God pays attention to families and to ordinary individuals, not only to the great figures. Think about those who went before you in faith or in your own family, and give thanks for them. Consider also what legacy of faith and character you want to leave to those who come after you.
exp.20:29:
This verse says that the tabernacle Moses made in the wilderness, along with the bronze altar of burnt offering, was at that time at the high place in Gibeon. But David could not go there to seek God's guidance, because he was terrified of the sword of the angel of the LORD. The word "terrified" here means very frightened, filled with fear.

This is the narrator's explanation. After the plague that fell on Israel because of David's census, the king saw that God had answered him at the threshing floor of Ornan and offered his sacrifice there. The text makes clear why he did not go to Gibeon, where worship normally took place. His fear was so strong that he did not feel able to go any further. Later, that place in Jerusalem would become very important for the temple.

For today: when fear or guilt leave us unable to move, God does not ask us to reach some perfect place. We can draw near to Him with humility, right where we are, and He hears us.
exp.3:39:
This verse tells how some families of the tribe of Simeon found rich, good pasture and a spacious land. The land was peaceful and quiet, free from conflict and disturbance. The verse also notes that some Hamites, descendants of Noah's son Ham, had lived there before them.

It is part of the lists of families of Judah and Simeon in Chronicles. The author, whom tradition calls the Chronicler, recalls how these families grew greatly and looked for land for their flocks. The text that follows says they drove out the earlier inhabitants in the days of King Hezekiah. That passage is harsh, and there is no agreement on all the historical details.

For today: the need for space and provision is real, but the text invites us to reflect. Let us seek provision with diligence, give thanks to God, and take care not to gain our own well-being at the cost of harming others.
exp.5:11:
It says that Ahitub was the father of Zadok, and that Zadok was the father of Shallum. This is part of a list of generations of priests. The names are spelled as they appear in the older translation, so Achîtob is Ahitub.

This list appears in 1 Chronicles, a book whose narrator cannot be identified with certainty; Jewish tradition often attributes it to Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for the people who returned from exile, and it aimed to show them where they came from and that priestly service in the temple had an unbroken line. Here the descent of Levi, the tribe of the priests, is followed.

For today: God pays attention to every generation, even though some names may seem to us like nothing more than a list. Your faith and your service, even if they are simple and little seen, can be a link that God uses to bless those who come after you.
exp.5:64:
This verse says that the cities for the Levites were assigned by lot, meaning the choice was made by casting lots, and that these cities came from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin. The cities themselves are named in the verses that follow. The pasture lands around each city are the open fields that belonged to it.

The writer of Chronicles does not speak in the first person; it is a narrative that reviews the family records of Israel. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, because their service was the worship of God. For this reason the people gave them cities within their own lands. This passage seems to draw on Joshua 21, although scholars note some differences between the two lists.

For today: those who serve God need the support and care of their community. We can ask ourselves how to support, with prayer, time, or practical help, the pastors, teachers, and missionaries who serve us.
exp.26:1:
This verse says that Jashobeam, son of Zabdiel, was in charge of the first division of men, the one assigned to the first month of the year. That division had 24,000 men. The phrase "in charge of the first division" means he was its leader.

The passage describes how King David organized the service of the kingdom. Twelve divisions took turns, one each month, to serve the king. In this way no one had to carry the whole year alone. Some think this Jashobeam is the same brave warrior mentioned in 1 Chronicles 11, but the Bible does not state this clearly.

For today: God values orderly and shared service. In your family, your church, or your work, do your part faithfully when it is your turn, and let others serve too, so that no one is worn out.
exp.11:34:
This verse says that from the tribe of Dan came 28,600 men prepared for battle. It is part of a list of warriors from each tribe.

The writer of Chronicles lists the tribes that came to Hebron to make David king after the death of Saul. The narrator is speaking here, not a character. Such large numbers have been understood in more than one way: some take them literally, and others think the word "thousand" might refer to military units. The central point is the broad and united support for David.

For today: when God is at work, He often brings together many people with different gifts and places. Ask yourself how you can join, with commitment and sincerity, in what God is doing in your church or community, rather than standing on the sidelines.
exp.8:33:
This verse says that the Levites mentioned earlier were heads of their families, according to their lists of descent. In addition, they lived in Jerusalem. "Family lines" means family lineages or genealogies. "Leaders" are the heads of family groups.

It is part of the long lists in 1 Chronicles 9, which record who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. The author, traditionally identified as Ezra though this is not certain, writes to remind the people of their roots and of the value of worshiping God. Just before this, he speaks of singers and those in charge of the showbread, who served day and night.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is quiet and steady. There are tasks no one applauds, but God remembers them. Today you can serve in your church or family with consistency and humility, trusting that your work is not forgotten.
exp.6:37:
This verse is part of a family list. It names three sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara. Jether could be the same person as Ithran in the previous verse, though this cannot be stated with certainty.

The book of Chronicles has no narrator that can be identified with certainty; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, but this is debated. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their origins and their identity. Here the tribe of Asher is reviewed, and the lists show that every family mattered and had its place among God's people.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today you can remember that your life has value before Him, and be encouraged to value and give thanks for those who, without being famous, serve faithfully in quiet ways.
exp.17:10:
This verse says that King David set apart for God, as an offering, the gold, silver and bronze vessels that Tou sent him, along with the silver and gold he had taken from several nations: Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines and Amalekites. "Dedicated to the LORD" means that he set these things apart for the service of the LORD.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who reviews the history of Israel. Tou, king of Hamath, sent gifts to congratulate David on defeating Hadadezer. David did not keep those treasures or the spoils of the wars for himself, but dedicated them to God. Scholars understand that this material would later serve for the temple, although this verse does not say so directly.

For today: what God allows us to achieve or gain is not only for ourselves. We can set apart a part of our time, money and talents for God and for serving others, recognizing that everything comes from Him.
exp.1:18:
When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur. The phrase "bore him" describes her giving birth to him.

Here the speaker is not a character in the story but the chronicler, who writes a long list of the families of the tribe of Judah. His purpose was to record the family lines of the people after the exile. Hur is important because from him comes Bezalel, the craftsman whom God filled with skill to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1-5). Some scholars understand this Caleb to be a different ancestor from the famous spy Caleb, son of Jephunneh.

For today: God works through ordinary lives, even those marked by loss. A widow or widower who starts over may be part of what God does in the generations that follow. Trust that your story also matters.
exp.25:14:
This verse says that the lot for the South Gate fell to Obed-edom, and his sons were assigned the storehouses. The reader's wording makes clear that these were two separate duties, one at a gate and one at the storerooms. The storerooms are not described in detail here, so the exact nature of the work is not fully known.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, recounts how David organized the Levite gatekeepers. The duties were distributed by lot, the small and the great alike, so that the assignment would be impartial and no one would feel looked down upon. Guarding the gates and storerooms protected worship.

Today, God values faithfulness more than visibility. If you are given a simple service, such as opening a door, looking after something, or helping quietly, do it gladly. In that too you are serving God.
exp.24:13:
It says that the seventh turn of service, or shift, fell to Jesarelah, together with his sons and his brothers, twelve in all. This passage describes a group of temple musicians who were assigned to their turn.

It is part of a list in 1 Chronicles 25 about how David and the leaders of the service organized the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to serve with music in the house of God. The text is not a speech but a narrative record. The turns were decided by lot, and each family received its place.

In other passages this name appears as Asharelah, so there are variations in the spelling.

God values orderly and shared service. No one had all the work, and each person had his place. Today we can serve faithfully in the church or the family, without comparing ourselves to others, joyfully doing the part that falls to us.
exp.18:11:
Joab tells his brother Abishai that they should come to each other's aid. If the Arameans prove too strong for Joab, Abishai will come to his rescue; and if the Ammonites are too strong for Abishai, Joab will come to his rescue. "Rescue" here means to come to the aid of someone or deliver them from danger in battle.

Joab, the commander of Israel's army, is the one speaking. The Ammonites had joined forces with the Arameans, and the army found itself under attack in front and behind. Joab divided the troops into two groups to face each enemy. With this promise of mutual help, he gave them courage and unity before the fighting, and then called them to be strong and to trust that God would do what seemed good to him.

For today: you do not have to face every battle alone. In your family, your church, or your work, offer your help and also accept the help of others. Do your part with courage, and entrust the outcome to God.
exp.28:15:
This verse says that everything the people gathered to build the temple comes from God and belongs to him. The word "provided" in the verse means got ready or gathered together. The "house for your holy Name" is the temple, where God would be honored. David recognizes that, in giving, they are only returning to God what he had first given them.

David speaks in prayer before all Israel. The leaders and the people had just given generously for the future temple, which his son Solomon would later build. David rejoices, but he takes no credit for himself. He sees himself as a stranger passing through, with days as brief as a shadow, and he asks that God keep the heart of the people faithful to him.

Everything you have, your time, your talents, and your money, is a gift from God. When you give or serve, do it with humility and joy, without pride, remembering that you are only returning what he has entrusted to you.
exp.20:12:
David is in a very difficult position here. God offers him three punishments: famine, defeat before his enemies, or a plague. David says he is deeply distressed. He would rather fall into the hands of the LORD, because His mercies are very great, than into the hands of men.

David, king of Israel, is speaking with the prophet Gad. Earlier, David had ordered a census of the people, and this displeased God (the text presents it as sin, although it does not explain all the reasons). Now he must choose one of the consequences. His answer shows that, even in his guilt, he trusts God's compassion more than human cruelty. The following passage shows that God did have compassion.

When we fail and face the consequences, we can draw near to God instead of running away from Him. He corrects, but He also has mercy. Confessing with humility and trusting in His goodness is the best way.
exp.13:14:
Here David is told to wait for a sign: the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees. When he hears it, he is to move out to battle, because that sound will mean God has gone out before him to strike the Philistine camp. Here "strike" means to defeat. "As soon as" means immediately.

God is answering David, who had asked Him for guidance. The Philistines had come again to attack the valley, and David did not want to decide alone. God gave him a different plan from the one he had used before: to circle around the enemy and wait for his signal. David obeyed and won.

For today: before acting, ask God and wait for His direction, even if you have faced something similar before. What worked yesterday may not be today's plan. Obeying with patience, and moving when He indicates, is trusting that God goes ahead.
exp.28:12:
This verse is a response of thanksgiving. Here "give thanks" means to acknowledge and declare with joy who God is and what he has done. To "praise" is to speak highly of someone with admiration. So David says: "Our God, we give you thanks and praise your glorious name."

David is praying before all of Israel. The people had just given generous offerings to build the temple, which his son Solomon would later build. Before giving thanks, David recalls that everything belongs to God, and he immediately admits that what was offered had already come from God's hands.

Today we can begin our generosity with gratitude. Before giving time, money, or talents, it is good to say to God: "Everything I have comes from you." In this way we give with humility, without pride, and we praise God for what he has entrusted to us.
exp.13:12:
This verse tells us that the Philistines came back to attack the valley, that is, the valley of Rephaim, where they had already been defeated. The phrase "raided the valley" means that they returned and launched another attack across that area. Today we would say: "Once again the Philistines raided the valley."

The writer of Chronicles explains how God confirmed David as king. He had just won a battle and burned the idols of the enemies. Even so, the danger came back. The important part comes next: David does not repeat the earlier plan out of habit, but asks God again, and God gives him a different strategy.

For today: a past victory does not guarantee that the same method will work for the next problem. When something difficult returns, ask God for direction again, instead of relying only on experience or on what worked before.
exp.22:13:
This verse says that the descendants of Moses, whom it calls "the man of God," were counted among the tribe of Levi. The phrase "were counted" means they were officially registered as part of the Levites. They were not given a separate place or a higher rank; they were simply Levites, like everyone else.

The book of Chronicles, whose author is not named with certainty (Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra), goes through the lists of families when David organizes the service of the temple. Aaron and his sons were priests, while the sons of Moses remained among the Levites who assisted. It is striking that the son of a great leader did not inherit a special office.

For today: serving God does not depend on the fame of our family or on a great name. God values faithfulness in the place that belongs to us, even when it is simple. Serve with joy where He has placed you.
exp.22:11:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Kohath, of the tribe of Levi, had four sons: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The names are spelled a little differently from how some readers may know them, but they refer to the same people.

These lists appear when David, now old, organizes the Levites for the service of the temple that his son Solomon would build. The writer of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the families to show that the service to God had order and roots. From the line of Amram would come Aaron and Moses.

For today: God knows and remembers each person by name, even those who seem to be only names on a list. Your service, though simple and little seen, matters to Him. Serve Him faithfully, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.6:8:
It says that their genealogies were recorded according to their families, and that the number of mighty men of valor was 20,200. "Families" here are the family lines, "heads of families" are the leaders of each clan, and "mighty men of valor" means men who were brave and capable for war.

It is part of the genealogies in Chronicles, within the tribe of Benjamin. Jewish tradition attributes the book to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was probably written for the people who were returning from exile, to remind them who they were, where they came from, and that their history had not been lost.

For today: God knows each person and each family, even when history records only names and figures. Give thanks to those who went before you in the faith, and live with courage and faithfulness, for your life also has a place in God's history.
exp.12:7:
David and all the Israelites were celebrating before God with all their might. They used songs and many instruments: harps and lyres (stringed instruments), tambourines (small hand drums), cymbals (metal plates), and trumpets. The phrase "celebrating before God" means they were festive and joyful.

This is part of the account in the book of Chronicles, written as narrative. David brings the ark of God to Jerusalem, and all Israel takes part. The ark represented God's presence. However, the following verse shows that although there was much enthusiasm, they moved the ark on a new cart, and Uzzah died when he touched it. Many understand that the people failed to obey the way God had specified for carrying it.

For today: worshiping God with joy in our hearts is good, but enthusiasm does not replace obedience. Let us seek to serve Him with gladness and also with careful attention to what He says in His Word.
exp.10:46:
This verse closes the list of David's mighty men with three more names: Eliel, Obed, and Jaasiel. Jaasiel is called "the Mezobaite," which may refer to a place or to a family; scholars are not sure which. Here "mighty men" refers to outstanding warriors.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra, though this is not certain, lists the men who supported David in becoming king. He writes after the exile, and he wants the people to remember that the kingdom was raised up with the help of many people, including some who are little known. Here only their names are mentioned.

For today: God notices those who serve faithfully, even when no one applauds them. If your service is small or quiet, go forward with confidence. God sees it and remembers it. Today you can encourage someone who serves in silence.
exp.0:52:
This verse follows a list of chiefs of Edom. The word "chief" here refers to a clan or tribal leader, the Hebrew word for a head of a family group, rather than a title from European nobility. Three more are named here: Kenaz, Teman and Mibzar. With them, the list nears its end.

These genealogies are found in 1 Chronicles, a book that Jewish tradition associates with the period after the exile. We do not know for certain who wrote it; many think of Ezra, but that is an opinion. Edom descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. The chronicler recalls this history to show his people where the neighboring nations come from and how they fit into the story of Abraham.

For today: God knows and remembers names that seem unimportant to us. If He takes account of each person, then you too are seen by Him. Today, treat someone ordinary with respect, remembering that they have value before God.
exp.8:34:
The verse says that Jeiel, called "the father of Gibeon," lived in Gibeon, and that his wife was named Maacah. "The father of Gibeon" probably means he was the founder or leader of the town, though some understand it in another way.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), is not speaking here to one person but to the people who returned from exile. After naming the Levites, he goes through the families of Benjamin, the tribe from which King Saul came. He wants them to remember their roots and their place in Israel.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who hardly appear in the stories. Your family, your work and your simple place matter. Live faithfully where God has placed you, and give thanks to those who held the faith before you.
exp.11:0:
This verse begins a list of men who came to David at Ziklag. At that time David was banished from Saul's presence and living in hiding, because he was fleeing from Saul, the son of Kish. The men who came to him are described as among the mighty men who helped him in battle, meaning brave warriors who stood with David in the fight.

Here the Chronicler speaks, an author who wrote after the exile to remind the people how God raised up David as king. Ziklag was a place where David lived while Saul was still reigning. The author probably wants to show that, even in difficult times, God was gathering people around him.

For today: when we go through seasons of separation, hardship or uncertainty, God can bring people who walk alongside us. We can also ask ourselves whom we can help, coming to their side with loyalty and courage just when they most need it.
exp.28:5:
This verse tells us that the leaders of the people responded with generosity. The leaders of the families and the officers of the tribes were the heads of the clans. The commanders of thousands and of hundreds were leaders over a thousand and over a hundred soldiers. The officials in charge of the king's work looked after the king's property. All of them gave willingly, that is, by their own decision and with gladness, without anyone forcing them.

David is speaking before the whole congregation. He had already given from his own possessions for the future temple, which his son Solomon would build. Then he asked: "Who is willing to consecrate himself this day to the LORD?" The leaders were the first to respond, and their example encouraged the people (v. 9).

For today: God values willing and joyful giving more than the amount. Those who lead others, in the church or in the family, teach a great deal through their example. We can ask ourselves what I can give today, gladly, for the work of God.
exp.6:20:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Ephraim: Zabad, Shuthelah, and also Ezer and Elead. Then it records a tragedy: Ezer and Elead were killed by the natives of Gath, because they went down to steal their livestock. The livestock were the animals the men were after, and the text presents their raid as the reason for their deaths.

The writer of Chronicles, writing after the return from exile, goes over the genealogies of the tribes to remind his people where they come from. Here a brief and painful episode appears within the history of Ephraim. The text does not explain every detail, such as the exact date or the names of the others involved, so it is not wise to invent them. What follows, the mourning of Ephraim, shows the weight of the loss.

For today: taking what does not belong to us can cost very dearly. Let us seek what is ours with honesty and patience, without trampling on others.
exp.14:13:
This verse says that the priests and the Levites prepared themselves spiritually, or "consecrated" themselves, to bring the ark of the LORD up to Jerusalem. To consecrate oneself means to set oneself apart and make oneself clean in order to serve God with reverence, as the Law required.

The one speaking just before this is David. The first time they tried to move the ark, they carried it on a cart, and Uzzah died when he touched it (1 Chronicles 13). Now David acknowledges that they had not sought God as He had commanded, that is, in the way He had specified. For this reason he asks that the Levites carry the ark on their shoulders, as Moses had commanded.

For today: draw near to God with humility and obedience, not only with good intentions. Before you serve, set aside time to pray, confess your failings, and seek how God wants you to do things.
exp.17:2:
It says that David defeated Hadadezer, king of Zobah, an Aramean kingdom north of Israel. "Defeated" here means that he beat him in battle. The verse says the king had marched out to establish his dominion along the Euphrates River, which means he was trying to extend his control over the region all the way to that river. The verse names Hamath as the place the battle reached, and it is not entirely clear from the wording whether the king or David is the one who went to Hamath, so some scholars read it one way and some the other.

The one telling the account is the chronicler, an author who wrote centuries later, when the people had returned from exile. He recalls David's victories to show that God was fulfilling what He had promised in the previous chapter: to give his kingdom rest and firmness.

For today: God remains faithful to His promises, even when they take a while. When you face something that seems too big, remember how He has sustained His people and trust in His care.
exp.25:18:
This verse closes the list of the temple gatekeepers. It says that their shifts, or "divisions," were assigned to the descendants of Korah and Merari, both Levite families. A gatekeeper watched over the doors and entrances of the house of God.

The book of Chronicles explains how King David organized the service of the temple before he died. The author, whose name is not known for certain, records these details to remind the people that worship had order. Every gate and every storeroom had responsible men, identified by name and family.

For today: God values simple and steady service, even when no one applauds it. Watching over a door, opening a church, or helping quietly is also worship. Ask yourself what small task you can carry out faithfully this week.
exp.6:7:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Becher, a son of Benjamin, had nine sons: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth and Alemeth. The line "all these were Becher's sons" closes the list and makes clear that this is the full count of his sons.

First Chronicles does not name its author in the text. Many believe it was written or compiled by Ezra, although this is not certain. It was written for the people returning from exile, and these genealogies reminded them of their origins, their tribes and their lands. Here the tribe of Benjamin is in view, and its brave men are highlighted.

God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today you can thank God that your life and your family matter to him. And you too can value those who serve without being famous.
exp.3:40:
This verse says that the men of Simeon, whose names are recorded, came in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. They attacked the Hamites in their dwellings and the Meunites who lived there, and they destroyed them completely. The phrase "to this day" means until the time the book was written. Then they settled in that place, because there was pasture there for their flocks.

The passage is a historical record within the genealogies of Simeon. We do not know with certainty who wrote it; tradition mentions Ezra, but this is uncertain. It seems meant to help the people remember their history and their identity. It recounts what happened; it does not say that God approved of every action.

For today: the need for provision is real, but it is worth asking how we seek it. Trust God for your daily needs, and aim to get ahead without trampling on others, with justice and respect.
exp.8:19:
This verse says that Phinehas, son of Eleazar, had been in charge of the gatekeepers in earlier times, and that the LORD was with him. The phrase "in charge" means he was the one leading and overseeing these guards. The phrase "in earlier times" means this was in the past, long before the chronicler's own day.

It is part of a list of the Levites who guarded the gates of the tabernacle, written by the chronicler after the return from exile. He wants to show that this service came from long ago, with roots in the history of Israel. Phinehas appears in Numbers 25 and is remembered for his zeal for God. The passage does not say here at what exact moment he led these guards.

For today: service that seems small, like guarding a door, matters to God. What counts most is not the position, but that the LORD is with us as we serve faithfully.
exp.18:14:
It says that when the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had fled, they too ran away before Abishai, Joab's brother, and went into their city. Then Joab stopped chasing them and went back to Jerusalem.

Here the account describes Israel fighting on two fronts: Joab against the Arameans and Abishai against Ammon. Earlier, Joab encouraged his brother, saying, "Be strong, and let us act bravely," and he left the outcome in God's hands. The battle turned in Israel's favor, though the war was not yet over, as what follows shows.

For today: do with courage what falls to you, and lean on those who are with you. Then entrust the outcome to God, without believing that everything is finished just because relief has come.
exp.11:30:
From the half tribe of Manasseh, the group that lived west of the Jordan, eighteen thousand men came. They were designated by name, that is, recorded individually, to go to Hebron and make David king.

The passage is a chronicle that lists the tribes that joined David after the death of Saul. No particular person speaks; the chronicler tells the story to show that all Israel supported David. The numbers in these lists are understood in several ways, and it is not certain what their exact meaning is.

For today: God often accomplishes his purposes when many people, each with their own part, come together with a willing heart. Ask yourself what place you can faithfully fill in your church or family, even if it does not get much notice.
exp.16:18:
Here David tells God that all the good he has received comes from God's goodness and purpose. The phrase "for the sake of Your servant" means for David's sake, the one whom God chose. The phrase "according to Your own heart" means according to what God himself willed.

David speaks in prayer, after the prophet Nathan brought him God's promise: his descendants would reign and his house would endure. David feels very small before such an honor. For this reason he does not boast of himself, but acknowledges that God accomplished this great thing and made known these great promises.

For today: when you receive blessings, do not see them as your own achievements. Thank God, and ask yourself how your life can help others see his goodness.
exp.10:27:
Ira, son of Ikkesh, was from the town of Tekoa, and Abiezer was from Anathoth. These are two more names in the list of David's mighty men. The words "Tekoite" and "Anathothite" simply show which town each man came from. Tekoa and Anathoth were towns in Judah and Benjamin, near Jerusalem.

No single person is speaking here. The chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), goes through the list of men who supported David when he was acknowledged as king in Hebron and Jerusalem. It resembles the list in 2 Samuel 23. The names are recorded to remember that his reign was upheld with the help of many.

For today: God notices the humble servants and forgets no one. Faithfully do your part, even when no one applauds it; in the kingdom of God, every labor counts.
exp.26:15:
This verse begins a list of the leaders who stood at the head of the tribes of Israel. Two are named here: Eliezer son of Zichri, leader of the tribe of Reuben, and Shephatiah son of Maacah, leader of the tribe of Simeon. The opening word, "Furthermore," means "in addition" or "also."

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not known for certain, describes how David organized the kingdom at the end of his life. Earlier he spoke of the military divisions that served in shifts each month. Now he lists the leaders of each tribe. This shows that the kingdom had order and that each tribe had someone to represent it.

For today: God values order and those who serve in less visible places. These men are hardly mentioned elsewhere, but God remembered them. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even when no one applauds you.
exp.5:8:
This verse continues a list of fathers and sons: Ahimaaz was the father of Azariah, and Azariah was the father of Johanan. The word "father" here names the son's direct parent. In Bible genealogies, generations are sometimes left out, so "father" can also mean "forefather."

The book of Chronicles does not clearly say who wrote it. Many think it was an author writing after the exile, sometimes called "the Chronicler." This list follows the line of priests descended from Aaron. It was probably recorded to remind the people returning from exile who they were and that temple service had ancient roots.

For today: God remembers people we barely know. Give thanks for those who served faithfully before you, and serve with steadiness, even when no one notices.
exp.2:12:
It says that Ahaz was the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah was the father of Manasseh. This is part of a list of kings of Judah, descendants of David. Here "was the father of" means "had as his son." The names are written in an older style, but they match the names in the verse above: Ahaz, Hezekiah and Manasseh.

The book does not say with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written after the exile in Babylon. Its purpose was to remind the people that the line of David was still alive and that God had not forgotten his promises. This list shows good and bad kings, but the family continues.

For today: Ahaz was a wicked king, Hezekiah was a faithful king, and Manasseh was very wicked at the start. Each generation made its own choices. Your family history does not decide your faith: you can choose to trust God, and He keeps working even amid human failures.
exp.1:13:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Jesse, the father of David. It says that the fourth son was Nethanel and the fifth was Raddai. They are only names, with no further details. "Nethanel" is commonly explained to mean "God has given." Other texts do not mention these two brothers, so we know very little about them.

The book of Chronicles was written by an author whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, although this is not certain. He wrote for the people who were returning from exile, and he wanted to remind them of their roots. Here he traces the family of Judah, which leads to David, the most remembered king. That is why he includes even the lesser-known brothers.

For today: God notices people whom the world forgets. Nethanel and Raddai hardly appear, yet they were part of God's history. Your quiet work, your faithfulness in small things, and your place in your family also matter to Him, even when no one applauds it.
exp.15:20:
It says that God did not let anyone oppress his people. Instead, out of care for them, he rebuked and judged kings who threatened them. "Oppress" means to treat cruelly or unjustly. "Rebuked" here carries the sense of confronting with correction or judgment.

This is part of the song of thanksgiving that David gave when the ark arrived in Jerusalem. It recalls how God protected Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when they were few in number and lived as strangers. A common reference is the episode of Pharaoh and Abimelech in Genesis, though the text does not name the kings. The purpose is to praise God for his faithfulness to the covenant.

Today it reminds us that God cares for his own even when we feel small, weak, or out of place. We can trust that he does not forget us. Today, thank him for a time when he protected you, perhaps without your even realizing it.
exp.15:3:
David appointed some of the Levites to serve before the ark of the LORD. Their work was to celebrate, to give thanks, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel. Celebrating meant remembering what God had done, giving thanks meant acknowledging his goodness, and praising meant honoring him for who he is.

The Chronicles writer tells us that David had just brought the ark to Jerusalem. After the sacrifices, he blessed the people and handed out food. Then he set up the worship service with Levites and musicians, including Asaph. In this way, worship was put in order and made ongoing, not just a one-day celebration.

For today: make gratitude a habit. Each day, set aside a few minutes to remember what God has done in your life, to give him thanks and to praise him, with a prayer or a song.
exp.8:40:
This verse names the four sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz. Micah was the son of Merib-baal and the grandson of Jonathan, the son of King Saul. The sons listed here are Micah's descendants.

The text is a genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, part of the family lists found in 1 Chronicles. Its author, traditionally Ezra or a writer known as "the Chronicler," wrote for the people who returned from exile. They wanted to remember who they were and where they came from. The same list appears in 1 Chronicles 8:35. About the rest of these men we know very little.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who are barely mentioned. Your faithfulness in everyday life, and what you leave to your family, also matters. Today you can give thanks to those who came before you in the faith.
exp.14:22:
Berechiah and Elkanah were to be guardians of the ark. A guardian was someone who watched over the entrance and protected a sacred place. Here they were assigned to watch over the ark, the chest that represented God's presence among his people.

The passage is part of the chronicler's account of when David brought the ark to Jerusalem. Earlier, the attempt to move it had gone wrong because it was not done as God had commanded. Now David organizes the Levites in order: singers, musicians, priests with trumpets, and guardians. The narrator speaks here and lists names to show that each person had their place. The guardians did not sing or play music, but their task was necessary.

Today we can learn that God values simple and quiet service. Perhaps no one will applaud you for opening the door, preparing a chair, or caring for others, but God sees that faithfulness. Serve gladly wherever you are needed.
exp.24:9:
The third lot fell to Zaccur. His group was made up of him, his sons, and his brothers, twelve in all.

This verse is part of a list written by the chronicler, an author who is not identified with certainty in the text. It tells how David and the leaders organized the temple musicians into 24 shifts. Lots were cast so that the division would be fair, without favoritism. Within the same passage it says that both the small and the great took part, the teacher and the student.

For today: in the church, every service counts, whether great or small. God values the faithfulness of those who serve quietly, even when their name appears little. Ask yourself today which shift of service is yours, and do it with joy.
exp.1:14:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Jesse: Ozem sixth, and David seventh. The names are those of male children, listed in birth order.

The book of Chronicles does not clearly say who wrote it; an ancient tradition attributes it to Ezra. It was written for the people who were returning from exile, and the genealogies reminded them of their roots and of the promise made to David's family. Here is an interesting detail: 1 Samuel speaks of eight sons of Jesse, but Chronicles names seven. It is possible that one of them died without having children, although the Bible does not explain this.

For today: God works in ordinary families and often chooses the one nobody expected. David was the youngest, and yet God used him. Do not measure yourself by your place or by what others think of you.
exp.23:21:
It says that among the descendants of Izhar (the Izharites, a family of the tribe of Levi), the leader was Shelomoth, and that Shelomoth's son was called Jahath. The word "from" points to the family line, and the Berean wording makes plain that Jahath came from Shelomoth. It is simply a record of names.

The context is a list of Levite families. The chronicler, who according to tradition may have been Ezra (though this is not certain), recalls how David organized the Levites to serve in worship of God. Recording names and families showed that each one had a place and an assigned task in the house of the Lord.

For today: God does not forget those who serve quietly. Even when no one remembers your name, your faithful service, whether cleaning, teaching, helping or accompanying others, has value before Him. Serve with steadiness, without seeking applause.
exp.14:17:
This verse gives a list of Levites chosen as assistants, described as "their brothers next in rank," meaning a second group after the main leaders. Among them were Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, and others. Obed-edom and Jeiel are named as "the gatekeepers," the men who guarded the gates. The "harps" and "lyres" mentioned nearby were stringed instruments.

The book of Chronicles tells that David was preparing to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. After a first attempt failed, he ordered the Levites to carry it out with order and reverence. For this reason he commanded the Levite leaders to appoint singers and musicians to praise with joy. This list shows that each person had an assigned place.

For today: God values those who serve in the background, such as the assistants and the gatekeepers. Serve faithfully in the place you are given, without seeking recognition, because God sees and remembers every name.
exp.15:15:
This verse continues the call to remember God's covenant. "The covenant He made" refers to a solemn promise God established with Abraham. "The oath He swore" is a promise confirmed by God himself, which he later renewed with Isaac.

This song of thanksgiving appears in Chronicles when David brings the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. Together with the Levites who lead the praise, he invites the people to remember that God keeps what he promises. The promises made to Abraham and Isaac included the land and a numerous descendants, as seen in Genesis.

For today: when you doubt God, call to mind his promises and how faithful he has been before. Write down some of them and thank him. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens hope and helps you trust in him, even in difficult times.
exp.16:3:
God tells Nathan to carry a message to David, whom he calls "my servant." The message is clear: David is not the one to build God a house to live in.

Here God is speaking. David wanted to build a temple, and Nathan, without first consulting God, told him to do what was in his heart. That same night God corrected that answer. Then, in verse 5 and following, God explains that he had never asked for a house of cedar. Later he promises something greater: that he will build a house for David, meaning a lineage of descendants. This passage does not explain why David could not build the temple; another passage (1 Chronicles 22:8) connects it with David's wars.

For today: a good desire is not always God's plan. Before acting, let us seek his direction in prayer and in his Word, and accept his answer with humility.
exp.1:20:
Hezron, a son of Judah, married the daughter of Machir, of the tribe of Manasseh, when he was already sixty years old. The verse says he "slept with" her, and the BSB puts it plainly: he married her, and then they had relations. From that union Segub was born. The phrase "father of Gilead" probably means that Machir was the founder or leader of the people of that region.

This is part of the long lists of families that open 1 Chronicles. The author, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), wrote them for the people who were returning from exile, to remind them where they came from. Here the line of Judah stands out, the line from which David would come. Segub became the grandfather of towns in Gilead.

For today: God is not limited by age or by the later stages of life. He can plant something valuable at any time, and every life matters in his plan.
exp.20:2:
Joab answers King David with a blessing and a question. He prays that the LORD would multiply His troops a hundred times over. He reminds the king that they are already all his servants. And he asks why the king wants to do this, since it will bring guilt on Israel. "Guilt" means blame or wrongdoing. "Want to" means desire or intend.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. David has just ordered that all the men of the people be counted, and the text says that Satan incited the king to do it. Joab senses that counting the people out of pride or from trusting in military strength would be a sin before God. Even so, the king insists. Commentators explain David's exact sin in several ways, but the passage makes clear that it was a serious mistake.

Today, when someone we trust warns us with respect, it is wise to listen. Let us ask God for humility, so that we do not rely on numbers, achievements, or resources, but on Him.
exp.16:8:
God says he will provide a place for his people Israel. He "plants" them like a tree, so that they may live in a place of their own, with firm roots and without being disturbed. To be "disturbed" means to be unsettled or troubled. The "sons of wickedness" are wicked people who oppress. God promises that they will no longer oppress his people as they did at the beginning.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan, addressing David. David wanted to build a temple, but God answers by reminding him that it was he who took him from tending sheep and made him king. Then he promises stability for the people and a house, that is, a descendant who will reign.

For today: God is the one who gives security and firm roots. When you feel unsettled or afraid, remember how God has sustained you before, and rest in the knowledge that he continues to care for your future, even when you cannot see the whole path.
exp.27:19:
David tells his son Solomon to be brave and get to work. "Be strong and courageous" means having heart and strength. "Do not be afraid or discouraged" means not losing heart and giving up out of fear or weariness. David assures him that the LORD God is with him and will neither fail him nor forsake him until the work on the temple is finished.

David, now old, is speaking publicly before he dies. God did not allow him to build the temple, so he hands Solomon the plans he received from the LORD. He knows the task is enormous, so he encourages Solomon and reminds him that he will have help: priests, Levites, craftsmen, and the people.

For today: when God gives you something big to do, don't wait until you feel capable. Take the first step, trust that God goes with you, and accept the help of other people.
exp.28:8:
This verse says that the people rejoiced because they had given freely to the LORD. The word "rejoiced" means they were glad and happy. They gave "freely," meaning by their own choice, with no one forcing them. They gave "wholeheartedly," meaning with complete sincerity and no hidden motives. King David also rejoiced greatly.

The passage tells what happened when King David encouraged the leaders and the people to give toward building the temple, which his son Solomon would later build. They had already given gold, silver, bronze, iron, and precious stones. The writer of Chronicles emphasizes that their joy came from giving with a whole heart. Right after this, David praises God and acknowledges that everything belongs to Him.

For today: giving to God, whether time, money, or talents, should not be a burden. When we give sincerely and remember that everything comes from God, our giving becomes joy and worship.
exp.8:20:
This verse says that Zechariah, son of Meshelemiah, was the gatekeeper at the entrance to the tent where God met with his people. The sacred tent was the place of worship, and a gatekeeper watched over its entrance.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes to the Israelites who returned from exile. He presents them with lists of Levite families to remind them that worship of God had order and that each servant had a place. Zechariah appears within a list of gatekeepers, descendants of Korah.

For today: God values small and unseen work, such as opening a door or welcoming others. If you serve quietly in your church or in your home, your faithfulness counts and God remembers it.
exp.1:3:
It says that Tamar, Judah's daughter-in-law, bore to him Perez and Zerah. In this way, Judah had five sons in all. The word "bore" here means gave birth. A daughter-in-law is the wife of a son.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), gathers the family records of Israel for the people who were returning from exile. Here he starts with Judah, the tribe of David. The story of Tamar is in Genesis 38, where Judah wronged her. Chronicles does not give the details, but it shows that Perez was an important ancestor, and from his line came David and later Jesus (Matthew 1:3).

God can continue his plan with imperfect people and families. If your story has mistakes or wounds, it is not outside God's care. Trust that he can work with grace and bring redemption, even when you do not understand the whole path.
exp.8:36:
This verse continues a list of names. It mentions other sons of Jehiel, the founder of Gibeon: Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth. The word that appears next, meaning "was the father of," shows how the family line is recorded. Here the names do not tell a story; they simply record who made up that family.

This part of Chronicles is a genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. It is believed that the author, traditionally called the Chronicler, wrote it for the people who were returning from exile, so that they would remember their roots and their place in Jerusalem. The list ends by linking to the family of King Saul.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom history barely mentions. If sometimes you feel that your work goes unnoticed, remember that God sees and values what you do faithfully. Your name matters to Him.
exp.15:12:
This verse calls God's people by three names: "offspring of Israel," "sons of Jacob," and "his chosen ones." "Offspring" means descendants, and "servant" here refers to Israel, or Jacob, as God's servant. In this way it reminds them who they are: the people God chose.

This is part of a psalm of thanksgiving that David handed to Asaph and his brothers when the ark of the covenant came to Jerusalem. The verses before it call people to seek the Lord and remember his works. This verse names those who receive that call, and the next one continues with God's covenant with them.

For today: if you belong to Christ, your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on the fact that God called you. That identity encourages you to seek him every day and to remember with gratitude what he has done for you.
exp.23:26:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that the descendants of Merari, traced through Jaaziah, were Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri. Merari was one of the three great groups of Levites, along with Gershon and Kohath.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), tells how David organized the service of the temple. He records the names of the Levites so that the people would remember who served in the house of God and to which family they belonged, even after the exile.

For today: God knows people by their name, not only the famous ones. Your service, though simple and little seen, matters to Him. Today you can serve faithfully and give thanks for those who serve in silence.
exp.3:18:
The verse mentions the wife of Hodiah, who was the sister of Naham. Her sons were the founders of two places: Keilah, the Garmite, and Eshtemoa, the Maacathite. In Hebrew, "father of" often means founder or leader of a people. Some of the names here may be people or cities, and it is not always known for certain.

This passage is part of the long lists of families of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles. The author, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, recorded these family lines for the people who were returning from exile. In this way they remembered their history, their lands, and their identity as God's people.

For today: God forgets no one, not even people whose names we barely know. If you feel small or unseen today, remember that God knows you and that your life has a place in his story. Serve faithfully where you are.
exp.7:1:
This verse follows a list of the sons of Benjamin. It says that Nohah was the fourth son and Rapha the fifth. The word "fathered" means that he was the father of them, and "firstborn" is the eldest son. The names in this passage differ from other lists of Benjamin in the Bible (such as Genesis 46 or Numbers 26), and the reason is not known with certainty; several explanations have been proposed.

Chronicles is a book written after the return from exile in Babylon, and it is not known with certainty who its author was; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra. Its purpose was to remind the people who they were, which families they came from, and that God had not forgotten them. That is why there are so many genealogies.

For today: God knows people by name, even those who barely appear in the story. You can remember that your life and your family matter to Him, and treat others with that same value.
exp.28:9:
King David rejoiced greatly and praised God in front of the whole gathered assembly. In this verse, "blessed" means that David praised God and gave thanks to him. The phrase "from everlasting to everlasting" means that God deserves praise without end. David declares that the Lord, the God of Israel, is worthy of blessing forever.

David speaks here as an old man, near the end of his reign. The people and their leaders had just given generously of gold, silver and precious stones for building the temple, which his son Solomon would later build. David is filled with joy at seeing their willing hearts, and he responds with a public prayer of worship.

For today: when you give your time, your money or your talents, do it with joy and sincere devotion, and remember that everything comes from God. Give thanks to Him instead of feeling proud of what you give.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that Ram was the father of Amminadab, and that Amminadab was the father of Nahshon. Nahshon is described as a leader of the descendants of Judah, that is, a chief of his tribe. The phrase "was the father of" simply means that one man was the parent of the next in the family line.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile in Babylon. Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. Its author goes through the family lists to remind the people who they were and where they came from when they returned. This list follows the line of Judah, which leads down to King David. Nahshon appears as a leader of Judah in the wilderness, according to Numbers 1 and 2.

God works through generations, even when their names seem little known to us. This line reaches to David and, according to Matthew 1, to Jesus. Your faithfulness each day in your family, though it may seem small, can influence those who come after you.
exp.3:2:
This verse names the sons of Etam from the tribe of Judah: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash, and it also names their sister, Hazzelelponi. The phrase "sons of Etam" likely refers to the founders or leaders of the town of Etam rather than only his direct children. The Hebrew in this verse is hard to read with confidence, so the exact meaning of some words is uncertain.

The book of Chronicles was written after the people returned from exile in Babylon. Its author, traditionally thought to be Ezra though this is not certain, compiled family lists to help the people remember who they were and where they came from. This list is part of the descendants of Judah, the tribe of David.

For today: God forgets no one. Even names that sound strange to us were written into his story. This reminds us that your life, though it may seem small or hidden, has value before God.
exp.5:74:
This verse is part of a list of cities. It says that the tribe of Asher handed over two more cities to the Levites: Hukok and Rehob. The phrase "together with their pasturelands" refers to the open land around each city, where the Levites could raise their livestock.

The writer of Chronicles reviews how Israel distributed cities to the Levites, who did not receive an inheritance of land like the other tribes. This list, written after the exile, reminded the people that the service of God was always sustained by the community. Some place names vary in other passages, such as Joshua 21, and scholars explain those differences in several ways.

Today we can learn to care for those who serve God in the church. Think of a pastor, a teacher, or a volunteer, and help them with your time, a word of encouragement, or your concrete support.
exp.5:70:
The Gershomites received the following: from the clan of the half-tribe of Manasseh, they were given Golan in Bashan and also Ashtaroth, together with their pasturelands. These were cities for the Levites, who did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. The pasturelands around each city were the open land where they could keep their livestock.

This verse is part of a list of Levitical cities. God arranged for the Levites to live spread out among all the tribes rather than in one region. The book does not name its author; many think it was written by someone after the exile, though there is no certainty. It was meant to remind the people how the service of God was organized.

Today we can ask ourselves how we care for those who serve God among us. One practical way is to support your church or a servant of God with offerings, prayer, or concrete help.
exp.15:29:
Verse 30 calls all the people of the earth to tremble before God. Here "tremble" does not mean a paralyzing dread but honoring him with awe because he is great. It also says that the world is firmly established and cannot be moved, because God upholds it.

David handed this song to Asaph and his companions when the ark of the covenant arrived in Jerusalem. It was a time of celebration and worship. The people were inviting all the nations to acknowledge the LORD as King. That is why the call follows that the heavens, the earth, and the sea should rejoice.

For today: when everything around you seems unstable, remember that God remains firm. Begin your day with a moment of respect and gratitude toward him, and entrust your concerns to the one who holds up the whole world.
exp.15:33:
He says we should give thanks to God because He is good, and His loving devotion never comes to an end.

This psalm of thanksgiving appears in 1 Chronicles 16 and was given by David to Asaph and his brothers when the ark of the covenant arrived in Jerusalem. The people were celebrating God's presence. Before the verse, all of creation joins in the praise, because God comes to judge the earth. Afterward, the people ask for salvation and respond with "Amen".

For today: when your mood depends on your circumstances, pause and thank God for one concrete sign of His goodness. Remembering that His loving devotion endures forever helps you trust and keep going.
exp.2:8:
These were all the sons of David, not counting the sons by his concubines, who were secondary wives with a lower legal standing. The verse also mentions Tamar, who was their sister. The word "besides" here means "apart from" or "in addition to."

This is part of a genealogy of David's family in 1 Chronicles. Nobody knows for certain who wrote the book; Jewish tradition often names Ezra. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots and the promise made to David. Tamar is mentioned because her story was well known and painful, as told in 2 Samuel 13.

God works through royal and imperfect families, with difficult histories. Our family history, even if it carries wounds, does not stop God from fulfilling his purpose. Entrust your past and your family to him today.
exp.25:25:
This verse says that Shelomith and his brothers were in charge of all the treasuries holding the things set apart for God, meaning the gifts dedicated to him. Those gifts had been given by King David, by the heads of families, by the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and by the army commanders. The heads of families are the leaders of the clans, and the commanders of thousands and of hundreds are military officers.

The book of Chronicles, written by an unnamed author, reviews the history of Israel and shows how David organized the service of the temple. The Levites had different duties, and some of them looked after the treasures. The verses that follow say that part of those offerings came from wars and would be used to repair the house of the Lord.

For today: what is dedicated to God deserves honest care and good order. If you serve in your church with money or resources, do it with transparency, remembering that it is not yours but God's.
exp.27:7:
David says that, before all the people and before God himself, he asks that they keep and seek out all the commandments of the Lord their God with care. To seek out means to search for and examine closely. An inheritance is what is passed down to descendants. The purpose is that they may possess this good land and leave it to their descendants forever.

David speaks as an old man, before the leaders of Israel gathered together. He is handing over the kingdom to his son Solomon and preparing for the building of the temple. Before addressing Solomon, he reminds the whole people that God's blessing is tied to obedience. The promise had conditions, and the people were also responsible.

For today: how we live in obedience to God influences those who come after us. We can ask ourselves what we are leaving to our children or to younger people: not only possessions, but also an example of seeking God and his Word with steadiness.
exp.8:10:
Azariah is presented in this verse as a priest who, according to the text, was the chief official in charge of the affairs of God's temple. His family line is traced back through Hilkiah, Meshullam, Zadok, Meraioth, and Ahitub. The phrase "chief official" here means the head or leading authority over the temple, not a king's son.

The chronicler, writing after the return from exile in Babylon, lists those who came back to live in Jerusalem and serve in the temple. His purpose was to show the restored people that their life of worship had ancient and unbroken roots. Some scholars think this Azariah is the same person who appears in Nehemiah 11:11 under the name Seraiah, though there is no complete certainty.

God values the faithfulness of those who serve from one generation to the next. Although names like this may seem like nothing more than a list, they remind us that God knows every person who serves him. Today we can serve steadily in our church and family, knowing that what is simple and faithful is also kept before God.
exp.10:32:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions two more warriors: Azmaveth, who was from Baharum (that is why he is called "Baharumite"), and Eliahba, from Shaalbon (that is why "Shaalbonite"). Names ending in "-ite" indicate the place of origin. Some of these places are not known with certainty today.

Context: The author of Chronicles, traditionally identified with Ezra though this is not certain, lists David's mighty men, the men who supported him in becoming king over all Israel. He writes for a people returning from exile, to remind them of their history and that God had sustained their king through faithful people.

For today: God notices people who sometimes seem unimportant. Of these men only the names remain, but they were written down. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one applauds you; God does not forget your work.
exp.24:11:
This verse says that the fifth turn of service fell to Nethaniah, along with his sons and his brothers, making twelve in all. The word "lot" does not appear in this verse, but it is understood from the context: the turns were assigned by casting lots. That is how the service by turns was known.

The writer tells how King David organized the musicians of the temple. They were the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, and they served with harps, lyres, and cymbals. They were arranged into twenty-four groups of twelve, and each group had its turn. This was done so that the praise of God would be orderly and constant.

For today: God values each person who serves, even when their name is little known. There is a place for everyone in worship, and serving with order and as a team honors God.
exp.14:12:
This verse says that the first time they tried to move the ark, God burst out in anger against them. The reason was that the Levites had not been carrying it, and the people had not consulted God about the proper way to do it, that is, in line with what He had commanded. "You" in this verse is simply the ordinary word for "you."

David speaks to the chief priests and Levites. Earlier, the ark had been placed on a new cart, and Uzza died when he touched it (1 Chronicles 13). Now David acknowledges that the law required the Levites to carry it on their shoulders by the poles. For this reason he asks them to sanctify themselves, that is, to prepare and set themselves apart for this service.

For today: good intentions and enthusiasm are not enough. It is wise to seek God according to His Word, not merely according to what seems practical or comfortable to us. If we make mistakes, we can acknowledge them with humility and begin again.
exp.10:17:
This verse tells how three of David's mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines, drew water from the well of Bethlehem, which was by the gate, and brought it to David.
