The phrase "brought it" is the act of carrying the water to him. David would not drink it, but poured it out to the Lord.

The writer of the book describes a moment in David's life. He was in a stronghold, and the Philistines held Bethlehem, his hometown. David, longing for home, expressed a wish, and these three men risked their lives to fulfill it. By pouring out the water, David acknowledged that something so costly was fit only for God. Scholars explain the gesture in several ways, but the text makes clear that he regarded it as sacred.

For today: value the sacrifices others make for you, and do not use their efforts merely for your own comfort. Respond with gratitude, and honor God.
exp.10:4:
The verse tells that the people of Jebus, a city that would later become Jerusalem, said to David, "You will never get in here." Even so, David captured the fortress of Zion, and from then on it was called the City of David.

David had just been anointed king over all Israel in Hebron, according to what God had said through Samuel. The Jebusites, who lived there, were confident that their city could not be taken. Their words show mockery and certainty. Afterward David offered a reward: whoever attacked first would become commander, and Joab achieved it. With this conquest, Jerusalem became the center of the kingdom.

For today: when someone tells you "you will never make it," or you face a great obstacle, remember that God keeps what He promises. Move forward with courage, with prayer and with work, trusting that He is the one who sustains your calling.
exp.21:13:
In this verse David tells his son Solomon that he has gathered a great deal of material for building the temple. David says he has taken great pains to provide it. Solomon is told that David has prepared gold, silver, bronze, iron, timber and stone. The amounts are enormous, and many scholars consider them very large or possibly exaggerated figures; there is no certainty about their exact meaning.

David speaks shortly before his death. God did not allow him to build the temple, so he devoted himself to having everything ready for Solomon. He asks Solomon to continue the work and to be faithful to the law of God.

For today: not all of us finish what we begin, but we can prepare the way for others. Serve God with what you have, and help those who come after you to move forward.
exp.10:16:
In this verse, David expresses a deep longing: he says he wishes someone would bring him a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem. The phrase "Oh, that someone would get me" is a way of saying "I wish someone would bring me."

David is the one speaking. He was in the stronghold, and the Philistines had taken control of Bethlehem, his hometown. His wish seems to be a sigh of longing, not a command. Three of his mighty men heard him and risked their lives to bring him the water. When David received it, he did not drink it, but poured it out before the LORD, because he felt it was too precious to use for his own pleasure.

For today: value the sacrifice of those who serve you, and be careful with your wishes, because they can cost others dearly. And offer to God with gratitude what you have received at a high price.
exp.1:54:
The verse mentions the clans of the scribes, that is, people who copied and cared for written texts, who lived at Jabez. They are named as the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites. They are said to have been Kenites, a people who were not originally Israelite. "Came from Hammath" points to a founder or ancestor of that clan, the father of the house of Rechab. It is not known for certain where Jabez was, or whether Hammath is a place or a person.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often associates with Ezra, though this is not certain, records family lines for the people who returned from exile. He wanted them to know where they came from, and that each family had its place, including groups of foreign origin who had joined Israel.

For today: God notices people who work quietly, like these scribes. Do your work faithfully, even when no one notices, and welcome gladly those who come from other places.
exp.6:39:
This verse closes the list of the descendants of Asher. It says that all of them were heads of families, chosen men, brave, and leaders among the chief men. When they were counted according to their family records, there were 26,000 men fit for battle.

The book of Chronicles does not clearly state who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their identity, their families, and their inheritance. That is why it includes these long lists. The count was made according to family records, and scholars debate the period in which the count was taken.

For today: God pays attention to every family and every person, even when their name seems small. You can serve with courage where you are, caring for your family and strengthening your community of faith.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that Ashhur, who is called "the father of Tekoa," had two wives: Helah and Naarah. The phrase "father of" most often means founder or leader of a town or a family, not necessarily a direct father.

Here no individual character is speaking; it is the chronicler, who writes lists of families from the tribe of Judah. He probably wanted to preserve the memory of the family lines after the exile, so that the people would remember their roots. Ashhur also appears in 1 Chronicles 2:24, and Tekoa was a town in Judah. The details about his life are few, and scholars do not agree on everything.

For today: God pays attention to families and to names that seem small. Give thanks to those who came before you, and care lovingly for your family, because your life matters to God too.
exp.4:9:
In the days of King Saul, the tribe of Reuben fought against the Hagrites and defeated them. The phrase "defeated at their hands" means the Reubenites won the battle. Afterward, the Reubenites settled in the homes of the Hagrites across the whole region east of Gilead.

The Hagrites were a desert people, and the exact origin of their name is explained in several ways.

Here the chronicler, who writes a list of the families of Israel, is speaking. He is talking about Reuben, whose descendants had many cattle and needed land to graze. The author wants to remember how this tribe grew and occupied its territory east of the Jordan.

For today: the blessings and places we live often come with effort and challenges. We can work with courage, while recognizing that everything good comes from God.
exp.5:58:
This verse continues a list of cities given to the descendants of Aaron, the priests. Here Ashan and Beth-shemesh are named, along with Juttah. The pasturelands mentioned are the open land around each city, where the people could keep their animals.

The chronicler reviews the records of the Levites, the tribe dedicated to the service of God. Since they did not receive a territory of their own, they lived in cities spread among the other tribes. This had been commanded in the time of Moses and Joshua. The readers of Chronicles, who were returning from exile, needed to remember that service to God had a place and an order among his people.

God cares for those who serve him and places them near the people. Today we might ask ourselves: in what place has God put me to serve and bless those around me?
exp.7:37:
It says that Azel had six sons and gives their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. It ends by repeating that all of them were sons of Azel, as if to make clear that none is missing. The idea behind this family record is simply that he was their father or ancestor.

This is part of the family lists of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles. There is no character speaking; it is the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes after the exile in Babylon, and these lists helped the people who were returning to remember their roots, their land, and their identity. Azel was a descendant of King Saul, according to the previous chapter.

For today: God does not see people as mere numbers. Here are six names that were preserved in his Word. Today you can remember that your name and your story matter to God, and also value your family and the ordinary people around you, praying for them by name.
exp.3:13:
It says Meonothai was the father of Ophrah, and Seraiah was the father of Joab. This Joab is called "father," meaning founder or head, of the people living in Ge-harashim, the name given to the place because its people were craftsmen. The name means "valley of craftsmen," because the people there were skilled workers.

It is a genealogy within the descendants of Judah. The writer of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), records these names for the people returning from exile. He wanted to remind them of their origin and identity. This Joab is not the famous general of David. He is another man with the same name.

For today: God values manual work and skilled trades. An entire people was remembered for its craftsmen. Do your work, whether humble or prominent, with dedication, as a service to God and to others.
exp.17:14:
Joab, son of Zeruiah, commanded David's army, and Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, held the post of recorder. The term recorder points to a role that was probably that of keeper of the king's records or chronicler. Some think he may also have served as a spokesman or adviser, but this is not known for certain.

Here the speaker is not a character in the story but the author of Chronicles. After describing David's victories, he lists his main officials. He wants to show that the kingdom was well organized and that God sustained it, since the preceding text says that the LORD preserved David wherever he went.

For today: God uses people with different tasks, both visible and quiet. Serve faithfully in what is yours to do, without comparing yourself to others, trusting that God values your part.
exp.4:24:
This verse says that the half-tribe of Manasseh, together with Reuben and Gad, was unfaithful to the God of their ancestors. "Prostituted themselves" here means that they abandoned their loyalty to God by worshiping idols, like someone who breaks a sacred promise of faithfulness. They turned to the gods of the people of the land, that is, of the nations that God himself had driven out before them.

The chronicler, writing after the exile, explains why these tribes east of the Jordan were carried away captive by Assyria. He describes them as brave and numerous people, but their strength did not save them from unfaithfulness. The author seems to want his readers to understand that the exile had a spiritual cause.

For today: achievements and blessings do not replace faithfulness to God. Today it is worth asking ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts and returning to him with humility.
exp.16:11:
This verse says that a descendant of David will build a house for God, and that God will make his kingdom firm forever. The word "forever" is the meaning of the original wording here. "Throne" is the place of authority of a king, and to "establish" means to make firm and secure.

Here God speaks, through the prophet Nathan, to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God answers that He will build David a "house," that is, a dynasty, a family of kings. This promise was first fulfilled in Solomon, who built the temple. Many Christians believe it is fully fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David, whose kingdom has no end.

For today: God keeps what He promises, even when it takes generations. When your plans do not turn out as you expected, trust that God is still working with a purpose greater than yours.
exp.10:15:
This verse places us in the setting. David was in the stronghold, a safe refuge, and the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem. A garrison means a group of soldiers who occupied and guarded the place. "At that time" marks when these things were happening.

The writer of the book tells this to prepare the story that follows. Bethlehem was David's hometown, and it was held by the enemy. That is why, when David felt thirsty and longed for the water from the well of his homeland, three of his mighty men took the risk of bringing it to him. Some scholars connect the stronghold with the cave of Adullam, but the text does not say this with complete certainty.

For today: value those who serve you with love and sacrifice, and offer to God what you hold most dear, as David did with the water.
exp.22:8:
This verse gives a list of names: three sons of Shimei, who are Shelomoth, Haziel and Haran. It says they were the heads of the families that descended from Ladan. It is unusual that another list of Shimei's sons appears later, so some think it refers to a different Shimei or to a different way of ordering the list. It is not entirely clear.

The chronicler tells how David, already old, organized the Levites for the service of the temple that Solomon would build. Each Levite family had a place and a responsibility.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those whom almost no one remembers. Serve where God has placed you, faithfully, without worrying about whether you are applauded or not.
exp.22:5:
This verse says that David divided the Levites into groups, or "divisions," according to the three sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The phrase "divided the Levites into divisions" refers to groups organized with set duties.

The book tells that David, now old, had made his son Solomon king and was preparing everything for the future temple. The Levites were the tribe dedicated to the service of God. David organized them so that each one knew his work: to build, to judge, to keep the gates, and to praise. After this, the text begins to list the descendants of Gershon.

For today: God values order and each person having a place. In your church or community, ask what concrete task you can take on, large or small, and do it faithfully, knowing it serves a greater purpose.
exp.15:24:
For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; He is to be feared above all gods. It says that the LORD is great and deserves to be praised with the whole heart. It also says he is to be feared, that is, held in deep reverence, above all gods. The verse also speaks of praise, and the verse before it speaks of salvation.

This passage is part of a psalm of thanksgiving that David handed to Asaph and his companions when the ark of the covenant was brought to Jerusalem. They sang it to celebrate God's presence among his people. They called all the nations to know him. The gods of the peoples were idols, and the text that follows says they are nothing compared to the LORD, who made the heavens.

For today: when something worries you or takes your attention, pause for a moment and praise God for who he is. Recognizing his greatness puts your problems in perspective and renews your trust.
exp.28:23:
This verse says that all the officials and the mighty men, along with all of King David's sons, pledged their allegiance to the new king, Solomon. The phrase "pledged their allegiance" in the verse means that they publicly acknowledged his authority and promised their loyalty to him.

It is part of the ending of 1 Chronicles. The chronicler tells how David, now old, handed the kingdom to Solomon in a great gathering before God. He highlights that even Solomon's brothers accepted him. This is significant because, on other occasions, the succession to the throne had caused conflict among David's sons.

For today: recognizing the authority God has placed over us, with humility, helps to maintain unity. In the family, the church, or the workplace, we can support those who lead without pride or rivalry, and pray for them.
exp.11:21:
It says that men kept coming to David day after day to help him, until he had a great army. The comparison "like the army of God" is a way of saying it was an enormous and impressive force. The phrase about help refers to men who joined to support him.

This passage is part of a list compiled by the chronicler, an author who is not identified with certainty. It speaks of the warriors who joined David while he was fleeing from Saul, at Ziklag, before he became king. The men of Manasseh were brave and were commanders. The author wants to show that David's reign was backed by many people from different tribes.

For today: God often sustains his work through people who join in and serve. Ask yourself whom you can help with your time, your gifts, or your support, and do it faithfully, day by day.
exp.5:32:
This verse begins the list of the Levite musicians who served in worship. The verse says these men served, together with their sons, meaning they were present and on duty. Heman is named, described as the singer, a descendant of Kohath (the Levite family of the Kohathites), and his family line is given: the son of Joel, the son of Samuel.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, reviews the genealogies of Israel to remind the people of their roots and of the value of worshiping God. He tells that David placed these men in charge of the music when the ark finally rested in Jerusalem. They served with song before the tabernacle, and later in Solomon's temple. Many understand this Samuel to be the prophet, though not everyone agrees.

For today: God values constant and orderly service, even the kind that seems small. Serve faithfully in your church, without seeking prominence, remembering that praising God is a task that many have received and passed on from generation to generation.
exp.11:24:
From Simeon came 7,100 brave and strong men, ready for battle, who arrived at Hebron. They are described as mighty men of valor, meaning men of spirit and courage. They are part of a list of groups who joined David.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes long after these events, records the tribes who went to Hebron to make David king, in keeping with what the LORD had said. His purpose is to show that all Israel supported David and that this fulfilled what God had promised. Some scholars note that Simeon, a small tribe, contributed many men, though the exact reason is not explained in the text.

For today: God counts on you, even if you come from a small or little-known group. When God is at work, every person who joins with courage and unity has a place in his plan.
exp.14:5:
This verse says that David gathered the descendants of Merari, one of the clans of the Levites. Their leader was Asaiah, and together with his relatives they numbered two hundred and twenty men. The word "chief" means the leader or head of the group, and "relatives" refers to the members of his clan.

The one telling this is the chronicler, who describes how David prepared the moving of the ark of God to Jerusalem. Earlier, the attempt to move it had ended badly. Now David calls the Levites, because they were the ones who were to carry it according to the law of God. That is why the list names each family with its leader.

For today: God values order and obedience, and he also values each person. No group was left unnamed. Serve where God has placed you, even when your task seems small, and try to do things his way.
exp.9:10:
This verse says that the people of Jabesh-gilead learned of what the Philistines had done to Saul after he was killed in battle: they took away his armor, carried off his head and his weapons, and displayed them in the temples of their gods. Here, "heard about" means received word of or learned about.

This is the account of the writer of Chronicles, who was writing to a people returning from exile. He wants to remind them how Saul's reign ended. Jabesh-gilead was a town that Saul had rescued at the beginning of his reign (1 Samuel 11). That is why its men react with gratitude and courage, as the next verse shows.

For today: gratitude is shown through deeds. Think of someone who helped you in the past, and look for a way today to honor them or serve their family, even when they can no longer repay you.
exp.25:7:
This verse sums up the list of Obed-edom's family. It says that all of them were descendants of Obed-edom, and that they, along with their sons and brothers, were capable men with strength to do the work. In all, there were sixty-two of them. The word "work" here refers to service in the temple.

This chapter is part of an account in Chronicles, written by an author who is not named in the text. It tells how David organized the Levites, and here the gatekeepers, who guarded the gates and the storerooms of God's house. Obed-edom also appears in the story of the ark, but the text does not explain in detail why his family was so large. Some see it as a sign of blessing.

For today: God values steady service, even in simple tasks. Offer your strength and abilities with joy, alongside your family or your church.
exp.17:12:
It says David placed garrisons, that is, groups of soldiers, in Edom, and that all the Edomites became subject to him. The text gives the reason: the Lord made David victorious wherever he went. "Subject" here means people under his rule who paid tribute.

This is part of the Chronicler's account of David's victories. The chapter recalls that Abishai defeated the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, and that David dedicated the gold and silver taken to God. The writer, addressing a people returning from exile, wants to show that David's success came from God, not only from his strength.

For today: we will not always see triumphs like these, but we can trust that God cares for those who walk with Him. When something goes well, let us acknowledge His help and give Him thanks, as David did when he dedicated what he had received to Him.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that David took up residence in the fortress he had just captured, and because of this the place came to be called "the City of David." It marks the moment when a conquered stronghold became his home and his capital.

The one telling this is the writer of Chronicles, who reviews the history of Israel. Earlier, the people of Jebus, the Jebusites, thought no one could take their city. David captured it, and Joab was the first to go up, so he received the position of commander. Now David makes that place his capital. Afterward it says that God was with him.

For today: David did not stop at the victory but settled in and built. After an achievement or a difficult stage, we can take firm steps, serve faithfully, and remember that what truly grows, grows with God.
exp.11:27:
He says that Zadok was a young man, mighty and brave, and that he came with twenty-two commanders from his own family. "Young man" means a youth. "Mighty of valor" means strong and full of courage. "Commanders" are the leaders or heads.

The author of Chronicles makes a list of the warriors who joined David at Hebron to make him king over all Israel. This Zadok appears among the Levites and priests, alongside Joiada. Many identify him with the priest Zadok who served in the times of David and Solomon, but the text does not say so clearly. The book wants to show that all the people supported David.

Today we can learn that God values those who put themselves at his disposal with courage and loyalty. Zadok did not come alone, but brought his family with him. Ask yourself whom you can encourage to serve God alongside you.
exp.7:9:
This verse ends a list of the sons of Shaharaim, a man of the tribe of Benjamin. It names three more: Jeuz, Sachia and Mirmah. It says they were "heads of families," that is, leaders or chiefs of their households and clans. Their father had them with Hodesh, his wife, in the land of Moab.

No one speaks here in particular; it is the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes after the return from exile in Babylon. He wanted the people to remember their roots, their land and their families. Why Shaharaim was in Moab and left his other wives, the text does not explain.

For today: God does not forget any name, even though we may pass over lists like this one. You can remember that your life and your family matter to God. Today, take a moment to give thanks for someone who shaped you in the faith.
exp.27:1:
David rose to his feet in front of the leaders of Israel and spoke to them warmly, calling them "my brothers" and "my people." He tells them that it had been in his heart to build a house as a resting place for the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and as a footstool for our God. The footstool is an image: the place where God, like a king, rests his feet. David says he had made preparations for the building, meaning he had already gathered the materials.

David speaks at the end of his reign, before the chiefs, commanders, and officials he had himself summoned to Jerusalem. He explains his desire to build the temple, but in the verses that follow he says that God did not allow it. He wants everyone to understand that the task will pass to his son Solomon.

For today: sometimes we have good plans for God and he tells us that they are not for us, or not for now. David did not become bitter; he kept preparing the way for others. We can serve with joy even when we do not see the final result.
exp.16:14:
This verse says that the prophet Nathan passed on to David the entire message God had given him, leaving nothing out. The phrase "all the words of this entire revelation" means the whole message from God, and "revelation" refers to what God made known to Nathan. Nathan delivered it faithfully, word for word in substance.

Nathan was a prophet, and David wanted to build a house for God. But God answered that he would instead build David a house, that is, his family and his descendants. He promised him a son whose kingdom would be firm. Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of Jesus, although it first referred to Solomon and the kings who would come after him.

For today: when we share what God says in his Word, let us do it with faithfulness and humility, without changing it to make it sound better. And like David, we can respond with gratitude.
exp.28:6:
This verse lists what Israel's leaders gave for building the temple: 5,000 talents of gold and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze, and 100,000 talents of iron. A talent was a very large unit of weight, and the exact value of these figures is debated.

King David had gathered the heads of families, tribes, and armies. He himself had already given from his own possessions, and he asked: "Who is willing to bring an offering to the LORD today?" The leaders responded with generosity. His son Solomon would build the temple later, and the people rejoiced to give freely.

For today: God values the disposition of the heart more than the amount. We can give time, gifts, or money with joy and sincerity, without pressure, recognizing that everything we have comes from Him.
exp.10:29:
This verse names two of David's warriors: Maharai and Heled, son of Baanah. Both were "Netophathites," that is, from Netophah, a town near Bethlehem. The list does not tell of their deeds; it only keeps their names.

The chronicler does not speak in the first person, but presents a list of the mighty men who supported David when he was established as king of Israel. He writes after the exile, and he wants his people to remember that the kingdom was sustained with the help of many people, not only the king. Nothing more is known about these two men beyond this mention, and the parallel text in 2 Samuel 23 presents them with slight variations.

For today: God values faithful service even when it goes unnoticed. Perhaps no one applauds your daily work, but God sees it. Serve steadily where you are, without needing to be famous.
exp.15:2:
In this verse, the narrator tells how David, after blessing the people, gave to every Israelite, both men and women, a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake.

The word "gave" in this verse means that he handed each person their share.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who recounts that David had just brought the ark of God to Jerusalem and offered sacrifices. It was a day of great joy and worship. David wanted no one to be left out of the celebration, and so he shared food with all the people.

For today: true worship is lived out in community and comes to the table. We can celebrate what God does by sharing food, time, and joy with others, leaving no one out, especially those who are alone or in need.
exp.10:25:
Here begins a list of brave men from David's army. First named is Asahel, the brother of Joab, and then Elhanan (Elchanan), the son of Dodo, who was from Bethlehem. "Mighty men" means strong soldiers who stood out among the troops.

The author of Chronicles, who writes long after these events, remembers those who supported David when he became king. His list aims to honor these men and to show that the kingdom was sustained by the effort of many people, not only by the king. Asahel also appears in other books of the Bible as a very swift young man who died in battle.

God takes note of people whom almost no one remembers. Perhaps your service is not famous, but it counts. Be faithful in your place, without seeking applause, and support those whom God has placed near you.
exp.24:3:
This verse lists the sons of Heman, one of the three leaders of music at the temple. There are fourteen names in the list, and the verses that follow add that he also had three daughters. "Seer" means someone who received a vision or message from God.

The author of the book, which tradition often associates with Ezra (though this is not known for certain), describes how David organized the musical service for the temple. Heman, Asaph, and Jeduthun led groups made up of their own sons. The names sound strange, and some, according to scholars, could be phrases or words of praise, but this is debated.

For today: God values steady service carried out within the family. None of the people on this list is famous, yet God remembered them by name. Serve where you are, even when no one applauds you, and teach your own family to worship.
exp.14:3:
It says that King David gathered together the descendants of Aaron, who were the priests, and the Levites, the tribe in charge of service in the sanctuary. The word that means "gathered together" here is one that can also mean "summoned." The "descendants of Aaron" refers to the priests of his family.

David speaks after a failed attempt to bring the ark to Jerusalem, when it was not carried as God had instructed (1 Chronicles 13). Now he wants to do it correctly, so he calls together the people God Himself had chosen to carry the ark. The verses that follow list the leaders of each Levite family.

For today: good intentions are not enough; it also matters to serve God the way He asks. Before undertaking anything for God, let us look in His Word for how to do it, and let us work together with the people He has placed beside us.
exp.8:0:
This verse says that all Israel was recorded by their family lines, and that these records were written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. It also says that Judah was exiled to Babylon because of their unfaithfulness. "Exiled" means forced to leave their homeland and live far away. "Family lines" are the lists of ancestors and descendants.

The author of Chronicles wrote this, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes after the exile, for a people who had returned to their land. The genealogies of the previous chapters end here, and right after this he names those who came back to live in Jerusalem. The message is that, even after the punishment, God did not forget his people.

For today: God knows your name and your story, even if you have gone through painful consequences. Acknowledge your mistakes honestly, but trust that God always offers the chance to return and begin again.
exp.1:36:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Zabad was the father of Ephlal, and that Ephlal was the father of Obed. These are only names, but each one corresponds to a real person within the history of Judah.

The book of Chronicles was written for the people of Israel after they returned from exile, and it is not known for certain who the author was; a Jewish tradition mentions Ezra. Here the account follows the line of Jerahmeel, from the tribe of Judah. Lists like these helped the people remember their roots and their heritage, and that God had preserved their families.

For today: although it may seem that our life goes unnoticed, God knows our name and our story. We can live faithfully in everyday life, knowing that He values every life and every generation.
exp.18:16:
David received word that the Arameans were gathering again to fight. So he called together all Israel, crossed the Jordan River, advanced toward them, and lined up his army for battle. When David lined up to engage them in battle, the Arameans fought against him.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the history of Israel. The Arameans had been defeated, but they did not accept the defeat and called for reinforcements from across the Euphrates River. David did not wait for the danger to reach his own home, but went out to face it. The following passage shows that Israel won and that the Arameans stopped helping the Ammonites.

For today: when we face a problem that returns, it is wise to act with order and courage, without letting it grow. We can prepare ourselves, ask God for direction, and take the necessary steps with confidence in Him.
exp.28:2:
Here David says that, in addition to everything he had already gathered for building the temple, he now gives more from his own treasures. He does this because of his delight in the house of God, that is, because he loves this project and takes joy in it. The phrase "over and above" in the verse means beyond or in addition to what has already been provided. "My personal treasures" refers to his own possessions, not the treasury of the kingdom.

David speaks before the whole assembly of Israel. He already knows that he will not be the one to build the temple, but his son Solomon, who is young, will. So he gets everything ready and sets an example. Afterward he invites the people to give as well, as seen in verse 5.

For today: giving to God should not be only a duty, but a response of love. Before asking others to serve or give, it is good for us to give with joy and generosity from what we have.
exp.3:9:
Jabez prayed to the God of Israel and asked him for four things: a blessing, more land, for God's hand to be with him, and to be kept from harm so that he would be free from pain. The verse ends by saying that God granted his request.

This prayer appears within a long list of families from the tribe of Judah. It is a brief aside that describes a man more honored than his brothers. His name sounds like the Hebrew word for "pain," since his mother gave birth to him in suffering. The Bible tells us nothing more about his life, so we cannot know for certain what kind of harm or what territory he had in mind.

For today: Jabez teaches us to pray with simplicity and trust, asking God to bless and protect us, knowing that everything we receive depends on his hand and not only on our own effort.
exp.24:10:
The fourth lot, that is, the fourth shift of service in the temple, fell to Izri. He served with his sons and his brothers, and in total there were twelve of them. "Lot" here refers to the drawing of lots that was used to assign the shifts.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), tells how David organized the musicians of the temple. They were families from Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman, and they were divided into 24 groups of twelve. Lots were used so that the order would be fair and no one would be placed above another. This list was part of the preparation for worship in Jerusalem.

For today: God takes account of each person, even those who are not famous. Here each family has its place and its turn. Serve with joy in what has been given to you, without comparing yourself to others, because your service also matters to God.
exp.5:40:
This verse is part of a list of the ancestors of Asaph, a temple musician. It says that Asaph descended from Ethni, from Zerah, and from Adaiah. These are names of earlier generations, each introduced by the phrase "the son of." The names are written as they appear in this version.

The author of the book, whom Jewish tradition often associates with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the families of the Levites. He wants to show who served in worship, going back to the time of David. Asaph sang at the right hand of Heman, and his line goes back to Levi, which confirms that his service had a legitimate place.

For today: God pays attention to people who sometimes seem unknown. Many names in this list hardly appear anywhere else, yet God remembered them. Serve faithfully even when no one applauds you; your life is also part of what God does from generation to generation.
exp.13:10:
This verse says that David and his men went up to a place called Baal-perazim and there defeated the Philistines. David acknowledges that it was God who burst out against his enemies, the way a flood breaks through and sweeps everything before it. "Defeated" means that he beat them in battle, and the name of the place is understood to mean "Lord of bursting forth" or "Lord of breakthrough."

The narrator tells what happened, and then he gives David's words. Before the fight, David had asked God whether he should go up and whether God would give him the victory. God answered yes. That is why David does not take credit for the win but sees it as God's work carried out through his hand.

For today: before making important decisions, we can pray and seek God's guidance, and when things turn out well, we can give Him the thanks instead of boasting about our achievements.
exp.8:28:
This verse says that some of the Levites were put in charge of the furnishings and other articles of the sanctuary. They also looked after the supplies used in worship: the fine flour, the wine, the oil, the frankincense, and the spices. The verse uses the word "furnishings" for the items in the sanctuary, and "articles" for the other things set apart for the sacred space. The spices meant here are the fragrant ones.

The writer here is the chronicler, an author whose name is not known with certainty (Jewish tradition often points to Ezra, but this is not certain). He writes after the exile in Babylon, and he wants to remind the people who returned how the service in the temple was organized. He shows that every task, even the smallest, was assigned with order.

For today: God values faithful service that goes unseen. Perhaps no one will applaud you for caring for the small things, but what you do faithfully in your church, your family, or your work has value before Him.
exp.2:22:
This verse names the three sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam. It is part of a family list. Neariah appears in the previous verse as one of the six sons of Shemaiah, who descended from the royal line of King David. The names are given as they appear in the Berean Standard Bible.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for a people who were returning from exile in Babylon. The list shows that the line of David was still alive, even after the fall of the kingdom. Some details of this genealogy are interpreted in various ways, but the general purpose is clear: to remember God's promise to David.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your life counts before Him. You can live with the confidence that God keeps His promises, generation after generation.
exp.5:80:
This verse ends a list of cities given to the Levites from the tribe of Gad. It names two more: Heshbon and Jazer. The pasturelands are the open lands around each city, used mainly to graze livestock.

The book of Chronicles does not say who wrote it. An ancient tradition points to Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for the people who returned from exile, and it reminded them of their history, their tribes, and the place of the Levites. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own. They lived in cities spread among all the tribes, to serve God and teach the people.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and he also calls us to support generously those who dedicate their lives to teaching and caring spiritually for others. Think today of someone like this and look for a way to support them with a prayer or a concrete help.
exp.10:39:
Verse 40 names two men: Ira and Gareb, both called "Ithrite." In the Berean Standard Bible, the verse simply lists them as "Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite." The word "Ithrite" indicates that they came from a family or town called Jattir, or from a clan known as the Ithrites. Scholars are not completely sure of their exact origin.

We are in a long list of David's mighty men, the warriors who supported and strengthened his kingdom. The chronicler, who writes after the exile, wants to remember everyone who served faithfully, even those of whom we know only the name. Ira and Gareb also appear in the parallel list in 2 Samuel 23.

God remembers the faithful who serve without being famous. Your quiet, steady, and loyal work in the family, the church, or the workplace has value before Him, even though almost no one notices it.
exp.3:16:
This verse is part of a list of families from the tribe of Judah. It names four sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher and Jalon. Then it says that Mered's wife Bithiah gave birth to Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah, and that Ishbah was the father of Eshtemoa. "The father of" a place usually indicates that he was its founder or leader. It is not entirely clear how the children are linked to their parents, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

The author of Chronicles, who was of Jewish tradition, gathered these genealogies for the people who were returning from exile. He wanted them to remember their roots, their tribes and their place in the land that God had given them. God does not speak directly here; it is a family record.

For today: God cares about people, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your name and your story matter to him. Value your family and give thanks to those who came before you.
exp.16:0:
David had already settled into his palace when he told the prophet Nathan that something was bothering him: he was living in a house of cedar, a fine and costly wood, while the ark of the covenant of the Lord was still under a tent. "Came to pass" means "happened," and "remaineth" means "stayed" or "lived on."

David, the king of Israel, speaks after establishing his kingdom and settling in Jerusalem. The ark represented God's presence among his people. David wished to honor God with a worthy place. Nathan at first encouraged him, but that same night God spoke to him with another plan, according to the text that follows.

For today: examine whether your comforts stand above your devotion to God. And when you have a good desire, present it to God with humility, ready to accept his answer and his timing.
exp.0:19:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Joktan was the father of four sons: Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth and Jerah. Joktan was the brother of Peleg and a descendant of Shem.

The book of Chronicles has no narrator who speaks within the scene. It is a historical work whose author is not named with certainty. It was written for the people who were returning from exile, to remind them of their roots. The names in this passage link Adam with Israel and show that all peoples have a common origin.

For today: God takes notice of every person, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your name and your life matter to him. Serve faithfully in small things, and value those who go unnoticed around you.
exp.1:49:
These were the descendants of Caleb. The verse names the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, a name tied to the region of Bethlehem. Shobal appears as the father of Kiriath-jearim, that is, the founder or leader of that town. The word "father" here usually points to an ancestor or chief of a town, not only to the head of a household.

The author of Chronicles, writing after the exile in Babylon, gathers genealogies to show the returning Israelites that they had firm roots and a place among God's people. The names of towns linked to names of people recall how Judah gradually settled the land. Some details of these lists are difficult to reconstruct with certainty.

God remembers every person and every family, even when history forgets their names. Today you can give thanks for those who went before you in faith, and think about what legacy of faith you will leave to those who come after you.
exp.4:19:
It says that the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh received help in the war against the Hagrites and all their allies. Their enemies were delivered into their hands, meaning that they won. The reason is that they cried out to God in battle and put their trust in God. "They were helped against their enemies" means that God answered them and was on their side. The Hagrites were a neighboring people on the east side of the Jordan, whom the Bible connects with Hagar.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, recalls this victory for a people who were starting over. He wanted to show that Israel's strength never rested only in its soldiers, though they were brave and well trained, but in trusting God. The following verses tell about the spoil and say that the war belonged to God.

For today: when you face a difficulty, do your part with effort, but pray from the beginning and trust God. It is not a trick for always winning, but an invitation to rest in him.
exp.1:39:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Elasah was the father of Sismai, and that Sismai was the father of Shallum. The word "father" here simply means that one person was the parent of the next, so the list traces a line from one generation to the next.

The writer is not a character in the story; he is the chronicler, a writer whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He wrote for the people of Israel, who were returning from exile. These family records, in this case of the line of Jerahmeel in the tribe of Judah, reminded them of who they were, where they came from, and that God had kept his people.

Although today these may seem to be only names, every person matters to God. We can give thanks for the generations that came before us and live in such a way that we leave those who come after us a legacy of faith, love, and faithfulness.
exp.10:36:
This verse names two of David's mighty men: Hezro, who was from Carmel, a town in Judah (not Mount Carmel), and Naarai, son of Ezbai. The word "Carmelite" simply means "from Carmel."

The author of Chronicles, who wrote after the exile (tradition connects him with Ezra, though this is not certain), lists the men who supported David in becoming king. A similar list in 2 Samuel 23 has some differences in the names. It is not known for certain why; it may be due to ancient copies or to different ways of spelling the names.

For today: God remembers people whom almost no one remembers. Your faithful service, even when it is quiet and goes unapplauded, has value to Him. Today you can help someone or do your work with honesty, trusting that God sees it.
exp.3:17:
This verse is part of a family list from the tribe of Judah. It says that Mered had a Judean wife, who gave birth to Jered, Heber and Jekuthiel, who are called the "fathers" of Gedor, Socho and Zanoah. Here "father" probably means founder or leader of those towns. It also mentions Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took as his wife. The verse says these were the children of Pharaoh's daughter Bithiah, which the list uses to describe who the sons were.

Context: There is no dialogue here; the author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), gathers genealogies. He writes for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots, their land and their identity. The names of towns show where the families settled. It is not clearly explained how the Judean wife relates to Bithiah; scholars interpret this in several ways.

For today: God pays attention to people by name, even in lists that may seem dull. Remember that your story and your family matter to Him, and give thanks for those who have contributed to your life.
exp.11:15:
This verse tells that a group of men from the tribes of Benjamin and Judah went to David. The word "stronghold" refers to a fortified place of safety and defense, probably located in a hard-to-reach area. The phrase "came to David" means that they joined him.

The text is part of a list of warriors who joined David while he was fleeing from King Saul. The one telling the story is the chronicler, who highlights the support David received. That some men came from Benjamin, the tribe of Saul, and some from Judah, David's own tribe, is surprising, and for that reason David receives them with caution and asks about their intentions. They answer with loyalty and peace.

Today we can learn that approaching others with sincerity matters. Whoever seeks to join a good cause should do so with a clean heart, and whoever leads does well to act with prudence and openness.
exp.3:7:
This verse says that Koz was the father of Anub and Zobebah, and that he was also the ancestor of the clans of Aharhel, son of Harum. "Father" here means the one from whom these people descended. In these lists, "son" can sometimes mean a descendant, not always a direct son.

Here no character is speaking in a dialogue. It is the chronicler, who reviews the families of the tribe of Judah. After the exile, this list may have helped the people remember their roots and their place in Israel. Little is known about Koz and these names; the Bible gives no further details. Right after this, Jabez appears, a man who does stand out among so many names.

For today: God knows and remembers people whom almost no one mentions. Your worth does not depend on being applauded, but on God seeing you. Serve faithfully, even when no one notices.
exp.7:31:
It says that Mikloth was the father of Shimeah, and that this family lived in Jerusalem, alongside their relatives. Mikloth was the father of Shimeah, meaning he was their ancestor. The relatives mentioned here were from the same tribe, Benjamin.

Context: the author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records genealogies for the people who were returning from exile. They wanted to remember their roots and their place in the land. This passage is part of the list of Benjamin and prepares the way for the family of King Saul, who appears next.

For today: God values people whom almost no one remembers. Just as these names were written down, you also matter to Him. Make it a point to live near your family and your community of faith, leaning on them and serving them with steady faithfulness.
exp.5:12:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Shallum was the father of Hilkiah, and that Hilkiah was the father of Azariah. The phrase "was the father of" means that he had a son. The names are older spellings, but they belong to real people from the line of the priests.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies as Ezra though this is not certain, records the priestly line of Levi. He writes for the people who returned from exile in Babylon. This list reminded them who they were and that service in the temple had deep roots. The list ends with Jehozadak, who was taken captive, and that shows that their history went through pain, but was not lost.

For today: God remembers people by name, not only the famous ones. Your everyday faithfulness also counts, and it can leave a mark on those who come after you.
exp.0:50:
After the death of King Hadad, Edom no longer had kings in this list, but "chiefs." The verse names the first of them: Timna, Alvah, and Jetheth.

The chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews the families of Edom, descendants of Esau, brother of Jacob. He does this within the genealogies that open the book, to show where each people stands in history. Some think these leaders governed one after another, and others think they governed at the same time.

For today: God remembers names that we forget. Today you can live with the confidence that your life, though it may seem small, matters to God, and serve faithfully where you are, without seeking applause.
exp.18:4:
When someone came and told David about his men, he sent messengers to meet them, since the men had been thoroughly humiliated. He told them to stay in Jericho until their beards had grown back, and then to return.

David had sent these men to comfort Hanun over the death of his father, the king of Ammon. The Ammonite princes suspected that they were spies, and Hanun humiliated them: he shaved off half of their beards and cut off their garments. Among the Hebrews, the beard was a sign of dignity, so David gives them time to recover in private. The war will come later.

Today we can learn to tenderly care for those who have been humiliated, without exposing them further. We can also learn not to view the good intentions of others with suspicion, because that can cause great harm.
exp.21:1:
This verse tells how David gave orders to gather the foreigners living in the land of Israel. From among them he appointed stonecutters, men who cut and shaped stone, to prepare finished stones for building the house of God.

The chronicler relates this after David had settled on the place where the temple would be built. David was already old and knew that his son Solomon would be the one to build it. For that reason he got the materials ready. The text does not say why he drew on foreigners for this work; some think it was forced labor, but the passage does not make this clear.

For today: preparing ahead serves the work of God. We may not see finished what we begin, but we can lay foundations for those who come after us, generously using the resources and the people that God places within our reach.
exp.15:31:
This verse calls the sea and everything that fills it to resound with joy. It also calls the fields to exult, along with all that is in them. "All that fills it" means the waters of the sea and the creatures that live in them. "All that is in them" refers to what is in the fields: plants, animals, and everything that lives there.

This is part of a song of praise that David gave to Asaph and his brothers when the ark of God was brought to Jerusalem. All the people were celebrating. The song invites the whole of creation to acknowledge that the LORD reigns and that he comes to judge the earth with righteousness.

For today: when you see the sea, a field, or a garden, let it lead you to give thanks to God. Take a moment this week to go outside, look at his creation, and praise him out loud.
exp.26:3:
This verse says that the division for the second month was led by Dodai the Ahohite, and that Mikloth was the leader under him. In that division there were twenty-four thousand men. The word "leader" here means the main person in charge of the whole group. Dodai is described as an Ahohite, meaning he belonged to the family or clan of Ahoh. Some think he may be the same man as the Eleazar son of Dodo named in 1 Chronicles 11:12, but this is not certain.

The chronicler is showing how David arranged Israel's army into monthly shifts. Each group served for one month of the year, so there was always a group ready for duty. This list was written to preserve the order and good management of David's kingdom.

For today: God values order and shared service. No one had to carry the whole year's load alone; each person fulfilled their turn. In the church and the family, sharing responsibilities prevents exhaustion and lets everyone serve.
exp.20:24:
David tells Ornan that he will not accept the threshing floor as a gift. He insists on paying the full value of the land. He says he will not offer to God something that costs him nothing, or a burnt offering that does not cost him anything.

David speaks here after having counted the people, something that displeased God, and a plague fell on Israel. God had told him to build an altar on the threshing floor of Ornan. Although Ornan offers everything to him for free, David insists on paying. The text does not explain all his reasons, but it shows that he wanted a sincere and personal offering. The payment in gold is mentioned in the following verse.

Today we can ask ourselves what we give to God. It is not a matter of buying his favor, since his grace is a gift. But a sincere devotion may involve time, effort, or money, not only what we have left over or what is convenient for us.
exp.9:13:
The verse says that Saul died because he failed to inquire of the LORD. "Inquire" means to ask for guidance or direction. "Turned over" means that God handed the kingdom from one person to another, in this case to David, son of Jesse.

The one speaking is the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, who sums up Saul's life after describing his death in battle. The verse just before this one says that Saul had turned to a medium for guidance instead of turning to God. The author presents this as a summary of Saul's rebellion. There is one detail worth noting: the account in Samuel says that Saul did ask the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him. So the text seems to describe a life that had drifted away from God, not just a single moment of failure.

For today: when you face difficult decisions, seek God first in prayer and in his Word, before turning to other sources or to your own opinion.
exp.25:17:
Here is how many gatekeepers guarded a place on the west side of the temple: four watched the highway and two watched the court. A court is an open area or enclosed space attached to the main building. The Hebrew word behind the phrase "the court on the west" is uncertain: it may refer to a courtyard, a porch, or a depot.

The writer of Chronicles, who wrote after the exile, recalls how David organized the Levites in shifts. He wanted the house of God to be well cared for and everything done in order. The gatekeepers were Korahites and Merarites.

Today, this verse reminds us that God values faithful service, even the kind that almost no one sees. Watching a door did not seem important, but it was part of worship. Do with willingness the small task that falls to you in your family or in your church, because God sees your faithfulness.
exp.2:2:
This verse continues the list of David's sons born in Hebron. It mentions the fifth, Shephatiah, whose mother was Abital, and the sixth, Ithream, whose mother was Eglah, David's wife. The names appear here in their older spelling.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, goes through David's family to remind the people that God sustained the royal line. Nothing more is said here about Ithream or Shephatiah. Why Eglah is singled out as David's wife is not clear, and there are several opinions, but the text does not explain it.

God also works through people who are little known, and He forgets none of them. Even if no one remembers your name or your labor, your life has value before God. Serve faithfully wherever you are, without seeking applause.
exp.26:18:
This verse names two tribal leaders from the time of King David: Ishmaiah son of Obadiah, who was over the tribe of Zebulun, and Jerimoth son of Azriel, who was over the tribe of Naphtali. The words "over Zebulun" and "over Naphtali" show which tribe each man was responsible for.

The writer here is the Chronicler, who records the history of Israel after the exile. He is describing how David organized the kingdom: army divisions serving in rotation, officers in charge of the royal property, and leaders set over each tribe. This list shows that every part of the people had its place and its representative. Beyond these two men, we know very little, and that is all we can say with certainty.

For today: God notices those who serve in places that are not seen. Even if no one remembers your name, your faithfulness matters. Serve steadily where God has placed you, without seeking applause.
exp.5:59:
This verse says that from the tribe of Benjamin, the Levites were given Gibeon, Geba, Alemeth, and Anathoth, along with the pasturelands around them. These were the places where the Levites could keep their flocks and herds. In all, the Levites received thirteen cities, divided among their families.

The writer of Chronicles, whom many believe wrote after the exile in Babylon (though no one knows for certain who he was), goes over the lists of the tribes. He wants to remind the people that the Levites, who served God in worship, did not receive a territory of their own, but cities within the other tribes. This follows what is told in Joshua 21.

For today: God cares for those who serve in his house, and he does so through his people. Think about how you can support the pastors, teachers, and servants of your church with prayer, time, or resources.
exp.24:0:
David and the commanders of the army set apart some of the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy with the accompaniment of lyres, harps, and cymbals. The verse introduces the list of the men who carried out this service.

The writer does not speak in his own voice here. The passage is part of a record of how David organized worship before the temple was built. He arranged it so that the praise of God would have order, preparation, and people responsible for it. Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun were Levites, that is, members of the tribe set apart for sacred service.

For today: God values service offered with dedication and preparation. If you have a gift, whether music, teaching, or practical help, offer it carefully to God and to your community.
exp.5:71:
Here two cities are named that the tribe of Issachar gave to the Levites, the descendants of Gershon: Kedesh and Daberath. Each was given along with the pasturelands around it, where the Levites could keep their animals.

The book of Chronicles, whose author is uncertain (tradition often says Ezra), goes through the genealogies of Israel. The Levites did not receive territory of their own, so each tribe gave them cities to live in. This list shows that the people supported them. In Joshua 21 a similar list appears with some different names, and the reason for those differences is not known for certain.

Today we can learn to care generously for those who serve in the church, and to support their work with our time, prayer, or resources, so that they can devote themselves to teaching and walking alongside others.
exp.11:17:
The Spirit of God is said to have come upon Amasai, the leader of the Thirty, and he declared his loyalty to David. The phrase "came upon" here means that the Spirit covered him or filled him. "Peace" means well-being and goodwill. A "band" was a troop or armed company. David accepted them and made them leaders of his troops.

David is in the stronghold, fleeing from King Saul. Men come to him from Benjamin and Judah, and David tests them with a question about their intentions. Amasai answers on behalf of all of them: they are with David because they see that God is helping him. Scholars do not agree on whether this Amasai is the same person who appears in other passages; the text does not make this clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we surround ourselves with and what loyalty we offer. When we see that God is at work in a just cause, let us support it sincerely, without duplicity, and seek peace with those who serve the Lord.
exp.5:10:
Azariah is said to be the father of Amariah, and Amariah the father of Ahitub. In Bible genealogies, the phrase "was the father of" can sometimes point to an ancestor rather than a direct son.

The book of Chronicles has an uncertain author, and tradition attributes it to Ezra. It was written for a people returning from exile. This list follows the line of the priestly Levites, from Aaron through to the temple of Solomon and beyond. It showed that the service of God had not been lost and that the people still had roots. Names repeat often, so it is not always easy to tell which Azariah is meant.

God remembers people, even those whom almost no one mentions. Your faithfulness in everyday, ordinary things counts. Think about who taught you to believe, thank them, and live in a way that others can learn from you too.
exp.19:7:
This verse closes the account of several battles against Philistine giants. It says that the descendants of Rapha, who lived in Gath, were defeated by David and his warriors. "His servants" here means his loyal men, his army. Rapha was an ancestor of families of great stature; the name is related to the "Rephaim," though not everything about them is known for certain.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, summarizes Israel's victories under David. Earlier, the account tells how Jonathan, David's nephew, killed a giant who had challenged Israel. At the end, the text stresses that the victory was shared: David and his people. For a people returning from exile, it was a reminder that God had given Israel strength against enemies who seemed enormous.

For today: big problems are rarely overcome alone. God often works through people who struggle together. Seek support from your family or your church, and offer yours to others.
exp.25:6:
This verse lists the sons of Shemaiah, who was a son of Obed-edom: Othni, Rephael, Obed, and Elzabad. His brothers, Elihu and Semachiah, are also named. The verse says that these men were capable men, meaning able and brave.

The author is the Chronicler, who probably wrote long after David. Here he describes how the gatekeepers of the temple were organized, the ones who guarded the gates and the entrance to the house of God. The text makes clear that Obed-edom's family was large because God had blessed him. This list shows that humble service was also valuable to God.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it goes unnoticed. We can serve in our church or family with steadiness and courage, without seeking applause, trusting that God cares for and blesses those who serve him.
exp.21:2:
This verse tells us that David gathered materials for the temple. He provided a large quantity of iron to make the nails for the doors of the gateways and for the fittings, and he also gathered more bronze than could be weighed. He likewise gathered cedar wood without number. Here "provided" means got ready, leaving everything in place for later use.

The chronicler recounts what David did. He knew that his son Solomon was young and inexperienced, and that the house of God had to be magnificent. David would not build it himself, but he wanted to leave everything ready before he died. The Sidonians and Tyrians had supplied him with cedar.

Today we can learn that serving God includes preparing the way for others. We may not see the result of what we sow, but God can use our generosity and effort. Think about something you can leave ready to help others serve better.
exp.23:16:
This verse continues a list of the twenty-four families of priests. Here the twenty-first, that of Jachin, and the twenty-second, that of Gamul, are named. The phrase "the twenty-first" means number 21. The names are those of the heads of the priestly households.

The author, traditionally identified as the chronicler, tells how David organized the descendants of Aaron into shifts to serve in the temple. The order was decided by casting lots. This was done so that all the service to God would be carried out in good order, and so that no one would be left out or overburdened. There are not many details about Jachin and Gamul, so it is best not to invent more.

God cares even for names that seem small. Today, your service in the church, even if it is quiet, also counts. Serve faithfully, and respect the order and the turn of others.
exp.17:13:
This verse says that David ruled over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people. "Justice" means deciding cases rightly, and "righteousness" means acting in a way that is right and fair, treating each person as they deserve, without favoritism.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition has linked with Ezra, though there is no certainty, summarizes David's reign. Before this, he tells of David's victories and says that the LORD preserved him. After this, he lists his officials. This verse brings both together: the power God gave him was used to govern with fairness.

For today: if you have any authority, in your home, at work, or in your church, use it to treat everyone with justice. Ask God to help you decide with honesty, even when it would be more convenient to do otherwise.
exp.1:16:
Abigail, David's sister, had a son named Amasa. Here the verse says she was his mother. Amasa's father was Jether, described as an Ishmaelite, meaning a descendant of Ishmael. In 2 Samuel 17:25 the name appears as Ithra, and there he is called an Israelite. Manuscripts and sources differ on this detail, so the exact identity is not easy to pin down.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), lists the families of Judah. He wrote for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. Here he mentions David's relatives, among them Amasa, who later became commander of Absalom's army.

For today: God forgets no one, not even those who have a different background or a complicated story. Every person counts in his plan. Treat others today with that same value.
exp.22:21:
This verse tells us that Eleazar, a descendant of Levi through the family of Merari, died without sons and had only daughters. Their cousins, the sons of Kish, married them. The word "cousins" here refers to close relatives, not to a more distant connection.

It is part of a list of Levite families, probably written by the chronicler, when David organized the Levites to serve in worship. Here it is recorded that Eleazar's line continued through his daughters. According to Numbers 36, heiresses married within their own tribe in order to keep the family inheritance.

God takes notice of every family, even those that seem to be left without continuation. We can value the people others overlook and remember that our place among God's people does not depend on what the world considers important.
exp.23:23:
He says that Uzziel had a son named Micah, and that Micah had a son named Shamir. It is part of a list of Levite families. The verse uses the word "and" in the same way.

This passage is part of a long list of names. The chronicler, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), recalls how King David organized the Levites to serve in the temple. The lineages of Levi are recorded, generation by generation. This showed that the service of God had order and that each family had a place. Here the interest is in the descendants, not in a direct teaching.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to the names that almost no one remembers. Your simple and steady service, though it goes unnoticed, has value before Him. Today you can faithfully do a small task, as if it were for the Lord.
exp.1:37:
Here the verse says that Obed was the father of Jehu, and that Jehu was the father of Azariah. The verse names each man as the father of the next, and each name links one generation to the next in a family list.

The book is anonymous, although Jewish tradition usually attributes it to Ezra; this is not certain. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their origins. This passage follows the line of Jerahmeel, within the tribe of Judah. We know almost nothing about these people, apart from their names.

For today: God notices people the world forgets. Even if your name does not appear in great stories, it matters to Him. Today you can give thanks for those who went before you in faith and in family, and live faithfully in your own generation, knowing that God uses ordinary lives.
exp.10:12:
This verse tells of Eleazar, one of David's three mighty men. It says he was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines gathered there for battle. At a place with a field full of barley, the troops fled from the Philistines.

The verse is part of a list of David's most courageous men, written by the chronicler. Its purpose is to honor those who supported the king and to show how God worked through them. The verse on its own does not finish the story, and the next verse describes how they stood firm in the middle of the field, defended it, and won.

Today we can learn that when everyone around us gives up or runs away, God can use one steadfast person to hold on to what is important. It calls for the courage not to abandon what is right, even when it seems like a small thing, like a field of barley.
exp.5:4:
This verse continues a family list. It says that Abishua was the father of Bukki, and that Bukki was the father of Uzzi. The verse uses the plain phrase "was the father of," so the relationships are stated directly. The names are spelled in a style that looks a little different from what modern readers may expect.

It is part of a genealogy of the priests, descendants of Levi and Aaron. The book of Chronicles has no author identified with certainty; many believe it was written after the return from exile in Babylon. Its purpose seems to be to remind the people of their roots and of the continuity of service in the temple.

For today: God pays attention to people, even when their names are hardly mentioned in the story. These names appear only once, but they are part of his plan. Your faithfulness day by day, in the hidden places, also counts and can leave a mark on those who come after you.
exp.15:40:
He says that David placed Heman and Jeduthun, along with the other men who were chosen and named one by one, alongside Zadok and the priests. Their task was to give thanks to the LORD. The reason: his loving devotion endures forever.

The verse of the word "chosen" is that it means selected for that task. The mention of those "named one by one" means that each of them was identified individually.

The account is told by the chronicler. David had brought the ark to Jerusalem and organized the service of worship. While the priests offered the daily sacrifices at Gibeon, where the tabernacle was, these musicians and singers praised God. It was an orderly and constant worship.

For today: praising God is not an ornament, it is a valuable task. Today you can choose a fixed time of day to thank him, remembering that his love does not run out.
exp.17:1:
It says that David defeated Moab, and that the Moabites became subject to him. As a sign of their submission, they brought him tribute, that is, payments owed to a ruler. The verse says David "defeated" them, which means he won the victory in battle. The word "subject" describes a people who were under David's authority and obliged to obey him.

The author of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, summarizes David's victories over his neighbors. He wants to show that God established David's kingdom and gave him rest from his enemies. The passage is very brief and does not explain the details of the war. Other texts, such as 2 Samuel 8, tell of similar events in more detail.

We can remember that God knows how to sustain and establish what He Himself has entrusted. If we face struggles that seem greater than we are, it is wise to trust that God works faithfully, and to act with humility and gratitude when He gives us victories.
exp.27:13:
David gave gold and silver, weighed out with exactness, for making all the articles needed for the temple. Each article used in service was assigned its own amount of metal. The phrase "by weight" means that every amount was carefully measured. "Articles" here does not mean only cups, but every kind of item used in worship.

The writer of Chronicles tells how David, now old, hands over to his son Solomon the plans for the temple, which he said he had received by the Spirit. David would not build it himself, but he prepared everything with order. The materials and the arrangement of the services were set down so that Solomon could carry them out.

For today: God values order and devotion in what is done for him. We can prepare with care and generosity what others will continue, serving without seeking credit, trusting that God uses the work of each generation.
exp.7:0:
This verse opens a family list. It says that Benjamin was the father of several sons, and it names Bela as the first, Ashbel as the second, and Aharah as the third. "Firstborn" means the eldest son, the one born first.

Here the speaker is not a character in the story; it is the chronicler, an author that tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He wrote after the return from exile in Babylon. He wanted the people to remember where they came from and to know that their history had not been lost. Lists of the names of the tribes, like this one for Benjamin, helped rebuild their identity. The names of Benjamin's sons vary a little in other passages, and that is explained in different ways.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those who appear only as a name. You too have worth and a place in his story. Give thanks today for those who went before you in the faith, and remember that God knows you by name.
exp.20:14:
This verse tells us that God sent an angel to Jerusalem to destroy it with a plague. But while the angel was carrying out the destruction, the LORD looked on, and he relented from the disaster. He told the angel who was destroying the people, "Enough! Withdraw your hand now!" The verse ends by placing the angel of the LORD beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, the place where the punishment was halted.

The narrator describes what happened after David sinned by counting the people. David chose to fall into God's hands rather than into the hands of his enemies, because he trusted in God's mercy. By then seventy thousand people had already died. Some scholars explain that God's relenting is not a mistake being corrected, but his compassion responding to the grief and humility of his people.

When we face the consequences of our mistakes, we can come to God with humility and without fear, because his mercy is great. He sees our suffering and takes no delight in punishing.
exp.11:26:
This verse mentions Jehoiada, a leader or chief of the house of Aaron, that is, of the family of the priests. With him came 3,700 men. The word "leader" here means chief or commander, not the son of a king. "Family" here means descendants or relatives.

The book of Chronicles lists the tribes that went to Hebron to join David and make him king over all Israel. No single person speaks here; the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra though this is not certain, notes the groups that joined. Here the Levites and the priests appear, who supported David with their people.
