For today: God works through people of every kind, including those without a famous position. Jehoiada and his people chose to back what God was doing. Ask yourself where you can join in, even in simple ways, with the work of God in your church or community.
exp.16:19:
He says that there is no one like the LORD and that there is no God but him. David affirms that this is not only his own idea, but something confirmed by what Israel has heard of God's works. The phrase "according to everything we have heard with our own ears" means that this belief rests on what has been passed down and witnessed by the people.

David speaks in prayer, after God promised him through the prophet Nathan that his house and his kingdom would be established. He feels very small before such goodness and responds with wonder and worship. Right away he remembers how God rescued Israel from Egypt and made them his people.

For today: when you receive blessings, do not stop at asking for more. Do as David did and pause to remember what God has already done, and give him thanks and praise. That strengthens faith and keeps the heart humble.
exp.16:13:
He says God promises to set a descendant of David over His house and His kingdom, that is, over God's house and the kingdom that belongs to Him. "Forever" means for all time, and "established" means firm and secure, not falling. The throne of this son will not be taken away.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple, and God answers that He Himself will build him a "house," that is, a dynasty. It first refers to Solomon, but many Christians see that the promise is fully fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David. Jews and Christians understand it in different ways.

For today: we can rest in the fact that God's plans do not depend on our strength. When everything seems unstable, let us trust that Christ reigns and his kingdom does not end.
exp.14:7:
It says that, from the Elizaphanites, a group of the Levites, the leader was Shemaiah, and 200 of his relatives came with him. "The chief" means the leader or head of that group. "His relatives" refers to the people from his family line who served alongside him, not only to brothers by blood.

The text is part of the chronicler's account. David is preparing to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem. This time he gathers the Levites, because God had established that they were to carry it. That is why the families are listed one by one, with their leaders and their numbers.

For today: God notices each person and each family that serves, even when their name appears only once. Your service in the church, however small or quiet it may seem, counts. And when we do something for God, it is good to do it in order, as He directs, and together as a team.
exp.22:10:
This verse says that among the four sons of Shimei, Jahath was the first and Zizah the second. Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, so their descendants were counted together as one family and given a single assignment.

This is part of a list of Levites, the tribe in charge of service in the temple. Here the narrator (tradition attributes this to the writer of Chronicles) tells how David, now old, organized the Levites for the service of God. This Shimei belongs to the family of Gershon. Each group was recorded so that the tasks could be fairly distributed. Scholars do not fully agree on how the names are grouped in this passage.

For today: God takes everyone into account, even those who seem few or little noticed. Jeush and Beriah were recorded. If today you feel that your contribution is small, remember that God sees you and gives you a place in his work. Serve faithfully wherever you are.
exp.18:8:
The Ammonites marched out of their city, Rabbah, and arrayed themselves for battle at the entrance to the city. The kings who had been hired as allies came and stayed apart from them, standing by themselves in the open country. The phrase "arrayed themselves" means they took up their positions, ready to fight.

Here the narrator is the chronicler, who is recounting the events. The Ammonites had insulted David's messengers and knew they would be in trouble, so they paid Aramean allies to help them. That arrangement left Joab, the commander of David's army, facing enemies on two fronts.

For today: trusting only in human resources, such as money or alliances, can give us false security, especially when we act from an uncorrected mistake. It is better to acknowledge our wrongs in time and seek God's help, rather than relying only on what we can buy.
exp.0:20:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Joktan: Hadoram, Uzal, and Diklah. The name Hadoram also appears in some other spellings, such as Adoram, but it is the same person.

The book of Chronicles begins with long lists of families, starting from Adam. The one who wrote them (Jewish tradition often thinks of Ezra, though this is not certain) wanted to remind the people of Israel where they came from and that they were part of the history of all nations. The sons of Joktan are usually connected with peoples of Arabia, but it is not always known with certainty where they lived.

God does not forget anyone, not even those who barely appear in history. If the Bible keeps these names, every person has value before Him. Today you can rest in the knowledge that God knows you by your name, even when you feel you go unnoticed.
exp.5:49:
This verse begins a list of the descendants of Aaron, the first priest of Israel. It names three generations in a row: Eleazar, his son Phinehas, and his son Abishua. The name "Phinehas" is spelled this way in the verse, and "son" here can mean a direct descendant, although in biblical genealogies some names are sometimes left out.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra though this is not certain, writes after the exile in Babylon. He wants to remind the people that their roots are still alive. After speaking about priestly service, he shows the line that sustained it, since the priests had to be descendants of Aaron.

For today: God remembers names that sometimes seem to us like simple facts. Each generation received a faith and passed it on to the next. Today we can ask ourselves whom we are serving and teaching faithfully, knowing that God values what is steady and simple.
exp.28:7:
This verse says that everyone who owned precious stones gave them to the treasury of the LORD's house. They handed them over under the care of Jehiel, a descendant of Gershon, a Levite.

David had gathered materials so that his son Solomon could build the temple. Then the leaders of the tribes and of the families offered gold, silver, bronze, and iron of their own free will. The people also gave precious stones. Jehiel seems to have looked after that treasure, though the Bible gives few details about him. The account stresses that they gave with joy and with a whole heart.

God values the heart with which we give more than the amount. Today we can give time, talents, or money with joy, and do it with order and honesty, as they did here by entrusting everything to a responsible person.
exp.27:9:
It says that God chose Solomon to build the temple, here called "a house for the sanctuary," that is, a holy place for worshiping God. David tells him to consider this carefully, to be strong, and to get to work.

David speaks before all Israel, already old, and hands his son Solomon the task he himself had wished to do, but which God entrusted to his son. Earlier he had advised him to know God and serve him with his whole heart. Right after this, he gives him the plans for the temple. Thus the work did not depend only on talent, but on a life faithful to God.

For today: when you feel that God has given you a task, whether in your family, your church, or your work, do not put it off. Ask him for strength, seek his guidance, and take the first step with courage and a sincere heart.
exp.15:25:
This verse says that the gods of the nations are worthless, meaning they have no real power or value, but it is the LORD who made the heavens. The Hebrew word behind "worthless" is often used for empty idols without strength.

Here we hear a song of thanksgiving that David handed to Asaph and his companions when the ark of the covenant was brought to Jerusalem. The text invites Israel to tell the glory of God among all peoples. Its strength lies in the contrast: idols are made by human hands, but God is the Creator.

Today we can ask ourselves what things hold the place of God in our hearts, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Today, give thanks to God for something he created, and entrust to him in prayer whatever is weighing on you.
exp.5:13:
This verse continues a list of descendants of Levi, from the line of the priests. It says that Azariah was the father of Seraiah, and Seraiah was the father of Jehozadak. The word "father" here simply shows that one man was the parent of the next. The name "Seraiah" appears in this form, and "Jehozadak" is the same name in its fuller form.

It is part of the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, which tradition attributes to Ezra, though this is not known for certain. They were written for the people who returned from exile, to remind them of their identity and of the continuity of the priesthood. The next verse says that Jehozadak was carried away captive to Babylon. This line reaches exactly that painful moment.

God does not forget people, even though history can seem to us like nothing more than a list of names. Even in times of loss and exile, He preserves His work from generation to generation. Today we can give thanks for those who passed on the faith to us, and think about how to pass it on to others faithfully.
exp.4:6:
It says that the relatives of Beera, arranged by their clans and recorded in their genealogy, had Jeiel and Zechariah as their leaders. The word "chief" here does not refer to royalty but to a leader or head of a family group. The phrase "recorded in their genealogy" refers to the family lists that tracked each line.

The author of Chronicles (traditionally thought to be Ezra, though this is not certain) reviews the tribes of Israel, and here speaks of Reuben. He writes for a people who had returned from exile and needed to remember their roots. After mentioning the deportation of Beera by the Assyrians, the text makes clear that this tribe still had its own leaders and order.

For today: God pays attention to people and remembers their names, even the little-known ones. Serve where you are, faithfully; your family, your church, or your work may need your humble leadership.
exp.7:6:
Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera were among the sons of Ehud, heads of families in Benjamin. The verse says that Gera carried them into exile, meaning he took these people away from their home to another place. The verse also says he was the father of Uzza and Ahihud.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the chronicler, who writes a long list of genealogies. It is believed he wrote after the return from exile in Babylon, to remind the people who they were and where they came from. The text is brief and does not explain why they were taken away, nor is it clear whether "who" refers to Gera or to someone else; scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: God remembers each person by name, even those we hardly know. Value your family history and that of others, and trust that your life also matters to Him, even in times of upheaval or change.
exp.14:15:
David told the leaders of the Levites to appoint their relatives as singers, lifting up their voices with joy and accompanied by musical instruments: harps, lyres, and cymbals.

King David is speaking. He had already learned that the ark of God had to be carried as God commanded, and the Levites had consecrated themselves. Now, as the ark is brought to Jerusalem, David wants its arrival to be marked by order and celebration. The praise was not improvised but organized and placed at the service of God.

For today: when we worship God, let us do so with a prepared heart and sincere joy. Serving with order and gladness, in church or at home, honors God.
exp.10:7:
He says that David built up the city all around, from the supporting terraces to the surrounding wall. "Built up" here means that he strengthened and enlarged it. The "supporting terraces" seem to have been areas of embankment or fill in Jerusalem, although it is not known exactly what they looked like. Joab restored the rest of the city, that is, he repaired what had been lacking.

The writer of Chronicles tells how David captured the stronghold of the Jebusites and made it his capital. Joab was the first to go up, and for that reason he was made chief. Then the two work together to strengthen the city. The text shows that David's kingdom grew because God was with him.

For today: God often works through people who share the work. David built up one part and Joab restored another. Serve where you are needed, without competing, trusting that God joins everyone's efforts together.
exp.13:5:
This verse continues a list of David's sons. Nogah, Nepheg, and Japhia are the names of three of them, born in Jerusalem. They are little-known names, and the Bible tells us almost nothing more about these sons.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes long after these events, shows that God established David's kingdom. After David was recognized as king over all Israel, the list of sons points to family, descendants, and blessing. Scholars note that some names repeat or vary in other lists, such as "Beeliada," but the reason is not known with certainty.

For today: God does not overlook ordinary people, even when no one remembers them. Your life and your name matter to him. Today you can serve faithfully in small things, trusting that God sees what others do not notice.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that Eber had two sons. One was named Peleg, a name connected with the idea of "division," because in his days the earth was divided. The other son was named Joktan.

It is part of a long list of family records at the beginning of Chronicles. The author, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra though this is not certain, reviews history from Adam to remind the people who returned from exile who they were and where they came from. The text does not explain what the division of the earth consisted of. Some think it refers to the scattering of the nations after Babel (Genesis 11), and others to a division of territories; the text does not make this clear.

For today: God cares for specific people, with names and families, even in lists that may seem dull. Your story matters to him too; pray, giving thanks for your family and your roots.
exp.2:19:
This verse lists five sons of Meshullam, who was a son of Zerubbabel: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed. The text says there were five of them in all. They are only names, and the Bible tells us nothing more about these people.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the family of King David. He writes for the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon. The list follows the royal line through Zerubbabel, the leader of the return. In this way he reminded them that God's promise to David was still alive, even though there was no longer a kingdom.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who seem to be minor figures. Every name counts in its story. This encourages us to serve him faithfully in ordinary things, trusting that he values what we do even when it goes unnoticed.
exp.5:9:
Johanan was the father of Azariah, who served as priest in the temple that Solomon built in Jerusalem. The phrase "was the father of" means that he was his father or an ancestor, since these family lists sometimes skip generations. It is not known with certainty which Azariah this is; some think of one from the time of Solomon and others of a later one.

The author of Chronicles writes for the people who were returning from exile. With this list of priests, from Aaron down to his own time, he wants to show that the worship of God and the service of the temple had a continuous and legitimate line. In this way he encouraged those who were returning to rebuild their spiritual life.

For today: God cares for the generations, and our faithfulness in the simple things can influence those who come after us. Serve God with constancy, even when no one remembers your name.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that Judah had three sons with a Canaanite woman, Bath-shua: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er was the firstborn, and he was wicked in the eyes of the LORD, so the LORD put him to death. "Wicked in the sight of the LORD" means that his conduct did not please God. "Put him to death" means that God brought his life to an end. The Bible does not explain here what his wickedness consisted of.

The book of Chronicles begins with long lists of families to help the people of Israel remember who they were and where they came from. It is believed to have been written after the exile in Babylon. The author begins with Judah because the line of King David would come from him. Even so, he does not hide that there was sin and judgment in that family. Genesis 38 tells more of this story.

For today: God sees our real life, not just our family name or our family background. Today we can ask him for a sincere heart and live in a way that pleases him.
exp.27:6:
God promises to establish Solomon's kingdom forever, but on one condition: that he keep resolutely carrying out God's commandments and ordinances, just as it was being done on that day. The phrase "resolutely carries out" means "keeps at it steadily and with determination," and "ordinances" refers to God's just rulings and laws.

King David, now an old man, speaks before the leaders of Israel. He tells them that God chose Solomon to build the temple. David repeats what God said to him: the promise depends on continued obedience. Some readers understand that "forever" also points to Christ, a descendant of David, although the text speaks first of Solomon.

For today: God's blessings are not sustained by good intentions held for only one day. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time for prayer, and ask God for strength to keep it up.
exp.13:13:
It says that David asked God again what to do in the face of a new attack by the Philistines. God answered him not to march straight up after them, but to go around and attack them in front of the balsam trees. The balsam trees are named here, and some think they could have been mulberry trees, but this is not certain. The phrase "asked again" means that he inquired once more.

The one speaking is God, answering King David. Shortly before, David had already defeated the Philistines and had burned the idols they left behind. Now they had returned to the valley, and David did not assume he would use the same strategy as the previous time. He preferred to ask again.

For today: a past victory or a wise decision does not replace present prayer. Even when a situation resembles another, it is worth asking God again for direction, because He can guide us in a new way.
exp.7:27:
These were the heads of families, the chiefs according to their family lines, and they lived in Jerusalem. The verse says that the men mentioned earlier were the leaders of their families, according to their genealogies. "Genealogies" refers to the family lines that traced each household's descent, its family tree. The verse adds that these families lived in Jerusalem.

First Chronicles reviews the genealogies of Israel, and Christian and Jewish tradition usually attributes it to an author or writer from after the exile (Ezra is often mentioned, though this is not certain). Here the descendants of Benjamin are summarized. These lists helped the people, who were returning from exile, remember their identity, their inheritance, and their place in the land.

For today: God does not forget people, even when many names seem distant to us. Your family, your history, and your place matter. You can give thanks for those who came before you and consider how to serve God with your influence in your home and your community.
exp.7:22:
This verse is part of a list of names: Abdon, Zichri, and Hanan. They are three men from the family of Benjamin. Some versions write "Abdon" as "Adon," so this may be a variant spelling of the name. The text tells us nothing more about them.

These lists are part of the genealogies of Benjamin. Here they appear as sons of Shimei, heads of families who lived in Jerusalem. The book is traditionally attributed to Ezra, though this is not certain. It seems to have been written for the people who returned from exile. They wanted to remind them who they were, where they came from, and that God had not forgotten their families.

For today: God knows people by their names, even those whom history hardly mentions. Your quiet work, your faithfulness in small things, and your family matter to Him. Today you can thank someone who serves without being noticed, and remember that you too are seen by God.
exp.5:38:
Asaph is described as Heman's kinsman, the one who served at his right hand, meaning he stood beside him in a place of support and honor. Asaph is named as the son of Berechiah, who was the son of Shimea. "At his right hand" means at his side. The word "kinsman" most likely points to a close relative from the same tribe of Levi.

The writer of Chronicles, traditionally identified with Ezra though this is not certain, records the family lines of the Levites. After the exile, the people needed to remember who had served in worship and where they came from. Heman and Asaph led the music in the temple under David, and this list shows that their service was rooted in the tribe of Levi.

For today, God values those who serve faithfully, even when their place seems humble. Asaph stood beside another, supporting him. We can serve in the church with joy, without needing to be at the center, trusting that God remembers every name and every labor done with love.
exp.26:19:
This verse is part of a list of the leaders of the tribes of Israel. It says that over the Ephraimites was Hoshea, son of Azaziah, and over one of the half-tribes of Manasseh (the part west of the Jordan) was Joel, son of Pedaiah.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews the organization of David's kingdom. Each tribe had a recognized leader. It was written for a people returning from exile, and it reminded them of their history and their order. This Hoshea is not the prophet Hosea; he is another man with the same name.

God cares for people one by one, even when they are almost unknown. These men appear in the Bible only by their names, but they were remembered. Today, serve faithfully where you are, even when no one applauds you. God sees and remembers your work.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that Ahitub was the father of Zadok, and that Zadok was the father of Ahimaaz. In Hebrew genealogies, the phrase "was the father of" can sometimes indicate a wider descent, such as a grandfather or an ancestor, and for that reason some lists skip generations.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile in Babylon. Its author is unknown; Jewish tradition often names Ezra, but this is not certain. This list follows the line of the priests descended from Aaron. Its purpose was to remind the people who returned from exile that serving God in the temple had ancient and continuous roots.

For today: God cares for the generations and uses ordinary people, whose names we hardly know, to sustain his work. Your faithfulness in small things, such as praying, serving in your church, or teaching the faith to your children, can be the link that helps others come to know God in the future.
exp.16:15:
In this verse, King David goes in and sits down before the LORD, and he speaks to him with humility. He asks who he is and what his family is, that God has brought him this far. "House" here means his family or descendants. "Sat before the LORD" means that he prayed in God's presence. "This far" refers to his present position as king.

David speaks after the prophet Nathan had passed on God's promise to him: his family and his kingdom would be established forever. David does not respond with pride but with wonder. He had come from being a shepherd of sheep, and now God was making him enormous promises. Many Christians see in this promise a sign that points to Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when you receive blessings or achievements, remember that they come from God. Before taking pride in them, pray with gratitude and acknowledge that he has brought you to where you are.
exp.16:9:
God tells David that, since the time he appointed judges over his people Israel, they have suffered at the hands of their enemies, but now He will bring those enemies down. The phrase "I will subdue" means to bring low or defeat. The phrase "I tell you" means simply that God is making His word known to David. Building a house does not refer to a physical building but to establishing a family or dynasty.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple for God, but God responds that it will be He who builds a "house" for David, that is, a royal lineage. Later, the promise speaks of a son who would reign, and many Christians see its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: before we think about what we can do for God, let us remember what He has already done and continues to do for us. We can serve Him with gratitude and confidence, knowing that He sustains our future.
exp.5:16:
He says that Gershom, son of Levi, had two sons: Libni and Shimei. It is part of a list of names. There are no very difficult words here, only proper names.

The book of Chronicles does not have a narrator who identifies himself clearly; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written after the return from exile in Babylon. That is why it mentions the deportation of Judah. The author presents the genealogy of the Levites, the tribe in charge of service in the temple, to remind the people of their identity and their place before God.

For today: God knows and remembers each person by name, even those whom almost no one mentions. Your service, even if it is quiet, has value to Him. Today you can thank someone who serves without anyone noticing.
exp.0:17:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Arphaxad was the father of Shelah, and that Shelah was the father of Eber. "Was the father of" means the same as "had as a son." These are three generations in a row among the descendants of Shem, son of Noah.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written for a people who were returning from exile and needed to remember their roots. The genealogies showed that God had kept his people through the course of time. Eber is important because Peleg and Joktan descend from him, and later the line that leads to Abraham.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even to those who appear only as a name in a list. Your life and your faithfulness, though they may seem small, are part of what God does from generation to generation.
exp.16:17:
Here David says he has nothing more to ask. God has shown him so much honor that any words of his would fall short. The word "honoring" in this verse means showing respect or making someone great. "Servant" is David himself, who presents himself as a servant of God. He ends by saying that God knows him completely: his intentions, his heart, and his needs.

David speaks in prayer, after the prophet Nathan brought him God's promise. He had wanted to build a temple, but God told him that instead he would build a house for David, that is, a lineage. Overwhelmed, David sits before the Lord and responds with wonder and humility, acknowledging that he did not deserve such favor.

For today: when God blesses you, do not rush to ask for more or to show off. Stop and give thanks. And when you do not know what to say in prayer, remember that God already knows you, and you can rest in his care.
exp.26:9:
He says that the commander for the seventh month was Helez, an Ephraimite. He is called "the Pelonite," which probably points to his place or clan of origin, though this is not known for certain. His division, the group of men under him for duty, numbered 24,000.

The writer of Chronicles, who tells the story of Israel for the people, describes here how King David organized his army. Each month a different group served, with its own commander, so that no one carried the whole year. List after list, the same number is repeated, which shows order and planning.

Today: God values orderly and shared service. If you are called to serve in your church, family or work, do it faithfully in your turn, without comparing yourself, and trust that your part matters within the care of everyone.
exp.0:33:
It says that Abraham was the father of Isaac, and that Isaac had two sons: Esau and Israel. "Was the father of" is the meaning of the verb here. "Israel" is the other name of Jacob, the name God gave him later (Genesis 32:28). Here the text calls him Israel, and not Jacob, because it looks at the whole nation that would come from him.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes this list of families after the exile in Babylon. He wanted to remind the people who were returning to their land where they came from and that they still belonged to God's promise. Before continuing with Israel, he first goes over the side branches, such as those of Keturah and Esau.

For today: God cares about the stories of families, even about names that seem unimportant. If you feel forgotten, remember that your life also has a place in God's plan.
exp.3:20:
This verse is part of a list of families from the tribe of Judah. It names the sons of Shelah, son of Judah: Er, "father of Lecah," and Laadah, "father of Mareshah." Here "father" usually means the founder or leader of a town. It also mentions the clans of linen workers at Beth-ashbea, that is, people who made cloth.

Context: This is not a speech but a family record within Chronicles. The author, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), wrote for a people returning from exile. He wanted to remind them of their origins, their families, and their trades. The verses that follow mention potters who worked for the king.

For today: God values ordinary work, such as weaving or making pots. Your daily job, done with honesty and care, can also be a way of serving God and others.
exp.7:7:
It says that a man named Shaharaim had sons in the country of Moab after he had divorced his wives, Hushim and Baara. The word "country" here means a region or territory. The phrase about divorcing his wives is stated plainly in this verse, so it can be read as it is.

Context: there is no character speaking; this is part of the lists of family lines from the tribe of Benjamin that the chronicler gathered. These genealogies helped the people, who were returning from exile, remember their roots and their land. It does not explain why Shaharaim divorced his wives or how he came to be in Moab; the Bible does not say, and it is not wise to guess.

For today: God cares that every name and every family story matters, including those that involve separations and parts that are left unexplained. If your own story has painful or confusing chapters, you can trust that God knows it and is still at work in your family.
exp.23:18:
This verse closes the list of the 24 shifts of the priests. It says that each group was placed in its appointed order of service for entering the temple, "the house of the LORD," according to the regulations already set down. "Appointed order" means the fixed arrangement or schedule. "According to the regulations prescribed by their forefather Aaron" means that they followed the pattern handed down from the ancient priest Aaron, and that the service was carried out as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded him.

The author is the Chronicler, who recounts how David organized the service of the temple. According to the text, the priests were divided into shifts so that everything would be done in order. Because of their family origin, the text links them to Aaron. The final phrase points to a command from God, though the passage does not say where it is given.

For today: God values service done with order and responsibility. If you serve in your church, carry out your turn faithfully, without wanting to be the center, because every task matters.
exp.13:11:
The verse tells that the Philistines, when they fled defeated, abandoned their gods there. Then David ordered that they be burned in the fire. "Gods" here means the images or figures they worshipped, and being "burned in the fire" means they were destroyed completely.

The account is from Chronicles, written to remember the history of Israel. David had just consulted God before fighting and saw that God gave him the victory. Burning the idols showed that he did not regard them as a trophy or as a useful power, but as something to be removed. In the parallel account in 2 Samuel 5:21 it says that David and his men carried them off; some think they first gathered them and then burned them.

For today: when God gives us a victory, let us not keep as a memento whatever competes with Him. We can ask ourselves what thing occupies in our heart a place that only God should have, and let it go with courage.
exp.21:9:
This verse says that Solomon, David's son, will build the temple to honor God. God promises to treat him as a son, being a father to him, and to establish his reign over Israel forever. The words "He is the one who will build a house for My Name" mean that he will build a temple where God is worshiped.

Here David speaks to his son Solomon, repeating what God had told him. God did not allow him to build the temple because he had taken part in many wars. So the task passes to Solomon, a man of peace. Some understand that "forever" also points to Jesus, a descendant of David, although others see it first in David's dynasty.

For today: God takes care of his plans and distributes the tasks as he wishes. If you are not given something you desire to do, you can prepare the way and support others with joy, trusting that God carries out his work.
exp.26:5:
This verse says that Benaiah was a brave man, outstanding among the Thirty, a group of elite warriors who served King David, and that he was even placed over them. A "division" means an organized unit of soldiers. His son Ammizabad was in charge of that division. Some understand that Ammizabad was in charge of it or was its second-in-command; the text does not make this clear.

The writer of Chronicles lists how David organized the army into twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand men each, with each one serving one month of the year. Benaiah, son of the priest Jehoiada, commanded the third. This list shows an orderly kingdom, where the service was shared so that no one carried the whole load.

For today: God values orderly and steady service, not only heroic acts. Ask yourself what your turn of service is: in your family, your church, or your work. Do it faithfully, and if you can, prepare others, as Benaiah did with his son.
exp.22:26:
It says that, following the final instructions of King David, the Levites twenty years of age or older were counted. The phrase "final instructions" refers to David's last commands, and "counted" means enrolled or registered. Earlier in this same chapter, the Levites had been counted from thirty years old.

The one telling the account is the chronicler, who recalls what David did at the end of his life, when he was preparing Solomon to reign. Since God had given rest to Israel and the temple was going to be built in Jerusalem, the Levites no longer had to carry the tabernacle. So their work changed: now they would serve in the house of God. More helpers were needed, and that is why the age was lowered. The texts do not explain every detail of this change.

When circumstances change, God may ask us for new ways of serving. We can offer him what we are and adapt with humility, without holding on to what was before.
exp.27:12:
This verse continues the list of what David handed over to Solomon: the plans for the temple. Here he adds the divisions of the priests and Levites, all the work of service in the house of the LORD, and all the articles used in that service. The articles here means the containers and objects of the temple, not only cups.

David speaks to his son Solomon, before the people, near the end of his life. He could not build the temple himself, so he hands over the plans. The text says David had received them by the Spirit (v. 12), and later says God made him understand them in writing (v. 19).

For today: God cares as much about the people who serve as about the details of the service. Serve with order and care in what is given to you, even when it seems small.
exp.13:16:
This verse says that news of David's victories spread through all the neighboring countries. It also says that the Lord caused the nations to fear him. The phrase "his fame went out" means that the news of him was made known and reported everywhere. "Nations" means the peoples or nations.

Here the chronicler, who tells the story of Israel, speaks just after David, now king, obeyed God's instruction and defeated the Philistines, from Gibeon to Gezer. The text emphasizes that his fame and the authority he had were not merely human achievements: they are presented as the work of the Lord. In this way it shows that God backed his reign.

For today: when we obey God step by step, we do not need to seek fame or force ourselves on others. We can do well what he asks of us and leave the outcome in his hands, remembering that any recognition that comes is a gift from him.
exp.13:2:
This verse says that David took more wives in Jerusalem and became the father of more sons and daughters. The phrase "became the father of" means that he was the parent of these children. "Jerusalem" is the city, and "and" is the ordinary word for joining two parts of a sentence.

The author of Chronicles, who writes looking back on the history of Israel, is not a character speaking here; he is the narrator. This comes right after David is established as king and receives help from Hiram. Then the list of his children follows. The text only reports the fact; it neither approves nor criticizes it. Other passages of the Bible show that having many wives brought problems to David's family, and the law warned kings about this (Deuteronomy 17:17).

For today: success and power do not make us immune to bad decisions. Take care of your relationships and your family with wisdom and faithfulness, and seek God's guidance also when everything is going well.
exp.10:35:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions two men: Hepher, who is called "the Mecherathite," and Ahijah, who is called "the Pelonite." These names ending in "-ite" are not family surnames like ours. They indicate the place or clan each man came from. Where Mecherathite was located is uncertain; scholars debate it.

Here the chronicler reviews David's mighty men, the men who supported him when he began to reign over all Israel. The writer is not a character in the story but the author of the book, who wrote for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots and those who served God and their king faithfully.

For today: God remembers those who serve, even when almost no one knows them. Your faithful and quiet work also has value before Him.
exp.24:26:
This verse says that the twentieth group, under the leadership of Eliathah, was made up of twelve people: him, his sons, and his brothers. The number "twentieth" means "number twenty," and "his brothers" here refers to close family relatives.

It is part of a list in the book of Chronicles, written by an author whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. Here it is recounted how David and the leaders of worship organized 24 groups of musicians to serve in the temple. Each group was assigned its turn by lot. Eliathah was one of the family heads of these groups.

For today: God values steady, organized service, including the kind that almost no one notices. Ask yourself what simple task you can carry out faithfully in your church or family, knowing that God does not forget those who serve.
exp.25:8:
This verse says that Meshelemiah had sons and brothers, eighteen of them in all, who were capable men. The word "capable" here means men who were able, dependable, and well prepared for their work. Meshelemiah (also called Shelemiah in other passages) was a Levite from the family of the gatekeepers.

The author, who according to tradition was the chronicler, lists how David organized the Levites to care for the gates and storehouses of the temple. It is not about one particular person; it is an orderly record. Families, numbers, and qualities are named, because service to God was arranged with care, and each family had its place.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is quiet, like watching over a gate. Ask yourself what simple task you have been entrusted with in your church or family, and do it with effort and steadiness, knowing that He sees and remembers every service.
exp.1:23:
This verse tells us that Hezron died in a place called Caleb-ephrathah, and that afterward his wife Abijah bore him a son, Ashhur, the father of Tekoa. Ashhur is called "father of Tekoa," an expression that is usually understood to mean founder or leader of that town. The text is brief, and some details of the original Hebrew are difficult, so scholars interpret it in several ways.

Here it is not a character who speaks but the chronicler, who compiles lists of families from Judah. He wrote for a people who had returned from exile and needed to remember their roots, their land, and their identity. Each name showed that God had cared for the families of his people.

For today: God takes notice of each life, even of names that almost no one remembers. Remember that your story matters to him, and give thanks to those who went before you in the faith.
exp.12:12:
It says that David did not move the ark of God with him into the City of David, as he had intended. Instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, who was from the city of Gath (which is why he is called "the Gittite"). The phrase "took it aside" means moving it away from its intended destination.

The author of Chronicles is the one telling this. David had just seen what happened when Uzzah died after touching the ark, and he was left sad and full of fear. That event showed that God must be treated with reverence and according to what He had commanded. So David paused before going on. Afterward, the text says that God blessed the house of Obed-edom.

Today, when something confronts us or does not turn out as we expected, we can stop, recognize that God is to be obeyed with humility, and examine our hearts and the way we seek Him, without giving up the desire to draw near to Him.
exp.10:10:
This verse begins the list of David's mightiest warriors. The first one named is Jashobeam, son of Hachmoni, the chief of the officers. It says that on one occasion he wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them. The word "wielded" means that he swung or drove the weapon with force. In the parallel passage (2 Samuel 23:8) a different number appears, eight hundred, and scholars explain this in several ways; there is no single certain answer.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, recalls those who helped David become king over all Israel. His central point is that they acted "according to the word of the LORD," and that God was with David.

For today: great achievements are almost never the work of one person. Value those who walk alongside you, and serve with courage wherever God places you.
exp.15:6:
On that day, when the ark arrived in Jerusalem, David first committed to Asaph and his associates a song of thanksgiving to the Lord. Giving thanks here means thanking and praising God, and committing the song to Asaph meant entrusting them with leading it.

The one acting is David, the king of Israel. The book of Chronicles tells how the ark of the covenant, the sign of God's presence, was brought into the city with great celebration. The Levite musicians, with harps, lyres, cymbals and trumpets, were already in their places. Then David gave them the first song of thanksgiving, which continues in the verses that follow.

For today: praise to God does not have to be only a private feeling. This week, write down one specific reason for gratitude and share it with someone, or sing it with your family or your church.
exp.13:3:
This verse begins a list of the sons born to David in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. The words "born to him" simply mean that they were his children. In other passages, the name Shammua also appears as Shimea or Shammuah, and the list continues in the next verse.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, tells us that God had established David as king over all Israel. He then mentions David's family as a sign of stability and blessing in his kingdom. The Bible also shows that David committed serious mistakes with his wives and his children, so this list does not tell the whole story. Solomon appears at the end, and later he will be the king who succeeds David.

For today: God cares for people one by one, even in lists of names. Every life counts to Him. Value your family, pray for it, and do not neglect it, because success without a firm home is incomplete.
exp.11:25:
From the tribe of Levi, 4,600 men came forward. The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve the temple and the things of God, so this is a count of their descendants who joined the others. The verse is part of a list and explains nothing more.

The book of Chronicles counts the warriors of each tribe who went to Hebron to join David and make him king over all Israel, after the death of Saul. It is not about one person; the chronicler, whose name the Bible does not give, tells the story. It is notable that Levites appear, since their main task was religious, and the text does not explain why they took part armed. Some think they supported David's reign as something desired by God.

Today we can learn that God values every person who joins his work, even when their name is not mentioned. Offer your gifts and your time gladly, knowing that your service counts.
exp.24:4:
This verse says that all those named before were sons of Heman, who is called "the king's seer" and is linked to the promises of God. A "seer" is someone who receives and passes on messages from God. The BSB says these sons were given to Heman "to exalt him," and that God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters. The original phrasing about "lifting up" points to honoring God's gifts and calling, though some understand it as giving strength or honor to Heman's position.

The author is the Chronicler, who describes how King David organized the musicians of the temple. Heman, Asaph, and Jeduthun led whole families dedicated to praise. It is noteworthy that Heman's sons are seen as a blessing from God.

For today: our abilities and our families can be a way of serving God. Think about what gift you have and how you can use it, together with others, to praise him faithfully and humbly.
exp.3:30:
This verse continues the list of towns where the tribe of Simeon lived. The names Beth-marcaboth and Hazar-susim probably mean "house of chariots" and "village of horses," though it is not known for certain why they were called that. The words "These were their cities until the reign of David" show that these towns belonged to them up until that time.

The author is the Chronicler, who wrote for the people of Israel after the exile. Tradition often names Ezra, but this is not certain. He wanted them to remember their families, their lands, and their history, so that they would know God had not forgotten them.

For today: God pays attention to the details of our lives, even to places and names that seem unimportant. Thank him for your family, your home, and your history, and live faithfully where he has placed you.
exp.6:22:
Ephraim, after losing his sons, came together with his wife again. She became pregnant and had a son. He named him Beriah, a name that sounds like a Hebrew word connected with "trouble" or "misfortune." The phrase "again he slept with his wife" simply describes the two of them coming together as husband and wife.

This is a genealogical list, written by an author who is not named in the text (Jewish tradition often points to Ezra). Earlier, it tells that Ephraim's sons were killed in a raid by the men of Gath, and that he mourned for many days. The child's name recalls that sorrow, but it also shows that the family went on. Some scholars debate details of this story, because the text is brief.

When we go through a loss, it is good to weep and to remember. But God can also give us new beginnings. We can ask him for comfort, lean on our family and our church, and take steps of hope without forgetting what we have lived through.
exp.8:29:
This verse says that some of the sons of the priests mixed the spices. These were fragrant blends used in the worship of the temple.

Context: It is part of a list of duties in the temple after the return from exile. The chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records who did each service. The Levites took care of the vessels, the flour, the wine and the incense. The priests were given this delicate work, because the law of Moses regulated how the holy oil was to be made (Exodus 30:22-33).

For today: God cares about the details and values hidden service. No one saw the work of mixing spices, but it was part of worshiping God. Do with care and faithfulness the task that has been entrusted to you, even when no one notices it.
exp.4:25:
God moved the will of Pul and Tiglath-pileser, kings of Assyria, so that they invaded the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, east of the Jordan. They were taken into exile and brought to places such as Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan.

The phrase "stirred up the spirit" means that God roused or drove the kings' will to act. The words "to this day" show that, when this was written, those people were still far from their land.

The chronicler tells the story plainly: these tribes abandoned God and followed the idols of the neighboring peoples. Their turning away from God is described as spiritual unfaithfulness. Some believe Pul and Tiglath-pileser are two names for the same king; others think they are two different people. The Bible presents this as God's judgment for their idolatry.

God takes our faithfulness seriously, but He also corrects us in order to call us back. Today we can examine whether anything has taken God's place in our hearts, and return to Him in humility before the consequences grow.
exp.26:24:
This verse names two officials who were in charge of the treasure during David's reign. Azmaveth, son of Adiel, was in charge of the royal storehouses, which means what was kept in the palace. Jonathan, son of Uzziah, was in charge of the storehouses in the country, in the cities, in the villages, and in the fortresses. The word "treasures" here may include harvests, supplies, and goods.

The writer of Chronicles presents a list of David's officials. It is not a speech but an administrative record. It shows that the kingdom was well organized, with someone responsible for each area. The verses before it speak of the census that Joab did not finish, and the verses after it continue with those in charge of the farming and the vineyards. The exact details of these positions are not known beyond what the text says.

God values order and faithfulness in what may seem ordinary. If you are in charge of money, goods, or tasks, whether at home, in the church, or at work, look after them with honesty and transparency, as one who serves God.
exp.6:17:
This verse says that Hammolecheth, the sister of Gilead, had three sons: Ishhod, Abiezer and Mahlah. The phrase "gave birth to" describes what she did for each of them. "His sister" refers to the sister of Gilead, grandson of Manasseh. It is striking that a woman is named, which is unusual in these lists.

Here the speaker is not a character but the author of Chronicles, who is thought to have written after the return from exile. His purpose was to remind the people who they were, what tribe they came from, and that God had cared for every family. These genealogies helped them reconnect with their heritage and their land. Scholars do not know much more about Hammolecheth and her sons, so it is best not to invent details.

For today: God remembers names that history has almost forgotten. You too are known to Him. Today, value someone in your family whom no one mentions, and thank them.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that Naarah, one of the two wives of Ashur, had four sons: Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. The word "bore" in the verse means "gave birth to." The names here are spelled a little differently today, and the verse ends by calling them the descendants of Naarah.

This is not a character speaking, but the chronicler, who arranges lists of families from the tribe of Judah. Ashur is presented as the father of Tekoa, and his two wives, Helah and Naarah, each have their own list of children. The Israelites who returned from exile needed to remember their roots and their place among the people. Some details of these genealogies are understood in different ways, because they may refer to people or also to towns.

For today: God pays attention to every person, and every name matters. Think of your family and of those who care for you; give thanks for them and pray for each one by name.
exp.24:2:
This verse lists the six sons of Jeduthun, who served under the direction of their father. In the reader's wording, the sons are named as Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six in all. Jeduthun "prophesied with the harp," that is, he spoke and sang on God's behalf with music, giving thanks and praise to the LORD.

The text itself gives no reason to doubt the list, so it can be read as given.

The chronicler tells how David and the captains of the army set apart the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun for musical service in worship. It was an organized ministry, not an improvised one.

Today we can see that praise is an important service. If you have a gift, use it with order and humility, and if possible, teach and encourage your family so that they worship God together.
exp.1:42:
This verse is part of a family list. It names four sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema. Hebron here is a person, a descendant of Caleb, although there is also a place with that name. Some names are spelled differently in older texts: the name Tappuah is spelled Thaphua there, and the name Rekem is spelled Recem.

No one speaks here in the first person. The author, whom tradition calls Ezra (this is not certain), gathers genealogies of the tribe of Judah. He probably wrote them for the people who were returning from exile, so that they would remember their roots and their place in God's story. Some of these names also seem to indicate peoples or clans, not only individuals, and scholars interpret this in various ways.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those we barely know. Today you can give thanks for your family and for those who passed on the faith to you, and remember that your life also matters to God.
exp.27:11:
This verse says that David also gave Solomon the plans for everything he had in mind: the courts of the temple, the rooms around it, and the storehouses where the treasures of God's house and the dedicated things were kept. The word "plans" means a design or blueprint. The "rooms" are the surrounding chambers, and "dedicated things" are objects set apart for God.

David speaks as an old man, in front of the leaders of Israel and his son Solomon. God did not allow David to build the temple, so he prepared everything he could so that Solomon would build it. The text goes on to say that David received this plan by the Spirit, and the passage stresses that the work came from God.

For today: preparing well for the future of others is also serving God. Even if we do not see the work finished, we can lay solid foundations, teaching, and order for those who come after us.
exp.28:27:
This verse tells how the life of King David came to an end. He died at a ripe old age, "full of years", that is, having lived a long and complete life. He also had riches and honor, which here are called "glory". After him, his son Solomon became king.

The one speaking is the author of Chronicles, who is not named with certainty. He closes the account of David's reign, which lasted forty years. The book was written for a people returning from exile, and it wanted to remind them of God's faithfulness to his promise about David's family and the continuity of his kingdom.

For today: a life well lived is not measured only by success, but by having served God in one's time and leaving a path open for the next generation. We can ask ourselves what we are leaving to those who come after us.
exp.11:38:
These fighting men who came to Hebron stayed with David for three days, eating and drinking. The phrase "had provided for them" means that their relatives had already gotten everything ready to welcome them.

Here the writer of Chronicles tells how the tribes of Israel came together to make David king. After mentioning the armies who came with a "perfect heart," that is, with sincerity and complete devotion, the account describes a great feast. Neighbors from other tribes brought much food because there was joy throughout the people. The Bible does not give more detail about how it was organized, so it is not wise to add details.

For today: when God unites his people, it is worth celebrating together. We can serve with generosity, preparing something for others, whether a meal, a space, or our time, and so help unity be lived out with joy.
exp.0:30:
This verse says that Keturah, Abraham's concubine, bore six sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. A concubine was a wife of secondary standing, and the phrase "bore" means "gave birth to." Further on the text writes "Jobshan," a variant spelling of the name Jokshan.

The author is a chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He was writing for the people returning from exile. The family lists reminded them where they came from and how they were related to other peoples. They also show that God's promise to Abraham, to make him the father of many nations, still stood.

For today: God forgets no one, not even those who are hardly mentioned in the story. If you sometimes feel small or unimportant, remember that God knows you by name and has you in his plan.
exp.23:17:
This verse closes the list of the twenty-four families of priests. The family of Delaiah held the twenty-third place, and the family of Maaziah the twenty-fourth.

Here the author of Chronicles, who reviews the history of Israel, speaks. David organized the descendants of Aaron into shifts to serve in worship. Lots were cast to set the order of the shifts, so everyone had their place and the service was not disordered. Many scholars think the book was written after the exile, to remind the people of their roots in worship.

For today: God cares about order and values each person, even those who appear at the end of the list. Serve where God has placed you, without comparing yourself, because your place matters.
exp.14:4:
Among the Levites whom David gathered, the verse says, from the Kohathites, Uriel was the leader, and he had 120 relatives with him. The word "leader" here means the head of the family, and "relatives" in this verse means members of the same clan.

The writer of Chronicles recounts how David gathered Israel in Jerusalem to bring the ark of God to the tent he had prepared. Earlier, the ark had been moved in the wrong way, and now the Levites, who were the ones responsible for carrying it, are organized. This list of families shows order and care. Beyond this text, not much more is known about Uriel.

God values orderly service, and he values people who are unknown to the world. Names and numbers are mentioned here because each one counted. Today, we can serve in the church with humility and order, knowing that God sees and remembers our work even when others do not notice it. Doing what God asks, in the way he asks it, is important.
exp.11:35:
From Asher came forty thousand men fit for service and prepared for battle. The phrase "fit for service" and "prepared for battle" describes men who were ready, equipped and willing to fight. They were not improvised volunteers but trained soldiers, ready to serve.

The writer of Chronicles, who wrote long after these events, gives a list of the tribes who went to Hebron to make David king after the death of Saul. The text stresses that they came with a wholehearted heart, that is, with sincerity and loyalty. The exact numbers in these lists have been debated, but the clear emphasis is the unity of all Israel.

For today: God values those who come forward with a sincere and united heart. Ask yourself how you can put your abilities at the service of God's people, without dividing, with loyalty and willingness.
exp.0:53:
This verse ends the list of the chiefs of Edom, that is, the leaders or heads of clans. Magdiel and Iram are the last two names. These men were leaders of their families or tribes, not rulers in any modern sense.

Here no single character speaks; it is the chronicler, who is writing a genealogical list. Edom comes from Esau, the brother of Jacob. By going through the families of the neighboring nations, the author places Israel within the wider story of humanity. Its readers, who were returning from exile, needed to remember their roots. We know nothing more about these two chiefs.

For today: God knows and remembers names that history has almost forgotten. That reminds us that no one is invisible to him. Today you can value the ordinary people around you, whatever their fame, and serve with confidence, knowing that God sees what you do.
exp.23:11:
This verse continues a list of the 24 divisions of the priests. Here the eleventh division is named, which corresponds to the family of Eliashib, and the twelfth, which corresponds to the family of Jakim. The word "lot" indicates that the lot fell upon that family group. Each name represents a priestly household, not just an individual.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records how David organized the service in the temple. There were many priests, so lots were cast to assign the shifts so that everything would be done in order. This list reminded the people after the exile that their worship had an orderly foundation.

God cares about details and values that each person has a place in his service. Even if your task seems small or little seen, doing it faithfully counts. Ask yourself today: what is my turn to serve, and am I fulfilling it with order and care?
exp.14:18:
This verse says that three music leaders, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, played bronze cymbals. Cymbals were two metal plates struck together to make a loud, clear sound. They are also called "musicians," because they had a musical ministry before God.

The passage is part of the account of when David brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. The chronicler tells us that the Levites chose these men to lead the music at that celebration. Each is named with his Levitical family, and others are mentioned who played harps and lyres (stringed instruments). Nothing more is said about exactly how that music sounded.

For today: praise to God deserves order, preparation, and the participation of many. If you serve in your church, even in something simple, do it with dedication, because each contribution helps everyone worship together.
exp.5:2:
This verse lists the family of Amram, from the tribe of Levi. His children were Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. Then it names the four sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

The text is a genealogy within 1 Chronicles, a book that tradition often attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for the people who were returning from exile. It reminded them who the legitimate priests and Levites were, and that their service in the temple came from a line established by God, going back to Aaron.

For today: God pays attention to families and to people with their names and family histories. Even famous leaders like Moses came to their service with a family story. Think about who taught you to believe and thank them. Also consider what faith you want to leave to those who come after you.
exp.8:38:
This verse is a family list: Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul, and Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal. Esh-baal seems to be the same son whom other passages call Ish-bosheth.

The author of Chronicles, who according to tradition may have been Ezra (this is not certain), writes to a people who had returned from exile. He recalls the families of the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem. Some wonder how Ner fits with other texts that mention him, and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: God does not forget people or their families, even when their story has both light and shadow. Ask yourself what faith and what values you are leaving to those who come after you.
exp.20:8:
The verse says that the LORD instructed Gad, David's seer. A seer was a prophet, someone who received messages from God and passed them on. The name of God in this verse is the LORD, and the word "instructed" introduces the message that follows.

David had just taken a census of the people, and this displeased God. David recognized his error and asked for forgiveness. Now God does not speak to David directly, but instructs Gad to bring a word about the consequences. This is how prophets acted: they were messengers between God and the king.

For today: when we recognize our sin, God still speaks to us, although at times we must also face the consequences. Let us seek his voice in the Bible and in wise counselors, and receive his correction with humility, trusting that his mercy is great.
exp.27:8:
Solomon is told to truly know the God of his father David and to serve him wholeheartedly and with a willing mind, not out of mere duty. The verse says the LORD searches every heart and understands the intent of every thought, so God sees what lies beneath outward actions. If Solomon seeks him, he will be found by him; but if he forsakes him, God will reject him forever.

David speaks before all Israel, already old, as he hands the kingdom to his son Solomon and charges him to build the temple. He gives him a father's advice: what matters most is not the building but his relationship with God. The warning is serious, and the story shows that Solomon later turned away.

For today: outward compliance is not enough. Set aside a few minutes each day to speak with God honestly, and ask him for a heart ready to serve him with joy.
exp.3:11:
This verse is part of a list of families from the tribe of Judah. It says that Eshton was the father of three people: Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah. Tehinnah is called "father of Ir-nahash," which probably means he was the founder or leader of that town. "Was the father of" means "had as a son" or "was the ancestor of." The "men of Recah" seem to be a family group; we do not know for certain who they were.

There is no character speaking here; the writer is the chronicler, who reviews genealogies for the people of Israel returning from exile. He wanted to remind them of their origins, their identity, and that God had cared for every family, even the little-known ones.

For today: God knows names the world forgets. Even if your life seems small or unknown, you have a place in his story. Today, thank someone who passed faith or care down to your family.
exp.20:17:
In this verse David speaks with God and owns his guilt without making excuses. He admits that he himself gave the order to count the people, that he sinned, and that he did wrong. He calls the people "sheep," since they had done nothing to deserve this. He asks that the punishment fall on him and his family, and that the blow stop. The word translated as "I have sinned" means "I committed a sin," and the word for the punishment refers to a disease or judgment that kills many people.

David had already ordered a count of the people, and God sent a plague as a consequence. David had just seen the angel with a drawn sword standing over Jerusalem. The text does not explain in detail why that count was wrong. Many readers think it reflected pride or confidence in military strength, but this is an interpretation.

Today we can learn to recognize our mistakes with humility, without blaming others. If our decisions affect other people, as in family or work, we should take responsibility and seek God sincerely.
exp.25:29:
From the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his relatives, 1,700 capable men, had charge of the affairs of Israel west of the Jordan. Their work covered everything connected with the worship of the LORD and the service of the king. In other words, they handled both religious duties (matters related to worship and the temple) and government duties (matters of administration).

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, describes how David organized the kingdom before his death. The Levites not only cared for the temple but also helped with civil duties. The verses that follow mention another group on the east side of the Jordan. Some details of the numbers and the regions are difficult to pin down.

For today: serving God and fulfilling our daily responsibilities can go together. Doing our work well, with integrity, is also a way of honoring the Lord.
exp.11:28:
It says that three thousand men from the tribe of Benjamin, the same tribe as King Saul, joined David. "Kinsmen of Saul" means relatives from his tribe. It adds that up to that point most of them had remained loyal to Saul's family.

The writer of Chronicles lists the warriors who came to Hebron to make David king after Saul's death. That Benjamites came was notable, because they were setting aside the loyalty they had shown to their own tribe. Scholars understand this as a sign that the kingdom was uniting around David.

Today, we sometimes find it hard to let go of old loyalties, habits, or comforts to follow what God is doing. Ask Him for courage to obey Him even when change costs you, and do it with humility and peace.
exp.4:21:
This verse says that many enemies fell, because the battle belonged to God and did not depend only on human strength. The phrase "fell wounded" would be better read as "fell slain," meaning they were struck down and died. Afterward, the people occupied those conquered lands until the exile, when they were taken away as prisoners to another country.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews the genealogies of Israel. Here he speaks of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, east of the Jordan. They cried out to God in the battle and trusted him. The text also recalls that their peace ended when they were carried off into exile.

For today: when you face a struggle, seek God first in prayer and trust him. But do not take a past victory for granted; remain faithful, because what God gives should be cared for with obedience.
exp.23:9:
This verse is part of a list. It says that the seventh round of service in the temple went to the family of Hakkoz, and the eighth to the family of Abijah. The word used here, translated as "went to," means the turn was assigned to them. These were work shifts for the priests.

The text was written by the Chronicler, who tells the history of Israel. He recalls that King David organized the descendants of Aaron into 24 groups, and that the order was decided by casting lots. In this way the service was arranged in an orderly and fair way. Later, the New Testament mentions Zacharias, of the course of Abijah (Luke 1:5), which shows that this order was remembered for centuries.

For today: God cares for what is orderly and values every service, even one that seems small. Serve faithfully in the place and at the time that is yours, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.24:19:
The thirteenth lot fell to Shubael, and he, his sons, and his brothers made up a group of twelve people. The verse uses the word "brothers" for close relatives who served together in the same family group.

The passage is part of the account of how King David organized the music for worship. Lots were drawn to assign 24 shifts among the musicians from the families of Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman, who sang and played instruments. The repeated listing shows order, and that each group had its own assigned place.

For today: God values steady and orderly service, even when it is seen by few. Shubael receives no special description, yet his name is recorded. Serve faithfully in your own place without comparing yourself to others, and trust that God sees your work.
exp.11:10:
Attai was the sixth and Eliel the seventh in a list of warriors. These are names of men who joined David.

Context: Here no single character speaks; the chronicler is recording a list. These are men from the tribe of Gad who came over to David when he was hiding from Saul in the wilderness. The text describes them as brave, ready for battle (verse 8). Their names and their order are recorded, which shows that each one was remembered.

For today: God notices people who seem ordinary and remembers them by name. Today, serve faithfully even when no one applauds you, and value those who serve quietly beside you. A simple "thank you" can encourage someone a great deal.
exp.15:18:
This verse recalls the people of Israel when God promised them the land of Canaan. They were few in number, very few indeed, and they were strangers in the land, people passing through without a place of their own. The word "everlasting" means eternal, and "statute" refers to a firm, established promise.

These words are part of the psalm that David delivered when the ark of the covenant came to Jerusalem. It reminds the Israelites that God kept his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when they were few and vulnerable. It is noted that God protected them as they moved from place to place.

For today: when you feel small, weak, or out of place, remember that God does not care only for the strong. His faithfulness does not depend on your size or your circumstances. Trust that He keeps what He promises, even in times of waiting.
exp.8:25:
This verse says that four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, were entrusted with the rooms and the treasuries of the house of God. Their work was to look after the storerooms of the temple, the places where its valuables and supplies were kept, and to guard the gates. The word "gatekeepers" names the people who watched over the entrances, and being "entrusted" means they had been given a responsibility that others relied on them to carry out.

The text is part of a list of families and servants who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. The author, traditionally called the Chronicler, is not identified with certainty. He wants to show that worship in the temple had order, and that each person had a concrete task.

For today: God values faithfulness in the small and the hidden. If something has been entrusted to you, whether money, time, or the care of others, look after it with honesty and constancy, as a service to God.
exp.25:20:
The verse names the descendants of Ladan, who were Gershonites through Ladan and belonged to the family of Gershon, one of the sons of Levi. Jehieli is named as one of the heads of the families of Ladan the Gershonite. "Heads of the families" here means the leaders of each family group.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes long after David, reviews how the service in the temple was organized. Here he tells who took care of the treasures: the offerings and the objects dedicated to God. The sons of Jehieli, who come next, had that responsibility. The names are recorded so that the people would remember that every task was important.

For today: God notices those who faithfully care for what has been entrusted to them, even when their work is quiet. Manage honestly what God has given you.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that Cush was the father of Nimrod, who began to be a mighty one on the earth. A "mighty one" is someone strong, with great influence or authority.

The chronicler is not giving a speech; he is putting together family lines after the exile in Babylon. He wants to show that the people of Israel belong to the story of all humanity, going back to Adam. Here he repeats a list from Genesis 10, where more details about Nimrod are given. Even so, the Bible does not explain here whether his power was good or bad, and some interpreters see it in different ways.

For today: power and influence are a call to responsibility. If God gives you authority, at work, in the family, or in the church, ask yourself how to use it to serve and not only to stand out.
exp.10:20:
Abishai was doubly honored above the other two men in his group of three, and because of this he became their commander. Yet he was not included among David's first three mighty warriors.

The chronicler is listing David's mighty men. He speaks of two groups of three men. Some scholars read this verse this way, although the text does not explain it fully. Abishai stood out for his bravery, but the Bible recognizes that others surpassed him.

God sees and values the service of each person, even when that person is not the best known. We can do our task well, rejoice in those who stand out more, and not live with envy. What matters is being faithful where God has placed us.
exp.15:35:
Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. That is the heart of this verse: a call to bless God, who is the same God for all time, past and future. Then the people answer with a shout of agreement, "Amen!" and "Praise the LORD!"

This verse closes a song that was sung when David brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem. The people celebrated with music and thanksgiving, and the chosen musicians led the song. Here we see that the whole gathering joined in, not only the singers, because the praise belonged to everyone present.

We can respond the same way today. When we pray or sing together, or when someone gives thanks to God, we can answer from the heart with a sincere "Amen." We can also praise the LORD on our own each day, not only as someone watching from the side but as one who takes part.
exp.11:31:
