This verse says that from the tribe of Issachar came two hundred leaders who "understood the times," meaning they knew how to read the situation of the moment and what Israel should do. Their fellow tribesmen followed their counsel and were guided by what they said.

This is part of a list of the tribes that came to Hebron to make David king after the death of Saul. The chronicler, who writes a long time afterward, emphasizes that the tribes came together. Issachar does not stand out for the number of soldiers, but for its wisdom. The text does not say exactly how they "understood the times"; some think it was political wisdom, and others, spiritual discernment.

Today, God gives different gifts: some help with strength, others with counsel. Ask Him for discernment to understand what is happening around you, and seek wise, humble counselors who are faithful to God.
exp.23:8:
This verse continues a list of the 24 families of priests. It says that the fifth lot fell to Malchijah and the sixth to Mijamin. "Lot" here means the turn that was assigned by casting lots, a way of deciding without favoritism.

The author is the Chronicler, who reviews the history of Israel for the people who were returning from exile. He explains how David, with the help of the priests Zadok and Ahimelech, organized the descendants of Aaron into turns to serve in the temple. The lots showed that each family received its place from God, not through rivalry. Scholars don't know much about most of these men; they are only names in the list.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is little seen. Perhaps no one will remember your name, but your task in the church or in the family matters. Do your turn with joy and without comparing yourself to others.
exp.11:5:
This verse gives five more names from a list of men who joined David: Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam. All are described as Korahites, that is, they belonged to the family or clan of Korah, from the tribe of Levi, although some scholars think it could also refer to a place.

The chronicler tells how, when David was fleeing from King Saul and living in Ziklag, brave warriors from various tribes came to support him. This long list honors each one by name. Here the ones who came from Benjamin, the same tribe as Saul, stand out, which shows that their loyalty to David was a difficult and costly decision.

God notices ordinary people who quietly stand on the right side. Although we do not remember their deeds today, their names were written down. Your faithful and quiet service, in the church or at home, also matters.
exp.1:19:
It says that Hur had a son named Uri, and that Uri had a son named Bezalel. "Was the father of" simply means that he had a son. It is a short line within a family list from the tribe of Judah.

The author of Chronicles, whose identity is not known for certain, writes after the exile in Babylon. He wants the people to remember their roots and their history with God. This Bezalel seems to be the craftsman whom God filled with his Spirit to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1-5). Some think this Hur is the same one who helped hold up Moses' arms, but this is not certain.

God uses ordinary people, with families and simple names, to do important work. Today, your skills and your work can also serve God and others.
exp.10:19:
Abishai, the brother of Joab, was the leader of a group of David's brave warriors. "Wielded his spear" means that he held it and used it with force in battle. "Killed them" means that he took their lives. He became famous for defeating three hundred men.

The writer of Chronicles gives a list of David's bravest warriors, who helped him establish his kingdom. The text says that Abishai was the chief "of the Three," but then says that he did not reach "the first three." This can be explained in several ways, and it is not entirely clear.

Today: be grateful to those who sacrifice for you, as David was with the water. And if you have strength or talent, use it to serve others, not to boast.
exp.1:48:
Here the verse says that Maacah, one of Caleb's wives, also bore Shaaph, the father of Madmannah, and Sheva, the father of Machbenah and Gibea. "Father of" most likely indicates the founder or leader of those towns, though some understand it as a direct family relationship. At the end, the verse says that Acsah was the daughter of Caleb.

No one is speaking in a sermon here; it is the chronicler, copying family lists after the exile in Babylon. He wanted the people to remember where they came from, which tribe they belonged to, and where their lands were. Caleb was from Judah, and his family occupied important cities. That a daughter, Acsah, is named is uncommon and draws attention.

For today: God does not forget the "small" people or their names. He values your family history and your place, and serves where God has put you, even when no one notices.
exp.20:26:
David built an altar to the LORD in that place and offered burnt offerings, which were burned whole, and peace offerings, which expressed thanks and fellowship with God. Then he prayed, and the LORD answered him by sending fire from heaven onto the altar.

This is the account of what followed the plague that fell on Israel because of the census David had ordered. Here the chronicler tells how David bought the threshing floor of Ornan, a Jebusite, paying the full price. He wanted to offer something that cost him. The fire from heaven showed that God accepted the offering and heard his repentance. Many understand that this is the same place where the temple was later built, though the text here does not say so directly.

Today, we can learn that coming to God with sincerity means real surrender, not just words. When we fail, God invites us to return to Him with humility, and He responds with mercy.
exp.12:3:
This verse says that the whole assembly of Israel agreed to David's proposal. They agreed because the idea seemed right to all the people. The word "assembly" here refers to the gathering of the people, and the note about an old spelling has been removed because that spelling does not appear in the verse you are reading.

David is the one who has spoken before, and now the account describes the people's response. David wanted to bring back the ark of God, which had been neglected since the days of Saul. Before acting, he consulted the leaders and asked them whether it seemed right to them and whether it was God's will. The people answered with unity.

For today: seeking God's will with humility and consulting other wise believers helps us move forward together. Even so, the fact that something seems good to everyone is not enough; we should also ask whether it pleases God and whether we are doing it in his way.
exp.28:19:
It says that David invited the whole assembled people to bless the LORD their God, that is, to praise and give thanks to Him. Everyone responded by blessing the LORD, the God of their ancestors. They bowed down and paid homage to the LORD, and they also bowed down before the king. The "assembly" is the gathering of the people; the "ancestors" are those who came before them.

David, now old, speaks at the end of his reign. He has just prayed and gathered offerings for the temple that his son Solomon would build. After this moment of devotion, he leads the people in worship. Bowing before the king was a sign of respect for his authority, distinct from the worship given to God alone.

Today we can learn that giving and serving should be accompanied by gratitude. Before asking or planning, take a moment to bless God out loud, alone or with others, acknowledging that everything comes from Him.
exp.9:1:
The Philistines chased Saul and his sons closely, and they succeeded in killing three of them: Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. "Chased" here means they caught up with them while they were running away. The names are spelled the way the reader's version gives them.

Context: the speaker is the chronicler, who summarizes Saul's last battle on Mount Gilboa. Israel had been defeated and the army was fleeing. The author wrote after the exile, and he wants to show how Saul's reign ended in order to prepare for David's coming. Books such as Samuel give more detail about the causes of this fall.

For today: life sometimes brings painful losses that we cannot avoid. We can learn to live faithfully with God now, without letting our own choices, like Saul's, lead us to a bitter end, and trust that God still guides history.
exp.8:14:
This verse continues a list of Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. It names Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah, and for the last of these it gives his family line: he was the son of Mica, the grandson of Zichri, and the great-grandson of Asaph. Asaph is the name of the Levite musician from the time of David. The phrase "son of" can also mean "descendant of."

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes for a people who had returned from exile. He wants to remind them who they are, which families they come from, and that service in the temple has deep roots. That is why he records names, not only events.

For today: God notices faithful service, even the kind that goes unseen. Almost no one remembers these names, yet they were preserved in the Bible. Serve where God has placed you, without seeking applause, and trust that he sees and remembers.
exp.23:6:
This verse begins to list the order in which the priests would serve in the temple. Lots were cast, and the first fell to the family of Jehoiarib and the second to the family of Jedaiah. "Lot" here means the drawing by which a decision was made. "Fell" means that the turn landed on that family.

The author of Chronicles is unknown; Jewish tradition often attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. It tells how David organized the descendants of Aaron into 24 groups, so that service in the sanctuary would be orderly and fair. Lots were used to prevent favoritism among the families of Eleazar and Ithamar, and everything was recorded with witnesses.

For today: God values order and humility in service. Serve where you are placed, without competing or comparing, trusting that every task, even the one no one sees, matters to Him.
exp.16:21:
It says that God chose Israel and made them his very own people forever, and that the Lord himself became their God. The phrase "You have made Your people Israel Your very own" speaks of God establishing them as a people belonging to him. The phrase "You, O LORD, have become their God" speaks of a close relationship and commitment, not only of power.

The speaker is King David. God had just promised him, through the prophet Nathan, that his house and his line would be secure. David answers with a prayer of wonder and gratitude. He remembers how God rescued Israel from Egypt and acknowledges that there is no other God like the Lord. His prayer shows confidence that God will fulfill what he promised.

For today: God relates to us out of love and faithfulness, not because of our merit. We can pray as David did, remembering what God has done, giving him thanks, and trusting his promises.
exp.3:26:
Shimei is said to have had twenty-two children in all: sixteen sons and six daughters. By contrast, his brothers did not have many children, and their whole clan did not grow to be as numerous as the sons of Judah. The idea here is that their family did not become as large.

This passage is part of the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, which tradition attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain. It speaks of the tribe of Simeon, who lived to the south, within the territory of Judah. The writer records the names so that the people, returned from exile, would remember their roots and their place in God's history. Simeon is compared with Judah, which was a very large tribe.

For today: do not measure yourself by size or by other people's numbers. God values every life and every family, even when they are small. Be faithful where He has placed you, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.3:10:
It says that Chelub, brother of Shuhah, was the father of Mehir, and that Mehir was the father of Eshton. "Was the father of" simply means "had as a son." It is a very brief family list, with names we hardly know.

The passage is part of the genealogies of Judah in Chronicles. Tradition often attributes the book to Ezra, but this is not certain. It was probably written for the people returning from exile, to remind them of their roots. This Chelub does not seem to be the famous son of Jephunneh, though there is no certainty. After the prayer of Jabez, the list continues its course and shows that God also works in ordinary families.

Today we can remember that God knows every name, even those no one remembers. Your life and your family matter to Him, even when they seem simple. Serve faithfully where you are and leave the result in His hands.
exp.0:43:
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah took his place as king. Bozrah was a city in Edom, and Jobab was from there. The words "when Bela died" simply mark the moment his life ended, and "took his place" means that Jobab succeeded him on the throne.

This verse belongs to the family lists that open 1 Chronicles. No one is speaking here; the chronicler is recording the kings of Edom, the people descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. These kings reigned before Israel had a king. The list does not show the throne passing from father to son, and each king is named with his hometown. Scholars discuss how best to understand this kind of succession.

For today: every leader's time comes to an end, and only God remains. We can serve where we are with humility and faithfulness, knowing that our true worth does not depend on a position.
exp.15:14:
It says that the people must always remember God's covenant, that is, the commitment he made to them. The word "remember" here means "do not forget." "Forever" means without end. It also says that God ordained his word "for a thousand generations," an expression that speaks of a very long time, without any practical end, and not so much an exact number.

King David gives this psalm of thanksgiving to Asaph and the Levites when the ark of the covenant arrives in Jerusalem. It speaks to the people of Israel, descendants of Jacob. It asks them to remember that God was faithful to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and that this faithfulness still holds.

For today: remembering what God has done strengthens trust. You can write in a notebook the times God helped you, and read them when you doubt or feel afraid, to remember that he keeps what he promises.
exp.14:2:
It says that David assembled all of Israel in Jerusalem to bring the ark of the LORD to the place he had prepared for it. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence with his people.

The chronicler tells what David did after building his palace and preparing a tent for the ark. Earlier, a first attempt to bring it had gone wrong (1 Chronicles 13), and so now David insists on doing it as God commanded: with the Levites. He wants the whole people to take part and to carry it out with reverence.

For today: when we want to draw near to God or serve him, good intentions are not enough. Let us seek to do it with reverence, following what he teaches, and let us do it together as a community, not alone.
exp.5:56:
It says that to the descendants of Aaron, who were priests, cities were given within the territory of Judah. Hebron and Libnah are named. A "city of refuge" was a place where a person who had caused a death by accident could flee. The pasture lands around each city are the areas that belonged to it.

Here the chronicler speaks, reviewing the lists of the Levites. This rests on what was commanded in Numbers 35 and Joshua 21: the Levites did not receive a land of their own, but cities distributed among the tribes. Hebron was a city of refuge, but its fields and villages were left for Caleb. In this way both promises were respected.

For today: God cares for those who serve him and also for those who need protection. We can be, like those cities, a place of welcome for someone who is wounded or needs help.
exp.5:18:
This verse closes the list of the sons of Levi. Merari, the third son of Levi, had two sons, Mahli and Mushi. With them the three main branches of the Levites are complete: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The verse calls these the clans of the Levites, listed according to their fathers, which means each family is recorded in the line of descent from its father.

The author is the Chronicler, a Jewish writer who probably wrote after the return from exile in Babylon. His name is not known for certain; some think it was Ezra, but that is an opinion. He records these genealogies to remind the people who the Levites were, who served in worship, and to reaffirm their identity and their place before God.

For today: God remembers every name, including those that almost no one remembers. You can live with the confidence that your faithful service, even when it is quiet, has value to Him.
exp.26:26:
It says that King David put two men in charge of the vineyards. Shimei the Ramathite was in charge of the vineyards themselves. Zabdi the Shiphmite was in charge of the produce of the vineyards, meaning the wine kept in the wine vats. The words "Ramathite" and "Shiphmite" tell us where each of the two men came from. The "wine vats" were the containers where the wine was stored.

The writer of the book describes how David's kingdom was organized at the end of his life. This list names the people in charge of the king's properties and goods. Reading it, one sees an orderly government, with tasks shared among many people. Exactly where those places were is not known.

For today: God values faithful and orderly work, even the kind that seems small or little seen. Do with care what has been entrusted to you, whether at home, at work, or in the church, and recognize the effort of those who serve alongside you.
exp.22:1:
This verse tells that David gathered all the leaders of Israel, as well as the priests and Levites. The word "leaders" here refers to the heads of the people. The Levites were members of the tribe of Levi, responsible for service in the worship of God.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles speaks. David was already old and had made his son Solomon king. Before he died, he gathered those responsible for the people to organize the service of the future temple. What follows is a count of the Levites and the division of their duties. David would not build the temple, but he prepared the way.

For today: if God gives you a responsibility, also think about those who will come after you. Prepare, organize and teach in time, so that others can continue the work with order and unity.
exp.5:60:
The verse says that the descendants of Kohath who had not yet received cities, that is, "the rest of the Kohathites," were allotted ten cities from the half-tribe of Manasseh. The cities were assigned by lot, a method of deciding that was understood to be guided by God.

This list in 1 Chronicles 6 reviews how the cities were divided among the Levites, the tribe set apart for the service of God, which did not receive a region of its own as the other tribes did. The chronicler, who writes after the exile, wants to remind the people that the Levites had their place and their place of service. Some lists agree with Joshua 21, although there are differences in the names that scholars explain in various ways.

God cares for those who serve. Just as he provided a home for the Levites, he also provides what is necessary for those who dedicate themselves to serving him. We can support with generosity those who work in the church and trust that God forgets no one.
exp.24:1:
These four sons of Asaph are named: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asarelah. They worked under the direction of their father Asaph, who "prophesied under the direction of the king." Here "prophesying" does not mean only predicting the future, but praising God with inspired music. Asaph acted under the direction of King David.

The author of the book, traditionally called the Chronicler, tells how David organized the musical service for worship in Israel. Together with the army commanders, he set apart the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun. The names are recorded because the Chronicler wanted to show that each person had a place in the worship of the people.

For today: God values orderly and team-based service. Whatever your gift, use it with humility, learning from those who lead you and serving alongside others to praise God.
exp.25:10:
This verse continues a list of the sons of Hosah, a Levite from the family of Merari. After Simri, it names Hilkiah, Tebaliah and Zechariah. In total, Hosah had thirteen sons and close relatives who served as gatekeepers of the temple. "Brothers" here can mean relatives or fellow members of the same family.

Context: No character is speaking; it is the chronicler, who records how David organized the service in the house of the LORD. The gatekeepers looked after the gates and the order of the holy place. The names are written down because each person had an assigned task. Not much more is known about these men.

For today: God values simple and steady service, even when no one applauds it. Ask yourself what small task you can carry out faithfully in your church or family, knowing that God knows your name and your work.
exp.14:20:
This verse names six Levites who were to lead the music with lyres "according to Sheminith." That last phrase is hard to understand. Some believe it refers to a low pitch or a melody in octaves; others think it means an instrument with eight strings. The word "lead" may mean that they directed the music. It is not known for certain.

The writer of Chronicles tells how David organized the Levites to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem. Music was an important part of that celebration. Each group had an instrument and a task, and they are named one by one.

For today: God values those who serve faithfully, even when their task seems small. There is a place for every gift in worship. Today you can offer what you know how to do, with order and from the heart, without seeking the spotlight.
exp.8:17:
This verse says that the gatekeepers from the Levite camp, organized into teams or shifts, were stationed at the King's Gate on the east side. "Gatekeepers" are the guards of the entrances, and the "teams" are the groups they worked in.

Here the chronicler speaks, an unknown author whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes after the return from exile in Babylon and lists who came back to Jerusalem and what service they performed. He wants to show that worship and order in the temple continued. The gate was probably the eastern entrance used by the king, but the exact details are not known with certainty.

For today: no service is small before God. The gatekeepers guarded a gate, and their task was recorded. Serve faithfully in the ordinary, even when no one notices.
exp.15:37:
David assigned Obed-edom and his sixty-eight relatives to serve in the worship. He also appointed Obed-edom son of Jeduthun, and Hosah, as gatekeepers. "Gatekeepers" were those who watched over the entrances and kept order at the holy place. Some scholars believe the two Obed-edoms are the same person, and others that they are different. The name "Hosah" may correspond to the name "Asa," but this is not certain.

The one who tells the account is the chronicler of Israel. He explains how David organized the service after bringing the ark to Jerusalem. He wanted worship to be constant and orderly, with each person in their task.

For today: God values simple services. Guarding a gate is not very visible, but it sustains worship. Serve faithfully in small things, without seeking applause.
exp.26:16:
This verse names two leaders. Hashabiah, son of Kemuel, was over the tribe of Levi. Zadok was over the house of Aaron, that is, the descendants of Aaron, the family of the priests. Here "over" means the head or chief of their group.

The book of Chronicles is anonymous, though tradition often attributes it to Ezra; this is not certain. The author lists how King David organized Israel at the end of his reign, with a leader for each tribe. These lists reminded the people, long afterward, that Israel had order and that the service of God had a place for everyone.

Today: God knows names and tasks, even the ones almost no one remembers. Serve faithfully in the place you have been given, without comparing yourself to others, because God values every service done with honesty and love.
exp.14:1:
David says that only the Levites may carry the ark of God, because the LORD has chosen them to carry it and to serve before Him forever. The word "forever" means continuing over the course of time. The phrase "no one but" means that only the Levites are allowed to do this work.

David speaks after he has prepared a tent for the ark in Jerusalem. He had earlier tried to move it on a cart, and that attempt ended with the death of Uzzah (1 Chronicles 13). Now David recognizes that he should follow what God had laid out in His law. For this reason he gathers the Levites before moving it.

For today: serving God with a good heart is not enough; it also matters to do it the way He directs. Before undertaking anything for God, it is wise to seek His guidance in the Bible and to act with humility and reverence.
exp.6:12:
This verse is a short list of the sons of Naphtali, one of the twelve sons of Jacob. It names Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, and Shallum. It identifies them as descendants of Bilhah, the woman who served Rachel and was the mother of Naphtali.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, reviews the genealogies of the tribes of Israel. He writes for the people who returned from exile and needed to remember who they were, where they came from, and that God had preserved their families. Naphtali appears briefly, among longer lists.

For today: God knows names, not just crowds. Even if your life seems small or little seen, he knows you and remembers you. Today, thank someone whose service goes unnoticed, and remember their name.
exp.1:34:
It says that Sheshan had an Egyptian servant named Jarha, and that he gave his daughter to him in marriage. From that marriage Attai was born. The word "gave" is the one the verse uses, and "bore" means that she gave birth to him.

It is a genealogical list within the descendants of Judah, in the family of Jerahmeel. There is no speaker who teaches; the chronicler records names. Since Sheshan had no sons, his line continued through his daughter and Attai. We do not know with certainty all the reasons, but this is how the family line was preserved. It is notable that the husband was a foreigner and a servant.

For today: God does not measure a person's worth by their origin or social position. We can receive with respect those who seem different or who are in humble places, remembering that God also writes history with them.
exp.1:0:
This verse begins a list of the names of the sons of Israel, that is, of Jacob. Six appear here: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The names are written in an older style, as "Issachâr," which today we say as Issachar. The other six sons follow in the next verse.

The author of Chronicles is unknown; Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. He writes for the people who returned from exile, and he begins with genealogies to remind them who they were, where they came from, and that they still were God's people. Afterward the list focuses on Judah, the tribe of David.

God works with real families, with imperfect stories, and forgets no one. Knowing your family history, with its lights and shadows, can help you be thankful for God's faithfulness and decide how you want to live now.
exp.14:21:
This verse says that Chenaniah, the head Levite, was the director of the music. The word "music" here refers to the singing and playing that went with the ark's procession. The Berean wording says he was "highly skilled," which means he had real knowledge and ability for the job. Some readers also know that the Hebrew word for "song" can be understood as "burden," which has led some to think he directed the carrying of the ark. Scholars do not fully agree on this.

The writer of Chronicles tells how David brought the ark of God to Jerusalem. This time he did it in an orderly way, assigning each Levite a task: singers, musicians, gatekeepers, and priests with trumpets. After an earlier failed attempt, the aim was to honor God with care.

For today: if you serve God in something, prepare yourself and do it with excellence and humility. God values the giving of the heart as much as the effort of learning to do things well.
exp.24:29:
The twenty-third lot, for the musical service in the temple, fell to Mahazioth. His group was made up of him, his sons, and his brothers, twelve people in all. The number 23 is simply the twenty-third in the order of the groups.

This passage is part of an account the writer of Chronicles gives about King David. David organized the Levites, the family dedicated to the service of the temple, into 24 groups of musicians. Each group had twelve members, and their turns were assigned by casting lots. The writer wrote to remind the people, after the exile, that worship was to be carried out with order and with the participation of everyone.

For today: God values the service of each person, even that of those whom almost no one remembers. Mahazioth appears only in a list, but his place mattered. Serve where God has placed you, faithfully, even when no one notices.
exp.0:46:
This verse says that when King Hadad died, another man named Samlah took over as ruler in his place. Samlah came from Masrekah, a place in Edom. The phrase "when Hadad died" simply means "after Hadad had died."

Here the chronicler is not speaking as a character; he is copying a list of the kings of Edom, the people descended from Esau. This list appears within the genealogies that open 1 Chronicles, and it is very similar to the one in Genesis 36. These kings were not sons of one another, and not much more is known about them. It seems the office did not pass from father to son.

For today: every leader and every position is temporary; only God remains. Live with humility and serve well where you are, knowing that your time is brief and that God still governs.
exp.5:72:
This verse continues a list of cities given to the Levites of the family of Gershon. Here Ramoth and Anem appear, in the territory of the tribe of Issachar, each one together with its pasturelands. The pasturelands were the grazing land around each city, where the Levites could keep their livestock.

The chronicler reviews how Israel distributed cities among the Levites, who did not receive a land of their own as the other tribes did, since their inheritance was to serve God. The other tribes supported them by giving them cities. The names of some cities vary a little in other passages, such as Joshua 21, which is common in ancient lists.

For today: just as Israel cared for those who served God, we can support with generosity and gratitude those who dedicate their lives to teaching and caring for the church.
exp.1:40:
Shallum was the father of Jekamiah, and Jekamiah was the father of Elishama. It is part of a list of descendants. In lists like this, the word "father" can sometimes also cover a more distant ancestor, not only a direct son.

This passage is in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, which were most likely compiled for the people of Israel after the exile in Babylon. This line belongs to the family of Jerahmeel, within the tribe of Judah. The author is not identified in the text; Jewish tradition often attributes it to Ezra, but this is not certain. Its purpose was to remind the people of their origin and identity.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even to names we hardly know. Your life counts for Him, even when it passes quietly. Live faithfully in everyday life and give thanks to those who came before you in the faith.
exp.12:4:
David gathered all the people of Israel, from the River Shihor in Egypt to Lebo-hamath in the north. He wanted them to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim. The verse says David "assembled" the nation, meaning he brought everyone together. The River Shihor is probably a stream on the southern border, though no one knows for certain which one it was.

David speaks with the leaders and with the people. Since the days of Saul, the ark, the symbol of God's presence, had been neglected. Now David wants to put it back at the center of the nation's life, and everyone agrees.

Today we might ask ourselves whether God sits at the center of our lives or whether we have pushed Him into a corner. Seeking Him again, together with others, is a good beginning. And it is wise to do so with attention to what He has said, not just with good intentions.
exp.16:16:
David is amazed. God had already given him a great deal, yet he also spoke about the future of his family, his house, which would continue for a long time to come. "As if this was a small thing" means that what God had already done was not the end of it, because God wanted to give even more. "Regarded me as a man of great distinction" means that God treated him as someone of great honor, although David did not see himself as deserving it.

David speaks in prayer, after the prophet Nathan had told him God's promise: that his descendants would reign and that a son of his would build the temple. David comes before the Lord and responds with humility and gratitude, without boasting about anything.

For today: when you receive blessings, do not take them as a right or as your own merit. Do as David did: pause, thank God simply, and acknowledge that everything comes from his goodness.
exp.16:1:
Nathan answers David: "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you." The words "God is with you" are a word of encouragement and support.

David was living comfortably in a palace of cedar, while the ark of God was still kept behind curtains. For that reason he wanted to build a temple. Nathan, the prophet, spoke according to what he saw as good intention in David. But that same night God corrected Nathan and told him that David would not be the one to build the house. So we see that even a good prophet can speak without having first consulted God.

For today: a good desire and a well-meant piece of advice do not replace prayer. Before you act, ask God and listen to his answer, even when it tells you "no" or "not yet."
exp.4:16:
It says that all the men of the tribe of Gad mentioned earlier were recorded in the genealogies. This took place during the reigns of Jotham, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel. "Recorded" here means written down in official lists of family descent.

The author of Chronicles is unknown; tradition attributes the book to Ezra, but this is not certain. He probably wrote for the people who returned from exile, to remind them who they were and where they came from. That is why he notes dates and names. The two kings mentioned reigned in periods close to each other, although scholars debate the exact years.

God does not forget anyone, not even people who today appear only as names on a list. You too have a place and a story before Him. Today, give thanks for your family and for those who went before you in the faith, and live in a way that honors that inheritance.
exp.8:18:
This verse introduces Shallum, from the family of Korah, the Korahites. Together with his relatives, he was assigned to guard the thresholds of the Tent. The phrase "work crew" means a group or shift of workers. It also says that their fathers had been assigned to guard the entrance to the dwelling of the LORD.

The book of Chronicles goes over the family records and the duties of the people after their return from exile. No one knows for certain who wrote it; one tradition points to Ezra. Its purpose is to remind readers that service in the temple went back many generations. It is notable that the Korahites are mentioned, since Korah rebelled in the wilderness (Numbers 16), yet his descendants continued to serve God.

For today: you do not need a famous job to please God. Guarding a door faithfully is also a ministry. And God can give a new purpose to a family, even one with a difficult past.
exp.15:42:
Once the great celebration was over, the text says, all the people went back to their homes. David also returned home, and with a purpose: to bless his household, that is, to pray for his family and ask God for good things for them.

This passage closes the account of the ark of God being brought to Jerusalem and placed in a tent. There were sacrifices, music, and praise, and David left Asaph and other Levites in charge of the service. The narrator (tradition attributes Chronicles to an author writing after the exile, though no one knows for certain who he was) shows that, after the public worship, David did not forget his family.

For today: after gathering with the church or sharing a special moment with God, we can carry that blessing into our home. Let us pray for our family, speak with kindness, and serve with patience.
exp.21:15:
David says that he has gathered gold, silver, bronze and iron in such amounts that they cannot be counted, along with craftsmen beyond number. Then he urges his son: "Now begin the work, and may the LORD be with you."

David speaks to his son Solomon. God did not allow David to build the temple, so he devoted himself to gathering all the materials and workers. Now he hands the task over to Solomon. The quantities he mentions may be meant to convey abundance rather than exact amounts; scholars interpret them in different ways.

God often gives us resources and companionship before asking us to act. If you feel that God is calling you to a task, do not wait until everything is perfect: begin with what you have, trust in his presence, and be thankful for those who prepared the way before you.
exp.0:21:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Joktan. It names three of them: Obal, Abimael, and Sheba. The word "begot" in the verse before means that Joktan was their father.

The author of Chronicles, who according to tradition was Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews the genealogies from Adam onward. He writes for the people who returned from exile, and he wants to remind them where they come from and that God has guided their history. Joktan belongs to the line of Shem, and the Bible says almost nothing more about these three sons.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who barely appear in the story. If you sometimes feel that your life goes unnoticed, remember that your name matters to God. And treat with courage the people around you who seem to count for little.
exp.0:6:
This verse lists the four sons of Javan, who was a son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah: Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittites, and the Rodanites. The names appear here in the spelling used by the Berean Standard Bible, so the name Tarshish is the same name that appears in the verse above. In some other ancient texts, the last name appears as Dodanim, and it is not known with certainty which form is original.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra though this is not certain, opens the book with lists of families. He writes for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. This list of the nations shows that Israel belongs to a larger story, the story of all humanity. Many believe these names relate to peoples of the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean, though the details are debated.

For today: God knows every person and every people by name. Today you can treat every person with respect, knowing that each one has worth before Him.
exp.5:5:
It says that Uzzi was the father of Zerahiah, and that Zerahiah was the father of Meraioth. Here the verse uses the plain phrase "was the father of," which shows a direct line from one generation to the next. In the Bible, a genealogy like this can sometimes skip generations or mean a more distant descendant, not always a direct son. It is part of a list of names from the priestly family.

No one speaks here in the first person; this is a genealogical record from the book of Chronicles, which tradition attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for the people who were returning from exile. The list connects Aaron with the later priests, to show that service in the temple had roots and continuity. Some scholars think the list may summarize generations.

For today: God notices people who may seem to us like nothing more than names. Your faithfulness in everyday life, even if no one applauds it, is part of a larger story that God cares for. Serve steadily where you are.
exp.7:38:
The verse says that Eshek, the brother of Asel, had three sons, named in order of birth: Ulam, the first; Jeush, the second; and Eliphelet, the third. "Firstborn" means the eldest son. Phrases such as "was his firstborn" and "the sons of" in these lists show family descent.

This passage is part of the family records of the tribe of Benjamin in Chronicles. The author is unknown; Jewish tradition often names Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written after the exile in Babylon, to remind the Israelites who were returning who they were and what family and tribe they came from. The following verse says that the sons of Ulam were brave warriors, skilled archers, and had many descendants. This shows that these lists are not just names but a record of noble families.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Value your family history and give thanks for those who came before you. And live in such a way that your life leaves a good mark on those who come after.
exp.26:4:
This verse says that the third army commander, who served as the leader for the third month of the year, was Benaiah, son of Jehoiada the priest. There were 24,000 men in his division. The word "division" refers to a group of men who served in rotation, and the title given to Benaiah's father is generally understood as "the priest," meaning he held a priestly role.

The chronicler describes how David organized Israel's army into twelve divisions, one for each month, each with 24,000 men. In this way the kingdom had a force always ready, but no one carried the service for the whole year. Benaiah appears in the verses that follow as one of David's mighty men.

For today: good order and shared service protect people from exhaustion. In the church, the family, or the workplace, sharing responsibilities in turns allows everyone to serve with strength and with joy.
exp.22:30:
This verse says that the Levites were to help present the burnt offerings to the Lord on the Sabbaths, on the New Moons, and at the appointed feasts. They were to serve regularly before the Lord, in the numbers prescribed for them. "Burnt offerings" are offerings that were burned up completely. "New Moons" were the beginnings of each month. The "appointed feasts" are the feasts God had set for his people.

This is in the account of King David, now old, when he arranges the service of the Levites for the future temple that his son Solomon would build. Their duties included helping the priests, preparing the bread and the flour, and praising God every morning and every evening. The text shows that worship was to be done with order and faithfulness.

For today: God values consistency. We can set aside fixed times to pray, give thanks, and praise him, not only when we feel like it, but as a simple and sincere habit.
exp.12:10:
David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah, striking him with a sudden blow that caused his death. That is why David named that place Perez-uzzah, meaning "the bursting forth against Uzzah," and it is still called by that name today, that is, up to the time the book was written.

Here the narrator speaks. David was bringing the ark of God to Jerusalem with great celebration, but they were carrying it on a cart, and not as God had commanded, which was on the shoulders of the Levites. Uzzah reached out and steadied the ark with his hand. Commentators explain the severity of this judgment in various ways, but all agree that God must be treated with reverence.

For today: even when our intentions are good, it is wise to seek God according to his Word and not only according to our own ideas. Let us approach him with respect, humility, and obedience.
exp.23:22:
This verse lists the descendants of Hebron, a son of Kohath, from the tribe of Levi. It names four heads of families in their order: Jeriah, Amariah, Jahaziel and Jekameam. Here "from the sons of" means the descendants, and "the first," "the second," "the third" and "the fourth" show the order in which their places were assigned.

The passage is part of a long list that organizes the Levites for service in the temple. It is traditionally associated with the time of King David, when worship was being arranged for the temple that Solomon would build. The text is a list, not a speech; that is why no one is speaking directly. The names and families were recorded so that the sacred work would be done in good order and it would be known who served in each turn.

For today: God values every person, even those whom few remember. Serve where He has placed you, with faithfulness and order, without seeking applause. No service done for God is small.
exp.17:3:
It says that David captured from Hadadezer a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. The phrase "hamstrung all the horses" means cutting the tendons of the back legs of the horses so they could no longer be used in war. He kept horses only for a hundred chariots.

The speaker is the chronicler, who summarizes David's victories. Some think David disabled the horses because of the law that told the king not to multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16), but the text does not say so. The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 8:4 gives different figures, and there are several ways to explain that.

Today: do not put your security in your resources or strength, but in God. Ask yourself what you trust in too much, and surrender it to God in prayer.
exp.3:0:
This verse opens a list of the descendants of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal. Here "descendants" does not always mean direct sons. In biblical genealogies the word can also refer to grandsons or more distant descendants.

The book does not name its author. Many believe it was written after the exile in Babylon, perhaps by Ezra, though this is not certain. Its purpose was to remind the people who were returning to their land where they came from, who their families were, and that God remained faithful to his promises. Judah was the tribe from which David would come.

For today: God knows people by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Value your family and faith history, give thanks for those who passed it on to you, and remember that your life also matters to God.
exp.5:61:
This verse says that the descendants of Gershom, a group from the tribe of Levi, were given thirteen cities. Those cities came from four tribes: Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Manasseh in Bashan. The verse names the clans directly, so no further comment on that wording is needed here.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, goes over the family records of Israel. He wants to remind his people that the Levites, who served in worship, did not have a territory of their own like the other tribes. For that reason the other tribes gave them cities to live in. In this way it was shown that the whole people supported the service of God.

For today: God cares for those who serve in the church, and we can do the same. Think of someone who teaches you or serves you in the faith, and support them with your time, your prayers, or your resources.
exp.25:13:
It says that the lot for the East Gate fell to Shelemiah. Then lots were cast for his son Zechariah, who is described as a wise counselor, that is, a man of wisdom and good judgment, and the lot for the North Gate fell to him. "Cast lots" means they included him in the drawing.

The author is the chronicler, who reviews how David organized the service of the temple. The gatekeepers, from the family of the Korhites, looked after the entrances of the house of the LORD. The gates were divided by lot, without favoritism, among younger and older men. The text does not explain why Zechariah was drawn separately; some think it was to share the responsibilities fairly, but this is not certain.

For today: God values simple and orderly service, even guarding a gate. Serve where you are needed, with wisdom and without comparing yourself to others, trusting that no work done for God is small.
exp.7:10:
This verse says that a man named Shaharaim had children with his wife Hushim, and that from her were born Abitub and Elpaal. The phrase "he also had sons by Hushim" simply tells us that he was their father.

It is part of the family lists of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles. No one speaks in the passage; the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), gathered the records for the people returning from exile. He wanted them to know where they came from, which tribe they belonged to, and what lands were rightfully theirs. The sons of Elpaal later appear as founders of towns such as Ono and Lod.

For today: God pays attention to each person and forgets no name. Even if no one else remembers you, your life has a place in his story. Live today with the assurance that you matter to Him, and value those whom others overlook as well.
exp.20:13:
This verse tells us that the LORD sent a plague upon Israel, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell dead. The word translated "plague" describes a deadly disease that spreads from person to person and kills many, which is the word your Bible uses here.

King David had ordered a census of the people, and this displeased God. The prophet Gad gave him three options for punishment. David chose to fall into the hands of the LORD, trusting in his great mercy, rather than into the hands of men. The account is told by the chronicler, and then it shows that God stopped the angel and had compassion. How to understand the death of so many people is difficult, and it is interpreted in various ways.

Today we can learn that our decisions, especially those of people who lead, affect others. When we fail, let us turn quickly to God with humility, because his mercy is greater than our error.
exp.25:15:
By lot, Shuppim and Hosah were assigned to guard the west gate, the gate of Shallecheth, on the ascending highway. The watches were posted one opposite the other, so that each guard was matched with another across from him. The meaning of "Shallecheth" is uncertain; some think it has to do with casting or throwing, but this is not certain.

The chronicler describes how David arranged the Levites who served as gatekeepers for the work of the temple. The lots divided the posts fairly, without favoritism, and each family received a specific duty in caring for the house of God.

For today: value quiet and steady service. Perhaps no one sees you at your post, but God does, and faithful work shared with others sustains the life of his people.
exp.8:5:
From the descendants of Zerah, a son of Judah, a man named Jeuel and 690 of his relatives lived in Jerusalem. The word "relatives" here means kinsmen, people from the same family line or clan.

The passage is a list of the families who came back to live in Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon. The author, whom many believe was Ezra though this is not certain, records these names to remind the people that their roots were still alive and that God had brought them home.

For today: God does not see numbers but people with names. Each of those 690 mattered. You also matter in your family, your church, and your community. Today, faithfully do your part, even if no one notices, because God does remember it.
exp.11:18:
Some men from the tribe of Manasseh went over to David when he was marching with the Philistines to fight against Saul. In the end, though, they did not help the Philistines, because the Philistine rulers talked the matter over and sent David away. They were afraid that David would switch sides to win back the favor of his master Saul, and that it would cost them their lives.

This is part of a list of warriors who supported David while he was fleeing from Saul and living in Ziklag. The chronicler shows that, even in difficult times, God was gathering people to stand with him. According to the account in 1 Samuel 29, David was dismissed by the Philistines; here we are told how, on his return, others joined him.

For today: God can use even the decisions of others, such as their rejection of us, to guide and protect us. When a door closes, trust that He is still at work and can bring you new support.
exp.5:53:
This verse begins the list of the places where the descendants of Aaron, the priests, were settled. The territories assigned to them were their homes and towns, and the first lot fell to them, which means their share of the land was decided by casting lots, a way of dividing the land that was understood to be guided by God.

Here the chronicler speaks, though no one knows for certain who he was, even if Jewish tradition often names Ezra. He writes after the exile, and he wants the people to remember their roots, their priestly line, and how God divided the land, including among the Levites, who did not receive their own territory as the other tribes did.

For today: God cares for each person and gives them a place and a purpose. Trust that the place where He has put you, whether simple or hard, is a place to serve Him faithfully.
exp.22:31:
The verse says that the Levites were responsible for the Tent of Meeting and the Holy Place, and that they were to serve under their brothers, the descendants of Aaron, in the service of the house of the LORD. The Levites were given the job of caring for the Tent of Meeting and the Holy Place, and they were also to work alongside their relatives, the priests descended from Aaron, in the service of the Lord's house. "Responsibilities" here means the duties and care entrusted to them, and the phrase "under their brothers" points to the Levites serving in a supporting role beneath the priests.

The passage comes where David, now old, arranges the Levites for the service of the temple that his son Solomon would build. It is a list of duties: praising, helping with the offerings, and caring for the holy place. The writer, traditionally identified as the Chronicler, is understood to want to show the order in the worship of God.

Today we can learn that serving God includes humble and unseen tasks, such as caring, keeping things in order, and helping. Think of a place where you can help in your church, without seeking applause, with faithfulness and joy.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that the relatives of these families of Benjamin, counted according to their genealogy, came to 956 men. "Genealogy" means the record of family descent. "Heads of families" were the leaders or those responsible for each household, that is, for each clan.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra though this is not certain, writes after the exile in Babylon. He is listing who returned to live in Jerusalem. He wants the people to remember their roots, to know that they are still the people of God, and to see that every family had a place in the rebuilding. The numbers and names gave identity to a community that had suffered greatly.

For today: God does not see people as a faceless crowd. Every name and every family matters to Him. And you too can serve where you are, without needing a famous position. Today, think of a specific place, such as your family or your church, and ask yourself how you can help faithfully.
exp.4:14:
This verse says that Ahi, son of Abdiel and grandson of Guni, was the head of his family. Being head means he held a position of leadership and was looked to for guidance and respect among his own people. The verse describes his role as one of responsibility for those who belonged to his family line.

The text is part of the family records of the tribe of Gad, who lived on the east side of the Jordan River. The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records these names so that the people would remember their roots after the exile. There are questions about how Ahi relates to the other names in the list, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

God takes notice of people who serve faithfully, even though today almost no one remembers their names. You can be a humble leader in your home, your church, or your work, caring for your own with responsibility and humility.
exp.21:6:
In this verse, David speaks to his son Solomon and shares something personal: that in his heart he had the desire to build a house for the Name of the Lord his God. The phrase "it was in my heart" means that he truly wished for it and had it on his mind.

David is near the end of his life and is preparing Solomon for a great task. He had already gathered many materials, but God had told him that he would not build the house, because he had fought in many wars. That task would belong to his son, to whom God would give peace. David does not complain; with humility he accepts God's plan and helps another person carry it out.

For today: sometimes God does not allow us to finish what we have dreamed of, but he does invite us to prepare the way for others. We can serve with joy, without needing recognition, trusting that God knows what our place is in his plan.
exp.15:5:
It says that two priests, Benaiah and Jahaziel, blew the trumpets before the ark of the covenant regularly, that is, the sacred chest that represented God's presence. The word "regularly" means that they did it again and again, as a steady service.

The Chronicler tells of the time David brought the ark to Jerusalem and arranged the worship. The Levites sang and played harps, lyres, and cymbals, while these priests blew the trumpets. It was an orderly way of remembering God, giving thanks, and praising him. Shortly afterward, David gave Asaph and his brothers a song of thanksgiving.

For today: worship does not depend only on great moments, but also on constant faithfulness. Even if your part seems small, like that of these men with their trumpets, God values your serving him regularly. Think of one simple practice, such as praying each day, and do it with consistency.
exp.3:22:
These were the potters who lived at Netaim and Gederah, a group of families from Judah who made clay vessels for a living. They lived in those places and served the king by doing his work.

The verse is part of the family records of Judah in Chronicles. The author, whom Jewish tradition associates with Ezra (this is not certain), records these trades to help a people returning from exile remember their roots and their place. Some details of the text are obscure, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God values simple and steady work. Even when no one remembers our names, doing our labor well, as for the King of kings, has value before Him.
exp.9:2:
The battle grew more and more fierce against Saul. The archers, that is, the Philistine soldiers who fought with bows, overtook him and wounded him. The phrase about the battle intensifying means the fighting became fiercer and more dangerous. The words about the archers wounding him mean that the arrows struck him.

Here the chronicler speaks, telling the history of Israel while looking back. Saul, the first king, had already lost his sons on Mount Gilboa. The book presents his death as the sad end of a reign marked by disobedience (1 Chronicles 10:13). Even so, the account is sober and gives no extra detail.

For today: the decisions we make over time take us somewhere. Today is a good day to return to God with humility and obedience, before pressures find us without strength.
exp.20:7:
In this verse, David admits before God that he committed a serious sin by ordering a census of the people. He asks God to take away the guilt of his servant, meaning himself. He says he has acted very foolishly, which means he behaved with great foolishness and without thinking clearly.

David is the king of Israel. He had ordered the people to be counted, although Joab, his military commander, did not agree. The text says this displeased God and that Israel suffered a blow. The biblical writers do not explain here in detail why it was so serious; many believe David put more trust in the number of his soldiers than in God.

Today we can learn from David: when we fail, the best thing is not to make excuses. We can tell God honestly what we did wrong and ask him for forgiveness, trusting in his mercy.
exp.1:53:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Bethlehem, the Netophathites, and the Zorites are linked to the descendants of Salma. The name "Atroth-beth-joab" is difficult: some believe it is the name of a place, and others that it refers to prominent families. It is not certain.

The text is from 1 Chronicles, written by an author who is not named with certainty. He probably wrote for the people who returned from exile. The genealogies reminded them who they were, where they came from, and that they had a place in God's story. Bethlehem appears here in passing, long before David or the Messiah are spoken of there.

For today: God does not overlook the small. A place or a name that seems insignificant may be part of a greater plan. Be faithful where you are, without despising your ordinary days.
exp.5:3:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Eleazar, son of Aaron, was the father of Phinehas, and that Phinehas was the father of Abishua. In this list "was the father of" can sometimes also mean "was an ancestor of," since biblical genealogies at times summarize generations.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, writes after the exile in Babylon. He presents the line of the priests who descend from Levi and Aaron. In this way the people who returned to their land could remember who served God in worship and where their responsibility came from.

For today: God pays attention to families and to every generation, not only to famous figures. Your faith can be an important link for others. Today you can pray for your children, nephews, nieces, or younger brothers and sisters, and live faithfully so that they see God in you.
exp.7:25:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Shamsherai, Shehariah, and Athaliah, who are among the descendants of Benjamin. In this list, these names appear alongside the sons of Jeroham, according to the following verse. The names are spelled differently in some English Bibles, so they may sound a little different from how you have heard them before.

No single character is speaking here. The chronicler, a Jewish writer who gathered the family records of Israel, notes these genealogies. He probably did so for the people returning from exile, so that they would remember their roots, their tribes, and their place in the land. The text says these men were heads of families and lived in Jerusalem.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those we hardly know. Today you can remember with gratitude the ordinary people who have been important in your family or your church, and thank God for them.
exp.26:21:
This verse closes a list. It says that Azarel, son of Jeroham, was the leader of the tribe of Dan. Then it sums up that everyone named before him were "the leaders of the tribes of Israel." The word "leaders" refers to the chiefs placed at the head of each tribe.

The book of Chronicles tells the story of Israel, and here the author describes how King David organized his kingdom. No character speaks; it is the chronicler who records the names. He probably wanted to remind the people that Israel had a well-established order and direction. This list appears just before the account of Joab's census, which provoked God's anger.

For today: God takes notice of people who serve, even when they are little known. These names hardly appear anywhere else, but they were written down. If your service goes unnoticed, remember that God sees it and values it.
exp.21:12:
It says Solomon will succeed if he carefully follows the laws and commands that the LORD gave to Moses for Israel. "Succeed" means things will go well for him. "Statutes and ordinances" are God's rules and decisions. Then comes the encouragement: be strong and courageous, do not be afraid, and do not be discouraged. ("Discouraged" means to lose heart or lose your confidence.)

King David, now old, speaks to his son Solomon. David wanted to build the temple, but God gave that task to Solomon. So David gives him advice and shows him everything he has already set aside: gold, silver, wood, stone, and workers. Solomon would not be starting from scratch.

For today: when God entrusts you with something big, do not rely only on your own strength. Obey His Word step by step, and remember that He has already been preparing resources and people to help you.
exp.1:5:
This verse lists the five sons of Zerah, one of the sons of Judah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara. The phrase "five in all" simply means that there are five of them altogether.

The book of Chronicles begins with long lists of families. Its author, who according to tradition may have been Ezra (though this is not certain), wrote for a people who were returning from exile. He wanted to remind them of their origins and that God remained faithful to his promise. Some of these names appear in 1 Kings 4:31 among wise men, but it is not certain that all of them refer to the same people.

God does not forget people, even when today no one remembers their names. This family came from a very imperfect story, that of Judah and Tamar, and yet God included it in his plan. You can trust that God is also at work in your story, with its failures and all.
exp.25:23:
This verse says that Shebuel, a descendant of Gershom and a grandson of Moses, was appointed as the officer in charge of the treasuries. The phrase "in charge" here means the person with the greatest responsibility for the storehouses. The "treasuries" were the riches and valuable objects kept for the service of the temple.

Here no character is speaking; this is the chronicler's account, which lists the duties David organized for worship. The Levites did not only sing or guard the gates; they also managed what was dedicated to God. It is remarkable that a descendant of Moses held a position of trust, though he was neither a priest nor the leading figure. Some think that "son" can mean descendant, since many years had passed since Moses.

For today: God values faithful and orderly work, even the kind that almost no one sees. If you manage money or resources in your church, family, or workplace, do it with honesty and transparency, remembering that everything comes from God.
exp.8:41:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Ahaz was the father of Jarah, and that Jarah was the father of three sons: Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Then Zimri was the father of Moza. The word "father" here means a direct parent, though in the Bible it can also sometimes refer to a more distant descendant.

The writer is the Chronicler, an author whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. He writes after the exile in Babylon. Through these genealogies, he reminds the people who returned who they were. Here he follows the line of Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin, and connects it with Jonathan. Note: this passage gives names that differ a little from 1 Chronicles 8:36, which is explained by variations in copying or in spelling.

For today: God remembers every name, even the little-known ones. Your life, your family, and your simple service have value before Him. Today, give thanks for someone who passed on the faith to you.
exp.16:26:
In this verse, David says that God has chosen to bless his family, meaning his descendants, so that they will continue before Him forever. Here "house" does not mean a building but a family or dynasty. The word "forever" means for all time, without end. David recognizes that, since God has blessed this family, the blessing will remain.

David is praying after the prophet Nathan brought him a message from God. David had wanted to build a temple, but God answered that instead He would establish David's "house," meaning his line of descendants. Many Christians see in this promise an announcement of Jesus, a descendant of David, although Jews understand it in other ways.

For today: when God gives you a promise, respond as David did, with gratitude and trust. Pray by reminding Him of what He has said, and rest in the fact that His blessing does not depend on your strength, but on His faithfulness.
exp.5:73:
This verse lists two towns that were given to the Levites from the tribe of Asher: Mashal and Abdon. The open land around a town, used mainly as pasture for its residents' livestock, was included with each town.

The book of Chronicles, which tradition usually attributes to Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews the history of Israel for the people who were returning from exile. This list is part of the towns distributed to the Levites, who did not receive a territory of their own as the other tribes did. In this way the author reminded them that God had cared for those who served in his worship and that this service had a place among the people.

For today: God cares for those who serve others. We can support, with gratitude and in concrete ways, those who dedicate their lives to teaching, caring for others, and serving in the church.
exp.23:5:
Shemaiah, a scribe who was the son of Nethanel and of the tribe of Levi, wrote down the arrangement of the priests. He did this in the presence of the king, the officers, the priest Zadok, Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and the heads of the families of the priests and Levites. So one family was taken from Eleazar and then one from Ithamar, alternating between the two.

The chronicler, the narrator of this account, tells how David organized the service in the temple into shifts. Because there were more leaders among the descendants of Eleazar, the families were chosen by lot so that the work would be fair and orderly. That the names were recorded and witnessed before many leaders shows that the process was open and could be checked by everyone.

For today: in the church, the family, or the workplace, serving with order, clarity, and openness prevents quarrels and honors God. Writing down responsibilities and sharing them fairly helps everyone take part.
exp.2:16:
This verse lists the descendants of Jeconiah, a king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. The Berean Standard Bible names Shealtiel as his son. Scholars have discussed how this name relates to others in the family line, and the exact connections are not fully settled, so it is best to read the names as the text gives them.

The writer of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra though this is not certain, presents the line of David after the exile. He wants the people who returned to know that the royal family was not lost. Shealtiel later appears as an ancestor of Zerubbabel, the leader of the return to Jerusalem.

For today: even when it seems that everything has been lost, God continues to keep his promises. Trust that he can sustain his plan in times of crisis, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.3:32:
This verse says that all the villages of the tribe of Simeon, the ones surrounding their cities, reached as far as a place called Baal. The words "villages" and "settlements" are simply the reader's English terms here: "villages" means the small towns or communities, and "settlements" means the places where they lived, while "genealogical record" refers to their family record, that is, their lineage.

The one who speaks is the Chronicler, an author we do not know for certain (Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra, but this is not sure). He writes after the exile in Babylon to remind the people who they were and where their ancestors lived. Here he lists the territory of Simeon, in the south of Judah. Some think that "Baal" is a short form of Baalath-beer, although this is not completely certain.

For today: God pays attention to places and to people who seem small. Be thankful for your origins and your place, and serve faithfully where God has put you.
exp.22:25:
This verse says that the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle and its furnishings for the service. Before, that task was part of their daily work. The word "articles" here means the objects and tools used in worship, not just cups. "Service" means the work done for the Lord.

The context is the end of David's reign. He had already said that God had given rest to Israel and that God would dwell in Jerusalem forever. Since the people no longer moved from place to place, and a fixed temple was being planned, the work of the Levites would change. They would no longer carry, but would help the priests in the house of God, in the courts, the chambers, and the purification of the holy things.

For today: when God changes a season of your life, your service may change as well. Ask him to show you how to serve him now, with the same willingness, even though the task is no longer what it used to be.
exp.25:26:
This verse says that part of what had been set apart for God, taken in battles and from the plunder, was used to repair the house of the LORD, that is, the temple. "Dedicated" means given over and set apart for God. The "plunder" was the goods gained by defeating the enemy.

The writer of Chronicles, looking back on the history of Israel, explains how the service of the temple was organized. Shelomith and his brothers took care of the treasures of the offerings dedicated by David, the army commanders, and other leaders. It is not known in detail when each offering was set apart, but the text shows that the temple was supported by willing giving and good order.

Today we can learn that what God allows us to achieve, such as a job, an income, or a victory, can be dedicated to supporting his work. We can give with gratitude and manage what is given with honesty.
exp.21:3:
This verse says that the Sidonians and the Tyrians, people from the cities of Sidon and Tyre, brought David a large quantity of cedar logs. The phrase "more cedar logs than could be counted" means there was so much timber that no one could keep track of it all.

Here the narrator of the book is explaining how David gathered materials for the temple. David knew he would not be the one to build it; his son Solomon would. So he made sure everything was ready. Sidon and Tyre were neighboring cities, not Israelite, and they were known for their trade and their skill with wood. The text does not describe how they made this arrangement, so it is best not to assume more.

For today: God can use unexpected resources and people for his plans. We can also learn from David: to prepare generously for something that others may finish, serving with humility without seeking credit.
exp.14:9:
It says that from the Uzzielites, one of the Levite families, Amminadab was the leader, and that he and 112 of his relatives were counted among them. "The chief" means the leader or head of the family. "His relatives" refers to his extended family, not only his own brothers.

The writer of Chronicles makes a list of the Levites whom David gathered to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem. Earlier, the attempt to move it had failed because it was not done as God had commanded. Now David organizes each Levite family under its leader, so that it is done with order and reverence. Then he calls them to consecrate themselves, that is, to prepare themselves to serve God.

For today: God values every person who serves, even when their name appears only in a list. Doing what God entrusts to us with order, humility, and preparation honors him, even when the service seems small.
exp.10:11:
This verse introduces Eleazar, son of Dodo, as the next hero in David's list. The verse says "next in command," so the first sentence can be read straight from the wording: Eleazar is named right after the previous warrior, Jashobeam.

The passage is a list written by the chronicler, who remembers the men who supported David so that he would reign over all Israel, according to the word of the Lord. It shows that the kingdom was not held up by one leader alone, but by many who remained faithful to him. The next verse tells how Eleazar stood with David in a battle against the Philistines.

For today: God often works through faithful people who are not always famous. Ask yourself where you can steadily and bravely support others in the task God has given you.
exp.23:1:
Verse 2 says that Nadab and Abihu, two of Aaron's sons, died before their father did and had no sons. Because of this, the priestly service passed to their brothers Eleazar and Ithamar.

The phrase "served as priests" means that they carried out the duties of the priests.

It is part of a list of families that the chronicler writes to show how David organized the service in the temple in shifts. The book of Numbers tells that Nadab and Abihu died for offering fire that God had not commanded. All the priestly descendants, then, came from the two remaining lines.

For today: God takes care of his work even when people fail or are gone. Serve with seriousness and reverence, and do not rely on your own ideas to draw near to God.
exp.26:23:
Joab, the son of Zeruiah, began to count the men but did not finish. Because of this census, wrath came upon Israel, and the number was not entered in the Book of the Chronicles of King David. The word "wrath" means God's anger or punishment. The Book of the Chronicles was the official record of the events of the kingdom.

Here the writer is not quoting a character speaking; he is explaining why that number was left out of the official record. This connects with 1 Chronicles 21, where David ordered a census, Joab objected, and a plague came upon Israel. The text does not tell everything in detail, but it shows that the problem lay in David's heart, in trusting the strength of numbers more than the promise of God.

For today: trust God more than figures, resources, or achievements. When we feel secure because of what we have, we can turn our eyes back to the Lord, who keeps his promises.
exp.0:22:
This verse ends the list of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem. It names Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. The verse reads the same as the one you have, with the names listed plainly and the line "All these were sons of Joktan" closing the list.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. It was written after the exile in Babylon. The genealogies at the beginning reminded the people who had returned that they had roots, identity, and a place in God's history.
