Ophir later appears as a land famous for its gold, although its exact location is debated.

For today: God knows the name of every person, even of those who barely appear in a list. If you sometimes feel that your life goes unnoticed, remember that to God you are not a mere number. Thank him for your family, and pray for the people who have been part of your story.
exp.26:32:
It says that Ahithophel was King David's counselor, and that Hushai the Archite was the king's friend. A "counselor" is someone who guides the king with wisdom in his decisions. "Friend of the king" seems to be a title of trust, someone very close to David. The names here are Ahithophel and Hushai the Archite.

The chronicler presents the list of officials who served David. It is not a character speaking but the narrator, who arranges the offices of the kingdom. Other books tell that Ahithophel betrayed David and that Hushai helped to defeat his advice (2 Samuel 15–17). Here only their offices are named, without mentioning that.

Even a king needs good counselors and faithful friends. Seek people who speak to you with truth and wisdom, and ask God for discernment in choosing them. Also be someone trustworthy to those who ask you for advice.
exp.22:2:
This verse tells that a count was made of the Levites, the tribe responsible for service in the temple. Only those who were thirty years old or more were counted, and the total was 38,000 men. The phrase "counted" means that each of them was recorded individually.

The writer of Chronicles relates that David, now old, made his son Solomon king and gathered the leaders, priests, and Levites. He wanted to organize the service of the future temple before leaving the kingdom. The verses that follow assign these men to tasks: work on the temple, judges, gatekeepers, and musicians. Other texts give different ages for beginning service (for example, twenty years in this same chapter), and it is not entirely clear how that difference is explained.

God cares about order and values each person in their service. In the church, there is a place for everyone: some teach, others sing, others guard the door. Ask yourself today what simple task you can take on with joy.
exp.11:3:
This verse continues a list of warriors from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David. It names Ishmaiah, from Gibeon, who is described as a mighty warrior among the Thirty and a leader over the Thirty. That group seems to have been an elite company of David's soldiers, though the text gives no further details. It then names Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, and Jozabad the Gederathite.

The author of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, recalls those who supported David when he was fleeing from Saul, at Ziklag. He includes relatives of Saul, which shows that even some from Saul's own tribe recognized David. Scholars do not agree on all the details about the Thirty.

For today: God notices people whom others overlook. Serve faithfully and courageously wherever you are, even when no one applauds you; your name matters to Him.
exp.28:13:
This verse shows David feeling very small. He asks, "Who am I?" as if to say that neither he nor his people deserve the honor of giving so generously. He recognizes that everything they have comes from God, so when they give, they are only giving back what they first received from Him. "So generously" and "willingly" describe giving gladly, by one's own choice.

David is speaking in prayer before the whole assembly. He had gathered the leaders and the people to bring materials and gifts for building the temple, a work his son Solomon would later carry out. After seeing the generosity of everyone, David praises God and claims no credit for himself.

For today: when you give your time, your money, or your talents, do it with humility and joy. You are not the absolute owner of what you have; you are a steward of what God has entrusted to you.
exp.3:14:
This verse is part of a family list. It names Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and his three sons: Iru, Elah, and Naam. It also says that Kenaz was a son of Elah. Here the verse lists the sons of Caleb in a single line and then gives Kenaz as the son of Elah in a second line.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), gathers genealogies of the tribes of Israel. He writes for the people who returned from exile, to remind them who they were and that God had cared for their families. This Caleb is the one who appears alongside Joshua, from the tribe of Judah. Some details of these lists are hard to understand and are interpreted in several ways.

God knows and remembers names that sometimes seem unimportant to us. Your life and your family have value before Him. Give thanks today for those who came before you in the faith, and live in a way that leaves a good example for those who come after.
exp.23:29:
This verse lists the sons of Mushi, who were Levites from the family of Merari: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. At the end it sums up that these were the sons of the Levites, arranged according to their families. The phrase "according to their families" refers to their clans or family lines.

Here no character is speaking in a speech; it is the chronicler recording official lists. The chapter explains how David, together with the priest Zadok and Ahimelech, organized the shifts of service in the temple. Lots were cast to divide the order, and the following verse notes that this was done with equal treatment for the eldest and the youngest.

For today: God takes notice of each person, even of names that almost no one remembers. Your service, though it may be quiet, has value before Him. Serve faithfully wherever you are, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.0:47:
After Samlah died, a man named Shaul, from the city of Rehoboth on the Euphrates, became king of Edom. The place name is the important detail here, and the verse says he took the throne that had been left empty. The river is the Euphrates, as the verse itself states.

Here the writer is not describing one person's story; the chronicler presents a list of the kings of Edom, the descendants of Esau. This same list also appears in Genesis 36. Notice that these kings are not sons of the ones before them, but come from different places. In this way the writer places Edom within the history of the nations surrounding Israel.

For today: no one holds their place forever. Kings come and go, but God continues to work. Let us live with humility and do good in the time we have been given.
exp.1:38:
Verse 39 says that Azariah was the father of Helez, and Helez was the father of Elasah. The phrase "was the father of" is the plain way to say this. It is part of a list of descendants, one generation after another.

This passage belongs to the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, whose author is unknown; Jewish tradition often names Ezra. This list follows the line of Sheshan and his Egyptian servant Jarha, within the tribe of Judah. It was probably written for the people returning from exile, to help them remember who they were, where they came from, and that their history had not been lost.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who barely appear in the story. Every name in that list mattered. You also matter to God, and your daily faithfulness, though it may seem small, is part of something greater.
exp.23:25:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Merari had sons named Mahli and Mushi, and that Jaaziah had a son named Beno. Merari was one of the sons of Levi, so these people belonged to the tribe responsible for service in the temple.

The text is in 1 Chronicles, a book that tradition attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain. After the exile, the author reminds the people how King David organized the priests and Levites to serve God. Recording the names showed that each family had a place and that their spiritual inheritance had not been lost.

For today: God knows names and families, not only famous figures. Your service, even if it is simple or little seen, has value before Him. Today you can serve faithfully in something small, trusting that God sees it.
exp.9:12:
It says that Saul died because of his unfaithfulness to the LORD. The word "unfaithfulness" here means that he broke faith with God and failed in his duty. He did not keep the word of the LORD, and he also consulted a medium, a woman who was supposedly able to speak with the dead, instead of seeking God.

The chronicler, who looks back on the history of Israel, explains why the first king ended as he did. After telling of his death in battle and his burial in Jabesh-gilead, he gives the spiritual reason. The facts of his disobedience appear in 1 Samuel, such as when he consulted the woman at Endor. That account can be understood in several ways, but here the chronicler clearly condemns it.

For today: when we are distressed, let us first seek God in prayer and in his Word, not shortcuts or doubtful sources. Obeying him in small things protects us from falling into great ones.
exp.20:15:
This verse says that God himself commanded the destroying angel to stop. "Enough now" means "that is enough," and "hold your hand" means he was to stop punishing. The angel stopped beside the threshing floor of Ornan, a Jebusite, that is, the place where grain was threshed. "He relented" does not mean that God made a mistake, but that he changed his heart toward compassion and held back the punishment.

David had ordered the people to be counted, and that displeased God. A plague came and seventy thousand people died. Here God halts the judgment just as it was reaching Jerusalem. Afterward David acknowledges his sin and asks that the punishment fall on him, not on the people. That same place was later where the altar was built, and later the temple.

Today: God is just, but he is also compassionate and knows how to set a limit to punishment. When we fail, we can come to him without excuses, acknowledge the wrong, and trust in his mercy.
exp.15:21:
God protects the people he has chosen. "Do not touch My anointed ones" means do not harm them. The "anointed ones" are people set apart by God for a purpose, and "My prophets" are those who speak on his behalf. The verse that follows speaks of salvation, which means rescue and deliverance.

This is part of the song of David when the ark was brought to Jerusalem. It recalls how God cared for the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, when they were few in number and lived as strangers. God himself warned the kings who threatened them (Psalm 105 repeats these words). It is a song of gratitude for his faithfulness.

For today: trust that God cares for his people even when you feel small or vulnerable. And treat with respect those who serve God, praying for them instead of criticizing them or harming them with words. This does not mean they can never be corrected, but that it should be done with humility.
exp.22:0:
This verse says that David was already an old man, "full of years," meaning that he had lived a long life. Before he died, he installed his son Solomon as king over Israel.

Here the chronicler speaks, the one who tells the history of Israel. We do not know for certain who he was, though tradition often points to Ezra. David prepares the handover of the kingdom to Solomon and arranges everything for the service of the temple. For this reason, he soon gathers the leaders, priests, and Levites, and these are counted. Other passages, such as 1 Kings 1, show that this transition also had difficult moments.

For today: planning ahead with care for what we will leave to others is wise. Prepare the next generation in faith, service, and character, without clinging to your own place, and trust that God will continue his work.
exp.18:12:
It says that we must be strong and fight bravely for the people and for the cities that belong to God. At the end, the outcome is left in the hands of the Lord: "May the LORD do what is good in His sight" means that he decides whatever seems best to him. "Be strong" means be brave and resolute.

The speaker is Joab, commander of David's army. He was surrounded: the Syrians on one side and the Ammonites on the other. He divided the troops with his brother Abishai, they promised to help each other, and he encouraged everyone before the battle. The enemies ended up fleeing.

For today: do with determination what is your responsibility, without laziness or fear, and lean on others who help you. Afterward, leave the result to God, trusting that he works with wisdom even when things do not turn out just as you planned.
exp.3:42:
It says that a group of men from the tribe of Simeon attacked the survivors of the Amalekites, that is, those who had escaped destruction. Afterward they settled in that region.

The verse's wording "who had escaped" is the basis for calling these the survivors, the people who got away from earlier fighting. "To this day" means up until the time this record was written.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records the history of the tribes. Here he tells how Simeon sought new lands in the mountain of Seir, in the days of King Hezekiah. Amalek was an enemy people of Israel from the time of the desert (Exodus 17). These genealogies reminded the Jews after the exile that God sustained his people and their inheritance.

For today: God fulfills his purposes with patience, even after generations. We can trust that he finishes what he begins, and we too should be persistent in removing from our lives whatever harms our faith, without leaving survivors that later trouble us again.
exp.24:30:
This verse closes the list of the twenty-four groups of temple musicians. It says that the twenty-fourth turn of service fell to Romamti-ezer, together with his sons and his brothers, twelve in all. Here "turn" means the time of service that was assigned by casting lots. "Brothers" can include close relatives of the family.

The book of Chronicles was written after the exile, to help the people remember how worship was organized in the days of David. The author does not narrate a scene; he presents an orderly record. David and the leaders of the service set apart families from the lines of Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman to minister with harps, psalteries, and cymbals. The lots were cast so that the service would be orderly and without favoritism.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is little seen. Being last on the list does not make anyone less important. Serve faithfully wherever you are placed, alongside your family or community.
exp.1:21:
Segub had a son named Jair, and Jair came to hold twenty-three cities in the region of Gilead, east of the Jordan River. Here "was the father of" means that Jair was his son, and "had" means that Jair controlled or ruled those cities.

No one in particular is speaking here; it is the chronicler of Israel, who writes after the exile and goes over the lists of the families of Judah. He wants to remind his people where they come from. Segub was born of Hezron and of a woman from the family of Gilead, and that is why his descendants settled there. Some scholars see this as a mixing of the lines of Judah and Manasseh, though the Bible does not explain it in detail.

For today: God cares for the names and the stories of people whom almost no one remembers. Value your family and your history, and trust that your life, though it may seem small, matters to Him.
exp.11:20:
This verse says that the men of Manasseh who joined David supported him against the raiders, probably a group that had attacked Ziklag. Many understand them to be the Amalekites, although the text does not make this clear. They were brave men and commanders in the army.

The chronicler, who writes long after these events, lists those who supported David before he became king. These men of Manasseh came to Ziklag when the Philistine lords sent David away. In this way, the author shows that God was gathering a faithful people around his chosen one.

For today: God often uses brave people who loyally join his work. Ask yourself whom you can support with your time, your gifts, or your encouragement, even if your part seems small.
exp.23:7:
This verse continues a list of turns for the priests. It says that the third turn went to the family of Harim and the fourth to the family of Seorim. Here "lot" means the drawing of lots that was used to set the order of service. The word "wrote down" means "recorded."

The author is the chronicler, who recalls how David organized the descendants of Aaron into twenty-four groups to serve in worship. The scribe Shemaiah recorded each turn before the king, the leaders, and the priests. Lots were used so that the division would be fair and free of favoritism. Many understand that this showed trust that God guided the outcome.

For today: God counts on you, and also on those who seem to go unnoticed. These almost forgotten names had a place and a turn in serving God. Serve faithfully wherever you are placed, without comparing yourself to others, and cooperate in good order so that everything is done with reverence.
exp.16:24:
In this verse David says that God has revealed something to him, meaning that God spoke to him directly and personally. What God told him is that He would build him a house, that is, a family and a lasting line of descendants. That is why David felt encouraged to pray. The phrase "has found the courage" means that he felt bold enough to speak with God.

David speaks in prayer after the prophet Nathan had passed on God's promise to him. David had wanted to build a temple, but God answered that He would be the one to establish David's house, meaning his dynasty. David responds with gratitude and humility, asking that the promise be fulfilled.

For today: when we know what God has promised in His Word, we can pray with confidence. We do not pray with doubts, but rely on what He has already said. Look for a promise in the Bible and bring it before God with gratitude.
exp.0:28:
This verse begins the list of the descendants of Ishmael, the son Abraham had with Hagar. Nebaioth was the firstborn, and then Kedar, Adbeel and Mibsam are mentioned. The word "firstborn" means the eldest son, the first to be born. "Genealogies" refers to the family lines that came after.

The book of Chronicles was written for the people of Israel after they returned from exile in Babylon. We do not know for certain who wrote it; Jewish tradition names Ezra, but this is not certain. The author begins with long lists of families to remind the people where they came from. He includes Ishmael before going on to Isaac and his line.

God fulfilled his promise to make Ishmael a great nation, and here we see his names written down. For God, every person has a name and a story. Today we can remember that no one is anonymous before him, and treat with respect and attention every person we meet.
exp.10:18:
David says it is unthinkable for him to drink the water his three mighty men brought him. To him, that water is like their blood, because they got it at the risk of their lives. "God forbid" is his way of saying he would never do such a thing. Their lives were on the line to bring it to him. David did not drink it, and the text ends by noting that these three were the mightiest of all.

David speaks during a war against the Philistines, who held Bethlehem, his hometown. He voiced a wish, almost a longing, and three of his soldiers broke through enemy lines to fulfill it. David felt that a simple craving was not worth so great a risk. That is why he poured out the water before the LORD, as an offering and a sign of honor to God and to them.

For today: value the sacrifices others make on your behalf and do not use them for your own comfort. Give thanks with humility, and remember that what it costs someone in effort, time, or health deserves to be treated with respect and offered to God.
exp.17:16:
Benaiah was the leader of the Cherethites and Pelethites, who formed the king's personal guard. Many believe they were soldiers of foreign origin, although this is debated. David's sons held the highest positions at the king's side, serving as his chief officials.

This verse is part of a list of those in charge of David's government. The author of Chronicles, traditionally associated with Ezra (this is not certain), records this after the exile. He wanted to remind the people that David's kingdom had order, and that each person had a task.

God works through people with different roles, and none is left over. Today you can serve faithfully in the place that is yours, in your home, your work, or your church, without comparing yourself to others or despising what is small.
exp.4:23:
This verse lists seven heads of families from the half-tribe of Manasseh, which lived east of the Jordan River. It says they were "mighty men of valor," meaning strong and courageous. They were also "famous men," people who were well known and respected. The verse says they were "heads of their families," meaning they were the leaders of their clans.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), reviews the family records of Israel for the people who returned from exile. Here he presents these leaders and then tells how the people turned away from God and ended up carried off into exile by the Assyrians. In this way we see that strength and fame are not enough without faithfulness.

For today: if God gives you ability, influence, or leadership, use them with humility and obedience. Being strong or admired does not replace remaining faithful to God every day.
exp.21:10:
It says that David blesses his son Solomon with a wish: that the LORD be with him, that he succeed, and that he build the house of the LORD, just as God had said he would. The words "may the LORD be with you" are the verse's own wording, so no further explanation is needed there. The word "succeed" means that things go well for him in whatever he undertakes. "House" refers to the temple.

David speaks to Solomon toward the end of his life. God did not allow David to build the temple, because he had taken part in many wars, and He promised that his son would do it. David gathers materials and now encourages Solomon to carry out that task. The verses that follow make clear that success is tied to obeying God's law.

For today: when God entrusts you with something, do not rely only on your own strength. Ask for His company, seek His direction, and walk in obedience, trusting that He sustains what He asks you to do.
exp.0:39:
This verse lists the descendants of Shobal, one of the sons of Seir: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. It then mentions the sons of Zibeon, another son of Seir: Aiah and Anah.

Here there is no character speaking. The author of Chronicles, whom tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, presents lists of families. Seir was the ancestor of the Horites, the people who lived in the region of Edom before the descendants of Esau settled there. These genealogies helped the people of Israel, who were returning from exile, to place themselves in human history from Adam onward.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today we can value others and remember that no one is insignificant to Him.
exp.15:34:
This verse says that the people should ask God to save them, gather them together, and deliver them from the nations, so that they may give thanks to his holy name and take pride in praising him. "The God of our salvation" means the God who saves us. "Give thanks" here means to acknowledge and proclaim with gratitude. "The nations" are the foreign peoples. "Glory" means to rejoice and boast in God, not in ourselves.

This is part of a psalm of David, sung when the ark of the covenant arrived in Jerusalem. The Levites sang it at a great celebration. Israel lived surrounded by powerful peoples and needed to depend on God. Scholars debate whether "gather us together" speaks of bringing scattered people back together or of uniting the people; the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: when you feel weak or scattered, pray asking God for help, but end by giving him thanks. Your need can become praise.
exp.21:11:
David asks God to give his son Solomon insight and understanding, meaning the good judgment to know what to do. He also asks that God's direction be given to Solomon as he takes charge over Israel, which is to say, guidance for governing the people. The final wish is that Solomon keep the Law of the LORD his God, that is, obey it.

David is speaking to Solomon, his son. God did not allow David to build the temple, so he leaves everything prepared for Solomon to do it. Before handing him that great task, David blesses him with this prayer and reminds him that success depends on obeying God.

For today: before making important decisions, ask God for wisdom and seek to live according to his Word. Talents and resources help, but good judgment and obedience are what sustain what we do.
exp.20:5:
This verse says that when the census was taken, Joab did not count the tribe of Levi or the tribe of Benjamin. The reason given is that the king's command was detestable to Joab. He found the order repugnant and wrong. The verse describes the king's command as detestable to him, so the reader should understand it as a word meaning loathsome or deeply objectionable.

The chronicler explains what happened when David ordered the people to be counted. Joab, commander of the army, did not agree, but he had to obey and left the count incomplete. Then God was displeased with this, and David acknowledged that he had sinned. The text does not say with certainty why Levi and Benjamin were left out; some think Joab stopped before finishing, or that Levi had a separate service to God.

For today: when someone in authority asks us for something that our conscience sees as harmful, it is good to speak with respect and clarity, to seek God, and not to remain silent. And if we are wrong, let us do as David did: acknowledge it with humility and ask for forgiveness.
exp.15:26:
It says that before God there is splendor and majesty, and that His dwelling is filled with strength and joy. "Splendor" means brightness or beauty, "majesty" means greatness and dignity, and "dwelling" means a house or the place where someone lives. That is, God is mighty and glorious, and His presence is not sad or weak, but full of life.

This is part of the psalm of thanks that David gave to Asaph and his brothers when the ark of the covenant arrived in Jerusalem. The people were celebrating that God was among them. In contrast to false gods, which are worthless, the psalm exalts the God who made the heavens.

For today: when you feel tired or discouraged, draw near to God in prayer and praise. His presence gives strength and joy that do not depend on circumstances.
exp.5:78:
This verse mentions two more cities given to the descendants of Merari, from the tribe of Reuben: Kedemoth and Mephaath. The phrase "together with their pasturelands" refers to the grazing land around each city, where the Levites could raise their livestock.

This list is part of a long record of the Levitical cities. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. God commanded that they live in cities spread among all of them (Numbers 35). The chronicler, who writes after the exile, preserves these details to remind the people of their history and of the place of those who serve in the temple.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and his people are called to do the same. We can generously support our pastor and those who work in the church, so that they have what they need.
exp.5:14:
This verse says that Jehozadak, a descendant of the priestly line of Levi, was taken away as a prisoner when God allowed Judah and Jerusalem to be sent into exile by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The words "went into captivity" and "sent into exile" describe the same painful event, the forced removal of people far from their homeland, and they are the ideas the reader should keep in mind here.

It is part of a genealogy of the priests. No voice speaks in the first person; the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), records the families for the Israelites who returned from exile. This verse closes the list with a sad note: the priestly line also suffered the fate of the people.

For today: even in times of loss or painful change, God does not lose sight of his people or their names. We can trust that he keeps working and preserving his history, even when we do not understand the moment we are living in.
exp.15:27:
This verse invites all the families of the nations to recognize the LORD as the great God. To ascribe to Him means to give Him the credit that is due to Him. His honor and greatness are His glory, and His might is His strength. The thought is repeated twice to add force to the invitation.

It is part of the psalm of thanksgiving that David handed over to Asaph and his brothers, the Levites, when the ark of the covenant came to Jerusalem. It was a moment of great celebration. This song reminds us that the gods of the peoples are nothing, while the LORD made the heavens. That is why the invitation is not only for Israel, but for all the nations.

Today we can begin the day by recognizing that everything good comes from God. Before asking, give thanks to Him out loud for something specific, and do not take the credit for your achievements: share it with Him.
exp.10:13:
Eleazar and David took their stand in the middle of the field and defended it. They struck down the Philistines, and the LORD brought about a great victory. The field was a planted piece of ground, and by holding their position there, they protected what was theirs.

The chronicler lists David's mighty men and tells this story of Eleazar. While the people fled, he stood firm. The parallel account in 2 Samuel 23 gives the details somewhat differently, and it is not entirely clear who exactly the verse means by "they." But the central message is plain: the victory came from the LORD.

Today, when everyone around you gives way, do not be afraid to stand firm in what is right. Do your part with courage, but remember that the final victory belongs to God. Trust Him, and ask Him for strength.
exp.15:8:
This verse invites us to sing to God, to offer him songs of praise, and to tell of all the wonders he has done. The words "sing" and "tell" are commands given to the whole people. "Sing praises to Him" refers to songs of praise, probably accompanied by instruments.

The passage describes the day when the ark of the covenant was brought to Jerusalem. David handed this song of thanksgiving to Asaph and his brothers, the Levites in charge of the music. His purpose was that Israel would remember and proclaim what God had done. These words are very similar to Psalm 105, although scholars explain the relationship between the two texts in different ways.

Today we can make gratitude a habit. Every day, tell someone one good thing God has done for you, or hum it quietly while you work. In this way your faith grows stronger and others are encouraged.
exp.5:54:
They say that the descendants of Aaron, priests from the family of Kohath, were given the city of Hebron, in the land of Judah. They also received its surrounding pasturelands, the open ground around the city used for their animals and their livelihood.

The writer of Chronicles lists the cities the Levites received to live in, since they had no territory of their own like the other tribes. The verses that follow make clear that the fields and villages of Hebron already belonged to Caleb, so the priests received the city, but not all the land around it. Hebron was also a city of refuge. This is recorded to show that God took care of those who served in his worship.

Today we can learn to support generously those who serve in the church, and to trust that God provides for those who dedicate themselves to him. We can also be thankful for what he has given us, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.23:28:
This verse is very brief: it names Jerahmeel as a son of Kish. It is part of a list of Levite families from the line of Merari. "Kish" is the name as it appears in the verse, and "Jerahmeel" means something like "God has compassion."

The text is written by the chronicler, who reviews how David organized the service in the temple. The Levites divided their shifts by casting lots, so that it would be fair. This list appears right after the mention of Eleazar, who had no sons. In 1 Chronicles 23:22 it says that his daughters married the sons of Kish, their cousins. In this way his family did not disappear.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even to names that almost no one remembers. No service done faithfully is small to Him. Serve where God has placed you, without seeking applause.
exp.1:43:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Shema was the father of Raham, who was the father of Jorkeam, and that Rekem was the father of Shammai. "Father" here means ancestor, the one a person came from. Shema and Rekem were sons of Hebron, mentioned in the previous verse.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies as Ezra (though this is not certain), is not speaking here to any particular person. He records the genealogies of the tribes of Israel, in this case that of Judah, through the line of Caleb. These lists helped the people, who were returning from exile, to remember their roots and their place in God's promise. Some of the names may be people and others may be peoples or places, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those we barely know. Give thanks for the people in your family who came before you, and live in such a way that you leave a mark of faith.
exp.15:36:
This verse tells us that David left Asaph and his associates, the Levites, before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. Their work was to serve there regularly, each task according to the daily requirements. The word "minister" here means serving in worship, and "regularly" means steadily, day after day.

The one telling the story is the writer of Chronicles. He says David had just brought the ark to Jerusalem and celebrated with a song of praise. Then he arranged the service so that worship would not be just a one-day festival. He left some servants in Jerusalem, beside the ark, and others in Gibeon, beside the tabernacle.

For today: worship is not only an exciting moment, it is also daily faithfulness. There is a special value in serving steadily, even in small things and without applause. We can ask ourselves what simple task God has given us and carry it out with care, one day at a time.
exp.14:19:
This verse names eight Levites who were to play harps according to Alamoth. The instrument here is a harp, and "Alamoth" is an uncertain word: many think it refers to a high pitch, such as high voices or soft instruments, but this is not known for certain.

The writer of Chronicles tells how David organized the Levites to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. Each group had its own task: some played cymbals, others harps, others lyres, and Chenaniah led. No one does everything; each person fulfills his part so that the praise is orderly.

For today: God values simple service done well. Even if your name is not well known, your part matters in the church. Serve faithfully in whatever is entrusted to you, and rejoice in the work of others.
exp.17:11:
This verse says that Abishai, son of Zeruiah, struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.

The chronicler recounts the victories of David and his men. Abishai was one of his military leaders. The text ends by saying that the LORD preserved David wherever he went. Other passages give slightly different numbers or names for this battle (2 Samuel 8:13; Psalm 60, title). It may be that these refer to different phases of the war, or to different ways of giving credit for the victory, but this is not known for certain.

Today we can learn that God often accomplishes his purposes through many people. He works through teamwork, values the effort of others, and recognizes that, in the end, the protection comes from God.
exp.7:5:
This verse says that the sons of Ehud were heads of families who lived in Geba, and that they were later exiled to Manahath. "Heads of the families" means the leaders of households or clans. "Exiled" means that they were forced to leave their home and move to another place.

It is part of the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin. The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, records these names for the people who were returning from exile. In this way they remembered their origin and their inheritance. It is not clear who ordered the move or why; the text that follows mentions Gera, but interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: God knows families by name, even when the history seems to be only a list. If you have lived through moves or difficult changes, remember that your place and your story matter to God, and he continues to sustain you.
exp.1:47:
This verse says that Maacah, one of Caleb's concubines, was the mother of two sons, Sheber and Tirhanah. A concubine was a secondary-rank wife, something common in that time.

No one specific is speaking here; it is the chronicler, whose identity is not known for certain, who gathers family lists of the tribe of Judah. After the exile, these genealogies helped the people remember their roots, their lands, and their place among the tribes. Caleb is mentioned with his sons from several women, and even the women are named, which was not the usual practice in these lists.

For today: God notices people whom others would overlook. There are names almost unknown that were written down in his Word. This reminds us that your life and your family have worth before him, even when no one applauds you. Serve faithfully in the small things.
exp.17:0:
Some time after the events of chapter 17, where God promised David that his family would last, David defeated the Philistines, brought them under his control, and took the city of Gath and its surrounding villages from their hands. The phrase "took it from their hands" simply means he took it away from them.

Here no one is speaking: the chronicler, who writes after the exile, tells the story. His purpose is to encourage a people who were starting over, showing that God kept his word and gave David victory and rest from his enemies. The account is summarized; other passages, such as 2 Samuel 8, give similar details.

For today: when God makes you a promise, be patient and trust him; victories come in their time. In the meantime, walk in faith and obedience, not relying only on your own strength, but on the God who does what he says.
exp.24:7:
This verse says that the temple musicians were organized by lot, so that it could be decided who would serve in each shift. Casting lots was a way of sharing out duties without favoritism. No one was left out for being young or old: "young and old alike" covers both the younger and the older, and "teacher as well as pupil" refers to the one who taught and the one who learned.

It is part of David's list for organizing worship in Jerusalem. The writer of Chronicles explains how the 288 musicians were divided among the families of Asaph, Jeduthun and Heman. The aim was for praise to the Lord to be orderly and constant. The Bible does not describe here exactly how the drawing of lots was carried out.

For today: in the church, service is not only for the most experienced. We can make room for those who are just beginning, and those with more experience can serve with humility, knowing that all of us matter before God.
exp.25:0:
This verse begins the list of the temple gatekeepers. "Divisions" means the groups or shifts that took turns serving. The gatekeepers were the ones who guarded the doors of God's house. Here Meshelemiah is named, from the family of the Korahites, descended from Kore. The verse also says he was one of the sons of Asaph, but that is hard to explain: it may be another name for an ancestor, or a shortened form of the family line.

No one is speaking in a sermon; the chronicler records how the temple service was organized, set up in the time of King David. He wanted the people, who were returning from exile, to see that worship had order and that each family had a place.

For today: God values simple and little-seen services, such as opening a door or welcoming people. Think of a small task you can do in your church with faithfulness and joy.
exp.8:39:
This verse continues the family line of King Saul. It says that Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son named Merib-baal, and that Merib-baal was the father of Micah. The phrase "who was the father of" simply tells us the family connection. In other passages, such as 2 Samuel 9, this man appears as Mephibosheth; it is thought that these were two names for the same son of Jonathan, though the Bible does not explain the change.

This passage is part of the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, probably written for the people who returned from exile in Babylon. The author is not telling a story but preserving the memory of the families of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem. In this way people remembered who they were and where they came from.

For today: God does not forget people or their families, even when the world sets them aside. Give thanks for those who went before you in the faith, and live in such a way that your own life also leaves a good inheritance.
exp.15:17:
This verse recalls what God said to his people: "I will give you the land of Canaan." The phrase "as the portion of your inheritance" means that this land would be the share that came to them as their inheritance. God promised, and his promise was sure.

These words are part of a psalm of thanksgiving which, according to the account, David delivered to be sung when the ark of the covenant arrived in Jerusalem. The psalm invites the people to remember the covenant God made with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. They remember it in order to praise God for his faithfulness, even when they were few in number and lived as strangers.

For today: when your situation seems small or uncertain, remember God's promises and how he has been faithful before. Thank him today for one of his promises that you have already seen fulfilled, and trust him for what you are still waiting for.
exp.28:11:
This verse says that God is the owner of everything. Riches and honor come from him, and he is the ruler over all. The phrase about power and might points to his strength and authority. In his hands, the greatness and strength of all things depend on him, and nothing lies outside his control.

King David, now an old man, is speaking. The people have just given generous offerings to build the temple, which his son Solomon would later build. David praises God before the whole assembly and acknowledges that everything they gave already belonged to God. That is why he says afterward: "From Your own hand we have given to You."

For today: when you give your time, your money, or your talents, do it with humility, without pride. What you have is a gift from God, and giving it back is returning to him a part of what he entrusted to you.
exp.8:16:
This verse names the gatekeepers, the men in charge of guarding the doors of the temple and its entrances. It lists Shallum, Akkub, Talmon and Ahiman, along with their relatives, and says that Shallum was their chief. The word "relatives" here can refer to family members or to others from the same clan.

In this chapter the chronicler (traditionally thought to be Ezra, though this is not certain) lists those who returned to live in Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon. His purpose is to show that the service in the house of God continued, with order and with Levite families clearly identified. The gatekeepers were not a minor post: they protected the entrance to the holy place, and the passage goes on to say that their service came from generations before.

God values faithful service, even when it goes unnoticed. Perhaps your task in the church or at home is simple, such as opening a door or welcoming others. Do it with steadiness and with joy, because God cares for every detail of his house.
exp.16:2:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Nathan that very night. The phrase "the word of God came to Nathan" means that God gave him a direct message. "That night" shows that God's answer came right away, on the same day Nathan had spoken.

David was living in a palace of cedar and wanted to build a house for God, since the ark was kept under curtains. Nathan, without consulting God, told him to do what was in his heart. But God corrected that hasty advice and showed that his plan for David was different. The narrator is the one who tells how God intervened.

For today: even when an idea seems good and comes from someone we respect, it is wise to pray and seek God's direction before acting. He can correct us with love, and He has better plans than our own.
exp.5:65:
This verse says that some of the clans descended from Kohath, who were Levites, were given cities within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim. A "clan" is a group of families descended from one common ancestor. The land given with each city includes the pasturelands and boundaries around it, which provided room for their animals.

The chronicler reviews how Israel distributed cities to the Levites, because they did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. They lived among all the people to serve in the things of God. The text does not say who is speaking at this moment; it is a list of records. The cities were assigned by lot, and later cities of refuge such as Shechem are mentioned.

For today: caring for those who devote themselves to serving in the church is everyone's responsibility. We can support them with prayer, practical help and generosity, so that they can dedicate themselves to their calling.
exp.25:5:
This verse says that the sons of Shemaiah, the firstborn son of Obed-edom, became leaders in their father's household. The reason is that they were strong and capable men. The phrase "ruled over their families" means they were in charge of their own households, and "strong, capable men" points to people who were reliable and able to carry responsibility.

This appears in the lists of the gatekeepers of the temple, drawn up in the time of King David. It is not a speech but a record that the chronicler wrote to remember who served in the house of God. Just before this, the text says that God had blessed Obed-edom, and that blessing is seen in his large family dedicated to service. The details of how God blessed him are not explained here, although other passages connect him with the ark.

Today we can learn that faithful service can pass from one generation to the next. If you have children, nephews, nieces, or younger people around you, encourage them by your example to serve God with courage, responsibility, and steadiness.
exp.27:18:
This verse says that David tells Solomon that the whole plan for the temple came from God. The phrase "the LORD has made clear to me" means that God himself showed David the details and gave him understanding of them. The word "plan" refers to the design or blueprint of the work. Some understand that David received these plans in writing or by inspiration; the text does not make clear exactly how.

David speaks at the end of his life, before Solomon and the people. He could not build the temple himself, so he hands his son the plans, the gold, and the instructions. He reminds them that the work did not come from a human idea, but from God. Right after, he encourages Solomon to be strong and courageous, because God will not leave him alone.

For today: before undertaking a project, whether in the family, the church, or at work, ask God for direction. And when the path looks difficult, remember that He walks with those who obey.
exp.3:21:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Shelah, son of Judah. It names Jokim, the men of Cozeba, Joash and Saraph, who ruled in Moab, and also Jashubi-lehem. At the end, the text says that these names come from ancient records, which means the information is drawn from very old sources.

Here the chronicler speaks, the one who gathered family records after the exile in Babylon. His aim was to remind his people where they came from. Some details are hard to pin down: it is not known for certain whether these are names of people or of places, and the note about ancient records leaves open how the names were first written down. Even so, the passage shows families who worked at common trades, such as linen and pottery.

For today: God remembers ordinary people and their simple work. Value your daily labor and do it with gratitude, as something God sees and remembers.
exp.18:13:
Joab, the commander of Israel's army, advanced with his soldiers to fight the Arameans, and they ran away before him.

The Ammonites had shamed David's messengers and prepared for war with the help of the Arameans. Joab found himself surrounded, with enemies in front of him and behind him. He divided his troops, placing himself with his brother Abishai, and told him the words above: to help one another, to be brave, and to leave the outcome in God's hands. Then he advanced, and the Arameans fled.

When you face something difficult, do your part with courage and work as a team, but entrust the outcome to God. Joab planned well and acted, without believing that everything depended on him alone. That blend of effort and trust gives us peace and firmness.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that Jabez was more honored and respected than his brothers. The word "honorable" means distinguished, of good reputation. His mother gave him that name and explained the reason: she had borne him in pain. In Hebrew, the name sounds similar to the word for "sorrow," though scholars do not know for certain whether this was because of the birth or because of difficult circumstances in the family.

The speaker is the chronicler, who is in the middle of a long list of families from the tribe of Judah. Suddenly he pauses to highlight one single man, which is unusual in these lists. Nothing is known about who his father was or when he lived. The next verse shows that his honor came from his prayer.

A rough beginning or a name weighed down with sorrow does not have to define your life. You can bring your story to God and ask him to guide you forward.
exp.5:27:
This verse names the two sons of the prophet Samuel. "Firstborn" means the oldest son. According to 1 Samuel 8:2, the oldest was named Joel and the second was Abijah. Because the wording of this verse differs from that account, many scholars think the name "Vashni" is not a personal name but a Hebrew word meaning "and the second." This is not certain, but it is a common explanation.

The book of Chronicles, which tradition attributes to Ezra (though this is not known for certain), was written for the people who returned from exile. Here the families of the Levites, those responsible for worship, are listed to remind them of their identity and their place in serving God. Samuel appears as part of that line.

For today: God values each person, even those who appear only as names in a list. Your faithfulness every day matters, and you can leave your children a heritage of faith by praying for them and serving God with steadiness.
exp.1:8:
This verse lists the three sons of Hezron, a descendant of Judah: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb. The phrase "were born to Hezron" is plain modern English already, so it needs no change.

First, a word about the context: no one is speaking here. It is a genealogy, written by an author whom Jewish tradition identifies as Ezra, though this is not known for certain. Its purpose was to remind the people, after the exile, of their roots. From Ram comes the line that leads to Boaz and then to David, as the verses that follow show.

For today: God cares for families and for generations, even when their names seem simple to us. Your life and your faith count in the story of God. Today, give thanks for those who passed on their faith to you, and ask yourself what legacy of trust in God you will leave behind.
exp.10:0:
It says that all the tribes of Israel came together to David at Hebron. They told him, "Here we are, your own flesh and blood," an expression that means "we are of your own family, we are one with you."

Here the people of Israel, represented by their leaders, are speaking. Saul had already died, and the people recognize David as king. They do this because he had already led them in battles and because God had chosen him to be the shepherd of his people. This takes place at the beginning of David's reign over all Israel.

For today: unity is born when we recognize what God has already arranged and draw close to others as family. In the church, at home, or at work, we can set aside divisions and say with humility: "we are one, let us walk together."
exp.10:31:
This verse names two men from the list of David's mighty warriors: Hurai, who came from the brooks or valleys of Gaash, and Abiel, who was from a place called Beth-arabah or Arabah. In some older Spanish Bible translations the proper names are spelled differently from how we see them today, and in the parallel passage of 2 Samuel 23:30 the first name appears as Hiddai.

Here it is not a single character speaking; the chronicler, who wrote after the exile, lists the warriors who supported David when he was made king over all Israel. He wanted to remind the people that the kingdom was sustained by many people, and not only by the king. The exact location of some of these places is uncertain.

For today: God notices people who often go unnoticed. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even when no one applauds you; your name matters to God and your effort counts in his work.
exp.7:17:
It says that Ishmerai, Izliah and Jobab were sons of Elpaal. It is part of a list of names from the tribe of Benjamin. The names appear with older spellings; in modern versions you will see "Ishmerai", "Izliah" and "Jobab", and "Elpaal" as the name of their father. Names can vary from one translation to another.

The book of Chronicles does not say with certainty who wrote it; Jewish tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not sure. It was written for the people who were returning from exile, and it reminded them who they were, which families they came from, and that God had not forgotten them. Lists like this helped preserve the identity and rights of each family in the land.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those no one remembers. You are not a number to Him. You can live with peace, knowing that your life matters, and also learn to value those who go unnoticed around you, treating them with respect and kindness.
exp.14:10:
Here, it says that David summoned two priests, Zadok and Abiathar, and six Levites, who were responsible for the work in the sanctuary. The word "summoned" means that he called them together as the leaders of their families.

The passage tells what King David did. He wanted to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem, and the first attempt had failed because it was not done as God had commanded (2 Samuel 6). Now David gathers those responsible so that it is done properly, with order and reverence. Then he asks them to sanctify themselves, that is, to prepare themselves to serve God.

For today: when we want to do something for God, good intentions are not enough. It is wise to seek God's guidance in the Bible, prepare ourselves with humility, and work together with other believers.
exp.6:31:
This verse says that Heber, a grandson of Asher, was the father of Japhlet, Shomer, and Hotham, and also of a daughter, Shua. The phrase "their sister" means that Shua was the sister of those three sons.

These words are part of the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, probably written after the exile in Babylon. There is no speaker in the passage, only an author recalling the families of Israel. With this, the people returning from exile could remember their roots, their tribes, and their place in God's promise. Here the line of the tribe of Asher is being followed.

For today: God knows the name of every person, even of those whom almost no one remembers. Today you can value each person around you, and also remember that your life and your family matter to God.
exp.5:76:
The descendants of Merari who had not yet received cities were given Rimmono and Tabor, in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. The words "together with their pasturelands" refer to the open land around each city, where the Levites could graze their animals.

The book of Chronicles, written by an unnamed author, reviews the history of Israel and the list of Levite cities. The Levites had no territory of their own, so each tribe gave them cities to live in. Joshua 21 contains a similar list, but with some different names. It is not known with certainty why, and scholars explain it in several ways.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and his people share in that care. We can support, with generosity and gratitude, those who dedicate their lives to teaching and serving in the church.
exp.28:18:
Here David prays for his son Solomon. He asks God to give him a "whole heart," that is, a sincere heart given entirely to God. With that heart, Solomon will be able to keep God's commandments, decrees and statutes (the rules).

David speaks near the end of his life, before all the people. He has just gathered freewill offerings to build the temple, a building he himself would not be able to build. After thanking God for the people's generosity, he prays for the future: he knows the work depends on Solomon's heart being faithful.

Today we can pray this way for our children and for those who come after us. Rather than wishing them success, let us ask God to give them a sincere heart that loves and obeys Him.
exp.4:5:
This verse continues the list of Reuben's descendants. It says that Beerah, whom the translation renders as Beera, was taken captive by Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, and that he was a leader of the Reubenites. The phrase "carried into exile" means taken by force to another land.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra though this is not certain, recorded the families of Israel for the people who were returning from exile. He wanted them to remember their roots and to understand why they had been deported. This brief mention recalls the judgment on the tribes east of the Jordan. Later in this same chapter, it is explained that they were unfaithful to God.

Today we can learn that important positions and names do not protect us from the consequences of turning away from God. Beerah was a leader, and yet he shared the fate of his people. Let us ask God for faithfulness, especially if we lead others, because our decisions affect them too.
exp.0:12:
This verse says that Canaan was the father of Sidon, his firstborn son, and of the Hittites. The Berean wording makes clear that the Hittites are named as a people descended from Canaan, rather than as another son. The name Sidon later became attached to a famous Phoenician city on the Mediterranean coast, though scholars do not always agree on exactly how the person and the city are related.

This is a genealogical list within the early chapters of 1 Chronicles. Jewish tradition attributes the book to Ezra, although the Bible does not state this clearly. It was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. Here the nations descended from Ham are reviewed, and Canaan is the father of several peoples who lived in the promised land.

For today: God knows names and stories, even those of people who seem to us to be only a list. If He values each one, He also knows you and values you. Give thanks for your family and your history.
exp.25:19:
This verse says that Ahijah, a Levite, was in charge of two groups of possessions: the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated things. "Dedicated things" means items set apart for God, such as offerings and objects given over to his service. "Being in charge" means he was responsible for looking after them.

The author of Chronicles, whose identity is debated (tradition often points to Ezra), describes how David organized the service of the temple. Earlier the gatekeepers were discussed; now the passage turns to those responsible for the storehouses. The aim is to show that everything was done in an orderly way. Verse 20 names Ahijah's fellow Levites as the ones in charge of these treasuries.

Today we can learn that caring honestly for what is dedicated to God is an important service. If you handle money or resources for your church, do it with transparency and responsibility.
exp.20:19:
This verse says that David set out and obeyed what the prophet Gad had told him on God's behalf. "Went up" means that he went to the place God had shown him, which was on higher ground. "According to" means "in agreement with."

David had sinned by ordering a census of the people, and as a result a plague came upon Israel. He acknowledged his guilt and asked that the punishment fall on him and not on the people. Then God sent a message through Gad: David was to build an altar on the threshing floor of Ornan, a Jebusite. The text tells how David obeyed without arguing.

For today: when we recognize our failures, the next step is to obey God. Sincere repentance does not stay in words but shows itself in acting as God directs us, even when we do not fully understand it.
exp.21:7:
God told David, through a message, why he would not build the temple: he had fought many wars and shed a great deal of blood. The verse says that David had shed much blood and waged great wars, and that he was not to build a house for God's Name because of all the blood he had spilled on the ground before God.

David speaks to his son Solomon before handing him the task. He tells him that he had in his heart the desire to build the temple, but God told him no. The Bible does not say that David sinned through his wars in general, but God preferred that a man of peace, Solomon, carry out that work. Some see here a difference in calling, not only a punishment.

God can accept our good desires and still give us a role different from the one we dreamed of. We can trust his plan, and, like David, gladly support those who will continue the work.
exp.12:11:
That day David feared God and felt a deep sense of awe before him. He asked, "How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?" The word "feared" here does not mean only terror; it also includes reverence. The ark was the holy chest that represented God's presence among his people.

David was bringing the ark to Jerusalem in a great celebration. Uzzah touched it and died, and David was saddened and frightened. His question shows that he understood that drawing near to God is not a light matter. The text does not explain every detail, but it makes clear that God's holiness must be taken seriously. Afterward the ark stayed in the house of Obed-edom, where there was blessing.

Today we can draw near to God with confidence through Christ, but also with respect. Before doing anything for God, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are doing it as he asks, with humility and obedience.
exp.6:3:
It says that, in addition to the descendants of Uzzi, there were 36,000 troops ready for battle, listed according to their genealogy. The reason it gives is that they had many wives and children. The "genealogy" is the record of family descent. The "troops for battle" are those who could fight in the army.

This passage is part of the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, which the writer presents to a people returning from exile (Jewish tradition often names Ezra, though this is not certain). Here it speaks of the tribe of Issachar. It was meant to remind them of their identity and their history, and that God had sustained every tribe. It also shows that the number of warriors depended on large families, something common in that culture.

For today: value your family and your community of faith as part of a larger story. God cares for each generation, and your faithfulness can affect those who come after you.
exp.11:22:
This verse opens the list of the armed men and leaders who came to David at Hebron. The phrase "armed for battle" means prepared and equipped to fight. "To turn Saul's kingdom over to him" means to hand the kingdom from one person to another, in this case from Saul to David. All of this happened "in accordance with the word of the LORD," that is, in line with what God had said.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who reviews the history of Israel. After Saul's death, many tribes joined David. The author wants to show that this support was not only political, but part of the plan God had already announced.

For today: God keeps what he promises, and often he uses people who are willing to serve. Ask yourself how you can help with your gifts, and do it with confidence in God's word.
exp.20:10:
This verse says that the prophet Gad went to where David was and gave him a message from God. The words "This is what the LORD says" were the way of announcing that what was coming was not Gad's own words, but God's own. Gad is the one who brings the message.

Here Gad speaks, sent by God after David took a census of the people, something the Bible says displeased God. Gad comes with a consequence that David must choose. The text does not explain all the details of David's sin, but it shows that God speaks to him clearly and gives him a choice.

For today: when God corrects us, it is wise to listen with humility, without excuses. And like David, we can trust in God's mercy more than in any human help.
exp.0:8:
This verse lists the sons of Cush, who was a son of Ham: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Sabteca. Then it names the sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. Seba appears twice because it is a name that is repeated in different families.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes for the people who were returning from exile. He begins with long lists from Adam to remind them of their origin and their place among the nations. Here it is in what is often called the "table of nations," which many relate to peoples of the south, such as Africa and Arabia. Identifying each people precisely is difficult, and scholars do not always agree.

For today: God knows each person and each family by name. Today you can remember that no one is invisible to Him, and treat every person with respect, regardless of their origin.
exp.25:28:
This verse says that Chenaniah and his sons, from the Izharites, held positions of authority. They had the outside duties as officers and judges over Israel, meaning people responsible for organizing and settling matters. Their work was over Israel in affairs beyond the temple itself, such as administrative tasks and service to the people.

The one narrating is the chronicler, who lists how David organized the Levites before he died. Some looked after the treasures of the temple, and others, like Chenaniah, attended to matters outside it. It shows that worship of God included order, justice, and good administration. Scholars do not specify exactly what those outside duties were.

For today: serving God is not only about being in the visible or directly spiritual places. Managing things honestly, helping resolve problems, and working with justice are also ways of serving him. Faithfully do the task you have, even when few notice it.
exp.5:47:
This verse says that the Levites, relatives of the priests, were assigned to every kind of service connected with the tabernacle, which here is called "the house of God." The tabernacle was the sacred tent where Israel worshiped. "Service" here means work carried out in care of something sacred.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, is recalling the families of Levi. He writes for a people returning from exile who needed to remember how worship was to be organized. The next verse makes clear that only Aaron and his sons offered the incense and the atonement, so each had his own task.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is simple or little seen. Ask yourself what concrete task has been placed near you, in your church or family, and do it gladly and responsibly, without envying the work of others.
exp.26:25:
This verse says that Ezri, son of Chelub, was in charge of the workers in the fields, the people who farmed the land that belonged to King David. The verse uses the phrase "who tilled the soil," which means they worked and cultivated the ground.

The author of Chronicles does not speak in the first person; he recounts how David's kingdom was organized. This list of officials shows that there was order in the management of the king's property: treasures, fields, vineyards, olive groves, and storehouses. Each person had an assigned task. Beyond Ezri, we know no further details about him, since the Bible does not give them.

For today: God values simple and orderly work. Even when your labor seems little noticed, like Ezri's, it can be an important part of something greater. Do your work with faithfulness and responsibility, as serving the Lord.
exp.4:7:
This verse names Bela, a descendant of the tribe of Reuben, and says that his family settled in a region east of the Jordan River. Their land reached from Aroer to Nebo and Baal-meon, which were known places in that area. The phrase "settled in" tells us that Bela's people made their home there.

The chronicler is the one speaking here, not a character in the story. He writes out a list of Reuben's families, most likely to remind the people, after the exile, who they were and where each family line had lived. The verses that follow explain that Bela had a large herd of livestock and that his family spread out toward the desert. We do not know for certain when he lived, and scholars interpret this in various ways.

For today: God does not forget people or their stories, even when they seem small. We can live with gratitude in the place where God has put us and faithfully care for what he has entrusted to us.
exp.0:10:
This verse continues the list of Ham's descendants. Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. It says that from him came the Ludites, the Anamites, the Lehabites and the Naphtuhites. "Was the father of" means that he was the ancestor of these groups. Many understand that these names represent peoples, not just individuals, although not everyone is sure which peoples they were.

The author of Chronicles, traditionally identified with Ezra (though this is not certain), writes to the Israelites who returned from exile. He begins with genealogies from Adam to remind them of their identity and their place among all the nations. This list continues with the Philistines and the Caphtorites, neighboring peoples of Israel.

For today: God knows the origin of every people and every person. Today you can treat with respect those who seem different, remembering that we all come from the same origin and that God values them just as much as you.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that, after the return from exile, some people lived in Jerusalem. They were descended from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, and also from Ephraim and Manasseh. The word "lived" means that they settled there to make their home.

The one who tells this is the chronicler, an author we do not know for certain, although Jewish tradition often mentions Ezra. He writes for the people who returned from Babylon. He reminds them who they are, where they come from, and that they are still God's people. That Ephraim and Manasseh appear, tribes of the north, may show that God did not forget all of Israel. Some scholars see it this way, though not all agree.

God cares for his people and gathers them again, even after failures and punishments. If you feel far away or divided, remember that God knows your name and your story. He can give you a place to begin again.
exp.12:5:
David and all of Israel went up to Baalah, which is another name for Kiriath-jearim, a town of Judah. They were going to bring the ark of God, the LORD's ark, up from there. The words "who is enthroned between the cherubim" describe the figures of angels on the cover of the ark. The words "the ark that is called by the Name" mean that the ark bore God's name and belonged to Him.

Here the chronicler speaks, telling the story of Israel. The ark had been far from the center of worship for years, and David wanted God to be once again the center of the people's life. Everyone agreed. Later the story shows that it was not done in the way God had indicated.

For today: desiring God at the center of life is beautiful, but we must also seek Him as He asks, with reverence and obedience, not only with good intentions.
exp.7:28:
This verse says that a man named Jeiel, the father of Gibeon, lived in the town of Gibeon, and that his wife was named Maacah. The phrase "lived in Gibeon" means that they settled down there to make their home. "Jeiel" may be a personal name or a title, and scholars understand it in different ways.

Here the speaker is not a character; the chronicler, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, compiles genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin. He does so for the people who returned from exile, so that they would remember their roots. This passage begins the list of the family of Saul, the first king of Israel, which also appears in 1 Chronicles 9:35.

For today: God takes notice of ordinary people, with their names and families. Remember that your daily life, your home, and the place where you live matter to Him. Serve faithfully where God has placed you.
exp.22:23:
This verse closes the list of the descendants of Levi. It says they were the heads of families, registered individually by name, and that those twenty years of age or older served in the house of the LORD. "Heads" means the leaders of the families, and the listing "by their families" refers to how they were recorded by their households.

Here the chronicler speaks, telling how David organized the Levites at the end of his reign. Since the temple would soon be built, they would no longer have to carry the tabernacle, so David gave them new tasks. The age of service was set at twenty, and the text does not explain the reason in detail. Some think it was because more workers were needed.

For today: God knows each person by name and values service, even the kind that goes unnoticed. Serve faithfully where you are, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.8:27:
Some of the Levites, as this verse says, were in charge of the articles used in worship. The phrase "articles used in worship" refers to the containers and objects used in the service of God. Their task was to count them whenever they were brought in or taken out, so that none would be missing.

This verse is part of the lists of the families who returned from exile in Babylon and settled in Jerusalem. The chronicler, traditionally identified as Ezra (though this is not certain), shows how the temple service was organized. The gatekeepers lived near the house of God and watched over its gates and its treasures.

God values faithfulness in small and ordinary tasks. Counting and carefully caring for what is entrusted to us, whether time, money, or responsibilities in the church, is a way of honoring God and serving with integrity.
exp.19:4:
Once again there was war against the Philistines, and Elhanan, son of Jair, killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath the Gittite. The shaft of Lahmi's spear was as thick as a weaver's beam, which means the weapon was enormous.

The writer of Chronicles reviews the wars of David's reign and highlights how God gave victory over the Philistine giants, descendants of the Rephaim. A parallel passage, 2 Samuel 21:19, says that Elhanan killed Goliath. Scholars explain this in several ways: a copyist's variant, or two men with that name. There is no single certain answer.

Today's giants can be fear, debt, or an addiction. God often gives us victory through ordinary people who remain faithful. You don't need to be famous; you need to trust God and take the next step.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that Shaharaim had children with his wife Hodesh: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, and Malcam. Here "had children" means he was their father.

It is part of the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles. The author is unknown; Jewish tradition often points to Ezra, but this is not certain. It records the names so that the people, after returning from exile, would remember their roots and their inheritance. The text does not explain why Shaharaim put aside his other wives or how all these names relate to one another.

For today: God pays attention to people and remembers their names, even the ones almost no one mentions. This encourages us to value our family and history, and to know that no life goes unnoticed by Him.
exp.13:9:
David, facing the advance of the Philistines, did not act on impulse. He asked God whether he should attack and whether God would give him the victory. God answered yes: go up, for He would deliver them into his hand. "Inquired" means that David sought God's direction; "deliver them into your hand" means giving him the victory.

The account tells us that David had just been recognized as king over all Israel. When the Philistines heard of it, they came to attack him and spread out across the valley of Rephaim. David, as a responsible leader, wanted first to know God's will. Afterward, the victory is credited to God, not only to David's forces.

For today: before making an important decision, pray and seek God's guidance in His Word. Doing so does not remove the need for effort, but it reminds us that we depend on Him.
exp.28:17:
David asks God to keep alive always the sincere desire the people showed when they gave for the temple. The word "keep" in the verse means to guard or maintain. The word "forever" means always. The request that God direct the people's hearts toward him means asking God to guide their hearts toward himself.

King David speaks at the end of his reign. He and the people had just offered their goods willingly and with joy to build the temple, which Solomon would later build. David acknowledges that everything comes from God and that he is pleased by an upright heart. For that reason he prays that this giving will not grow cold.

For today: a generous and faithful heart is a gift from God, not only our own effort. We can pray each day that God keep our desire to serve him firm and direct our hearts toward him.
exp.24:12:
It says that the sixth turn of service in the temple fell to Bukkiah, together with his sons and his brothers, twelve people in all. The word "turn" is understood from the context. Bukkiah appears in other passages as well.

It is part of a list in 1 Chronicles 25, where the author, whom tradition identifies with the Chronicler, tells how David and the leaders of worship organized the Levite musicians.
