Lots were cast to divide the service into 24 turns, and each group had twelve members. In this way the service of praise was arranged in an orderly and continuous way.

For today: God values steady, orderly service, even when it is little seen. Think of one simple task in your church or family, and do it faithfully, knowing that God knows every name and every effort.
exp.5:57:
This verse continues a list of cities that were given to the sons of Aaron, the priests. The names in this part of the list are Jattir, Eshtemoa, Hilen and Debir. The cities came with pasturelands around them, where the priests could keep their flocks and herds.

The chronicler, who writes after the exile, goes back over the family records and the division of the land of Israel. He wants his people to remember that the Levites and priests had a set place among the tribes, including Judah. This list is similar to the one in Joshua 21, although some names appear in slightly different forms, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God cares for those who serve him and makes sure they have a place and what they need. We can generously support those who give themselves to spiritual service, and trust that God also provides for us.
exp.5:62:
This verse says that the descendants of Merari, one of the sons of Levi, were allotted twelve cities. Those cities were located within the territories of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun. The word "clans" refers to their family groups, and "allotted" means that the cities were assigned to them.

The passage is part of a list of the cities that Israel gave to the Levites. They did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, because their service was the worship of God. For that reason they lived scattered among all the people. Many believe the chronicler was reminding a community that was returning from exile of this, although who wrote the book and when is debated.

Today, God cares for those who serve in his house, and it falls to us to help. We can support our pastors and those who devote themselves to teaching the Word through offerings, prayer, and encouragement.
exp.27:5:
God chose Solomon to build the temple, which is called "My house" and "My courts" in this verse (the courts that surrounded the temple). The verse also says that God treats him as a son and that He will be his Father. The phrase about being chosen matches the words "I have chosen him" in the verse.

King David, now old, is speaking before the leaders of Israel. He had wanted to build the temple, but God did not allow it and chose his son Solomon instead. David tells this publicly so that the people will support Solomon. Furthermore, the promise of a lasting kingdom depends on Solomon's obedience to God.

For today: God does not only give us tasks, He also offers us His closeness as a Father. We can humbly accept the place He gives us, even when someone else has started the work, and keep obeying Him faithfully.
exp.20:23:
David had disobeyed God by counting the people, and a plague was killing many in Israel. An angel stopped by Ornan's threshing floor, and David went up there to build an altar and ask that the plague would stop. Ornan, respectful and generous, wants to help his king, so he offers the threshing floor for free, along with the oxen for the burnt offering, the threshing sledges as wood for the fire, and wheat for the grain offering. Ornan ends by saying, "I give it all." But David insists on paying the full price, because he will not take for the LORD what belongs to someone else, and he will not offer burnt offerings that cost him nothing.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our giving to God costs us anything real: time, money, comfort or effort. Giving without sacrifice is easy, but a sincere offering comes from a heart that values what God has done.
exp.28:24:
It says that the LORD raised Solomon to great honor in the sight of all the people of Israel. He gave him royal majesty such as no king in Israel before him had received. "Highly exalted" means that he lifted him up greatly. "In the sight of" means "in the presence of." The royal majesty that Solomon received is described as something no earlier king of Israel had been given.

The book of Chronicles was written by an author who is not named in the text, and it is thought he wrote after the exile in Babylon. Here it tells of the end of David's reign and the beginning of Solomon's. It stresses that Solomon sat on "the throne of the LORD," that is, that his kingdom belonged to God and not only to a man. All Israel accepted him.

Every position or success we receive comes from the hand of God. If He gives us responsibility or recognition, we can live it out with humility and gratitude, using it to serve others and not only for our own prestige.
exp.15:19:
This verse says that God's people moved from one place to another, passing through different nations and kingdoms. The word "wandered" means they kept travelling without settling in one fixed place. The phrase "from nation to nation" simply describes moving on from one people to another. It describes a people with no settled home, always on the move.

These words are part of a psalm of thanksgiving that David handed over to Asaph and his companions when they brought the ark to Jerusalem. It calls to mind the patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who were few in number and foreigners in Canaan. Although they lived insecurely, God promised them the land and protected them from powerful kings, as the verses that follow say.

For today: when you feel unsettled, lost or in times of change, remember that God cared for those who walked without security. Give thanks for the times he has protected you, and trust that he continues to keep his promises.
exp.4:10:
This verse says that the tribe of Gad lived next to the tribe of Reuben, in the region of Bashan, and that their land reached as far as a place called Salecah. "Lived next to the Reubenites" means they settled in the same area east of the Jordan River, beside Reuben's territory. Salecah was a town or boundary point of the land, at the edge of Bashan.

The book of Chronicles does not name its author, and it does not speak in the first person. It is a historical account, which tradition usually attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain. It was written for a people who were returning from exile. Lists of families and lands like this reminded them who they were and that God had given them a place and an inheritance.

For today: God cares for every family and every place, even when they seem like small details. If He remembers names and lands, He also knows you. Give thanks today for the place and the people God has given you, and care for them faithfully.
exp.25:12:
The passage says that the gatekeepers of the temple cast lots to decide who would guard each gate. They did this for every gate, "young and old alike," meaning that age did not decide who received a post. They did it "according to their families," that is, by family groups.

The text is part of a list the chronicler gives of how David organized the service in the temple. Here the gatekeepers are in view, descendants of Korah and Merari. No one chose his own post; the lot divided the work. In that time, casting lots was understood as letting God decide (Proverbs 16:33).

Today, this invites us to value every kind of service in the church, whether visible or hidden. God does not measure service by the size of the position. We can accept with humility the place where He puts us and serve with joy.
exp.3:6:
This verse says that Helah, one of the two wives of Ashhur, had three sons: Zereth, Zohar, and Ethnan. They are only names, with no further details.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the Chronicler, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra, although this is not certain. He wrote for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their roots. That is why he records the families of Judah, even the lesser-known ones, such as that of Ashhur, the founder or leader of Tekoa.

For today: God does not forget anyone, even when the world does not remember us. There are people whose names almost no one mentions, yet God knows them. Today you can value those who go unnoticed, and remember that your life matters to Him too.
exp.8:3:
This verse gives the name of a man from the tribe of Judah who lived in Jerusalem: Uthai, with his family line going back: son of Ammihud, of Omri, of Imri, and of Bani. All of them descend from Pharez, son of Judah. The name Pharez is the older way of spelling the name found in this verse's line of descent.

The book of Chronicles is a list of families that remembers who came back to live in Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon. We do not know for certain who wrote the book; tradition mentions Ezra, but this is not certain. This passage wants to show that the people had roots, and that God had not forgotten the families, even after very hard times.

For today: God knows your name and your story, not only the stories of famous people. Today, give thanks for those who came before you in faith or in family, and remember that your life also counts in God's plan.
exp.20:3:
The verse says that King David insisted on his order, and Joab, though he did not agree, had to obey. "Prevailed" means that the king's word won out and was imposed over Joab's objection. Joab then traveled throughout all Israel, came back to Jerusalem, and gave David the result of the count.

Joab, the commander of the army, had already warned David that counting the people would bring harm to Israel. David would not listen. The text presents the census as a grave error, and soon afterward God's judgment came. Some think David was trusting more in his military strength than in God, though the passage does not explain this in full detail.

For today: listen to wise counsel, even when it comes from someone who makes us uncomfortable. If we are in authority, humility means stopping to ask whether what we want to do honors God, and not simply imposing our own will.

sum.12: David consulted with the leaders and with all of Israel, and they agreed to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim with great joy, with music, and with a new cart. When Uzzah reached out to steady the ark, God struck him down and he died, and David felt fear and grief. Then he left the ark at the house of Obed-edom, and God blessed that household for three months.
sum.7: This chapter continues the family records of the tribe of Benjamin, naming its clans, leaders, and the places where they lived, such as Gibeah, Ajalon, and Jerusalem. It traces the line down to the family of King Saul and his descendants, and it ends by highlighting the sons of Ulam, brave men who were skilled archers. God keeps the record of every family and its place among his people.
sum.17: David defeats the Philistines, Moabites, Syrians, and Edomites, and these peoples either bring him tribute or come under his rule. The text says that the LORD gave him victory wherever he went. David dedicates the gold and silver he won to the LORD, and he reigns over Israel with justice, together with his officials.
sum.11: While David was at Ziklag and in the stronghold, hiding from Saul, brave warriors from Benjamin, Gad, Judah, and Manasseh came to him to give him their support. Then great armies from all the tribes went to Hebron with sincere hearts to make him king over all Israel. There were three days of feasting and great joy.
sum.1: This chapter lists the twelve sons of Israel and focuses on the descendants of Judah. It follows the line that runs through Hezron, Boaz, and Jesse to David, and it mentions other families, such as those of Caleb and Jerahmeel. It shows how God preserved the memory of the peoples and their lineages.
sum.0: This chapter is a list of families that begins with Adam and continues through Noah and his three sons. It then shows the peoples who came from them, the line that leads to Abraham, and the descendants of Ishmael, of Esau, and the kings of Edom. It reminds us that God knows the names and the stories of all the peoples.
sum.2: This chapter lists the sons of David: six born in Hebron and others born in Jerusalem, including Solomon. It then follows the line of kings descended from Solomon down to Josiah, and afterward the heirs after the exile, such as Zerubbabel. It shows that God kept David's family alive across many generations.
sum.14: David prepared a place for the ark of God and recognized that only the Levites should carry it, as God had commanded, because the first time they had not inquired of God in the proper way. The Levites consecrated themselves, carried the ark on their shoulders with singers, music and sacrifices, and all Israel celebrated with joy. Michal, however, despised him in her heart.
sum.15: David brings the ark of God into the tent he had prepared for it, offers sacrifices, blesses the people, and gives food to everyone. Then he appoints Levites to praise God with music, and David sings a song that calls people to remember his wonders and his covenant, and to worship him because he is great and good, and his mercy endures forever. After that he arranges the service, and everyone goes back home.
sum.22: In his old age, David makes his son Solomon king and organizes the Levites for service in the temple. He assigns them by family to tasks such as workers, judges, gatekeepers, and musicians. Since God had given Israel rest in Jerusalem, the Levites would no longer carry the tabernacle; instead, they would help the priests and praise God every day.
sum.5: This chapter records the genealogy of the tribe of Levi, tracing the priestly line of Aaron down to the exile in Babylon. It also names the Levites whom David appointed to be in charge of the music in the house of the LORD, such as Heman and Asaph. At the end, it lists the cities that were given to the Levites throughout Israel.
sum.23: David organized the descendants of Aaron into twenty-four divisions to serve in the house of God. They cast lots, with Eleazar and Ithamar, since Nadab and Abihu had died without sons. The other Levites were also recorded, and they cast lots in the same way. In this manner, the older and the younger served with order and fairness before God.
sum.3: This chapter traces the families of Judah and Simeon, mentioning trades such as potters and craftsmen. Amid all these names, Jabez stands out, honored for his prayer to God, who granted what he asked. At the end, the people of Simeon look for pasture and land, and settle in new places.
sum.6: This chapter lists the family records of several tribes of Israel: Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher. It highlights the number of their brave and war-ready men, and also Ephraim's grief over his sons who had died and the birth of Beriah. It shows that God remembers every family and every generation.
sum.18: David wanted to show kindness to Hanun, the king of Ammon, over the death of his father. But the Ammonite leaders became suspicious and disgraced David's messengers. Ammon then hired the Syrians to fight, and Joab and Abishai, trusting in God, defeated them. After that, David defeated the Syrians again, and they made peace with him.
sum.20: David, incited by Satan, orders the people to be counted, although Joab opposes it, and this displeases God, who sends a plague. David acknowledges his sin and asks that the punishment fall on him and not on the people. God stops the angel, and David buys the threshing floor of Ornan, builds an altar there, and offers sacrifices, showing repentance and that worshiping God costs something.
sum.19: In this chapter, Joab conquers Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, while David remains in Jerusalem. David then receives the king's crown and a great quantity of plunder. Afterward, Israel defeats several descendants of Philistine giants, and it is shown that God gave them the victory through their warriors. The text also tells how the defeated were treated, a harsh element that is not fully explained and is interpreted in different ways.
sum.16: David wanted to build a house for God, since he himself was living in a house of cedar while the ark of the covenant was kept under a tent. But God told David, through the prophet Nathan, that David would not be the one to build it. Instead, God would build a house for David, meaning a dynasty, and his kingdom would last forever. David responded with humility, thankful to God and praising him.
sum.13: God confirms David as king. Hiram of Tyre sends him materials and workers for his house, and David has children in Jerusalem. When the Philistines attack him, David consults God before fighting, follows his instructions, and wins twice. His fame spreads, and God puts the fear of David on the nations.
sum.4: This chapter tells the story of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Reuben lost his right as firstborn because of his sin. These tribes defeated their enemies when they cried out to God, but later they turned away to follow other gods, and the Assyrians carried them into exile.
sum.24: David and the army commanders set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to serve in the house of God with music and "prophesying," using harps, lyres, and cymbals. In total there were 288 trained musicians. They cast lots to divide them into twenty-four shifts of twelve people each, and in this the small and the great, the teacher and the student, took part equally.
sum.9: At Mount Gilboa the Philistines defeated Israel, and Saul died along with his sons. The Philistines displayed his weapons and his head in the temples of their gods, but the brave men of Jabesh-gilead rescued the bodies and buried them. The text explains that Saul died because he was unfaithful to God and because he consulted a medium instead of seeking Jehovah, and so the kingdom passed to David.
sum.27: David gathers the leaders of Israel and tells them that God did not allow him to build the temple, because he had been a man of war, and that God chose his son Solomon to build it. He hands over the plans and the materials to Solomon and asks him to serve God wholeheartedly. He encourages Solomon not to be afraid, because God will be with him.
sum.28: David encourages the people to give toward the temple, and the leaders offer willingly and wholeheartedly. Then David praises God, acknowledging that everything we have comes from Him, and prays for Solomon. Solomon is crowned king, and David dies after reigning for forty years.
sum.8: This chapter lists the first people who returned to live in Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon: people from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, as well as priests and Levites. It highlights the gatekeepers and other Levites who looked after God's house, its treasures, and its worship. It ends with the family of Saul.
sum.21: David prepared the materials for building the temple well in advance, because God did not allow him to build it himself, since he had shed a great deal of blood in wars. He entrusted the work to his son Solomon, promising that God would give Solomon peace. He encouraged Solomon to obey the law, to be courageous, and to trust in God. He also asked the leaders to help him.
sum.25: This chapter shows how David organized the Levites as gatekeepers who guarded the gates of the house of the Lord. The shifts were divided by lot, with the young and the old receiving their assignments alike. He also appointed those in charge of the treasuries of the holy things, and others to serve as judges and officials. Everything was done in an orderly way, to serve God and the king.
sum.10: All Israel came together to David at Hebron and anointed him king, in keeping with the word of the LORD. David captured Jerusalem with the help of Joab, and God was with him. Then his mighty warriors are named, whose courage and loyalty helped him, and David shows respect for life by refusing to drink the water that his men risked their lives to bring him.
sum.26: This chapter describes how David organized the kingdom: twelve divisions of 24,000 men who served in rotation, one month each, along with leaders over the tribes. It also names those in charge of his possessions (treasuries, fields, vineyards, livestock) and his counselors. It is clarified that David did not count those under twenty years of age, because God had promised to multiply Israel.
